_note: Multiple-choice quiz questions, generated offline by scripts/gen_quiz.py from the study cards in terms.json and validated there (exactly one correct option, a rationale on every option, four options, audited tier). Reviewed by hand before shipping. Served read-only by app/quiz.py; no model call happens at request time. Ids are opaque and never reused.

questions.question: What is the main thing a business owner changes when they pick a different legal form of ownership, such as sole proprietorship versus corporation?

options.text: The number of customers the business is allowed to serve
options.rationale: Customer count is not governed by ownership structure at all.

options.text: How much the business must spend on marketing each year
options.rationale: Marketing spending is a business decision unrelated to legal ownership structure.

options.text: Who is personally liable for debts and who controls decisions
options.rationale: The card defines ownership form as directly changing liability exposure and decision control.

options.text: The physical location where the business must operate
options.rationale: Location is a separate business decision, not a consequence of ownership form.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests direct recognition of what one concept, forms of ownership, actually determines. One concept, one reasoning step.

questions.question: When a business is closing down, what should happen before any remaining money is distributed to the owners?

options.text: The owners should split the cash evenly no matter what
options.rationale: Ignores that debts and creditor claims must be settled first regardless of split arrangement.

options.text: All known debts and creditor claims should be settled first
options.rationale: The card states debts must be paid before distributing what's left, in a legal, orderly sequence.

options.text: The owners should sign a new partnership agreement
options.rationale: A new partnership agreement is irrelevant once the business is dissolving.

options.text: The business should immediately reopen under a new name
options.rationale: Reopening under a new name is unrelated to proper wind-down procedure.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, direct first-order consequence: settle debts before distribution. One reasoning step.

questions.question: Two friends start a landscaping partnership on a handshake, splitting everything evenly. Two years on, one of them wants out. What should they have put in writing?

options.text: The name they trade under locally
options.rationale: A registration matter, not a partnership term.

options.text: How a partner leaves and is paid out
options.rationale: Exit terms are exactly what a partnership agreement settles while the partners still agree.

options.text: How many hours each works weekly
options.rationale: Useful and not what the exit turns on.

options.text: Which bank holds the business account
options.rationale: Administrative and not in dispute.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the term the missing agreement would have carried.

questions.question: A woodworker runs her furniture business as a sole proprietorship. A customer sues after a chair collapses and wins a judgment larger than the business's bank account. What happens next?

options.text: Her personal savings and property can be used to pay the judgment
options.rationale: In a sole proprietorship the owner and the business are the same legal person, so there is nothing between the judgment and her own assets.

options.text: The judgment is capped at whatever the business account holds
options.rationale: This is the protection a company structure buys, and a sole proprietorship is not one.

options.text: Registering an LLC now would cap the loss she still faces
options.rationale: A structure protects what happens after it exists; it does not reach back over this chair.

options.text: She owes nothing further without a signed personal guarantee
options.rationale: A guarantee matters for debts she agreed to; liability for harm needs no signature.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests one concept, forms of ownership, applied to a new liability scenario rather than just defining the term.

questions.question: A three-owner consulting firm is closing. They still owe $15,000 to a printing vendor and have $40,000 left in the account. One owner wants to split the $40,000 three ways immediately so everyone can move on. What is the risk of doing this?

options.text: The state will automatically dissolve the LLC without any filing needed
options.rationale: Dissolution still requires filing articles of dissolution; it doesn't happen automatically from a payout.

options.text: The owners could be personally liable if the vendor's claim later goes unpaid
options.rationale: Distributing funds before settling known debts is the classic wind-down mistake that exposes owners to personal liability.

options.text: The remaining cash must legally go to the state instead of the owners
options.rationale: Unclaimed funds going to the state applies to abandoned property, not standard owner distributions during wind-down.

options.text: The vendor loses all rights to collect once the business stops operating
options.rationale: Closing the business doesn't erase creditor claims; proper notice and a claims window still apply.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, applied: predicting the consequence of skipping the debt-settlement step in a specific closing scenario.

questions.question: A founder prints cards reading LLC, opens a business account and starts selling. She has filed nothing with the state. What is her actual position?

options.text: Filing can be done at the first tax year
options.rationale: Formation comes before operating, not after.

options.text: She is not yet operating as an LLC
options.rationale: The protection of a limited company comes from the filing, so until it is made she is trading personally.

options.text: A bank account creates the entity
options.rationale: A bank opens accounts, not companies.

options.text: The LLC exists once she uses the name
options.rationale: Using a name creates no entity.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: separate the paperwork from the appearance of a company.

questions.question: Two partners in a catering business never wrote a partnership agreement. One partner put in $70,000 and the other put in $10,000, but they split profits equally for years. Now they want to close the business. Their operating relationship has no buy-sell clause and no exit valuation method written down. What is the most likely consequence during wind-down?

options.text: Creditor claims come out of each partner's share after the assets have been divided between them
options.rationale: Debts are paid before anything is distributed, which is what makes an early split dangerous.

options.text: Dissolution is blocked until the partners draft and sign a written agreement covering the split
options.rationale: Closing does not wait on paperwork the partners never wrote; the default rules simply take over.

options.text: Default state partnership law splits what remains, likely evenly rather than by what each put in
options.rationale: With nothing written down the state's default rules fill the gap, and those tend toward equal treatment whatever each partner actually contributed.

options.text: The partner who put in $70,000 has the first claim on what remains, ahead of any even split
options.rationale: That priority is exactly what a written agreement would have created, and there is none.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding two concepts at once: what happens by default without a partnership agreement, and how that default interacts with the wind-down distribution sequence. Neither concept alone answers the question.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Partnership Agreements Essentials and Business Dissolution and Wind-Down. Deleting Partnership Agreements Essentials removes the reason the split isn't proportional to capital; deleting Dissolution removes the wind-down context entirely. Both are load-bearing, so this passes the break test.

questions.question: A sole proprietor registers a DBA ("doing business as") name for her bakery and starts operating under that name. She believes this protects her personal assets the way an LLC would. What is the flaw in her reasoning?

options.text: Sole proprietors are legally barred from registering a DBA unless they first obtain a business license.
options.rationale: False restriction: nothing in the cards ties DBA eligibility to holding a business license first.

options.text: A DBA registration requires an EIN filing, which automatically converts the business into a corporation for tax purposes.
options.rationale: Incorrect: an EIN is a separate filing step and doesn't convert ownership structure; a DBA is not a corporation regardless of EIN status.

options.text: A DBA only protects assets if the owner also files Articles of Organization within the same fiscal year.
options.rationale: Fabricated condition: no such time-limited rule connects DBA filing to Articles of Organization taking retroactive effect.

options.text: A DBA registration only creates a trade name and does not form a separate legal entity, so her personal liability is unchanged.
options.rationale: Correct: the cards distinguish a DBA name registration from actually forming an entity like an LLC, which is what creates the liability shield.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests the interaction between choosing an ownership form (and its liability consequences) and knowing which specific filing actually creates that legal form, rather than either concept alone.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Forms of Business Ownership and Business Formation Filing Requirements. Deleting Forms of Business Ownership removes the liability stakes, making it a pure filing-trivia question; deleting Filing Requirements removes the specific DBA-vs-entity distinction the question hinges on. Both needed, passes the break test.

questions.question: A regional bakery organized as an LLC is being acquired by a national food corporation. The deal is structured so the bakery's owners receive stock in the acquiring corporation and stay on as employees. After the deal closes, how does the ownership and liability picture change for the former bakery owners?

options.text: They remain personally liable for the bakery LLC's past debts since receiving stock does not affect an LLC's liability protections.
options.rationale: Confuses LLC liability protection for ongoing operations with the fact that the entity itself has been absorbed into the acquiring corporation; their exposure changes with the deal.

options.text: They now hold equity in the corporation and share in its risks and rewards, no longer bearing the LLC's original liability exposure.
options.rationale: Correct: the acquisition shifts them from LLC owners into shareholders of the acquiring corporation, changing both their control and liability position.

options.text: Since a merger occurred rather than an acquisition, the bakery owners retain full independent control over company decisions.
options.rationale: Misapplies 'merger' to a scenario the card frames as an acquisition where one company buys another, not a combination of equals.

options.text: Receiving stock automatically converts their ownership back into a general partnership with the acquiring company.
options.rationale: Nonsensical structure: receiving acquirer stock makes them shareholders, not partners in a partnership arrangement.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires connecting how an acquisition restructures a deal (M&A) with what that does to the owners' original ownership form and liability status, a genuine interaction rather than either concept in isolation.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Mergers and Acquisitions Basics and Forms of Business Ownership. Deleting M&A Basics removes any reason the ownership form would change at all; deleting Forms of Business Ownership removes the liability/control comparison the correct answer depends on. Passes the break test.

questions.question: Two business owners agree by handshake that one will supply goods 'for a fair price, sometime next month.' Why does this fall short of a real contract?

options.text: It was never reviewed by a licensed attorney.
options.rationale: Attorney review is not required for a contract to be binding; this misapplies a formality that isn't in the card.

options.text: It involves goods instead of services being exchanged.
options.rationale: The type of subject matter, goods versus services, doesn't determine whether terms are clear enough to form a contract.

options.text: It was not signed in front of a notary public.
options.rationale: Notarization isn't a general requirement for contract validity; students confuse this with special document types.

options.text: It lacks clear terms like exact price and delivery date.
options.rationale: Correct: vague price and timing means there's nothing specific to hold either side to.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (clear contract terms), one reasoning step: recognizing why vagueness undermines enforceability.

questions.question: A part-time cashier tells a delivery driver the store will double next week's order, even though only the store manager can approve vendor contracts. What is the main concern here?

options.text: A spoken promise carries less weight than a written purchase order.
options.rationale: Spoken agreements can bind; the trouble is who spoke, not how.

options.text: The delivery driver should have asked for the order in writing.
options.rationale: A written copy of an unauthorised promise is still unauthorised.

options.text: The cashier's promise may not actually bind the company to the deal.
options.rationale: Only people the business has actually given authority can commit it, and a part-time cashier has not been given it here.

options.text: Doubling an order is a change big enough to need a fresh contract.
options.rationale: Size is not what decides it; authority is.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (authority to bind), one reasoning step: identifying that lacking signing authority undermines whether a promise counts.

questions.question: A contract requires a printer to deliver 500 finished brochures by Friday. The printer delivers on time but only 200 brochures are usable, the rest are misprinted. How should this situation be classified?

options.text: As a misunderstanding, since brochure quality wasn't specified in writing.
options.rationale: Delivering usable, correctly printed brochures is an implied core obligation, not something requiring separate specification to enforce.

options.text: As no breach, since the delivery still arrived on the agreed day.
options.rationale: Meeting the deadline doesn't excuse failing the quantity and quality terms of the deal.

options.text: As a minor breach, since some brochures were usable.
options.rationale: Partial usability doesn't make the shortfall minor when most of the order fails to meet the contract's purpose.

options.text: As a material breach, since the core purpose of the order isn't met.
options.rationale: Correct: delivering far short of the promised quantity defeats the purpose of the deal, making it a material breach.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (breach recognition), one reasoning step: judging whether a specific failure counts as material breach.

questions.question: A delivery driver for a bakery tells a flour supplier over the phone, 'Sure, send us triple our usual order next week, we're good for it.' The bakery's owner never approved this. What should the supplier's business do before treating this as a confirmed order?

options.text: Cancel all future dealings with the bakery, since the driver's statement proves the company is untrustworthy.
options.rationale: Overreacts to an authority problem as if it were a trust or breach issue, not what the concept addresses.

options.text: Ship the tripled order immediately, since any employee speaking for the company creates a binding deal.
options.rationale: Assumes any staff member automatically has authority, which is exactly the mistake the concept warns against.

options.text: Draft a penalty clause for late payment before shipping the tripled order.
options.rationale: Addresses remedies for nonpayment, not the separate question of whether the order was validly authorized.

options.text: Confirm the order with someone at the bakery who actually holds purchasing authority before fulfilling it.
options.rationale: Correctly applies the concept: verify the person committing has real authority before relying on the promise.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (authority to bind) applied to a new scenario involving a driver instead of the card's warehouse associate; requires predicting the correct action, not just defining the term.

questions.question: A printing company contracted to deliver 1,000 flyers by Friday for a Saturday product launch. They deliver on time, but 950 of the flyers have the wrong event date printed on them. How should the client classify this?

options.text: No breach at all, since printing errors are a normal risk of doing business with vendors.
options.rationale: Excuses a real, specific failure to meet the agreed terms just because errors are common in the industry.

options.text: A breach only if the client had separately written a penalty clause for printing mistakes.
options.rationale: Confuses the existence of a breach with the existence of a remedy clause; a breach can occur even without a pre-set penalty.

options.text: A minor breach, because the flyers still arrived by the agreed Friday deadline.
options.rationale: Focuses only on the timing term while ignoring that the content itself failed the contract's purpose.

options.text: A material breach, since the error defeats the point of having the flyers
options.rationale: The wrong date on nearly all copies undermines the entire point of the order, matching the card's material breach standard.

notes.difficulty_justification: Applies the material-versus-minor breach distinction to a new fact pattern (wrong content instead of late/missing delivery), requiring reasoning about what defeats the contract's purpose.

questions.question: Before meeting a landlord, a shop owner writes down the rent she cannot exceed, the fit-out contribution she would trade away, and the point at which she leaves. What has she prepared?

options.text: Proof that the market rent is lower
options.rationale: Evidence she may want and did not gather.

options.text: A first offer designed to anchor low
options.rationale: A tactic, and not what she wrote down.

options.text: A schedule for the meeting agenda
options.rationale: Order of business, not negotiating position.

options.text: Her needs, her trades and her limit
options.rationale: Knowing the must-haves, the giveaways and the walk-away point before the room is what negotiation preparation means.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: recognise the three-part preparation in a concrete case.

questions.question: A regional sales rep emails a supplier detailed pricing, quantities, and a delivery date for a large order, and the supplier ships the goods believing the deal is final. The company later says the rep never had signing authority. What is the strongest reason the company may still be bound?

options.text: Because the rep is not a company officer, nothing said or written by them can ever create a legal obligation for the business.
options.rationale: Overstates the authority rule; non-officers can still bind a company under apparent or delegated authority.

options.text: The email listed clear terms, so any employee's written promise automatically becomes a binding contract.
options.rationale: Confuses clear terms with authority; well-specified terms don't grant someone the power to bind the company.

options.text: The supplier reasonably believed the rep had authority, so apparent authority may bind the company despite the lack of formal approval.
options.rationale: Correct: this combines authority (apparent authority doctrine) with the fact that formation looked complete, which is why the company can still be held to it.

options.text: Since the order was placed by email instead of on paper, the lack of a wet-ink signature means no contract could have formed at all.
options.rationale: Misapplies e-signature/formality concerns; format of communication isn't the issue here, and email agreements can still form contracts.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding both authority (who can legally bind the company) and contract formation (whether terms were specific enough to count as a deal) at once, since neither concept alone explains the outcome.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Authority to Bind the Business, Contract Formation and Terms. Removing authority leaves a simple 'were terms clear enough' question, and removing formation leaves a pure authority question with no term detail to reason about; both are needed to explain why the supplier's belief matters.

questions.question: A contract requires a printing vendor to deliver 5,000 flyers by Friday morning for a Saturday trade show, with a clause stating a 20% discount applies for any delivery after the deadline. The vendor delivers Friday evening, a few hours late but still in time for the show. What is the correct response?

options.text: Pay in full, since the flyers arrived in time for the trade show to use them.
options.rationale: The purpose was served and the contract still priced a late delivery, which is a term the buyer paid for.

options.text: Treat it as a material breach and cancel the order, since the contract deadline was missed outright.
options.rationale: A breach that still delivers the point of the deal is minor, and the contract already says what it costs.

options.text: Withhold payment until the vendor agrees to renegotiate the delivery terms for future jobs.
options.rationale: Invents leverage the contract does not give, and the remedy is already written.

options.text: Apply the 20% discount the contract specifies, since the late delivery triggered the agreed remedy.
options.rationale: The parties priced this exact failure in advance, so the remedy is the one they wrote rather than one argued after the fact.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests the interaction between recognizing the severity of a breach and knowing which remedy actually applies given that severity; a student who only knows one concept could not pick the right response.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Breach of Contract Recognition, Obligations and Remedies. Dropping breach recognition removes any reason to weigh material vs minor, and dropping remedies removes any way to know what to actually do about the late delivery; both are required to reach the correct action.

questions.question: A supplier's quote setting out goods, price and delivery date is accepted through a portal button, and the portal logs the user, the timestamp and the version agreed. The buyer now says nothing was ever signed. What is the position?

options.text: Binding only if the quote is reprinted
options.rationale: Reprinting adds nothing to the record.

options.text: Binding, as terms and consent are logged
options.rationale: The definite terms make it a contract and the verifiable electronic record supplies the assent, which is what a signature is for.

options.text: Not binding, as email is informal
options.rationale: Formality of medium is not the test.

options.text: Not binding without an ink signature
options.rationale: Paper is not what makes agreement count.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the terms are definite enough to form a contract and the electronic record is what carries the assent.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Contract formation and terms, Electronic contracts and e-signatures. Without definite terms the click agrees to nothing. Without the verifiable log the assent is deniable. Both are needed.

questions.question: A company writes a detailed code of conduct and posts it on the office wall, but offers no training, no reporting channel, and no consequences for violations. What is this company missing?

options.text: A hotline for employees to report retaliation after being fired
options.rationale: This narrows the issue to whistleblower retaliation specifically, when the scenario describes a broader lack of enforcement.

options.text: A public statement about its environmental impact
options.rationale: This describes CSR messaging, not the enforcement gap the scenario is pointing to.

options.text: Follow-through systems that make the written rules actually get enforced
options.rationale: This matches the common mistake: a policy on paper without training, reporting, or accountability isn't a real compliance culture.

options.text: A conflict of interest policy for its managers
options.rationale: Conflict of interest is a separate concept; the scenario is about following rules generally, not personal stakes in decisions.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of a single concept, the gap between having a policy and building a compliance culture, with one direct reasoning step.

questions.question: An employee's cousin owns a company that just submitted a bid for a contract the employee will help evaluate. According to conflict of interest recognition, when does the duty to disclose this relationship begin?

options.text: Once the cousin's company is shortlisted for the contract
options.rationale: Waiting for the shortlist means evaluating bids while the conflict sits undisclosed.

options.text: Once the employee is asked to vote on awarding the contract
options.rationale: By then the employee has already helped shape the evaluation.

options.text: Once a colleague asks about the employee's connection to a bidder
options.rationale: Disclosure prompted by someone else's question is not disclosure.

options.text: As soon as the employee learns the cousin's company is one of the bidders
options.rationale: The duty attaches to the existence of the interest, not to whether it ends up changing anything.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, direct recall of when the disclosure obligation starts, testing the common misconception directly.

questions.question: After an employee reports a safety violation to compliance, her manager doesn't fire her but starts excluding her from team meetings and cuts her hours. Why does this still count as a whistleblower protection violation?

options.text: Because retaliation includes quieter actions like exclusion or reduced hours, not just firing
options.rationale: This matches the common mistake: retaliation isn't limited to termination, it covers subtler punishments too.

options.text: Because the employee's identity was not kept confidential during the investigation
options.rationale: The scenario doesn't mention a confidentiality breach; the issue described is retaliation through exclusion and reduced hours.

options.text: Because whistleblower protections only apply once the government opens a formal investigation
options.rationale: Protections apply to any retaliation for a good-faith report, not just once an investigation is officially opened.

options.text: Because the manager must have a personal financial stake in the outcome for it to count
options.rationale: This describes a conflict of interest concern, not what defines retaliation under whistleblower protections.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, applying the definition to recognize that retaliation extends beyond obvious firing, still one direct reasoning step from the card's common mistake.

questions.question: A hiring manager at a marketing firm is reviewing final candidates for a copywriter role, and one candidate is her former college roommate, someone she hasn't spoken to in over a year. What should she do?

options.text: Disclose the past relationship to her supervisor and step back from the final decision.
options.rationale: Matches the correct handling: disclosure plus recusal protects the process even if she believes she'd stay objective.

options.text: Mention the friendship casually in a team meeting but continue leading the evaluation.
options.rationale: Disclosure without actually stepping back from the decision doesn't remove the improper influence.

options.text: Hire whichever candidate scores highest, since old friendships rarely sway a fair review.
options.rationale: Assumes the conflict doesn't matter unless bias actually shows up in the outcome, ignoring the duty to disclose regardless of result.

options.text: Quietly rate the friend lower than deserved to avoid looking biased to coworkers.
options.rationale: Overcorrecting in secret is still an undisclosed conflict distorting the outcome, just in the opposite direction.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (conflict of interest) applied to a new hiring scenario, requiring the student to identify the correct action rather than just define the term.

questions.question: A warehouse employee reports to HR that a supervisor is falsifying safety inspection logs. Two weeks later, with no explanation, her schedule is changed from day shifts to overnight shifts. What does this situation illustrate?

options.text: The schedule change likely counts as retaliation, since punishment can take quiet forms beyond firing.
options.rationale: Correctly recognizes that whistleblower protection covers subtler retaliation, not just termination or demotion.

options.text: The company is safe from liability as long as the shift change was labeled a routine staffing decision.
options.rationale: Labeling retaliation as routine doesn't remove liability if the timing and effect suggest punishment for the report.

options.text: Whistleblower rules only apply once a lawsuit or regulator gets involved, so nothing has happened yet legally.
options.rationale: Misunderstands that protections apply from the moment of the good-faith report, not only once external legal action begins.

options.text: No retaliation occurred, since she wasn't fired, demoted, or given a pay cut after her report.
options.rationale: Reflects the common mistake of only counting firing as retaliation while missing quieter forms like schedule changes.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept applied to a new scenario involving subtle retaliation, requiring the student to recognize the mechanism rather than recall a definition.

questions.question: A furniture company switches to a cheaper overseas supplier and issues a press release praising its new 'sustainability partnership,' but never sets up any audits or contract terms covering the supplier's labor or environmental practices. What is the problem with this approach?

options.text: It switched suppliers to cut costs, which sits badly with a sustainability claim.
options.rationale: Cheaper sourcing and responsible sourcing can coexist; what is missing is any check that they do.

options.text: It treats CSR as an announcement, not a standard backed by audits and terms.
options.rationale: A commitment with no audit and no contract term behind it is a press release, and the supplier's practices are exactly what it claims to have changed.

options.text: It is a reasonable first step, with the audits and terms to follow later on.
options.rationale: The announcement is the whole of it, and nothing is scheduled to follow.

options.text: It leads on environmental claims when the cost saving is the real story here.
options.rationale: Which story leads is a marketing choice, not the failure here.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept applied to a fresh supplier scenario, requiring the student to judge whether the described action satisfies real CSR standards rather than just recall the definition.

questions.question: A finance manager reports to compliance that her own supervisor is steering contracts to a firm owned by his spouse. After the report, the supervisor removes her from the contract review team and cuts her project hours. What did the company mishandle here?

options.text: It let the disclosed relationship stand instead of requiring recusal from the vote.
options.rationale: Names the conflict-of-interest failure but ignores the retaliation against the reporter, which is the actual event described.

options.text: It reassigned her duties in retaliation for a good-faith report of misconduct.
options.rationale: Correctly identifies that removing duties after a report counts as retaliation, even without firing, which whistleblower protections cover.

options.text: It only violated policy once she was formally terminated from the company.
options.rationale: Reflects the mistaken belief that retaliation must mean firing, when reduced duties and hours already qualify.

options.text: It failed to require the supervisor to disclose the relationship before any contract decision was made.
options.rationale: Addresses only the upstream conflict of interest, missing that the described harm is the retaliation after her report.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding two concepts at once: recognizing the underlying conflict of interest and correctly applying whistleblower protection to a non-termination form of retaliation.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Conflict of Interest Recognition, Whistleblower Protections. Deleting conflict of interest still leaves a valid retaliation question, but deleting whistleblower protections removes the reason the reassignment matters at all, so both concepts are needed to explain why the company's response, not just the original conflict, is the failure being tested.

questions.question: A clothing brand publishes a supplier code of conduct requiring safe factory conditions, but it never assigns anyone to audit factories or track violations. Why does this arrangement still leave workers at risk?

options.text: The code needs supplier disclosure of ownership conflicts before it can be effective.
options.rationale: Imports a conflict-of-interest fix that has no bearing on factory safety monitoring, which is the actual issue.

options.text: The code sets a real standard but has no internal system to enforce it consistently.
options.rationale: Correctly identifies that a written CSR standard without compliance follow-through, audits, accountability, is a policy that exists on paper only.

options.text: The code should have been replaced with a one-time donation to worker safety causes.
options.rationale: Suggests a weaker, PR-style substitute for ongoing standards rather than identifying the actual missing enforcement mechanism.

options.text: The code focuses on shareholder profit instead of factory worker welfare.
options.rationale: Misreads the scenario; the code is explicitly about worker safety, not shareholder returns, so this doesn't match the described gap.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests two concepts together: recognizing a CSR standard exists and diagnosing why it fails without a compliance culture's audit and accountability mechanisms behind it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Ethical Governance and Compliance Culture, Corporate Social Responsibility Standards. Deleting CSR leaves a generic compliance-culture question with no specific content to enforce; deleting compliance culture leaves a CSR question that can't explain why a written standard fails. Both are required to explain the gap.

questions.question: A sourcing director is choosing which overseas factory to certify under the company's new CSR safety code. She fast-tracks approval for a factory partly owned by her cousin without mentioning the family tie to anyone. What is the most complete problem with her decision?

options.text: She violated CSR standards by choosing a factory without checking its wage and safety records at all.
options.rationale: Assumes she skipped safety checks entirely, which isn't stated; the actual issue is the hidden relationship distorting the choice, not a missing audit.

options.text: She should have donated to worker safety programs instead of certifying any single factory.
options.rationale: Substitutes an unrelated PR-style gesture for the real issue, which is disclosure and recusal in the certification decision.

options.text: She only created a problem if the factory later fails a safety audit and gets caught.
options.rationale: Reflects the misconception that a conflict only matters once harm results, when the duty to disclose applies as soon as the conflicting interest exists.

options.text: She undermined the CSR audit process by letting an undisclosed personal tie shape which factory got certified.
options.rationale: Correctly links both concepts: the undisclosed relationship compromised the objectivity the CSR audit standard depends on to be meaningful.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires combining conflict of interest recognition with CSR audit standards to see how an undisclosed personal tie corrupts the integrity of a supposedly objective safety certification, which neither concept alone explains.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Conflict of Interest Recognition, Corporate Social Responsibility Standards. Deleting CSR leaves an ordinary conflict-of-interest question unrelated to factory certification; deleting conflict of interest leaves a CSR question with no explanation for why the certification is untrustworthy. Both are necessary to identify the full problem.

questions.question: A dispute where one company sues another for failing to deliver goods as promised in a signed agreement is best described as what type of matter?

options.text: A criminal matter, since the dollar amount involved is likely large
options.rationale: Reflects the common mistake of equating large stakes with criminal status, but size of damages doesn't make something criminal.

options.text: A criminal matter, since breaking a signed agreement is treated as an offense against the public
options.rationale: Confuses breach of a private agreement with a public offense; the state has no charge here.

options.text: A civil matter, since it involves a private dispute over harm from a broken agreement
options.rationale: Correct: this is a private dispute between two parties over harm from a broken contract, the hallmark of a civil case.

options.text: Neither, since only government agencies can bring legal action over broken agreements
options.rationale: Incorrectly assumes only government can sue; private parties routinely bring civil suits over contracts.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests only the single concept of civil versus criminal liability by asking the student to classify one scenario, a first-order recognition task.

questions.question: Why might a court dismiss a lawsuit even before looking at the facts of who did what?

options.text: Because the court decides it disagrees with the contract terms being disputed
options.rationale: Courts rule on legal disputes, they don't dismiss cases just because they dislike contract terms.

options.text: Because the court lacks the authority to hear that kind of case or dispute
options.rationale: Correct: jurisdiction is about whether the court has the legal power to hear the case at all, independent of the facts.

options.text: Because the defendant hired a more experienced lawyer
options.rationale: Attorney skill has no bearing on whether a court has jurisdiction over a case.

options.text: Because the plaintiff asked for too much money in damages
options.rationale: The amount requested doesn't determine dismissal for lack of jurisdiction, it may affect which court but not authority itself.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, tests recognition of what jurisdiction actually controls, one reasoning step from the definition.

questions.question: A business owner negotiates a special delivery schedule with a supplier in a signed agreement. Which source of business law governs that specific arrangement?

options.text: A federal statute passed by Congress
options.rationale: Statutes are broad public laws, not the private terms two parties negotiate between themselves.

options.text: A contract the two parties agreed to
options.rationale: Correct: a negotiated delivery schedule between two private parties is governed by the contract they signed.

options.text: A regulation issued by a government agency
options.rationale: Regulations come from agencies enforcing statutes, not from private negotiations between a business and its supplier.

options.text: A prior court ruling establishing precedent
options.rationale: Case law shapes how disputes are decided generally, but it doesn't create the specific negotiated terms between these two parties.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept task asking the student to identify which source of law applies to a given rule, a direct recognition step.

questions.question: A bakery owner substitutes cheaper ingredients than promised in a catering contract, causing a client's event to fall short of expectations, but nothing illegal happened. The client wants compensation for the difference in value. What kind of case does the client have?

options.text: A civil case, since it involves a breach of contract between two private parties
options.rationale: This matches the concept: a private dispute over harm or broken agreement is civil, resolved through a lawsuit for damages.

options.text: A criminal case, since the bakery deceived a paying customer
options.rationale: Deception alone isn't automatically criminal; no specific offense against the public is described here, just a private harm.

options.text: Neither, since only regulatory agencies handle ingredient disputes
options.rationale: This ignores that private contract disputes are resolved through civil lawsuits, not just agency oversight.

options.text: A criminal case, since the dollar amount at stake could be significant
options.rationale: Size of the loss doesn't determine criminal status; that depends on whether a law defines the act as a public offense.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept applied to a new scenario where the student must distinguish civil from criminal based on the nature of the harm, not surface features like dollar amount.

questions.question: A cafe owner can find no statute covering the exact refund dispute she is in, and the supply agreement she signed addresses it directly. Which source governs?

options.text: Whatever the local custom suggests
options.rationale: Custom does not override a written term.

options.text: The contract the two sides signed
options.rationale: A contract is itself a source of binding rules between the parties, and it fills the space where no statute speaks.

options.text: A statute written for another trade
options.rationale: A statute aimed elsewhere does not reach this deal.

options.text: Nothing, since no statute applies
options.rationale: Assumes statutes are the only source of law.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: pick the governing source for a concrete dispute.

questions.question: A Texas retailer and a Georgia supplier fall out over a shipment. Their signed agreement names Georgia courts for any dispute. Where should the retailer file?

options.text: In Georgia, as the agreement states
options.rationale: A venue clause is the parties' own choice of where a dispute is heard, and courts generally hold them to it.

options.text: In Texas, where the harm was felt
options.rationale: Where the loss lands does not override the clause.

options.text: In a federal court in both states
options.rationale: One dispute is not filed twice.

options.text: In either state, at its own choice
options.rationale: The clause exists precisely to remove that choice.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: read a venue clause and act on it.

questions.question: A bakery in Ohio signs a supply contract naming Ohio courts as the venue for any dispute. The supplier later ships spoiled flour, and it's revealed the supplier forged its health inspection certificate to win the contract. The bakery wants to sue for damages, and a state prosecutor separately wants to pursue the forged certificate. Which statement best matches each track to its proper handling?

options.text: Both matters must be filed together in Texas, since that's where the flour was delivered and consumed.
options.rationale: Confuses delivery location with the forum clause, and wrongly merges a civil claim with a criminal matter that the state controls independently.

options.text: The forum clause controls both the damages claim and the forgery charge, since one contract dispute triggered everything.
options.rationale: Wrongly assumes a private venue clause can bind a criminal prosecution, when the state acts independently of any contract terms between the parties.

options.text: The bakery's damages claim follows the Ohio forum clause, while the forgery charge proceeds separately through the state regardless of that contract.
options.rationale: Correctly separates the civil claim, which the venue clause governs, from the criminal forgery matter, which the state prosecutes independent of any private contract term.

options.text: Since the harm is serious enough to ruin the bakery's business, both issues automatically become criminal and bypass the venue clause entirely.
options.rationale: Mistakes severity of harm for the criminal/civil dividing line, when what actually matters is whether a specific law defines the act as an offense against the public.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding two concepts at once: distinguishing civil from criminal liability, and applying venue/jurisdiction rules only to the civil piece, since a contract clause cannot bind a state prosecution.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Civil Versus Criminal Liability, Jurisdiction and Venue Basics. Removing jurisdiction leaves only 'is this civil or criminal,' which loses the venue-clause reasoning; removing civil/criminal leaves only 'where do we file,' which loses the need to separate the prosecution from the contract claim. Both are needed, so it passes the break test.

questions.question: A marketing team sends 5,000 unsolicited promotional texts to numbers that never opted in, and one recipient's phone plan charges her extra fees she now wants reimbursed. Given how legal exposure and liability type actually work here, which outcome is most accurate?

options.text: Per-message penalties across the whole list, plus her separate claim.
options.rationale: The exposure scales with the 5,000 messages rather than with the single person who noticed, and her claim sits on top of it rather than instead of it.

options.text: Exposure is limited to the one recipient's fees plus a modest administrative fine.
options.rationale: Counts the harm that happened to one person and ignores the penalty attached to each message sent.

options.text: Since no criminal offence occurred, the matter ends with an informal customer complaint.
options.rationale: Civil and statutory penalties do not need a crime to bite.

options.text: The company faces a private claim from the recipient and nothing from any regulator.
options.rationale: Unsolicited messaging is regulated, so a regulator has standing whatever the recipient does.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires linking two concepts: recognizing the legal limit the campaign violated, and correctly sizing the resulting liability as statutory exposure distinct from an individual civil claim, rather than defining either concept alone.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Legal Environment Awareness, Civil Versus Criminal Liability. Removing legal-environment awareness leaves no reason the campaign is risky at all; removing civil/criminal distinction leaves no way to separate the individual's claim from the broader statutory penalty. Both are needed, so it passes the break test.
review_flags: The per-message penalty is closer to a civil statutory penalty than a criminal charge; option b avoids naming it as either to stay defensible, but a sharp student could ask whether TCPA penalties count as civil or criminal, worth flagging as a slightly underspecified area in the source card.

questions.question: A team confirms that no state statute bars its planned home delivery of wine, and stops there. It never reads the city ordinance, the delivery platform's terms or the licence it already holds. What is the flaw?

options.text: A delivery plan the team cannot fund
options.rationale: Cost is not what the team failed to check.

options.text: One source checked, three still binding
options.rationale: Legal limits arrive from statutes, local regulation, licence conditions and contracts at once, so clearing one of them clears very little.

options.text: A city ordinance that outranks the statute
options.rationale: Local rules apply alongside state law rather than above it.

options.text: State law read without a lawyer's help
options.rationale: Who read it is not the gap; how much was read is.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the awareness habit is present and the map of sources it should sweep is incomplete.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Legal environment awareness, Sources of business law. Without the check there is no partial diligence to fault. Without the several sources one check is enough. Both are needed.

questions.question: A company wants to legally protect its unique brand logo from being copied by competitors. Which legal tool is designed for this purpose?

options.text: A trademark registration
options.rationale: The card states names and logos need trademark protection, the correct tool for a brand identifier.

options.text: A patent application
options.rationale: Patents protect inventions and processes, not brand names or logos.

options.text: A trade secret policy
options.rationale: Trade secrets protect confidential know-how like recipes, not publicly displayed brand logos.

options.text: A copyright filing
options.rationale: Common mistake: assuming copyright covers business logos, when logos need trademark protection instead.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of which single legal tool matches a given asset type, one concept, one reasoning step.

questions.question: A company legally collected customer emails for order confirmations. What must it do before using those same emails for a new marketing campaign?

options.text: Sell the email list to a third party to offset campaign costs
options.rationale: Selling data without disclosure is the exact misuse the card warns violates data obligations.

options.text: Get new opt-in consent before using the data for that different purpose
options.rationale: The card explains data use has real limits, and reusing data for a new purpose requires fresh consent.

options.text: Use the emails freely since the data was already collected legally
options.rationale: Common mistake: assuming legal collection automatically permits any future reuse without new consent.

options.text: Wait one year before the original consent expires automatically
options.rationale: There's no such automatic expiration rule described; the issue is purpose, not time elapsed.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept applied to a direct first-order consequence, recognizing what obligation follows from collecting personal data.

questions.question: A sauce maker wants its recipe treated in law as a trade secret. What does that status actually require?

options.text: Renewing the secret every ten years
options.rationale: No renewal exists for secrets.

options.text: Filing the recipe with the state
options.rationale: Filing it would publish it.

options.text: Printing it on the bottle label
options.rationale: Disclosure ends the protection.

options.text: Real limits on who can see it
options.rationale: A trade secret is protected only while the business takes genuine steps to keep it secret.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify what earns trade secret status.

questions.question: A software company keeps its ranking algorithm on a shared company drive that all 200 employees can access, and stamps the file 'Confidential' at the top. A former engineer later joins a rival firm and uses the same algorithm logic. What is the most likely legal weakness in the company's position?

options.text: Trade secret protection covers formulas and recipes rather than software logic
options.rationale: The category of information is not the problem; how it was handled is.

options.text: Wide internal access and a label do not show the file was treated as secret
options.rationale: Protection follows the steps actually taken to keep something secret, and a file 200 people can open is not being kept secret.

options.text: The company should have trademarked the algorithm before hiring engineers
options.rationale: Trademarks cover brand identifiers, not the workings of a product.

options.text: The algorithm was never patented, so it had no protection to lose
options.rationale: Trade secret protection is an alternative to patenting, not a consequence of it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (trade secret safeguards) applied to a new scenario requiring the student to identify why the protective measures fail, not just define the term.

questions.question: A furniture designer owns a patented folding-chair mechanism and signs a deal letting a large retailer manufacture and sell chairs using it in exchange for a percentage of sales. Six months later the retailer starts selling far fewer units than expected, and the designer's royalty income drops sharply even though demand for folding chairs is strong industry-wide. What contract term would have most directly protected the designer against this outcome?

options.text: A minimum guaranteed royalty, whatever volume the retailer actually sells
options.rationale: A guaranteed minimum protects the licensor's income even if the licensee undersells the product, unlike a royalty tied purely to sales volume.

options.text: A clause transferring full ownership of the patent to the retailer after year one
options.rationale: Transferring ownership would end the designer's rights entirely rather than protect their income stream.

options.text: A requirement that the retailer file for its own separate patent on the mechanism
options.rationale: The retailer doesn't own the invention and filing a competing patent wouldn't address the low sales issue.

options.text: A copyright registration covering the folding-chair design
options.rationale: Copyright protects creative works, not a functional mechanical invention, and wouldn't fix the royalty shortfall.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (licensing terms) applied to a new licensing scenario where the student must predict which contract mechanism solves the described problem.

questions.question: A founder has traded under her bakery name in one city for two years and now wants protection across the country before she expands. What is the step?

options.text: Trade under the name in each state
options.rationale: Slow, costly and still unregistered.

options.text: Buy every matching domain name
options.rationale: Domains are addresses, not rights in a name.

options.text: Copyright the name and the logo
options.rationale: Copyright does not cover brand names.

options.text: Apply to register the mark federally
options.rationale: National protection against a confusingly similar name comes from federal registration, not from local use.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: pick the registration step that matches the protection wanted.

questions.question: A founder registers her snack brand name with the state and buys the matching domain name, then assumes a rival snack company can't use a nearly identical name elsewhere. What is she missing?

options.text: She needs a patent on the snack itself before the name can be defended
options.rationale: A patent covers an invention, which has nothing to do with the name.

options.text: A state filing and a domain are not a federal trademark
options.rationale: Those two secure a name in one state and at one address; stopping a confusingly similar name across the country is what the federal filing buys.

options.text: Trademark rights attach after the product has been on sale for a year
options.rationale: Invents a waiting period that does not exist.

options.text: Copyright is the route for a brand name, and she has not filed for it
options.rationale: Copyright covers creative works rather than names used in trade.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests whether the student can distinguish which legal tool actually secures a brand name, requiring both the general IP-protection judgment call and the specific mechanics of what trademark registration does versus other filings.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Trademark Registration Process, Intellectual Property Protection. Remove Trademark Registration and the question has no specific mechanism to correct her mistake. Remove IP Protection and there's no reason to frame this as a 'which tool' judgment rather than a pure procedure question. Both needed, passes break test.

questions.question: A fitness app licenses its workout-tracking software to a gym chain, and the licensing contract lets the gym access the app's full customer database to run its own separate marketing campaigns. What problem does this create?

options.text: The app company loses ownership of its software the moment any data access is shared with a licensee.
options.rationale: Licensing doesn't transfer ownership; this confuses licensing with a sale or assignment.

options.text: The gym chain now owns the trademark on the app's brand name since it received the data under contract.
options.rationale: Trademark ownership isn't affected by data-sharing terms in a licensing contract; this conflates two unrelated rights.

options.text: Customer data is being reused for a new purpose without the consent that was originally given for it.
options.rationale: Data collected under one purpose can't just be handed off for new uses like outside marketing without fresh consent, regardless of what the licensing deal permits.

options.text: The license becomes unenforceable because software cannot legally be licensed to a third-party company.
options.rationale: Software licensing to third parties is common and legal; this invents a restriction that doesn't exist.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires combining what a licensing deal legitimately transfers (software use rights) with the separate legal limit that customer data can't be repurposed without consent, even when a contract technically allows the data access.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Privacy and Data Obligations, Licensing IP Rights. Remove Privacy obligations and there's nothing wrong with the licensing terms as written. Remove Licensing and there's no contract mechanism creating the data-sharing scenario. Both are necessary, passes break test.

questions.question: A brewer licenses its trademark to a canning partner and, so the partner can actually make the beer, hands over the yeast process it treats as a trade secret. The licence covers the mark and says nothing about confidentiality. What is the exposure?

options.text: A secret that is now owned by the partner
options.rationale: Ownership does not transfer by disclosure.

options.text: A trademark that can no longer be used
options.rationale: Licensing a mark does not forfeit it.

options.text: A licensed mark and an unprotected secret
options.rationale: The licence carefully governs the asset it names and the secret travelled outside the business with no obligation attached to it.

options.text: A licence that must be registered first
options.rationale: Invents a filing requirement.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the licensing is done properly for one asset and the safeguard duty for the other was never carried across.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Licensing intellectual property rights, Trade secret safeguards. Without the licence the process never leaves the brewery. Without the secret the licence is complete. Both are needed.

questions.question: In a triple-net commercial lease, which added costs does the tenant typically pay beyond the base rent?

options.text: A share of the landlord's other tenants' rent shortfalls
options.rationale: Lease terms don't require one tenant to cover another tenant's unpaid rent.

options.text: The landlord's mortgage payments
options.rationale: Mortgage payments are the landlord's financing obligation, not a tenant charge under any standard lease type.

options.text: Property taxes, insurance, and maintenance
options.rationale: Correct: these are the defining extra charges of a triple-net lease.

options.text: The landlord's business income taxes
options.rationale: Income taxes are a personal or corporate obligation of the landlord, not a property-related lease charge.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, direct recognition of what triple-net lease terms mean without needing to apply it to a new scenario.

questions.question: What is the direct risk of signing a lease for a property before checking whether zoning allows the intended business use?

options.text: The lease automatically becomes void if zoning doesn't match
options.rationale: Leases don't self-void based on zoning; the tenant remains bound to pay even if the use isn't permitted.

options.text: The landlord becomes responsible for any zoning violation fines instead of the tenant
options.rationale: Liability for illegal use typically falls on the business operating there, not automatically the landlord.

options.text: The business could end up paying rent on a space it cannot legally use as planned
options.rationale: Correct: this is the first-order consequence described directly on the card.

options.text: The property's title becomes invalid until zoning is corrected
options.rationale: Zoning issues don't affect legal ownership or title validity; those are separate concepts.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, one reasoning step from the stated risk of skipping a zoning check to its direct consequence.

questions.question: Before buying a warehouse, a company pays for a title search on the property. What is that search for?

options.text: Checking the roof and the wiring
options.rationale: That is a physical inspection.

options.text: Valuing the building for the bank
options.rationale: That is an appraisal.

options.text: Finding claims against the property
options.rationale: A title search looks for liens, easements and competing claims that would survive the sale.

options.text: Confirming the zoning allows storage
options.rationale: Zoning is a separate enquiry.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: say what a title search covers.

questions.question: A boutique owner signs a lease quoting $18 per square foot base rent for a 1,000 sq ft store, but the lease is triple-net. After the first year, her total occupancy cost is much higher than the $18,000 she expected. What most likely explains the gap?

options.text: The title search on the property turned up an unexpected lien she must now pay off.
options.rationale: Liens relate to ownership history at purchase, not to a tenant's recurring lease costs.

options.text: The landlord raised the base rent mid-term without notice.
options.rationale: Base rent changes are governed by the lease term and typically require negotiated escalation clauses, not silent raises.

options.text: She underestimated how much local zoning fees would cost for her retail use.
options.rationale: Zoning approval fees are a land-use issue, not part of the rent structure described in the lease.

options.text: She is also paying her share of property tax, insurance, and maintenance on top of base rent.
options.rationale: A triple-net lease adds these three costs on top of base rent, which is exactly the gap the common mistake warns about.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (triple-net lease cost structure) applied to a new numeric scenario to identify the source of a cost overrun; requires using the mechanism, not just defining it.

questions.question: A buyer receives a signed deed transferring a small office building to her company and assumes the purchase is now completely safe. Based on how title works, what risk does she still face?

options.text: The lease terms on the building could be renegotiated by the previous tenant.
options.rationale: Lease terms are a landlord-tenant matter, unrelated to whether the deed proves clean ownership.

options.text: The building's insurance premium could increase due to rising construction costs.
options.rationale: Insurance cost trends are a market factor, not a title or ownership defect issue.

options.text: An old unresolved lien from a prior owner could still attach to the property.
options.rationale: A deed only shows a transfer occurred, it does not guarantee the property is free of past liens or competing claims, which is why a title search matters.

options.text: The zoning on the property could change without any warning at all.
options.rationale: Zoning changes are a separate land-use risk, not something a deed or title search addresses.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (deed versus clean title) applied to a specific buyer scenario to predict what could still go wrong, requiring use of the mechanism rather than its definition.

questions.question: A baker finds a cheap unit in a light industrial zone and plans to run a small cafe counter at the front of it. What should she confirm before signing?

options.text: That the rent is below market rate
options.rationale: A commercial question, not a permission.

options.text: That retail sales are permitted there
options.rationale: The zone allows production and the counter is a retail use, which the local rules have to permit separately.

options.text: That parking is free for customers
options.rationale: Convenience, not lawful use.

options.text: That the landlord will repaint it
options.rationale: A fit-out term, negotiated later.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: spot the second use hidden inside the plan.

questions.question: A retailer signs a 5-year triple-net lease on a storefront, satisfied that the base rent and CAM cap are both reasonable. After signing, she learns the lot's zoning bans walk-in retail without a conditional use permit that takes months to obtain. What is the real problem here?

options.text: Careful lease terms did not protect her from a zoning rule blocking her intended use.
options.rationale: She read the commercial terms properly and the question of whether the law lets her trade there sits outside the lease entirely.

options.text: The triple-net structure leaves her owing back taxes the seller never paid before closing.
options.rationale: Triple-net shifts ongoing costs forward, not the previous owner's arrears.

options.text: The landlord committed fraud, since the space was not zoned for her business at signing.
options.rationale: Checking the permitted use is the tenant's diligence, absent a false statement by the landlord.

options.text: Her CAM cap was pointless, because the landlord can revise those charges each year.
options.rationale: A negotiated cap binds; the cap is the part of this deal that worked.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding two distinct concepts, lease terms and zoning approval, and recognizing that satisfying one doesn't satisfy the other; a single-concept question could not produce this failure mode.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Commercial Lease Fundamentals and Zoning and Land Use Rules. Deleting zoning leaves a question about whether reading a lease carefully guarantees success, which loses its point; deleting lease terms leaves only a zoning question with no lease-diligence contrast. Both are needed, so it passes the break test.

questions.question: A company buys a vacant lot after running a full title search that turns up no liens or ownership disputes. It later discovers the lot is zoned strictly for agricultural use, blocking the warehouse expansion it planned. Which statement best explains why the purchase still went wrong?

options.text: Zoning designations are automatically voided once a title search confirms clear ownership of the land.
options.rationale: Invents a nonexistent legal effect; ownership and zoning are independent and clearing title has no bearing on land use rules.

options.text: A clean title search only confirms who legally owns the land, not what uses the local government permits on it.
options.rationale: Correctly separates ownership verification from use permission; title and zoning answer different questions entirely.

options.text: Title insurance would have covered the loss since it protects buyers against any restriction discovered after closing.
options.rationale: Overextends title insurance's purpose, which covers past ownership defects like liens, not future or existing zoning limitations.

options.text: The title search must have been incomplete, since a proper search always reveals zoning restrictions along with ownership history.
options.rationale: Misunderstands scope of a title search, which covers ownership claims and liens, not municipal zoning designations.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests whether the student can distinguish two concepts that are easy to conflate, ownership clarity and permitted use, and recognize that resolving one leaves the other completely unaddressed.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Property Ownership and Title Basics and Zoning and Land Use Rules. Removing zoning turns this into a plain title-search question with no twist; removing title basics removes the reason the buyer felt falsely reassured. Both concepts are required for the scenario to make sense, so it passes the break test.

questions.question: A landlord offers a tenant a 5-year triple-net lease on a building the landlord recently acquired, but records show an old contractor's lien on that property was never formally released. How should this affect the tenant's decision?

options.text: It is irrelevant, since a triple-net lease moves property risk onto the tenant by design.
options.rationale: Triple-net moves operating costs, not someone else's claim on the title.

options.text: It does not reach a tenant who pays rent and CAM and never takes an ownership stake.
options.rationale: A claim strong enough to move the building reaches whoever is occupying it.

options.text: It matters later if the tenant decides to buy, so it can be left for the purchase.
options.rationale: The risk to the tenancy arrives long before any purchase.

options.text: The lien is worth investigating, since an ownership claim could cut the lease short.
options.rationale: A five year commitment is only as good as the landlord's hold on the building, and an unreleased lien is a live claim against that hold.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires connecting lease security to the landlord's title status, a two-concept interaction that neither card addresses alone, and applying it to a new leasing scenario rather than restating either definition.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Commercial Lease Fundamentals and Property Ownership and Title Basics. Deleting title basics leaves an ordinary lease question with no lien to reason about; deleting lease fundamentals removes any reason the tenant would care about the landlord's title at all. Both are necessary, so it passes the break test.

questions.question: What is the core idea behind antitrust and fair competition laws?

options.text: Businesses should disclose known product defects even if a claim is technically true
options.rationale: This describes consumer protection and fair dealing, a different concept.

options.text: Businesses should win customers through better products instead of rigging the market with rivals
options.rationale: Correct: matches the definition of growing by being better, not by colluding or abusing power.

options.text: Businesses should keep advertising claims truthful and provable before publishing them
options.rationale: This describes advertising law compliance, not antitrust.

options.text: Businesses should only worry about competition rules once they become large corporations
options.rationale: This reflects the common mistake the card warns against: antitrust applies regardless of company size.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of a single concept's core definition with one reasoning step, no application to a novel scenario required.

questions.question: A company offers a 5-year warranty on its blenders but sets aside no money or staff process to handle future claims. What does this reveal?

options.text: The company is treating the warranty as just a sales pitch instead of a real financial obligation
options.rationale: Correct: this is exactly the common mistake described, no budget or process behind the promise.

options.text: The company is violating antitrust rules by offering an unfair advantage over competitors
options.rationale: Warranty length has nothing to do with antitrust or collusion.

options.text: The company is making a deceptive advertising claim by offering the warranty at all
options.rationale: Offering a warranty itself isn't deceptive advertising; the issue is failing to fund and honor it.

options.text: The company is required to disclose this gap under international trade regulations
options.rationale: International trade rules concern cross-border shipping, not domestic warranty funding.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, recognizing the direct consequence of not planning for a stated obligation, matching the card's core common mistake.

questions.question: A small skincare brand plans to start shipping orders to customers in other countries. What does it have to check first?

options.text: Whether rivals already sell there
options.rationale: Competition does not confer legality.

options.text: Whether the packaging looks local
options.rationale: A marketing question, not a legal one.

options.text: How long the shipping takes there
options.rationale: Service quality, not permission.

options.text: Which goods each country will admit
options.rationale: Import rules, ingredient restrictions and licences differ by destination and decide whether the parcel can lawfully arrive at all.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the trade rule that comes before the sale.

questions.question: A new bakery already has its general city business license and is ready to open. The owner assumes that single license covers everything needed to legally sell baked goods. What is the most likely problem with that assumption?

options.text: The licence will lapse before the bakery has turned its first profit.
options.rationale: Renewal timing is administrative, not what is missing.

options.text: A general business licence covers online trade rather than a storefront.
options.rationale: Invents a distinction the licence does not draw.

options.text: Food sales need separate health and handling permits beyond the licence.
options.rationale: A general licence says the business may trade; handling food for the public is regulated separately and by a different body.

options.text: The bakery has to hold off advertising until the first renewal.
options.rationale: Invents an advertising restriction.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (permitting scope) applied to a new, specific business scenario requiring the student to predict a compliance gap, not just define the term.

questions.question: An appliance store sells washing machines with a 5-year warranty but keeps no budget or reserve fund for future repair claims, treating the warranty purely as a selling point. What is the most likely consequence of this approach?

options.text: The warranty lapses once the store stops stocking that model of machine.
options.rationale: A promise to the buyer survives the store's stocking decisions.

options.text: The store can revise the warranty terms after a sale without telling the buyer.
options.rationale: Terms are fixed at the sale; that is what makes it a promise.

options.text: Customers will owe a service fee on each repair whatever the warranty says.
options.rationale: The warranty is what sets who pays, and it says the store does.

options.text: The store will face financial strain and complaints when claims start arriving.
options.rationale: A five year promise is a five year liability, and treating it purely as a selling point means nothing has been set aside to meet it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, applied to a new business situation to predict the real-world consequence of underfunding a warranty obligation, requiring more than definition recall.

questions.question: Two small, independently owned coffee shops in the same neighborhood agree over lunch to both raise their prices by a dollar so neither one has to compete on cost. What best describes this arrangement?

options.text: It is legal as long as the price increase is publicly announced to customers afterward.
options.rationale: Public disclosure doesn't make collusion legal; this misunderstands what makes price-fixing illegal.

options.text: It only becomes illegal if a third competitor also joins the agreement.
options.rationale: The card states there's no minimum threshold, so adding more participants isn't what triggers illegality.

options.text: It is legal because neither business is large enough to affect the overall market.
options.rationale: Misconception that antitrust only applies to giant corporations; the card notes there's no size threshold for illegal collusion.

options.text: It is illegal price-fixing even though it was an informal agreement between small businesses.
options.rationale: Matches the card's point that even a casual verbal agreement on pricing counts as collusion under antitrust law, regardless of business size.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept applied to a fresh scenario involving small businesses, testing whether the student can correctly identify collusion despite the common misconception about company size.

questions.question: A mobile nail technician holds her state licence and works out of a van she fitted herself, with no sink plumbed in. The trade standard requires running water at the station. What is her position?

options.text: Exempt, because the van is mobile
options.rationale: Invents an exemption.

options.text: Licensed, and not meeting the standard
options.rationale: Holding the licence is one requirement and the operation itself has to be built so the industry rules are actually met, not merely applied for.

options.text: Fully compliant, since she is licensed
options.rationale: Treats the licence as covering everything.

options.text: Unlicensed, so the standard is moot
options.rationale: She holds the licence.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: separate holding a licence from meeting the standard behind it.

questions.question: Two rival snack brands agree at a trade show to both advertise their chips as 'the freshest on the shelf,' a claim neither has tested, and to keep their prices matched at $3.99. Which statement best captures the legal problem here?
