notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: find the middle that serves both sides.

questions.question: A gym member who trains four times a week and pays for premium classes complains about a $15 late fee. The manager waives the fee and adds a free guest pass. A new member who visits rarely gets the same complaint handled the same way. What is the flaw in this approach?

options.text: The gym ignored that different members carry different long-term value, so effort should scale with worth.
options.rationale: Correct: it treats every customer identically instead of weighing future value against the cost of the concession, missing the balance the higher-value member actually merits.

options.text: The gym should have charged both members double to discourage future lateness.
options.rationale: This punishes rather than balances interests and has no basis in either concept.

options.text: The gym correctly treated both members the same since fairness means identical treatment for identical complaints.
options.rationale: This describes the mistake as a virtue; it ignores that lifetime value should shift how much effort a business spends per customer.

options.text: The gym should have refused both complaints to protect its stated late fee policy.
options.rationale: Enforcing policy rigidly ignores lifetime value entirely and risks losing the high-value member for a trivial fee.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding two concepts at once: recognizing that lifetime value should inform how much a company concedes, and that concessions must still be sized to what the company can sustain. Neither concept alone explains the flaw.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Customer Lifetime Value, Balancing Company and Customer Interests. Deleting lifetime value leaves only 'treat complaints identically,' which no longer explains why the flaw matters differently for different customers. Deleting balancing leaves only 'value the loyal customer more,' which doesn't address the sustainability trade-off in giving concessions. Both are needed, question holds.

questions.question: A software vendor calls a key client the moment it discovers a bug that will delay a feature launch, explains the cause, and proposes a fix timeline. A rival vendor waits for its client to notice the same kind of delay before responding. Both vendors also run quarterly strategy calls with these clients. Why does the first vendor build a stronger long-term partnership than the second?

options.text: It avoided the bug entirely, since no bugs occurred in the delayed feature launch.
options.rationale: The stem states a bug did occur and caused a delay, so this misreads the scenario.

options.text: It proactively disclosed the problem before being caught, which reinforces the trust that ongoing partnerships depend on.
options.rationale: Correct: early disclosure is the specific behavior that builds trust, and that trust is what sustains the partnership over the rival's reactive approach.

options.text: Its quarterly calls are more frequent, and frequency alone is what turns a vendor into a trusted partner.
options.rationale: Both vendors run quarterly calls; frequency is identical, so this can't be the distinguishing factor.

options.text: It offered a better technical fix, since partnerships are ultimately decided by product quality, not communication.
options.rationale: The scenario doesn't compare fix quality, only disclosure timing, so this introduces an unsupported factor.

notes.difficulty_justification: Both vendors share the partnership-building structure (quarterly calls), isolating transparency as the true variable; the student must see how disclosure timing feeds directly into whether the ongoing relationship holds up, not just recognize either concept alone.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Earning Customer Trust Through Transparency, Building Long-Term Customer Partnerships. Deleting transparency leaves two identical partnership efforts with no way to explain a difference in outcome. Deleting partnership leaves a simple 'proactive disclosure is good' fact with no long-term stakes attached. Both are required for the question to resolve.

questions.question: A car salesperson notices a customer only needs a basic commuter sedan but keeps steering her toward a loaded SUV that pays a bigger commission, while chatting warmly and asking about her family the whole time. Why does this fail to build a real customer relationship despite the friendly conversation?

options.text: The salesperson used friendliness to mask steering the sale toward what benefits him, not what actually earns lasting trust.
options.rationale: Correct: rapport requires honest guidance even at the cost of a sale, and this behavior fits the classic mistake of confusing chattiness with real trust-building.

options.text: The salesperson correctly built a relationship since he asked personal questions and kept the conversation friendly throughout.
options.rationale: This mistakes surface friendliness for rapport, exactly the common confusion the concept warns against.

options.text: The salesperson spent too much time on small talk instead of focusing on closing the sale quickly.
options.rationale: This treats efficiency as the problem, but the actual issue is dishonesty about the recommendation, not the amount of chat time.

options.text: The salesperson should have offered a bigger discount on the SUV to make the upsell easier to accept.
options.rationale: A discount doesn't fix the core issue of pushing an unsuitable product; it just makes the mismatch cheaper.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires distinguishing the surface behavior (friendly conversation, an ongoing relationship gesture) from the substance (honest recommendation) and seeing that relationship thinking only counts as genuine when paired with trustworthy rapport, not just repeated friendly contact.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Building Rapport and Trust, Customer Relationship Thinking. Deleting rapport/trust leaves only 'he talked to her a lot,' which wouldn't explain why that fails as relationship-building. Deleting relationship thinking leaves only 'he lied about which car fits,' a single trust violation without the framing of what counts as a real ongoing relationship versus a disguised one-time push. Both are needed.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of following up with a customer after a sale is complete?

options.text: To collect payment that was still outstanding
options.rationale: Confuses follow-up with billing, which isn't the purpose described.

options.text: To immediately pitch them on a more expensive product
options.rationale: Reflects the common mistake of turning follow-up into an upsell pitch.

options.text: To confirm the customer is satisfied with what they bought
options.rationale: Directly matches the definition of checking in to ensure the purchase worked out.

options.text: To ask the customer to stop posting reviews online
options.rationale: Mixes in review management, a different concept not related to post-sale check-ins.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, recognition of the stated purpose: one reasoning step.

questions.question: Which response to a negative public review best reflects taking real ownership of the problem?

options.text: Explaining calmly why the customer misunderstood what happened
options.rationale: Sounds calm but is still defensive, shifting blame rather than owning the mistake.

options.text: Ignoring the review since responding might draw more attention to it
options.rationale: Silence is the opposite of the recommended approach and doesn't earn a second look from readers.

options.text: Naming the specific mistake and describing exactly how it will be fixed
options.rationale: Reflects calm, specific ownership and a path to resolution as described in the card.

options.text: Posting a generic apology asking the customer to message privately without naming the issue
options.rationale: Matches the common mistake of a canned, non-specific reply that avoids real accountability.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, recognizing what genuine ownership looks like versus common failure patterns: one reasoning step.

questions.question: A cafe replies warmly to every glowing review and leaves the critical ones without any reply at all. What does that pattern tell someone browsing?

options.text: That its food is better than rated
options.rationale: Replies say nothing about the food.

options.text: That the cafe has very few critics
options.rationale: The critical reviews are visible.

options.text: That criticism gets no response here
options.rationale: Future customers read the replies as much as the reviews, and silence on the hard ones is itself an answer.

options.text: That replies are written by staff
options.rationale: Authorship is not the signal.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: read what the reply pattern communicates.

questions.question: A bakery receives a one star review saying a cake arrived late for a child's birthday. Which public reply does the most for the strangers who will read it?

options.text: Ask the customer to remove the review and call us
options.rationale: Treats the review as a problem to delete rather than an audience to answer.

options.text: Apologize by name, name the fix, offer to make it right
options.rationale: The reply is read by future customers, so a specific apology plus a stated change is what demonstrates the business is safe to buy from.

options.text: Explain that the delivery driver caused the delay
options.rationale: Assigning blame reads as defensiveness and tells a stranger nothing has changed.

options.text: Post that the shop takes all feedback seriously
options.rationale: The generic canned reply that never names the problem, which the card calls out directly.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose the reply that serves the public audience in a fresh case.

questions.question: A bike shop sold a first time rider a road bike on Saturday. Which follow up call on Tuesday fits the skill?

options.text: Ask how the fit feels and mention the free tune up
options.rationale: Checks genuine satisfaction at the moment problems surface, and reminds them of value already paid for.

options.text: Offer a discount on a second bike for a friend
options.rationale: A referral pitch before the first purchase has even been judged.

options.text: Pitch the clipless pedal upgrade they skipped
options.rationale: Turns the follow up into an upsell, the exact trap the card names.

options.text: Ask for a five star review before the week ends
options.rationale: Harvests reputation before earning it, and asks the customer for a favour first.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: pick the post-sale contact that serves the customer rather than the next sale.

questions.question: A client posts that a contractor left drywall dust across her living room. The crew says the mess was smaller than described. What should the public reply do?

options.text: Own the mess, state the fix, move to a repair date
options.rationale: Ownership plus a concrete next step is what converts a complaint into a resolution in front of an audience.

options.text: Ask the client to take the conversation private
options.rationale: Leaves every future reader with the complaint and no answer.

options.text: Set the record straight about the amount of dust
options.rationale: Arguing over degree in public loses the reader even if the crew is right.

options.text: Thank them and say feedback is taken seriously
options.rationale: Names nothing and fixes nothing, which reads as a form letter.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose the response that resolves rather than defends.

questions.question: A mattress store salesperson calls a customer one week after delivery, but only to ask if they want to buy a matching pillow set. The customer never mentions their sleep quality. What does this call risk in terms of word-of-mouth?

options.text: The customer feels pushed rather than cared for, so the story they share may turn.
options.rationale: A follow-up that is really a sales call converts a goodwill moment into a grievance, and that is what gets retold.

options.text: Nothing changes, since word of mouth travels from complaints rather than calls.
options.rationale: A pushy call is itself a story people repeat.

options.text: The customer reads the call as a sign the mattress has a known fault.
options.rationale: Invents a worry the case does not suggest.

options.text: The call produces a poor review whatever the customer thinks of the mattress.
options.rationale: Overstates a risk into a certainty.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires linking the follow-up card's specific mistake (upsell disguised as care) with the reputation card's mechanism (experiences become stories) to predict a downstream word-of-mouth effect, which neither concept alone fully explains.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Following Up After the Sale, Reputation and Word-of-Mouth. Deleting Reputation and Word-of-Mouth leaves only 'this follow-up is done wrong,' a state-level point; deleting Following Up After the Sale removes the reason this particular interaction risks becoming a bad story. Both are needed to reason from the flawed call to the reputational consequence.

questions.question: An owner answers every negative review within the hour, and each reply sets out in detail why the customer had misunderstood the policy. What is the effect on someone reading them?

options.text: A business that ignores its critics
options.rationale: It answers every one of them.

options.text: Fast replies that read as defensive
options.rationale: Showing up quickly is the right habit and the content of the reply is what a future customer actually judges.

options.text: Replies too slow to be noticed
options.rationale: They arrive within the hour.

options.text: Reviews that will now be deleted
options.rationale: Replying does not remove a review.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the review management discipline is exemplary and the way criticism is answered undoes the benefit.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Managing online reviews, Responding to public criticism. Without the fast replies there is nothing for readers to judge. Without the defensive content the habit pays off. Both are needed.

questions.question: A bike shop calls a week after every sale to ask how the bike is riding. One caller mentions a sore saddle, the shop swaps it free, and three of her friends come in that month. Reviews were never mentioned. What does the case show?

options.text: A referral scheme working as designed
options.rationale: There is no scheme here.

options.text: A good follow-up doing the talking
options.rationale: The call created something worth repeating, and word of mouth carried it outward without the shop ever asking.

options.text: A free repair that cost too much
options.rationale: A saddle bought three customers.

options.text: Customers who would have come anyway
options.rationale: The friends followed the saddle story.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the follow-up is the cause and the word-of-mouth ripple is the effect, and the case only makes sense with both.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Following up after the sale, Reputation and word-of-mouth. Without the call the saddle problem stays hidden. Without the ripple the fix helps one customer. Both are needed.

questions.question: An employee facing an angry customer stays calm and works toward a fair fix instead of arguing back or handing over everything demanded. What does this show?

options.text: The employee is managing a difficult interaction well
options.rationale: Correct: the card defines this as staying steady and steering toward a real solution rather than escalating or caving.

options.text: The employee is empowering another employee to solve the problem
options.rationale: That concept is about giving authority to fix issues, not about staying calm during conflict.

options.text: The employee is anticipating what the customer needs next
options.rationale: Anticipating needs is about proactive offers, not reacting to an already upset customer.

options.text: The employee is keeping service consistent across channels
options.rationale: Consistency across channels concerns matching answers across phone, chat, and email, not conflict handling.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept recognition, matching a described behavior to its defining term with one reasoning step.

questions.question: A grocery store clerk notices a customer buying baby formula and diapers, and quietly mentions the store's new parent discount card before the customer asks. What is this an example of?

options.text: Anticipating a need based on cues in the situation
options.rationale: Correct: the clerk noticed contextual signals and offered something useful before being asked.

options.text: Maintaining consistency across service channels
options.rationale: This is a single in-person interaction, not a comparison across different service channels.

options.text: Empowering employees to solve problems
options.rationale: No problem was being solved or authority exercised here, so this doesn't fit.

options.text: Managing a difficult interaction
options.rationale: There is no upset customer or conflict in this scenario.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept applied to a simple recognition scenario, requiring one step of matching behavior to definition.

questions.question: A customer is quoted one returns deadline on the phone, a different one in chat, and a third at the counter. What does the business lack?

options.text: A faster phone answering time
options.rationale: Speed is not the inconsistency.

options.text: One answer across every channel
options.rationale: The experience should not depend on which door the customer came through.

options.text: A shorter returns deadline
options.rationale: Length of the window is not the issue.

options.text: More staff trained on returns
options.rationale: Training without one agreed answer repeats it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what the three answers reveal is missing.

questions.question: A customer at a phone repair kiosk shouts that his screen replacement cracked again after one day and demands a free new phone. The technician quietly checks the repair log, then calmly offers a free re-repair within 24 hours plus a $20 credit, without raising her voice or agreeing to a new phone. What does this response demonstrate?

options.text: Matching his energy to show she takes the complaint seriously
options.rationale: She lowered the tension rather than matching his anger, which is the opposite of what happened.

options.text: Caving in completely to stop the confrontation quickly
options.rationale: She did not give the customer what he demanded; she offered a scoped fix instead, so this is not caving in.

options.text: Escalating the issue to a manager to avoid responsibility
options.rationale: No escalation happened here; she resolved it herself on the spot.

options.text: Staying calm while steering toward a concrete, reasonable fix
options.rationale: This matches managing difficult interactions: staying level-headed and redirecting anger toward an actual solution rather than matching the anger or surrendering to the demand.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, applied to a new scenario requiring the student to judge whether the response is calm-and-solution-focused versus caving or escalating, a single reasoning step beyond definition.

questions.question: A car rental agent notices a customer booking a one-way rental with a drop-off at an airport two hours before an international flight. Without being asked, the agent mentions the fastest route to avoid traffic and confirms the drop-off counter closes 30 minutes before boarding. What is this agent doing?

options.text: Waiting for the customer to raise a concern before responding
options.rationale: The agent acted before any concern was voiced, which is the opposite of a reactive approach.

options.text: Recognizing a time-sensitive pattern and offering help before being asked
options.rationale: The agent used the specific context, tight flight window and one-way drop-off, to surface a likely problem and solve it proactively, which is anticipating customer needs.

options.text: Offering the same standard checkout script given to every renter
options.rationale: A standard script would not respond to this customer's specific timing situation; this is tailored, not uniform.

options.text: Assuming the customer's needs based on a general stereotype
options.rationale: The agent is reading specific booking details, flight timing and drop-off location, not making a stereotype-based guess.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied to a new context: the student must distinguish genuine cue-based anticipation from stereotyping or reactive service, a single applied step.

questions.question: An older customer at a bank counter says plainly that she does not use apps, and the teller keeps pointing her towards the mobile service. What should the teller do?

options.text: Repeat the app instructions slowly
options.rationale: Volume and pace were never the barrier.

options.text: Serve her the way she can use
options.rationale: Serving people well means adjusting to the individual in front of you rather than running one approach on everybody.

options.text: Refer her to a different branch
options.rationale: Moves the customer, not the service.

options.text: Show her how to install the app
options.rationale: Still pushes the channel she declined.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: adjust the service to a stated individual need.

questions.question: A garage's customers mainly complain that they never know when the car will be ready. The owner is choosing between a loyalty app and an automatic text at each repair stage. Which serves the complaint?

options.text: Both, to cover every possibility
options.rationale: Spends twice on an unaimed guess.

options.text: The texts, which answer the question
options.rationale: Technology earns its place by making the service faster, easier or more personal against a real problem, not by being new.

options.text: Neither, since staff can phone them
options.rationale: What is already failing.

options.text: The app, which looks more modern
options.rationale: Novelty rather than usefulness.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: pick the tool that answers the stated complaint.

questions.question: A hotel gives front desk staff authority to comp up to $75 without manager approval. A guest is furious about a noisy room and demands a full refund of a $400 stay. The staffer stays calm, acknowledges the problem, but immediately grants the full $400 refund just to end the confrontation. What went wrong here?

options.text: The staffer should never have been given refund authority at all, since only managers can judge legitimate complaints.
options.rationale: Contradicts the empowerment concept itself, which exists precisely so frontline staff can resolve issues without escalating.

options.text: The staffer failed by not raising their voice to match the guest's anger before offering a solution.
options.rationale: Misunderstands managing difficult interactions, which calls for staying level-headed, not escalating tone to match the customer.

options.text: The staffer handled it correctly, since staying calm and resolving the complaint on the spot is the whole goal of empowerment.
options.rationale: Ignores that empowerment includes clear limits; resolving on the spot only counts as success within the authorized boundary, not by exceeding it.

options.text: The staffer used their granted authority in a way that exceeded its actual limit, giving in to pressure instead of solving within bounds.
options.rationale: Correct: empowerment came with a $75 limit, and caving to the full demand under pressure is exactly the failure mode where staying calm doesn't prevent overcorrecting past the authorized boundary.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding both the boundary-setting mechanism of empowerment and the discipline of not over-conceding under pressure from managing difficult interactions; neither concept alone explains why the outcome is a failure.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Managing Difficult Interactions, Empowering Employees to Solve Problems. Deleting empowerment removes the $75 limit, so there's no defined boundary to violate, and the question collapses to 'don't give free stuff to end conflict,' losing the authority-limit reasoning. Deleting managing difficult interactions removes the anger/pressure context, and it becomes just a policy-violation question. Both are needed, question holds.

questions.question: A retailer publishes a two hour reply standard and meets it on email every single time. Chat replies take a day and the phone line rings out. What is the position?

options.text: The two hour promise is too ambitious
options.rationale: It has been proved achievable.

options.text: A standard nobody in the firm meets
options.rationale: Email meets it every time.

options.text: Email is the wrong channel to promise
options.rationale: Email is where the promise is honoured.

options.text: A real standard kept on one channel
options.rationale: The standard is genuine where it is measured, and a customer who chose a different door never sees it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the quality standard is real and its reach across channels is not, so the customer's experience depends on which one they picked.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Delivering service quality, Consistency across service channels. Without the standard there is nothing to apply unevenly. Without the channel gap the promise holds everywhere. Both are needed.

questions.question: A chain advertises that any problem is resolved the same day, and requires a regional manager's written approval for any refund above ten dollars. What does that pairing produce?

options.text: Staff with too much spending authority
options.rationale: They have almost none.

options.text: A promise the front line cannot keep
options.rationale: A service standard is only as good as the authority the person facing the customer has to deliver it.

options.text: A standard that is far too generous
options.rationale: Generous is not why it fails.

options.text: Refunds that cost more than they should
options.rationale: The approval rule holds refunds down.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the published standard and the authority actually granted point in opposite directions.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Delivering service quality, Empowering employees to solve problems. Without the standard nothing is promised. Without the approval rule the front line can honour it. Both are needed.

questions.question: What does it mean for an employee to understand a customer's needs?

options.text: Greeting each customer with the same friendly script to keep service consistent
options.rationale: Consistency in greeting is unrelated to figuring out individual needs.

options.text: Assuming a customer wants the same thing as most other shoppers that day
options.rationale: This is guessing rather than actually finding out what the customer wants.

options.text: Recommending the store's highest-margin product to every customer who walks in
options.rationale: This is the common mistake of pushing a preferred product instead of finding out what the customer wants.

options.text: Asking questions to find out what the customer actually wants before recommending anything
options.rationale: Correct: matches the definition of listening and asking instead of guessing.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests a single concept at the recognition level: identifying what understanding customer needs actually is.

questions.question: A salesperson tells a customer a repair 'should be pretty quick' instead of giving an actual timeframe, just to keep the customer happy. What is the direct risk of this approach?

options.text: The customer will stop mentioning their real reason for wanting the repair done quickly
options.rationale: This confuses the situation with buying motives, not expectation-setting.

options.text: The customer will feel like just another number instead of an individual
options.rationale: That describes a lack of personalization, not a broken expectation about timing.

options.text: The customer will assume the business has no internal customers to coordinate with
options.rationale: Internal customers are a separate concept and unrelated to this vague-promise scenario.

options.text: The customer will feel misled once the real timeframe turns out to be longer than expected
options.rationale: Correct: vague, softened promises set up disappointment when reality doesn't match, per the card's core warning.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, one reasoning step: predicting the direct consequence of vague promises instead of honest timelines.

questions.question: Which situation best describes treating a coworker as an internal customer?

options.text: A manager reminds staff to smile and use a customer's name during checkout
options.rationale: This is a personalization tactic with an external customer, not recognition of an internal one.

options.text: A warehouse team ships orders quickly to a paying customer who placed a large order
options.rationale: This is service to an external paying customer, not an internal one.

options.text: A prepress team flags file errors quickly so the design team can fix them before printing
options.rationale: Correct: the design team relies on prepress's work internally, matching the card's example of serving a coworker who depends on your output.

options.text: A cashier asks a shopper follow-up questions to figure out what they actually need
options.rationale: This describes understanding customer needs with an external customer, not an internal one.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, recognition level: identifying which scenario matches the definition of an internal customer relationship.

questions.question: A client asks a printing shop to deliver 500 custom brochures by tomorrow morning, but the shop's fastest possible turnaround is three full days. What should the shop rep do?

options.text: Accept the order for tomorrow and let the client find out about the delay when they come to pick it up.
options.rationale: This avoids the conversation entirely, guaranteeing the customer is blindsided later, the opposite of setting expectations.

options.text: Say the order should be ready 'pretty soon' without naming a specific day, so the client doesn't get upset.
options.rationale: Vague reassurance instead of a specific honest timeline is the common mistake of softening bad news rather than communicating clearly.

options.text: Tell the client honestly that three days is the real turnaround, and offer a rush option if one truly exists.
options.rationale: This matches setting expectations correctly: being upfront about the real timeline and only offering alternatives that are actually possible.

options.text: Promise tomorrow morning to keep the client happy, then quietly try to speed up production later.
options.rationale: This is overpromising to close the deal in the moment, exactly the pattern that leads to disappointment and lost trust when reality falls short.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (Setting Customer Expectations) applied to a new, specific deadline scenario not covered in the card's own example, requiring the student to predict which response matches the concept's mechanism.

questions.question: A shopper at an electronics store keeps repeating 'I just want the cheapest laptop you have,' but also mentions twice that she travels for work every week and worries about her current laptop's battery dying mid-flight. What should the salesperson do?

options.text: Recommend a slightly pricier laptop with long battery life, framing it around reliability for her travel schedule.
options.rationale: This recognizes that her real motive is likely reliability and peace of mind while traveling, not just cost, and matches the pitch to that underlying reason.

options.text: Ask her to decide between two random mid-range models without mentioning battery life or travel at all.
options.rationale: This ignores the buying motive clues altogether and doesn't tie the recommendation to any identified reason for her purchase.

options.text: Show her the absolute lowest-priced laptop on the shelf since she stated price as her main concern.
options.rationale: This treats her stated price objection as the true motive without probing what's actually driving her decision, the common mistake called out on the card.

options.text: Offer her a payment plan so the cheapest laptop feels even more affordable.
options.rationale: This still assumes price is the true motive and just makes the cheap option easier to buy, ignoring the travel and battery clues entirely.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept applied to a fresh scenario requiring the student to infer the real motive from context clues rather than the stated request, one reasoning step beyond simple recall.

questions.question: An online shop finds that seventy percent of its carts are abandoned on the screen where shipping cost first appears. What does journey mapping tell it to do?

options.text: Add more products to the catalogue
options.rationale: Range is not where they are leaving.

options.text: Fix the step where people drop out
options.rationale: Mapping the path exists to show where customers stall, and the value comes from working on that point rather than the whole funnel.

options.text: Spend more on ads to bring traffic
options.rationale: Pours more people into the same leak.

options.text: Email everyone who abandoned a cart
options.rationale: Chases the symptom after the fact.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: act on the drop-off the map exposes.

questions.question: A hardware store groups shoppers by age and finds the groups behave almost identically. Its staff say the real split is between people fixing something urgently and people planning a project. What does needs-based segmenting suggest?

options.text: Split them by how much they spend
options.rationale: A result, not a need.

options.text: Add income bands to the age groups
options.rationale: More surface traits.

options.text: Stop segmenting the shoppers at all
options.rationale: The staff have found a real split.

options.text: Group them by the job they came to do
options.rationale: Segmenting by what customers are trying to get done separates groups that actually behave differently, which demographics here do not.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: re-cut the groups on the useful axis.

questions.question: A warehouse team tells the sales team 'no problem, we can always ship same-day,' even though during busy weeks same-day shipping is rarely possible. Sales then promises customers same-day delivery as a standard feature. What's the core issue here?

options.text: Sales should stop promising shipping and send customers to the warehouse
options.rationale: Pushes the customer around an internal problem.

options.text: The warehouse gave sales, its internal customer, a promise it could not keep
options.rationale: Sales depends on the warehouse the way a customer depends on sales, and the unreliable answer travelled straight out to people paying money.

options.text: Sales is at fault for repeating a claim without checking with a carrier
options.rationale: Sales checked with the team that owns the answer.

options.text: The warehouse should mind its own deadlines, since sales faces the customer
options.rationale: That is the attitude the internal customer idea corrects.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires linking two concepts: recognizing sales as the warehouse's internal customer, and seeing how an unreliable internal answer becomes a broken expectation for the external customer. Neither concept alone explains the chain of failure.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Identifying Internal Customers, Setting Customer Expectations. Deleting Identifying Internal Customers removes the reason the warehouse owed sales an honest answer in the first place. Deleting Setting Customer Expectations removes the reason the vague 'no problem' answer causes real harm downstream. Both are required, so it passes the break test.

questions.question: A salon's system greets each client by name and brings up her last colour. The stylist starts mixing it without asking, because the record says that is what she has. The client wanted a change. What is the fault?

options.text: Personal detail standing in for a question
options.rationale: Knowing a customer well makes the service feel individual and it is not a substitute for finding out what she wants this time.

options.text: Too much history stored on each client
options.rationale: The history is an asset here.

options.text: The stylist should not keep records
options.rationale: Records are what made the personalisation possible.

options.text: Greeting by name feels intrusive here
options.rationale: The greeting is not the misstep.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the personalisation is genuine and it quietly replaced the needs question it was supposed to support.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Personalizing the experience, Understanding customer needs. Without the stored history there is nothing to assume from. Without the missing question the personal touch is a plus. Both are needed.

questions.question: A buyer's real reason for purchasing is being ready for a trade show in three weeks. The representative reads that correctly, sells exactly the right machine, and never mentions the six week lead time. What went wrong?

options.text: The motive was read and then defeated
options.rationale: Identifying what the customer is really buying for is only useful if the promise made can serve it, and this one cannot.

options.text: The buyer's motive was really price
options.rationale: The case says otherwise.

options.text: The wrong machine was recommended
options.rationale: The machine fits the need.

options.text: Lead times are never worth raising
options.rationale: This is the one fact that mattered.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the motive is correctly identified and the expectation set against it makes the sale fail anyway.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Recognizing buying motives, Setting customer expectations. Without the deadline motive the lead time is unremarkable. Without the silence on delivery the sale serves the motive. Both are needed.

questions.question: What does it mean when a company achieves economies of scale?

options.text: It makes a product feel unique so customers stop comparing prices.
options.rationale: Describes product differentiation, a separate strategy unrelated to production cost per unit.

options.text: It blocks new competitors from ever entering the industry.
options.rationale: Describes a barrier to entry, not the cost mechanism of economies of scale, even though large scale can sometimes act as one.

options.text: It spreads fixed costs over more units so each item costs less to make.
options.rationale: Correct: this matches the core mechanism, fixed costs divided across higher volume lowers per-unit cost.

options.text: It raises prices because it has no remaining competitors in the market.
options.rationale: Confuses scale economies with monopoly power, a different concept about competitor count, not production cost.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of a single concept's definition with one reasoning step: identifying the direct mechanism of economies of scale.

questions.question: A new airline wants to launch flights out of a busy city airport, but every available gate is already leased long-term to existing carriers. What does this situation illustrate?

options.text: A form of monopoly power held by the new airline.
options.rationale: Monopoly power means controlling the market as the sole seller; the new airline is the one being kept out, not the one dominating.

options.text: An economy of scale that lowers the new airline's per-flight cost.
options.rationale: Economies of scale are about cost dropping with volume, not about being blocked from operating at all.

options.text: A barrier to entry that makes it hard for the new airline to compete.
options.rationale: Correct: limited gate access is a structural obstacle blocking a new competitor, the definition of a barrier to entry.

options.text: A product differentiation strategy used by the existing airlines.
options.rationale: Differentiation is about making a product distinct to customers, not about physically restricting a competitor's access to infrastructure.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept applied to a direct, first-order scenario: recognizing a structural obstacle as a barrier to entry.

questions.question: A business owner who plans only for one possible outcome and assumes sales, costs, and competitors will all behave exactly as expected is failing to account for what?

options.text: Business risk and uncertainty in the plan.
options.rationale: Correct: ignoring that the future could unfold differently than expected is the core failure this concept addresses.

options.text: Economies of scale in production costs.
options.rationale: Economies of scale concerns per-unit cost as volume grows, not planning for uncertain future outcomes.

options.text: Product differentiation from competitors.
options.rationale: Differentiation is about standing out on features, unrelated to failing to plan for uncertain future conditions.

options.text: Barriers to entry protecting the business.
options.rationale: Barriers to entry are about blocking competitors, not about the owner's failure to plan for uncertain events.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, recognition-level: identifying the described planning failure as a lack of accounting for business risk and uncertainty.

questions.question: A new streaming service wants to enter the market for satellite internet in rural areas, where launching and operating satellites costs hundreds of millions of dollars. What does this situation best illustrate?

options.text: The new company should expect easy entry once it secures enough marketing budget
options.rationale: Marketing spend doesn't offset the actual structural barrier here, which is the enormous fixed capital cost, not brand awareness.

options.text: The market must be in monopolistic competition since satellite service is a differentiated product
options.rationale: This confuses market structure labeling with barriers to entry; the scenario is about what blocks entry, not how many similar sellers already exist.

options.text: The existing satellite companies must be operating as an illegal monopoly
options.rationale: High costs to enter don't by themselves mean current firms control the whole market or lack any competitors, so calling it an illegal monopoly overreaches.

options.text: The high cost to enter functions as a strong structural barrier protecting current providers
options.rationale: Massive startup capital requirements are exactly the kind of structural barrier that keeps new competitors out for years, matching the airline gate-slot example on the card.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, barriers to entry, applied to a new industry scenario requiring the student to identify the barrier rather than recite the definition.

questions.question: A single company owns the only bridge connecting an island town to the mainland, and it recently raised the toll by 40% with no advance notice. Residents have no other route on or off the island. Which response best fits this situation?

options.text: Assume the toll increase is fair since any company can raise prices on its own product
options.rationale: This ignores that customers here have zero viable alternative, which is the specific condition that turns a price increase into an abuse of monopoly power.

options.text: Conclude it isn't really monopoly power since only one product, tolls, is involved
options.rationale: Monopoly power isn't about how many products are sold; it's about whether customers have any real alternative, and here they don't.

options.text: Wait for a competitor to naturally build a second bridge and undercut the price
options.rationale: Given the enormous cost of building a bridge, natural competitive entry is unlikely, so this ignores the real barrier keeping the company unchallenged.

options.text: Push for regulation or a price cap since residents have no alternative route
options.rationale: This matches the card's guidance that when one seller controls essential access with no substitute, regulation or capping price is the appropriate response to monopoly power.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, monopoly power, applied within a new scenario requiring the student to judge the appropriate response rather than just define monopoly.

questions.question: A bakery carries $6,000 a month in rent and equipment costs. It doubles output from 3,000 to 6,000 loaves using the same oven and the same premises. What happens per loaf?

options.text: Cost per loaf stays the same
options.rationale: Ignores the spreading of fixed cost.

options.text: Fixed cost per loaf halves
options.rationale: The same fixed amount spread over twice the units is half as much on each one.

options.text: Total fixed cost doubles
options.rationale: The rent and oven did not change.

options.text: Variable cost per loaf halves
options.rationale: Ingredients scale with output.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: work the fixed cost through a volume change.

questions.question: A national bakery chain runs huge mixing and baking lines that cut its per-loaf cost far below what any small bakery could match, and it also holds exclusive supply contracts with the region's wheat distributors. A new local bakery wants to enter the market. Which statement best explains why this local bakery faces a tougher entry than one facing only a cost disadvantage?

options.text: The chain's low costs alone prove it holds monopoly power over the whole bread market.
options.rationale: Misapplies monopoly power; having a cost edge over one entrant doesn't mean there's no viable alternative for customers across the market.

options.text: The local bakery faces no real disadvantage since differentiated products always escape cost competition.
options.rationale: Overstates differentiation's power and ignores that the input-access barrier exists regardless of how differentiated the product is.

options.text: The exclusive wheat contracts add a structural barrier on top of the scale-driven cost gap, so entry is blocked two ways at once.
options.rationale: Correctly combines both concepts: economies of scale explain the cost gap, while the exclusive contracts are a separate structural barrier restricting access to inputs, compounding the difficulty.

options.text: Since the chain achieved economies of scale, the local bakery just needs to grow production volume to match its costs.
options.rationale: Ignores the barrier from exclusive contracts; scaling up production doesn't solve a lack of access to the same supply deals.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding two distinct concepts, cost-based scale advantage and structural entry barriers, and reasoning about how they compound rather than defining either alone.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Economies of Scale, Barriers to Market Entry. Removing economies of scale leaves only a barrier question (why exclusive contracts block entry), which loses the cost-gap reasoning; removing barriers leaves only a scale question about matching costs. Both are needed for option b to be correct, so the pairing holds.

questions.question: A new sandwich shop opens on a street with six other sandwich shops selling similar subs at similar prices. The owner is deciding whether to drop prices below everyone else's or to build a spicy signature sauce recipe found nowhere else. Which choice best fits the market structure and why?

options.text: Build the sauce, since it raises barriers and keeps new shops off the street.
options.rationale: A sauce does not deter entry; it earns a preference.

options.text: Build the signature sauce, since a valued difference avoids pure price competition.
options.rationale: With seven near-identical sellers, the one thing that stops the street competing to the bottom is something customers can only get here.

options.text: Drop prices below the rivals, since that is how a similar seller wins custom.
options.rationale: Six rivals can match a price overnight.

options.text: Do neither, since six competing shops leaves nobody with any pricing power.
options.rationale: Crowding is why differentiation pays, not a reason to do nothing.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests whether the student can combine recognition of a specific market structure with choosing a differentiation strategy suited to it, rather than knowing either concept alone.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Market Structure and Competition, Product Differentiation Strategy. Removing market structure leaves a generic 'should this shop differentiate' question with no reason tied to rival count/similarity; removing differentiation leaves only a structure-identification question with no strategic choice. Both are needed to justify option b over a, so the pairing holds.

questions.question: A juice bar's only real edge is a recipe that any competitor could reproduce within a week of tasting it. Its three year plan assumes premium pricing throughout. What is the exposure?

options.text: Rivals who cannot enter the market
options.rationale: They can enter in a week.

options.text: A plan that undercharges for the juice
options.rationale: The premium is the assumption at risk.

options.text: A recipe too complex for the market
options.rationale: It is easy to copy, not complex.

options.text: A difference that will not hold the price
options.rationale: Differentiation only supports a premium while it is hard to copy, and the plan treats a week long lead as if it lasts three years.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the differentiation is real today and the risk assessment has to ask how long it survives a competitor's response.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Product differentiation strategy, Business risk and uncertainty. Without the differentiation there is no premium to plan on. Without the risk question the premium looks safe. Both are needed.

questions.question: In a market economy, who mainly decides what goods get produced and at what price?

options.text: A central government agency sets production levels and prices
options.rationale: This describes a command economy, the opposite of a market economy.

options.text: A national planning board allocating factory quotas
options.rationale: This is a command economy feature, not a market one.

options.text: Labor unions negotiating fixed wages for all industries
options.rationale: Wage negotiation isn't the defining mechanism of a market economy; price signals from supply and demand are.

options.text: Buyers and sellers interacting through supply and demand
options.rationale: Correct: in a market economy, prices and production are driven by voluntary exchange between buyers and sellers.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests direct recognition of one concept, who makes production decisions in a market economy, with no application to a novel scenario.

questions.question: What best describes a mixed economy?

options.text: Citizens vote directly on prices and production decisions
options.rationale: No economy allocates this way.

options.text: Industry is owned and run by the state across the board
options.rationale: That is a command economy.

options.text: Firms compete freely inside rules, taxes and services the state sets
options.rationale: A mixed economy is both at once: private firms making most decisions inside a frame the state sets.

options.text: Prices are set by supply and demand with government standing back
options.rationale: That is a pure market economy.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, straight recognition of the definition of a mixed economy without applying it to a scenario.

questions.question: In one town, allotment plots are leased to named holders for ten years. In the next town, plots are reassigned at random every spring. Which soil ends up better cared for?

options.text: Both, since gardeners are careful
options.rationale: Ignores what the incentive does.

options.text: Neither, as ownership means little
options.rationale: Ownership is exactly what differs.

options.text: The leased plots, whose holders invest
options.rationale: Secure ownership gives people a reason to put work in now that only pays off later.

options.text: The reassigned plots, shared by all
options.rationale: Nobody reaps what they improved.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: apply the incentive effect of clear ownership.

questions.question: A furniture maker enters a country where the government sets factory rents low and guarantees electricity, but also fixes how many chairs the factory may export each year and sets worker pay by decree. Which tradeoff is the company facing?

options.text: Higher operating risk in exchange for full control over prices and wages
options.rationale: Reverses the tradeoff; the scenario describes guarantees and restrictions, not risk and freedom.

options.text: Lower operating risk in exchange for reduced pricing and output freedom
options.rationale: Correctly names the command-economy tradeoff: guaranteed inputs and stability traded against fixed quotas and wages limiting flexibility.

options.text: Lower production costs in exchange for stronger patent and property protections
options.rationale: Property protection isn't part of this scenario; mixes in an unrelated concept.

options.text: Faster demand response in exchange for higher taxes on profit
options.rationale: Describes neither guarantee nor quota; misapplies a market-style tradeoff to a command setup.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (command vs market economies) applied to a new, specific scenario requiring the student to identify which tradeoff is occurring, not just define the terms.

questions.question: A private gym sets its own membership prices and class schedules, but must pass annual fire-code inspections and collect state sales tax on every purchase. Which feature of a mixed economy does this best show?

options.text: A pure market economy with no government involvement in daily operations
options.rationale: Ignores the inspections and tax collection, which are clear government functions.

options.text: Market pricing operating alongside government rules and tax collection
options.rationale: Matches the definition: private decision-making on price and services combined with regulatory and tax obligations from government.

options.text: A planned economy where government sets output targets for private firms
options.rationale: No output targets are set here; this describes command planning, which isn't present.

options.text: Government ownership of the gym paired with private hiring decisions
options.rationale: The gym is privately owned; nothing suggests government ownership.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (mixed economy) applied to a novel business situation, requiring the student to recognize both the market and government elements at play rather than just recall the definition.

questions.question: Several food trucks share one public parking lot with no assigned spots, and none of them clean up trash left behind after service. What does this situation best illustrate?

options.text: Government regulation lowering the trucks' overall operating costs
options.rationale: No regulation is mentioned in the scenario; this misattributes the cause.

options.text: Market competition driving the trucks to lower their prices
options.rationale: Pricing and competition aren't described here; this substitutes an unrelated market dynamic.

options.text: Unclear ownership reducing anyone's incentive to maintain the shared space
options.rationale: Matches the property rights concept: no individual owner means no one captures the benefit of upkeep, so the lot gets neglected.

options.text: Clear ownership encouraging each truck to invest in the lot's upkeep
options.rationale: States the opposite of what's happening; ownership here is unclear, not clear.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (property rights and incentives) applied to a new shared-resource scenario, requiring the student to connect neglect to the absence of ownership rather than just define the term.

questions.question: Two neighboring farms grow the same crop. Farm A is in a heavily planned economy where the government assigns land use and sets output quotas, but individual farmers still hold deeded title to their specific plots. Farm B is in a market economy, but the land is communally worked with no individual plots assigned. Which farm is more likely to see soil neglect, and why?

options.text: Farm A, because a planned system uses land less efficiently than a market one
options.rationale: Answers at the level of the system rather than the plot.

options.text: Farm A, because assigned quotas leave a farmer little reason to work the land hard
options.rationale: Plausible, and Farm A's plots are individually held, which is the part that matters.

options.text: Farm B, because unclear ownership of shared plots removes any reason to invest
options.rationale: Nobody improves ground they may not be farming next season, which is what shared and unassigned use produces whatever the wider system is.

options.text: Neither farm, since the economic system decides land care more than ownership does
options.rationale: Ownership is precisely the variable that differs here.

notes.difficulty_justification: Forces the student to separate the economic-system label from the ownership variable and see that property rights, not command-versus-market status, drives the neglect outcome, which requires holding both concepts and testing them against each other.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Command Versus Market Economies, Property Rights and Incentives. Deleting property rights leaves no way to distinguish the farms since both would just be 'command' vs 'market' with no ownership detail to explain the neglect. Deleting command-versus-market removes the deliberate mismatch (planned economy with ownership vs market economy without ownership) that makes the question test whether students conflate the two ideas. Both are required.

questions.question: A textile company operates in a country where private firms set most prices and freely enter or exit the market, but the government also runs subsidized state-owned mills that sell cloth below the private firms' cost, and it requires licenses to open a new factory. How should the company best classify this economic environment?

options.text: A command economy transitioning toward market reforms, since licensing requirements suggest the state is gradually loosening its grip.
options.rationale: Misreads a stable mixed system as a transition story; nothing in the scenario indicates change over time, only current coexisting features.

options.text: A pure command economy, since state-owned mills and licensing requirements mean the government is really directing production.
options.rationale: Overstates government control by ignoring that private firms still freely set prices and enter the market, which a pure command system would not allow.

options.text: A mixed economy, since private competition sets most prices while government-run mills and licensing rules also shape the market.
options.rationale: Correctly identifies both the private competitive function (price-setting, free entry) and the specific government functions (subsidized state mills, licensing) coexisting, which is what defines a mixed economy rather than either pure extreme.

options.text: A pure market economy, since most prices are set by private firms competing for customers.
options.rationale: Ignores the state-owned mills and licensing requirement, which are clear government interventions inconsistent with a purely market-driven system.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires distinguishing pure market and pure command extremes from the mixed reality by identifying specific market functions and specific government functions at once, rather than defaulting to a single label.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Command Versus Market Economies, Mixed Economy Characteristics. Deleting the command-versus-market framing removes the temptation to mislabel this as purely one extreme, but the question still needs that spectrum to make options a and b plausible wrong answers. Deleting mixed economy characteristics removes the correct answer's basis entirely. Both concepts are load-bearing.

questions.question: A country lets private firms own property and set most of their own prices, and it also runs the health system and caps what utilities may charge. A founder plans on the assumption that every price in her business is hers to set. What has she missed?

options.text: That private ownership is not allowed
options.rationale: It plainly is allowed.

options.text: That the country is a command economy
options.rationale: Most prices are privately set.

options.text: That utilities set their own prices
options.rationale: Those are the capped ones.

options.text: Private ownership inside public limits
options.rationale: Owning the business gives her the incentive and the control that comes with it still stops where the state has set a rule.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the ownership rights are real and the mixed system puts boundaries around them, so neither idea alone describes her position.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Property rights and incentives, Mixed economy characteristics. Without the ownership there is no control to overestimate. Without the public limits her assumption holds. Both are needed.

questions.question: A customer pays extra for groceries delivered to her door within one hour instead of driving to the store herself. Which type of value is she mainly paying for?

options.text: The utility of a wider selection of grocery brands to choose from
options.rationale: Selection isn't mentioned in the scenario and misattributes the value to variety instead of speed and access.

options.text: The utility of the groceries being a higher physical quality than store shelves
options.rationale: This wrongly assumes value comes from product quality, ignoring the convenience being described.

options.text: The utility of a lower total price compared to shopping in person
options.rationale: The scenario describes paying extra, not paying less, so this contradicts the given situation.

options.text: The utility of getting the groceries quickly and without leaving home
options.rationale: Correct: this describes time and possession utility, paying for speed and convenience rather than the product itself.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of a single concept, identifying which form of utility a customer is paying for in one straightforward situation.

questions.question: A factory's night shift creates loud noise that disturbs nearby homeowners who have no connection to the factory's business. What does this situation represent?

options.text: A form of economic utility the factory is providing to nearby residents
options.rationale: Utility describes value delivered to a customer, but the neighbors are not receiving any benefit here.

options.text: A trade-off the factory made between two internal spending priorities
options.rationale: Trade-offs involve the factory choosing between its own competing options, not an impact on outside neighbors.

options.text: A risk-reward decision about whether the factory will earn a profit
options.rationale: This scenario is about an outside cost to neighbors, not about weighing the factory's own potential profit against risk.

options.text: A spillover effect landing on people outside the factory's transactions
options.rationale: Correct: the noise is a side impact on third parties who are not buyers or sellers in the factory's deals.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of one concept, identifying an externality as the direct consequence of a single business action.

questions.question: A student club has $400 in its account and wants both a printed banner and a guest speaker. Each one costs $400. What does the situation illustrate?

options.text: Banners are cheaper than speakers
options.rationale: They cost the same here.

options.text: Picking one means giving up the other
options.rationale: Limited resources mean every choice carries the value of what was not chosen.

options.text: The budget was set at the wrong level
options.rationale: Any budget runs out somewhere.

options.text: Both can be had by fundraising more
options.rationale: Dodges the choice rather than naming it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the idea the situation shows.

questions.question: A student spends Saturday working a shift instead of at a review session. What is the opportunity cost of the shift?

options.text: The review session given up
options.rationale: Opportunity cost is the next-best thing the choice displaced.

options.text: The hours the shift ran
options.rationale: The input, not what it displaced.

options.text: The wages the shift paid
options.rationale: That is the benefit of the choice.

options.text: The travel cost to work
options.rationale: An out-of-pocket cost.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the forgone alternative.

questions.question: A kitchen adds cooks one at a time. The fourth adds 20 meals an hour, the fifth 12, the sixth 5. Total output still rises. What is this?

options.text: Each extra cook adding less
options.rationale: Diminishing returns is exactly this: output still grows while each added input contributes less than the one before.

options.text: Cooks of decreasing ability
options.rationale: The constraint is the kitchen, not the people.

options.text: A kitchen that is understaffed
options.rationale: The opposite is being shown.

options.text: Output falling with each cook
options.rationale: Total output is rising.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the pattern in the numbers.

questions.question: A cafe asks whether to stay open one more hour. What does marginal thinking compare?

options.text: That hour's extra takings and cost
options.rationale: The margin is the next unit only, so the whole day's figures are beside the point.

options.text: The whole day's profit and costs
options.rationale: Averages the decision away.

options.text: The rent paid for the month
options.rationale: Unchanged by the extra hour.

options.text: Last year's takings at that hour
options.rationale: History, not the next unit.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what the margin compares.

questions.question: A dry-cleaning app doesn't actually clean clothes any better than a corner shop, but it picks up dirty laundry from your door and returns it pressed within 24 hours. Which type of value is this app mainly selling?

options.text: Higher quality fabric care than any nearby competitor offers
options.rationale: The scenario explicitly says the cleaning itself is not better, so this contradicts the setup.

options.text: Time and possession utility from convenient pickup and fast turnaround
options.rationale: The value comes from not having to go to the shop and getting the item back quickly, which is time and possession utility, not a better core product.

options.text: Form utility from producing a physically superior cleaned garment
options.rationale: This assumes the product itself is upgraded, but the cleaning quality is described as no better than the corner shop.

options.text: A lower price than competitors for the identical cleaning service
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario mentions price at all, so this introduces an unsupported cost advantage.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (economic utility) applied to a new, specific business scenario requiring the student to identify which utility type explains the value, not just recall the definition.

questions.question: A print shop installs a new industrial fan system that vents strong chemical odors directly onto the sidewalk where a coffee shop's outdoor seating is located. The coffee shop isn't part of any deal with the print shop. What is this an example of?

options.text: A form of economic utility, since the print shop is creating value through its new equipment
options.rationale: This confuses value created for a customer with an unrelated cost imposed on a neighboring business.

options.text: A spillover effect, since the odor creates a cost for a nearby business outside the transaction
options.rationale: The coffee shop is a third party bearing a cost from a decision it wasn't part of, which is exactly what an externality describes.

options.text: A circular flow issue, since money is moving between the print shop and its customers
options.rationale: This describes normal buyer-seller exchange, not the side effect landing on someone outside that exchange.

options.text: A trade-off, since the print shop is choosing equipment over other spending
options.rationale: This mislabels the situation as a resource allocation choice rather than an outside impact on an uninvolved third party.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (externalities) applied to a new business situation requiring the student to recognize the third-party cost pattern, which is the mechanism, not just the definition.

questions.question: A three person print shop has everybody doing design, printing and packing in turn. Output per hour is low and the presses sit idle during every changeover. What should change?

options.text: Split the work by what each does best
options.rationale: Dividing the work removes the switching cost and lets each person get faster at one thing.

options.text: Add a fourth person doing everything
options.rationale: Adds cost and repeats the pattern.

options.text: Buy a faster printer for the shop
options.rationale: The press is already sitting idle.

options.text: Ask everyone to work a longer day
options.rationale: More hours at the same low rate.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: identify the productivity fix the setup calls for.

questions.question: A print shop's average cost per poster is $4. A customer wants 50 more on a run already set up, where paper and ink cost $1.20 each. What should guide the price floor?

options.text: The $4 average across all work
options.rationale: Loads sunk setup onto the extra units.

options.text: The total cost of the whole run
options.rationale: Includes costs already committed.

options.text: The price charged to the last client
options.rationale: A different job with a different setup.

options.text: The $1.20 the next poster costs
options.rationale: The setup is already paid for, so the extra run only has to beat what producing those 50 actually adds.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: price the next unit, not the average.

questions.question: An owner uses a shop unit she already owns, so she counts the premises as free. A neighbouring unit the same size rents for $2,000 a month. What is she missing?

options.text: The value the unit would sell for
options.rationale: A capital figure, not the monthly use.

options.text: The mortgage she still pays
options.rationale: A cash cost, not the forgone option.

options.text: The cost of maintaining the unit
options.rationale: Also a cash cost.

options.text: The rent she is not collecting
options.rationale: Owning it does not make it free; using it gives up the next-best use, which here has a market price attached.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: price an owned resource at its forgone use.

questions.question: A support team's first three agents cut response time sharply. The seventh and eighth barely move it, and the queue is now limited by one approval step. What should the manager conclude?

options.text: Response time cannot be improved
options.rationale: The approval step is unaddressed.

options.text: The team needs more agents still
options.rationale: Repeats what has stopped working.

options.text: The first three agents were wasted
options.rationale: They produced the sharp gain.

options.text: More agents is the wrong input now
options.rationale: Once added units of one input stop producing much, the gain is somewhere else, which here is the step actually holding the queue.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: read the falling increment as a signal to change input.

questions.question: A bakery has $10,000 and two uses for it: a delivery van projected to add $1,500 a month, or a storefront remodel expected to lift the foot traffic that already drives sales. Nobody has tested delivery demand. How should the owner reason?

options.text: Take the van, since its projection is the larger figure
options.rationale: Treats a projection as a certainty, the exact error the risk side of this warns about.

options.text: Weigh the untested projection against what is given up
options.rationale: One budget means the choice is also a refusal, and the van's number is a forecast carrying risk rather than a fact.

options.text: Take the remodel, since remodels rarely lose money
options.rationale: Right choice for a wrong reason, and it skips the comparison entirely.

options.text: Split the budget so both projects can start this spring
options.rationale: The we will do both answer that ignores the shared, limited budget.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: scarcity forces the either-or, risk weighting decides which side of it the uncertainty sits on.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Scarcity and Trade-offs, Profit Motive and Risk-Reward. Remove scarcity and option c is fine, since both can be funded. Remove the risk view and the larger projection simply wins, which is option b. Both are needed to make a the only defensible reasoning.

questions.question: A brewery can send 6am delivery trucks down a residential street at no extra cost, or use a back access road for about $6,000 a year. Sales are identical either way. What makes the back road defensible?

options.text: It raises the value customers place on the beer
options.rationale: Drinkers never see the delivery route; sales are stated as unchanged.

options.text: It buys down a risk the ledger does not show
options.rationale: The cost falls on neighbours, and neighbours turn into zoning fights and lawsuits, so the spend is insurance against a real exposure.

options.text: It removes the need for a zoning application
options.rationale: Invents a permitting requirement the case does not mention.

options.text: It lowers the fuel cost of each delivery run
options.rationale: The scenario says it costs more, not less.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the externality names a cost outside the ledger, risk weighting turns it into a number worth paying.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Spillover Effects and Externalities, Profit Motive and Risk-Reward. Without the externality the $6,000 buys nothing and the cheap route wins. Without the risk framing the neighbours' complaint is somebody else's problem rather than an exposure. Both are load bearing.

questions.question: A town's main factory plans layoffs to cut costs. A manager points out that roughly a third of the plant's output is bought by local households. What does the circular flow add to the decision?

options.text: Local buyers will switch to a national supplier
options.rationale: Possible, but it is a competition story rather than what the flow explains.

options.text: The layoffs will be reversed within two quarters
options.rationale: Asserts a timeline the case gives no basis for.

options.text: The plant should raise prices to cover the gap
options.rationale: Raising prices into a town with falling income compounds the problem.

options.text: The wages cut also cut the spending that returns
options.rationale: Money moves in a loop, so reducing household income in a town this concentrated reduces the demand the plant itself depends on.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts held together: the loop explains why the saving returns as lost demand, scarcity explains why the cut was on the table at all.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Circular Flow of Economic Activity, Scarcity and Trade-offs. Without the flow, a payroll cut is simply a cost saving. Without scarcity there is no pressure to cut and no trade-off to weigh. Remove either and the question stops being about the loop closing back on the firm.

questions.question: A consultant takes a small extra project because the fee comfortably beats the few hours of direct cost. Those hours come out of the one week she had set aside to pitch a retainer client worth ten times as much. What did the margin calculation miss?

options.text: The overhead that is spread across the whole year
options.rationale: Unchanged by this decision.

options.text: The direct cost of the extra hours
options.rationale: That was counted properly.

options.text: What those hours were already promised to
options.rationale: The marginal comparison was done correctly against cash cost and the scarce input had a far better alternative use that never entered it.

options.text: The fee the small project pays
options.rationale: Also counted, and it does beat the cost.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the marginal test is run correctly and omits the opportunity cost of the input it consumes, which is what reverses the answer.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Marginal thinking, Opportunity cost reasoning. Without the marginal framing there is no decision rule. Without the opportunity cost the rule gives the wrong answer. Both are needed.

questions.question: Each additional advert a shop buys brings fewer new customers than the last: the tenth brings 40, the eleventh 25, the twelfth 14. Each advert costs $300 and a customer is worth $18. Where should the shop stop?

options.text: At the first advert that brings less
options.rationale: Falling returns can still be profitable.

options.text: When total customers stop growing
options.rationale: Far past the profitable point.

options.text: When the budget has been spent
options.rationale: A constraint, not a decision rule.

options.text: Where the next advert stops paying
options.rationale: The falling increment is the pattern and the stopping rule is the unit where its extra benefit drops below its extra cost, here between the eleventh and twelfth.
