notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: diminishing returns describes the shape and marginal thinking supplies the stopping rule, and neither alone names where to stop.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Diminishing returns, Marginal thinking. Without the falling increments there is no reason ever to stop. Without the marginal rule falling returns look like a reason to stop immediately. Both are needed.

questions.question: A factory keeps adding staff to its busiest line, where each new hire now adds very little. The same people on an idle second line would each produce a full shift's output. The manager says the busy line is the priority. What is wrong?

options.text: Hires who are not productive enough
options.rationale: They are productive elsewhere.

options.text: A second line that should be closed
options.rationale: It is the better use.

options.text: Staff worth far more on the other line
options.rationale: The busy line has run into diminishing returns, which is precisely what makes the forgone use of each worker the deciding number.

options.text: A busy line that should be slowed
options.rationale: Nothing suggests reducing it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: diminishing returns on one line and the alternative use of the same worker have to be held together before the allocation is visible.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Diminishing returns, Opportunity cost reasoning. Without the falling returns the busy line is the right place. Without the idle line there is no better use. Both are needed.

questions.question: A government places a new tax on imported electronics. What is the most direct effect this has on businesses that import those electronics?

options.text: Their goods become exempt from later trade rules.
options.rationale: A tariff grants no exemption from anything.

options.text: Their cost of bringing in those goods goes up.
options.rationale: A tariff is a tax paid at the border by the importer, so it lands on the landed cost first.

options.text: Their domestic sales tax rate rises to match.
options.rationale: Sales tax is a separate instrument.

options.text: Their overseas supplier drops its price to absorb it.
options.rationale: A supplier may share the pain; nothing compels it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests the single, direct first-order consequence of one action (a tariff), requiring only recognition of what a tariff is.

questions.question: What is the main idea behind deciding to outsource a task based on comparative advantage?

options.text: Give it to whichever side gives up the least, not whoever is fastest.
options.rationale: Comparative advantage is about what each side forgoes, which is why the better producer can still be the wrong one to do the job.

options.text: Give it to whichever side has the most spare workers available.
options.rationale: Headcount is capacity, not advantage.

options.text: Give it to whichever side charges the lowest flat price for the work.
options.rationale: Price alone ignores what each side gives up to take it on.

options.text: Give it to whichever side is simply better at the task itself.
options.rationale: That is absolute advantage, the usual confusion.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept recognition of the core comparative advantage principle, requiring one reasoning step about opportunity cost.

questions.question: A furniture brand buys ninety percent of its components from a single overseas factory. A port strike there halts shipments for six weeks and the brand cannot build anything. What does that reveal?

options.text: That the brand should raise prices
options.rationale: Price does not restart production.

options.text: That ports are unreliable places
options.rationale: Blames the port rather than the design.

options.text: That the components were faulty
options.rationale: Quality is not the problem.

options.text: How much rides on one supplier
options.rationale: Concentrating supply in one place means any disruption there becomes a disruption to the whole business.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the risk the disruption exposed.

questions.question: A toy company imports plastic parts from overseas at $12 per unit. The government just imposed a new 30% tariff, pushing the cost to $15.60. A domestic supplier offers the same part for $14.50. What is the most sound response to this situation?

options.text: Wait several months to see if the tariff gets removed before making any sourcing changes
options.rationale: Treats the tariff as a temporary fixed blip rather than a real cost shift that could climb further, missing the urgency the card highlights.

options.text: Switch to the domestic supplier now, since it is cheaper than the tariffed import price
options.rationale: Recognizes the tariff flipped the cost comparison and acts on the new numbers, exactly the mechanism the card describes.

options.text: Keep buying overseas since that supplier was cheaper before the tariff was added
options.rationale: Ignores that the tariff has already changed the real cost comparison, clinging to outdated pricing.

options.text: Absorb the tariff cost fully and raise consumer prices by the full 30% immediately
options.rationale: Assumes the tariff must be passed straight to consumers instead of considering supplier switching as an alternative.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, tariffs, applied to a fresh sourcing decision requiring the student to use the mechanism of cost comparison rather than just define what a tariff is.

questions.question: A phone accessory company sources 90% of its charging cables from a single factory in Malaysia and has no backup supplier. A regional flood just shut that factory down for two months. Based on the risks of relying on one overseas source, what should the company have done beforehand?

options.text: Stopped importing and moved all production to domestic materials at once
options.rationale: An expensive overcorrection to a problem that needs a second source.

options.text: Negotiated a lower price with the same Malaysian factory to offset the risk
options.rationale: A discount does not keep the factory open.

options.text: Kept the single supplier, since imported materials carry this risk anyway
options.rationale: Spreading the sourcing is exactly what changes the risk.

options.text: Qualified a second supplier in another region at a somewhat higher unit cost
options.rationale: The premium is the price of not having the whole line stop when one region floods.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, supply chain dependence, applied to a new disruption scenario requiring the student to predict the appropriate risk mitigation, not just recall the definition.

questions.question: A bakery is excellent at both baking bread and decorating cakes, and is actually faster at decorating cakes than any local partner. But every hour spent decorating cakes is an hour not spent baking bread, which brings in much more revenue per hour. What does comparative advantage suggest the bakery should do?

options.text: Stop baking bread entirely since cake decorating is where it has proven speed
options.rationale: Reverses the correct specialization; ignores that bread is where the bakery's time is worth the most.

options.text: Outsource cake decorating to a partner and focus its own hours on baking bread
options.rationale: Reflects comparing opportunity cost rather than raw skill, the core of comparative advantage.

options.text: Decorate all its own cakes since it is faster at that task than any potential partner
options.rationale: Focuses on absolute advantage in speed while ignoring the higher opportunity cost of giving up bread baking time.

options.text: Split time evenly between bread and cakes to keep both skills sharp
options.rationale: Avoids specializing at all, missing the point that trading based on opportunity cost produces more total output.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, comparative advantage, applied to a fresh scenario where the student must reason through opportunity cost rather than just recall the term's definition.

questions.question: A cookware company gets 90% of its cast iron pans from one factory overseas, and its home country just imposed a new tariff on that country's metal goods. What is the most complete reason the company should act now rather than just eating the tariff cost?

options.text: One efficient supplier handles production, so the tariff is a cost to pass on.
options.rationale: Treats concentration as efficiency and the tariff as temporary.

options.text: The tariff will climb again soon, so waiting makes the eventual cost worse.
options.rationale: Speculates about the rate instead of reading the exposure.

options.text: Tariffs are a pricing matter, so the sourcing structure is a separate question.
options.rationale: The structure is what makes the tariff unavoidable.

options.text: Leaning on one overseas factory adds tariff cost to a chain with no backup.
options.rationale: The tariff is a cost and the single source is why it cannot be routed around, so the two compound rather than sit side by side.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding both tariff cost mechanics and supply chain dependence risk together; neither concept alone explains why urgency is warranted.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Global Supply Chain Dependence, Tariffs and Trade Barriers. Removing dependence leaves only 'tariff raises cost,' which doesn't explain the urgency of no backup option; removing tariffs leaves only 'diversify suppliers' with no cost trigger. Both are needed, question holds.

questions.question: A clothing company currently outsources fabric dyeing to an overseas partner because the partner's opportunity cost for dyeing is lower than the company's own. A new tariff on dyed fabric imports raises the landed cost above what it would cost the company to dye in-house. What should the company do?

options.text: Bring dyeing in-house, since the tariff has erased the advantage that justified it
options.rationale: Comparative advantage is a comparison of what each side gives up, and a tariff changes that arithmetic rather than sitting outside it.

options.text: Move to a domestic partner at once without comparing what either would cost
options.rationale: Right direction, reached without doing the comparison.

options.text: Keep outsourcing, since the partner remains the better place to do the work
options.rationale: Better at dyeing is not the test; the cost of the alternative is.

options.text: Ignore the tariff, since the advantage rests on skill and speed rather than taxes
options.rationale: Trade costs enter the comparison like any other cost.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires reasoning about how a tariff changes the underlying cost comparison that comparative advantage depends on; neither concept alone determines the right action.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Comparative Advantage, Tariffs and Trade Barriers. Removing tariffs leaves a static comparative advantage question with no reason to reconsider; removing comparative advantage leaves only 'tariff raised cost' with no framework for deciding in-house vs outsource. Both needed, question holds.

questions.question: An electronics retailer sources 100% of its circuit boards from a single manufacturer in one country. That country's currency suddenly strengthens sharply against the retailer's home currency. Why should the retailer be especially worried compared to a competitor who buys the same boards from three manufacturers in three different countries?

options.text: A single-source buyer tends to pick the country with the weaker currency
options.rationale: Invents a pattern, and currencies move either way.

options.text: Exchange rates reach single-source buyers more than diversified ones do
options.rationale: States the conclusion without the mechanism that produces it.

options.text: The retailer cannot shift volume elsewhere, so the full currency hit lands on it
options.rationale: A diversified buyer can move orders toward the cheaper currency; one supplier means the whole move is absorbed.

options.text: The competitor's spread of suppliers leaves it untouched by currency moves
options.rationale: It is cushioned rather than immune.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires connecting a currency trade force to the specific risk amplification created by single-source dependence, and contrasting it against a diversified alternative; no single concept explains the comparative risk.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Global and Trade Forces, Global Supply Chain Dependence. Removing the currency shift leaves no actual event to react to; removing supply chain dependence removes the reason this retailer is worse off than the diversified competitor. Both needed, question holds.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of antitrust enforcement by the government?

options.text: To stop companies from harming competition through price fixing or blocking rivals
options.rationale: Matches the card's definition that antitrust addresses harm to competition and consumers.

options.text: To prevent any single company from becoming the largest firm in its industry
options.rationale: Misconception that antitrust targets size alone rather than harm to competition.

options.text: To set the maximum price a company can charge for any product
options.rationale: Confuses antitrust with price controls, which is a different government tool.

options.text: To guarantee that every business earns roughly equal profits each year
options.rationale: Antitrust does not equalize profits, it addresses anti-competitive conduct.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of a single concept's definition with one reasoning step, no application to a novel scenario required.

questions.question: Why do private businesses typically fail to supply true public goods on their own?

options.text: Because non-payers can still benefit, so there's no profit incentive to provide it
options.rationale: Matches the card's free-rider explanation for why private markets under-supply public goods.

options.text: Because people who don't pay can still be excluded from using the good
options.rationale: Reverses the actual trait; public goods are non-excludable, so this is backwards.

options.text: Because government regulations forbid private companies from building infrastructure
options.rationale: Invents a regulatory ban that isn't part of the concept at all.

options.text: Because public goods always cost more than any private company can afford
options.rationale: Cost size is not the defining reason; the issue is non-excludability, not affordability.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, direct recall of the mechanism behind under-provision, one logical step.

questions.question: Which situation best reflects the common mistake businesses make with compliance costs?

options.text: A company budgets once for a permit fee and assumes it never needs renewal or review again
options.rationale: Matches the card's warning that compliance costs recur through renewals, audits, and rule changes.

options.text: A company hires an extra worker to get certified before opening to avoid a shutdown risk
options.rationale: This shows planning ahead for compliance, the opposite of the mistake.

options.text: A company raises its prices after estimating higher inspection fees for the coming year
options.rationale: This is proactive cost planning, not the mistake described on the card.

options.text: A company tracks quarterly inspection costs as part of its annual budget
options.rationale: This reflects treating compliance as an ongoing cost, which is the correct approach, not the mistake.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, tests recognition of the described common mistake through one reasoning step distinguishing it from proper practice.

questions.question: A landscaping company is deciding between two equipment leases. Lease A shows a higher pre-tax profit than Lease B, but Lease A's payments don't qualify for a tax deduction while Lease B's payments do. Applying the idea of deciding based on after-tax results, what should the owner do before choosing?

options.text: Recalculate both leases after tax, then decide between them
options.rationale: The decision rests on what the company keeps, and only one of these leases converts its pre-tax lead into an after-tax one.

options.text: Choose Lease B, since a deduction makes an option cheaper overall
options.rationale: A deduction helps and does not automatically close a pre-tax gap.

options.text: Ignore the tax difference, since both leases are business equipment
options.rationale: Both are equipment and only one payment qualifies.

options.text: Pick Lease A, since it already shows the higher profit on paper
options.rationale: Pre-tax profit is the figure the tax treatment changes.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied to a novel lease comparison, requiring the student to apply after-tax reasoning rather than recall its definition.

questions.question: A food startup's opening budget lists ingredients, rent, equipment and wages. It carries no line for inspections, the food licence or the labelling review. What is the flaw?

options.text: Wages counted twice in the figures
options.rationale: Invents a bookkeeping error.

options.text: Rent that is too high for a startup
options.rationale: No rent figure is given.

options.text: Ingredients priced above the market
options.rationale: Nothing suggests mispricing.

options.text: Compliance costs left out of the plan
options.rationale: Meeting the rules takes real money and real time, and a budget that omits it understates what opening actually costs.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: spot the missing cost category.

questions.question: A town's street lighting benefits everyone who walks the streets at night, including those who contribute nothing towards it. Why does government usually fund it?

options.text: Towns prefer to own the poles
options.rationale: Ownership preference is not the reason.

options.text: Private firms cannot install lights
options.rationale: They can install them perfectly well.

options.text: Lighting costs almost nothing
options.rationale: It is a substantial expense.

options.text: Nobody would pay for it alone
options.rationale: When the benefit cannot be withheld from non-payers, private buyers under-supply it and the funding has to be collective.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: explain the under-supply problem in a concrete case.

questions.question: A cleaning company owner compares hiring an employee versus a contractor for extra jobs. He counts the payroll tax savings of using a contractor but forgets that his city requires all cleaning contractors to carry a separate business license and pass an annual inspection, adding recurring fees either way. What is the real flaw in his comparison?

options.text: He failed to check whether the contractor arrangement would trigger antitrust scrutiny from regulators
options.rationale: Antitrust concerns market power and competition harm, not licensing or classification of a single small hire.

options.text: He assumed the government would subsidize the license fee as a public good for local businesses
options.rationale: Business licensing fees are a private compliance cost paid by the firm, not a non-excludable public good funded collectively.

options.text: He ignored an ongoing compliance cost that applies regardless of which option he tax-optimizes around
options.rationale: Correct: the license and inspection fees are a recurring compliance cost that hits both options, so the tax comparison alone is incomplete.

options.text: He should have based the decision purely on pre-tax wages since compliance fees never affect a hiring choice
options.rationale: Wrong direction: this dismisses both tax and compliance effects, which contradicts the core lesson of planning around after-tax and after-compliance reality.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding both the after-tax reasoning from taxation and the recurring nature of compliance costs at once; neither concept alone explains the flaw in his math.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Taxation and Business Decisions, Regulation and Compliance Costs. Deleting taxation leaves no reason he compared employee vs contractor at all. Deleting compliance costs removes the actual gap in his reasoning, leaving only a generic tax question. Both are needed, so this passes the break test.

questions.question: A city raises its minimum wage and, in the same year, changes its business tax structure so payroll taxes rise for firms with more than five employees. A restaurant owner only recalculates her menu prices based on the wage increase. What is she missing in her planning?

options.text: She should work from the tax change, since a wage floor rarely moves small-business pricing
options.rationale: Takes one of the two changes and drops the other, which is the mirror of her actual error.

options.text: She should set the wage rise aside, since tipped restaurant staff sit outside it
options.rationale: Tip credit rules vary and do not remove the wage change from her cost base.

options.text: She should treat both changes as one-off costs that will not recur next year
options.rationale: Both are structural changes to what staff cost her from here on.

options.text: She adjusted for the wage rise and left out the payroll tax that rose with it
options.rationale: Two changes landed in the same year and she priced for one, so her margin is short by exactly the tax she never counted.

notes.difficulty_justification: The student must recognize that a government policy change (wage law) and a tax structure change interact and compound, rather than treating either one in isolation, which requires combining both concepts to spot the gap.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Government's Role in the Economy, Taxation and Business Decisions. Deleting the government policy angle leaves a plain tax-only question. Deleting the taxation angle leaves only the wage cost question already modeled in the card's own connect example. Only combining both produces the compounding effect the question hinges on, so it passes the break test.
review_flags: The Government's Role card and Taxation card overlap conceptually since taxes are one channel of government's role; kept them distinct by making the wage law the government's role trigger and the payroll tax the separate taxation mechanism.

questions.question: Two firms that together hold eighty percent of a regional market agree privately to divide it by territory, so neither bids in the other's area. Both hold every licence and file every return correctly. What is the position?

options.text: Fine, as no prices were ever discussed
options.rationale: Dividing territory needs no price talk.

options.text: A licensing breach the regulator will act on
options.rationale: The licences are in order.

options.text: Compliant on rules, exposed on antitrust
options.rationale: Government shapes business through more than one instrument, and satisfying the licensing arm says nothing about the competition arm.

options.text: Lawful, since each holds its own area
options.rationale: Carving up a market is the classic case.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the firms are measured against two different arms of government and pass one while failing the other.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Government's role in the economy, Antitrust enforcement. Without the clean compliance record this is a simple lawbreaker. Without the market division the compliance settles it. Both are needed.

questions.question: What does GDP measure for a country?

options.text: The total amount of money the government spends yearly
options.rationale: Confuses GDP with government spending, which is only one part of the economy.

options.text: The interest rate set by the central bank
options.rationale: Confuses GDP with a monetary policy tool, not a production measure.

options.text: The total value of goods and services produced in a given time
options.rationale: This matches the definition of GDP as the total output value over a period.

options.text: The average income earned by all households
options.rationale: Confuses GDP with average household income, which GDP does not directly measure.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of a single concept's definition with no applied reasoning required.

questions.question: If prices rise faster than a worker's wage increase, what happens to that worker's purchasing power?

options.text: It depends only on how much the worker saves
options.rationale: Introduces an unrelated factor not tied to the direct relationship between prices and wages described.

options.text: It rises because nominal pay went up
options.rationale: Confuses nominal wage increase with real purchasing power, missing the inflation adjustment.

options.text: It stays exactly the same as before
options.rationale: Ignores that unequal rates of change mean real buying power shifts, not stays flat.

options.text: It falls because the wage buys less than before
options.rationale: Matches the card's core point that purchasing power drops when inflation outpaces wage growth.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, tests the first-order consequence of prices outpacing wages, one reasoning step.

questions.question: Local unemployment is rising, household spending is falling and three shops on the same street have closed. A retailer is planning a new store. What should she do?

options.text: Ignore it, as cycles always turn
options.rationale: True eventually and useless now.

options.text: Weigh the plan against the downturn
options.rationale: Reading the current conditions and letting them shape the decision is the whole point of watching the cycle.

options.text: Open two stores instead of one
options.rationale: Doubles the exposure.

options.text: Raise prices to protect the margin
options.rationale: Raises prices into falling spending.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: let the conditions inform the decision.

questions.question: A central bank raises interest rates sharply. What is the most direct effect on businesses?

options.text: Exports become more costly
options.rationale: A later, indirect currency effect.

options.text: Wages rise across the board
options.rationale: Not a direct effect of the rate.

options.text: Taxes increase on profits
options.rationale: Taxation is fiscal, not monetary.

options.text: Borrowing costs more to do
options.rationale: Rate changes work through the price of credit before anything else.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the first link in the chain.

questions.question: Factory jobs disappear permanently because the work is now automated, and those workers lack the skills the new jobs need. What kind of unemployment is this?

options.text: A downturn in overall demand
options.rationale: Cyclical, and the jobs would return.

options.text: A short dip between two jobs
options.rationale: That is frictional and brief.

options.text: A mismatch of skills to jobs
options.rationale: When the jobs themselves have changed shape, the gap is structural rather than a matter of the cycle.

options.text: A seasonal drop in the work
options.rationale: Seasonal work comes back.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: classify the unemployment.

questions.question: A central bank cuts rates to encourage activity. What chain is it relying on?

options.text: Higher taxes, then more revenue
options.rationale: That is fiscal policy.

options.text: Cheaper credit, then more spending
options.rationale: Lower rates make borrowing cheaper, which is meant to lift borrowing, spending and in turn output.

options.text: Fewer imports, then more output
options.rationale: Trade policy, not monetary.

options.text: Lower wages, then more hiring
options.rationale: Wages are not the instrument.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: trace the intended mechanism.

questions.question: A print shop owner wants to add a rush-order service. She calculates it will use $12 of extra ink and paper per order, and plans to charge $20 to feel like she's making a profit. She hasn't accounted for the fact that rush orders pull her one employee off regular print jobs for 45 minutes each time. What should she do before setting the final price?

options.text: Add the value of the employee's lost production time into the price before committing to $20
options.rationale: Correctly applies the concept: labor hours and lost productivity are real costs even when no extra cash leaves the register.

options.text: Lower the price to $15 to attract more rush customers and make up the difference in volume
options.rationale: Cuts price further without addressing the unaccounted labor cost, worsening the margin problem.

options.text: Charge exactly $20 since that already covers the materials with room to spare
options.rationale: Ignores that materials are only part of the real cost; labor time pulled from other work is uncounted.

options.text: Keep the $20 price since ink and paper are the only real costs of the rush service
options.rationale: Treats material cost as the whole picture, the exact mistake of ignoring labor and lost productivity.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept (Cost of Doing Business) applied to a new scenario requiring the student to identify an uncounted labor/productivity cost, not just define the term.

questions.question: A landscaping company gave every employee a 2% raise this year, and prices for gas, fertilizer, and equipment rose 5% over the same period. The owner tells his crew their pay went up, so they're better off. What is the flaw in his reasoning?

options.text: The raise doesn't matter because wages and prices always move together over time
options.rationale: Assumes wages automatically track inflation, which the scenario shows is false here.

options.text: The raise is meaningless unless the company also raises its own prices by the same percentage
options.rationale: Confuses the company's pricing decisions with the separate question of employee purchasing power.

options.text: There's no flaw, since a 2% raise is still more money than the crew had before
options.rationale: Focuses only on the nominal increase, missing that inflation eroded real value.

options.text: The crew's real purchasing power actually fell since their pay grew slower than prices did
options.rationale: Correctly applies the concept: a 2% raise against 5% inflation means real buying power dropped, even though nominal pay rose.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept applied to a fresh wage/inflation scenario, requiring the student to compare nominal versus real change rather than recite the definition.

questions.question: A boutique gym owner is deciding whether to take out a loan to open a second location. She notices the central bank just raised interest rates sharply and unemployment has been ticking up for three straight months. What is the most sound move given these signals?

options.text: Delay the loan-funded expansion and consider a lower-cost option that doesn't rely on expensive new debt
options.rationale: Correctly reads both signals together, rising rates make borrowing costlier and rising unemployment signals weaker consumer spending, pointing toward a cautious, cash-conscious move.

options.text: Proceed with the loan-funded expansion right away, since more locations always mean more revenue
options.rationale: Ignores the specific interest rate and unemployment signals entirely, treating expansion as risk-free.

options.text: Take the loan now to lock in current rates before they rise even further next quarter
options.rationale: Misreads the signal, rates are already described as having risen sharply, so the urgency logic doesn't fit; also ignores the unemployment warning.

options.text: Ignore the rate and unemployment data since gym memberships are unaffected by economic swings
options.rationale: Assumes gyms are recession-proof with no support from the scenario, dismissing relevant signals outright.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, applied by interpreting two specific indicators (interest rates, unemployment) together to shape a single business decision, rather than defining what an indicator is.

questions.question: A resort town's unemployment runs at 2 percent in July and 14 percent in January, year after year. What should a policymaker conclude?

options.text: The town is in a lasting recession
options.rationale: It recovers every July.

options.text: The pattern is seasonal, not a slump
options.rationale: Naming the type is what decides the response, and work that reliably returns each summer calls for something different from a downturn.

options.text: The figure must be measured wrongly
options.rationale: The swing is real and expected.

options.text: Workers there lack the right skills
options.rationale: They work each summer.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: classify from the pattern.

questions.question: A developer's whole model depends on cheap construction loans. The central bank signals several rate rises over the coming year. What should the developer do?

options.text: Raise the sale price of each home
options.rationale: Assumes buyers absorb it.

options.text: Re-test the model at higher rates
options.rationale: Policy moves through the cost of credit, and a model built on cheap borrowing has to be checked against what it will actually cost.

options.text: Wait for the rises to be confirmed
options.rationale: The signal is the warning.

options.text: Borrow far more before they rise
options.rationale: Doubles down before testing.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: act on a policy signal.

questions.question: A region's unemployment falls to 3 percent and a manufacturer cannot fill shifts at its usual wage. What does the labour market tell it?

options.text: The unemployment figure is wrong
options.rationale: The difficulty confirms it.

options.text: It must compete harder for workers
options.rationale: A tight market shifts the balance toward workers, so the usual wage no longer clears the vacancies.

options.text: Applicants are simply unwilling
options.rationale: Blames people for a market condition.

options.text: It should cut its wage to save
options.rationale: Moves the wrong way in a tight market.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: read a tight labour market from the firm's side.

questions.question: A government announces a large road building programme funded by borrowing. A construction supplier asks what it means for him. What is the direct effect?

options.text: Lower interest rates on his loans
options.rationale: That is monetary policy.

options.text: More public spending, more demand
options.rationale: Fiscal policy works through what the government taxes and spends, and a building programme puts demand straight into his market.

options.text: A stronger currency for imports
options.rationale: Indirect at best.

options.text: Fewer regulations on his industry
options.rationale: Regulation is a separate lever.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: trace fiscal policy to a specific business.

questions.question: A bakery owner sees interest rates jump from 4% to 8% and is considering taking out a loan to buy a new commercial oven that would speed up production. Her current oven works but is slower, requiring more staff overtime hours. What is the most sound way to weigh this decision?

options.text: Take the loan now, since a faster oven pays for itself in any conditions.
options.rationale: Assumes the return without checking it against the new cost of money.

options.text: Compare the extra interest at 8% against the overtime the old oven costs her.
options.rationale: A rate rise changes the hurdle rather than closing the question, and the overtime bill is what the loan is being measured against.

options.text: Skip the loan while rates are high and carry on paying the overtime hours.
options.rationale: Treats the rate as decisive without pricing what staying put costs.

options.text: Set the oven's sticker price against her savings, since rates affect borrowers.
options.rationale: She would be a borrower, which is the point she has missed.

notes.difficulty_justification: The question forces weighing a borrowing-cost signal against a real labor cost figure at the same time; neither the indicator reading nor the cost-of-business framing alone determines the right call.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Reading Economic Indicators, Cost of Doing Business. Deleting the interest rate signal removes any reason financing cost matters, turning it into a plain cost calculation. Deleting the labor cost concept removes the other side of the comparison, turning it into a plain 'rates are high, don't borrow' question. Both must stay for the trade-off to exist.

questions.question: A cafe holds its menu prices flat for three years as a gesture to regulars. Over the same period its ingredient and wage costs rose about eighteen percent. What has actually happened?

options.text: Costs that cannot have risen at all
options.rationale: The case states they did.

options.text: A gesture that cost the cafe nothing
options.rationale: It cost eighteen percent of input inflation.

options.text: A real price rise for the customer
options.rationale: Customers pay the same nominal price.

options.text: A quiet margin cut, not a price hold
options.rationale: The nominal price is unchanged and the real cost of producing each item is not, so the cafe absorbed the whole rise.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: a flat price and rising input costs have to be read together to see where the inflation actually landed.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Inflation and purchasing power, Cost of doing business. Without the cost rise the flat price is simply a flat price. Without the price hold the cafe passes it on. Both are needed.

questions.question: National GDP growth is positive. In the same region, unemployment has risen four quarters running and retail spending is flat. A manager cites the GDP figure as grounds for hiring six staff. What is the flaw?

options.text: One indicator read without the others
options.rationale: Indicators describe conditions only when read together, and two of the three here point the other way.

options.text: GDP measured at the wrong geography
options.rationale: National GDP is a real figure; it just is not the local one.

options.text: Hiring planned before the quarter closed
options.rationale: Timing is not what makes the argument weak.

options.text: Unemployment lagging behind the growth
options.rationale: A real effect, and four quarters is not a lag.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: reading an indicator correctly is only useful if it is set against the wider conditions it is supposed to describe.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Reading economic indicators, Economic conditions and cycles. Without the GDP figure there is no argument to fault. Without the contrary local conditions the figure supports hiring. Both are needed.

questions.question: A central bank cuts rates hard to bring unemployment down. A year later borrowing and investment have risen and unemployment has barely moved, because the jobless lack the skills the new roles require. What does this show?

options.text: A rate cut that was far too small
options.rationale: Borrowing and investment responded.

options.text: Unemployment that will fix itself
options.rationale: A skills gap does not close alone.

options.text: A tool aimed at the wrong kind of gap
options.rationale: Rate cuts work on demand, and a shortfall caused by a skills mismatch is not a demand problem, so the policy can succeed on its own terms and still miss.

options.text: Monetary policy that never works
options.rationale: It worked on what it reaches.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the policy transmission worked and the type of unemployment determines whether that transmission could ever have helped.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Monetary policy effects, Unemployment and the labor market. Without the rate cut there is no policy to judge. Without the type of unemployment the failure looks like weak transmission. Both are needed.

questions.question: A central bank raises rates to slow rising prices, knowing it will also slow hiring and output. A commentator calls this a policy failure. What is the better reading?

options.text: A tool that affects only prices
options.rationale: It plainly reaches output too.

options.text: A choice with no downside at all
options.rationale: The downside is explicit.

options.text: A cost accepted to buy something else
options.rationale: The slowdown is not a side effect that was missed; it is the price of the thing being bought, which is what makes it a trade-off rather than a failure.

options.text: A failure the bank did not foresee
options.rationale: It is stated as known in advance.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the policy mechanism explains what happens and the trade-off framing explains why it is not a mistake.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Monetary policy effects, Scarcity and trade-offs. Without the mechanism the slowdown is unexplained. Without the trade-off it reads as an error. Both are needed.

questions.question: A government can fund retraining for displaced manufacturing workers or short-term benefit top-ups, not both. The displaced jobs are gone for good. What does the trade-off argue?

options.text: Top-ups, which reach displaced people immediately
options.rationale: Faster relief for a gap it cannot close.

options.text: Both, since each serves a real need
options.rationale: The constraint rules that out.

options.text: Retraining, because the jobs are not returning
options.rationale: The type of unemployment decides which use of the limited money actually addresses it, and a permanent skills gap is not bridged by a temporary top-up.

options.text: Neither, as the market will correct
options.rationale: A structural gap does not self-correct.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the scarcity forces a single choice and the type of unemployment is what decides which choice fits.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Scarcity and trade-offs, Unemployment and the labor market. Without the constraint both could be funded. Without the type of unemployment either looks equally reasonable. Both are needed.

questions.question: What does market equilibrium describe in a market?

options.text: The price customers consider most fair or affordable
options.rationale: The card warns against treating equilibrium as the 'fairest' price rather than just where quantities match.

options.text: The lowest price a business can charge and still cover its costs
options.rationale: This describes a cost floor, not the point where supply and demand quantities match.

options.text: The price that gives sellers the highest possible profit margin
options.rationale: Equilibrium is about matching quantities, not maximizing seller profit.

options.text: The price where the amount buyers want matches the amount sellers offer
options.rationale: This matches the definition of equilibrium as the point where quantity demanded and quantity supplied line up.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests direct recall of a single concept's definition with one reasoning step, no application to a novel scenario.

questions.question: Which pair of products is best described as complements?

options.text: Two rival coffee shops located across the street from each other
options.rationale: These are substitutes since customers pick one cafe instead of the other.

options.text: A streaming subscription and a movie theater ticket for the same new release
options.rationale: These act as substitutes since a customer might choose one form of entertainment over the other.

options.text: Two competing brands of bottled water sold at the same store
options.rationale: These are substitutes since customers choose one over the other, not complements.

options.text: A movie ticket and a bucket of popcorn bought during the same visit
options.rationale: The card describes tickets and popcorn as complements since they are typically bought together.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires recognizing the definition of one concept, complements, applied to a straightforward example, one reasoning step.

questions.question: A heatwave arrives and a hardware store's stock of electric fans has not changed. Customers are queuing for them. What happens to the price?

options.text: It rises, as demand outruns supply
options.rationale: More buyers chasing the same quantity pushes the price up.

options.text: It stays put, because supply is fixed
options.rationale: Fixed supply is why it moves.

options.text: It falls, since stock stays the same
options.rationale: Unchanged supply does not lower a price.

options.text: It falls, as buyers grow more careful
options.rationale: Buyers are queuing, not hesitating.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: read the price effect of a demand shift.

questions.question: A cinema raises ticket prices 15 percent. Streaming at home is the cheap alternative, and popcorn and soda are bought alongside tickets. What should it expect?

options.text: More tickets, since higher prices signal quality
options.rationale: A positioning idea that does not survive an easy substitute at home.

options.text: Fewer tickets, and concession sales falling with them
options.rationale: The substitute pulls ticket buyers away, and the complements only sell when a ticket does, so the loss lands twice.

options.text: No change, since moviegoing is a fixed habit
options.rationale: Assumes inelastic demand in a market with an obvious alternative.

options.text: Fewer tickets, but concession sales holding steady
options.rationale: Gets the substitute right and forgets that concessions ride on attendance.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: trace a price move through both linked goods in a new setting.

questions.question: A food truck preps 70 tacos a day. At $9 it sells 40 of them; at $7 it sells about 70. What does the $7 point represent?

options.text: The lowest price the truck can charge and survive
options.rationale: That would be a break-even question, which needs cost data not given here.

options.text: The price that earns the most profit per taco sold
options.rationale: Per unit profit is highest at $9; equilibrium is about quantities matching, not margin.

options.text: The fairest price for the neighborhood it serves
options.rationale: The fairness reading is the trap: equilibrium carries no claim about what is fair.

options.text: Where the quantity sold matches the quantity prepped
options.rationale: Equilibrium is simply where the amount demanded and the amount supplied meet, leaving no surplus.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: identify equilibrium from a demand and supply pair in a fresh case.

questions.question: A cafe has three rivals within one block selling ordinary drip coffee, while its seasonal latte has no local equal. It needs more revenue this quarter. Where should the larger increase go?

options.text: On the drip coffee, which sells the most cups
options.rationale: Volume is exactly what is at risk: three rivals a block away make drip the switchable item.

options.text: On the latte, where switching is hardest
options.rationale: Sensitivity differs by item, and the drink with no nearby substitute absorbs a rise with the least lost volume.

options.text: Evenly across the menu, to look consistent
options.rationale: Treating every item as equally sensitive is the error the card names.

options.text: On food items, leaving all drinks untouched
options.rationale: Avoids the question rather than answering where sensitivity is lowest.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: compare sensitivity across two items and place the increase.

questions.question: At $40 a ticket, a venue sells out in nine minutes and a resale market springs up at $120. What does that tell you about the price?

options.text: It shows a surplus of seats on sale
options.rationale: The opposite condition.

options.text: It sits above where buyers will pay
options.rationale: That would leave seats unsold.

options.text: It is exactly at the clearing level
options.rationale: Equilibrium leaves no resale gap.

options.text: It sits below where the market clears
options.rationale: Demand far exceeding supply at the asking price is a shortage, and the resale price shows where buyers actually value it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: read a shortage from market behaviour.

questions.question: A furniture store manager wants to clear out an overstocked sofa line and rewards sales reps with a flat $50 bonus per sofa sold, regardless of price. Customers for this sofa line are highly price sensitive because several nearby stores sell nearly identical sofas. What is the most likely result?

options.text: Customer behavior will stay the same no matter what reps do, since price sensitivity only matters for company-wide pricing decisions.
options.rationale: Misunderstands price sensitivity as a policy-only concept rather than something that shapes individual customer reactions to any price a rep offers.

options.text: Reps will slash prices to close deals quickly, since the bonus rewards volume and price-sensitive customers respond strongly to discounts.
options.rationale: Correctly combines the incentive structure (rewarding units, not margin) with high price sensitivity (customers who will buy readily if discounted), predicting reps chase volume through price cuts.

options.text: Reps will raise prices to boost their bonus per sale, since customers will pay whatever is asked.
options.rationale: Contradicts the stated high price sensitivity; these customers have nearby substitutes and would walk rather than pay more.

options.text: Reps will hold prices steady, since the flat bonus removes any reason to change pricing behavior.
options.rationale: Ignores that a flat per-unit bonus still creates pressure to close sales fast, which interacts with how price-sensitive these customers are.

notes.difficulty_justification: Needs both the incentive's effect on rep behavior and the customer base's price sensitivity to predict the outcome; the bonus structure alone doesn't reveal how customers will respond, and price sensitivity alone doesn't reveal what reps will do.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Incentives and Behavior, Price Sensitivity. Delete incentives: no reason to expect reps to change pricing at all, just a note about customer sensitivity. Delete price sensitivity: no reason discounting would actually work to move volume. Both required to reach the answer.

questions.question: A city caps the price of a popular food truck's tacos below the level where the truck's daily prep quantity would match the number of customers wanting them. What happens as a direct result of the cap?

options.text: The market reaches a new equilibrium automatically, since price and quantity always adjust to match.
options.rationale: Misapplies equilibrium as something that happens regardless of constraints; a price cap prevents the price from moving to the equilibrium point.

options.text: A shortage forms, since more customers want tacos at the capped price than the truck is prepping to sell.
options.rationale: Correctly applies supply and demand under a price forced below equilibrium: quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage.

options.text: Nothing changes, since the truck can simply prep the same quantity as before at the lower price.
options.rationale: Ignores that lower price increases customer demand while supply behavior may not adjust, breaking the balance the cards describe as equilibrium.

options.text: A surplus forms, since the lower price discourages customers from wanting the tacos at all.
options.rationale: Reverses the basic demand relationship; lower prices increase quantity demanded, they don't reduce it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires combining what a price cap does to the supply-demand balance with the definition of equilibrium as the matching point; recognizing why a price below equilibrium specifically produces a shortage rather than a surplus needs both concepts together.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Market Equilibrium, Supply and Demand. Delete equilibrium: question becomes just 'what happens when price is low', losing the specific reasoning about why capping below the matching point creates imbalance. Delete supply and demand: no mechanism explains why quantity demanded and supplied diverge. Both necessary.

questions.question: A cinema raises ticket prices twenty percent in the same month that studios cut the gap before streaming release to two weeks. Ticket sales fall thirty five percent. What explains the size of the fall?

options.text: The price rise was too small to matter
options.rationale: Twenty percent moved sales sharply.

options.text: A close substitute made demand elastic
options.rationale: How far quantity moves with price depends on what else the buyer can switch to, and a two week wait is now a real alternative.

options.text: Cinema demand is always inelastic
options.rationale: The case shows the opposite.

options.text: Streaming is a complement to cinema
options.rationale: Here it competes rather than pairs.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: elasticity is not a fixed property of the product, it is set by what substitutes are available at that moment.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Elasticity of demand, Substitute and complement goods. Without the price rise nothing tests demand. Without the substitute the same rise costs far fewer sales. Both are needed.

questions.question: What is a key difference between paying with credit and paying with cash on hand?

options.text: Credit lets a buyer get goods now without ever owing more than the sticker price
options.rationale: Ignores that interest adds cost beyond the sticker price, the core misconception the card warns about.

options.text: Credit and cash always cost the same as long as the total is paid eventually
options.rationale: Denies that timing and interest change the real cost, which the card says matters.

options.text: Credit usually adds interest cost over time that cash payment does not
options.rationale: Matches the card's core point: borrowed money comes with a price tag and a clock attached.

options.text: Credit removes the need to ever repay the borrowed amount
options.rationale: Confuses credit with a gift; repayment is still required plus interest.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests direct recognition of one concept, the definition-level fact that credit carries interest cost cash does not, requiring one reasoning step.

questions.question: Why can a company's profit on an overseas deal change even if nothing else about the deal changes?

options.text: Because inflation runs faster abroad than it does at home
options.rationale: Inflation differs by country and is not what moves a single deal's profit.

options.text: Because business loan rates are reset every quarter by lenders
options.rationale: Borrowing cost is a separate line from the deal's conversion.

options.text: Because exchange rates shift the real cost or value of the deal
options.rationale: The same price in a foreign currency converts to a different sum at home once the rate moves.

options.text: Because international shipping is priced on each order placed
options.rationale: Freight is a cost, and nothing about the deal changed.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, recognition-level: identifying that exchange rate movement alone can change deal value, one reasoning step from the definition.

questions.question: A supplier offers a business either $10,000 today or the same $10,000 in two years, with no interest added. Which is worth more?

options.text: The sum now, which can be used
options.rationale: Money in hand can be invested or spent, so the same figure later is worth less today.

options.text: The later sum, if prices fall
options.rationale: Speculative and not the general rule.

options.text: They are worth exactly the same
options.rationale: Ignores what two years of use is worth.

options.text: The later sum, which is safer
options.rationale: Waiting adds risk rather than removing it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: compare two sums at different points in time.

questions.question: A US toy company pays a Japanese factory in yen. If the dollar strengthens against the yen before the next invoice is due, what happens to the company's cost in dollar terms?

options.text: The dollar cost rises, since the yen figure on the invoice goes up with it.
options.rationale: The yen amount is fixed; what changes is the dollars needed to buy it.

options.text: The dollar cost holds, since the rate matters to traders rather than buyers.
options.rationale: Anyone paying in another currency is exposed to the rate.

options.text: The dollar cost rises, since a strong dollar pushes import prices upward.
options.rationale: Reverses the direction a strong home currency works in.

options.text: The dollar cost drops, since each dollar now buys more yen than before.
options.rationale: The invoice is denominated in yen, so a stronger dollar buys that same yen total for fewer dollars.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (exchange rate movement changing real cost) applied to a fresh cross-border payment scenario, requiring the student to predict a direction of effect rather than recall a definition.

questions.question: A landscaping company's revenue grew from $150,000 to $180,000 over five years, a 20% increase, but prices in the economy rose about 18% over that same span. What should the owner conclude about the business's real growth?

options.text: Real growth cannot be judged unless the company's costs are also known.
options.rationale: Sounds cautious but sidesteps the actual tool the concept provides for comparing revenue across years.

options.text: Real growth is close to 20%, since the revenue figures already reflect true performance.
options.rationale: Ignores inflation entirely, treating the raw percentage change as if it were real growth.

options.text: Real growth is only about 2%, since most of the revenue increase just tracked rising prices.
options.rationale: Correctly separates the small real gain from the inflation-driven portion of the raw increase.

options.text: Real growth is negative, since any inflation automatically erases business gains.
options.rationale: Overcorrects by assuming inflation always outweighs nominal growth, which isn't the case here.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (adjusting nominal change for inflation) applied to a new company's numbers, requiring the student to compute the implication rather than just recall the definition.

questions.question: A shop can buy a $12,000 van outright with cash it already holds, or on credit at nine percent over three years while keeping that cash as a buffer. What does the decision turn on?

options.text: What the cash buffer is worth to it
options.rationale: Credit costs interest, so the question is whether keeping the cash available is worth more than what the borrowing costs.

options.text: Whether the dealer accepts cash
options.rationale: A mechanical detail, not the trade-off.

options.text: Whether the van will be reliable
options.rationale: Same van either way.

options.text: Which option looks better on paper
options.rationale: Appearance is not a criterion.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: price the cost of credit against the use of cash.

questions.question: A consultant is owed $50,000 for a project finished three years ago and is offered $50,000 today as final settlement, with no interest added for the delay. Over those three years inflation averaged about 4% per year, and the consultant could have earned 6% annually investing money elsewhere. Why is receiving $50,000 today actually a worse outcome than it looks?

options.text: It is no worse, since $50,000 is $50,000 whenever it finally arrives
options.rationale: This is the misconception the case is built to test.

options.text: The issue is inflation alone, since money never received could not have been invested
options.rationale: Had it arrived on time it could have been put to work, which is the second loss.

options.text: The payment lost purchasing power to inflation and three years of investment growth
options.rationale: Two separate losses stack: the same sum buys less than it did, and it earned nothing in the meantime.

options.text: The issue is the missing contractual interest, which is a legal point rather than economic
options.rationale: Names the remedy and skips what was actually lost.

notes.difficulty_justification: Demands recognizing two distinct erosions of value at once, purchasing power lost to inflation and growth opportunity lost to delay, neither of which alone explains why a flat late payment falls short.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Inflation-Adjusted Value, Time Value of Money. Deleting inflation leaves only a standard 'money delayed without interest' TVM question. Deleting TVM leaves only a standard 'inflation eroded purchasing power' question. The question only works because both losses stack on the same delayed payment, so it passes the break test.

questions.question: An importer borrows in dollars at six percent to settle a euro invoice falling due in six months. Over those months the euro strengthens ten percent against the dollar. What has happened to the total cost?

options.text: Interest plus a larger euro bill
options.rationale: The borrowing cost was known at the start and the exchange move added a second, separate cost to the same purchase.

options.text: Interest offset by the currency move
options.rationale: The move went against the importer.

options.text: A cheaper invoice than expected
options.rationale: A stronger euro costs more dollars.

options.text: No change, as the loan is fixed
options.rationale: The loan is fixed; the invoice is not.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the cost of credit and the currency exposure stack on the same transaction and have to be counted together.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Money, credit and interest, Currency exchange rates. Without the loan there is no interest to add. Without the currency move the cost is just the interest. Both are needed.

questions.question: A lender charges three percent a year on a one year loan. Inflation over that same year runs at five percent. What has happened to the lender in real terms?

options.text: It earns three percent in real terms
options.rationale: Three percent is the nominal rate.

options.text: It loses the whole principal sum
options.rationale: The principal returns, worth slightly less.

options.text: Inflation does not affect lenders
options.rationale: It affects them directly.

options.text: It is repaid in weaker dollars
options.rationale: The interest earned is less than the fall in what a dollar buys, so the money coming back is worth less than the money that went out.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the interest rate and the inflation rate have to be set against each other before the lender's real position is visible.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Money, credit and interest, Inflation-adjusted value. Without the interest rate there is nothing to adjust. Without the inflation figure three percent looks like a gain. Both are needed.

questions.question: What does it mean for an economy or business to be allocatively efficient?

options.text: Production costs have been reduced to the lowest amount possible.
options.rationale: Cost minimization is about efficiency of production, not about matching output to what people actually want.

options.text: A company is earning the highest possible profit margin on each unit sold.
options.rationale: High margins reflect pricing and cost control, not whether resources are aimed at what buyers value most.

options.text: Every machine and worker is being used without any idle time.
options.rationale: This describes operational efficiency, the common mistake of confusing lean operation with producing the right mix of goods.

options.text: Resources are producing the mix of goods that people value most.
options.rationale: This matches the core definition: producing what people actually want most, not just producing without waste.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of a single concept's definition with one reasoning step, no application to a novel scenario required.

questions.question: A woodworking shop has plenty of raw lumber and a large workshop, but only one saw that every worker must share, slowing output. Which factor of production is limiting this business?

options.text: Capital
options.rationale: Capital includes equipment like the saw, and the single shared saw is the bottleneck restricting output here.

options.text: Land
options.rationale: Land refers to raw materials and space, which the shop already has in abundance.

options.text: Labor
options.rationale: Labor refers to the workers themselves, who are present but limited by lack of equipment, not their own numbers.

options.text: Entrepreneurship
options.rationale: Entrepreneurship is the organizing and risk-taking role, not the physical equipment causing the slowdown.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires identifying which single factor of production is the bottleneck in a straightforward scenario, one concept applied through basic recognition of the category definitions.

questions.question: What is the main risk of switching to a cheaper input purely because it costs less?

options.text: It moves the business away from producing what people want most.
options.rationale: That is an allocation question, not an input quality one.

options.text: It leads to a lasting rise in what customers are willing to buy.
options.rationale: A cheaper input does not lift demand.

options.text: It raises the total quantity of other inputs the business needs.
options.rationale: Possible in some cases, not the general risk.

options.text: It might reduce output quality or speed enough to hurt sales elsewhere.
options.rationale: A cheaper input is only cheaper if what it produces still sells, and the saving is easy to measure while the damage is not.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests the direct first-order consequence of one concept, resource substitution, without requiring combination with any other concept.

questions.question: A print shop runs its presses at full capacity with zero downtime, spending most of that capacity on embossed invitations that sell slowly while turning away rush orders for business cards that customers request constantly. What does this situation show?

options.text: The shop needs to substitute a cheaper material for its current one
options.rationale: This is a resource substitution fix, but the scenario describes a mismatch in what's produced, not an input cost or quality problem.

options.text: The shop is operationally efficient but not allocatively efficient
options.rationale: Correct: the presses run without waste, but resources are tied up in low-demand output instead of the higher-value product customers actually want.

options.text: The shop has a shortage in its factors of production
options.rationale: The presses are running at full capacity, so the issue is what they're producing, not a missing resource.

options.text: The shop is both operationally and allocatively efficient
options.rationale: Ignores that turning away high-demand orders while making slow-selling items means the resource mix isn't matching what buyers value most.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (allocative efficiency) applied to a new, specific business scenario requiring the student to distinguish it from operational efficiency, not just define it.

questions.question: A landscaping company has plenty of land contracts, willing workers, and a founder eager to expand, but it only owns two mowers and both are constantly booked, forcing it to turn down new clients. What should the owner prioritize to grow output?

options.text: Investing in additional mowing equipment
options.rationale: Correct: capital (the mowers) is explicitly the bottleneck limiting output, so addressing it directly relieves the constraint.

options.text: Signing more land contracts to expand the client base
options.rationale: More contracts without more equipment would only worsen the existing bottleneck.

options.text: Bringing in a co-founder to share entrepreneurial duties
options.rationale: Entrepreneurship isn't described as lacking; the founder is already willing and available, so this doesn't address the stated limit.

options.text: Hiring more workers to cover additional job sites
options.rationale: Assumes labor is the constraint, but new hires would just be idle waiting for available mowers.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (factors of production) requiring the student to identify the specific bottleneck factor in a novel scenario rather than just list the four factors.

questions.question: A cafe's nightly washing up takes one member of staff four hours at $16 an hour. A machine costing $3,200 would cut that to thirty minutes. What does the comparison support?

options.text: Keeping the staff, who are flexible
options.rationale: Flexibility does not cover the gap.

options.text: Waiting until the current staff leave
options.rationale: Delays a saving already available.

options.text: Buying it, since it pays back in months
options.rationale: Saving three and a half hours a night at $16 recovers the purchase in roughly two months, which is what makes the substitution worth it.

options.text: Buying two machines for both sinks
options.rationale: Doubles the cost for the same job.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: test one input against another on the numbers given.

questions.question: A print shop switches from a costly premium paper to a cheaper recycled stock for all its jobs, cutting material costs by 20%. Customers who order wedding invitations, its highest-margin product, start canceling because the recycled stock feels flimsy, while customers ordering flyers, a low-margin product, don't notice or care. Why did this substitution hurt the shop overall?

options.text: The shop failed to identify entrepreneurship as its scarce factor of production before making the swap.
options.rationale: Misapplies factors of production, entrepreneurship as a bottleneck isn't the issue here; the problem is a substitution mismatched to customer value, not a missing organizing resource.

options.text: The shop picked a substitute based on cost savings without checking whether it would shift resources away from the product customers valued most.
options.rationale: Correct: the substitution ignored quality fit for the high-value product, moving resources toward outcomes customers valued less, which is the allocative failure the substitution triggered.

options.text: The shop simply chose a substitute that cost less without ever checking whether it changed output quality enough to hurt sales elsewhere.
options.rationale: This restates the substitution mistake alone but misses the deeper reason it mattered: the quality drop specifically hit the shop's most valued product line, an allocative efficiency consequence, not just a generic quality slip.

options.text: The shop ran its printing process with less waste after the switch, so the drop in sales must be unrelated to the paper choice.
options.rationale: Confuses operational efficiency with allocative efficiency; low waste doesn't mean the resource is going to its highest-value use, and the sales drop is directly tied to the paper choice.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding resource substitution (the paper swap) and allocative efficiency (matching resources to what customers value most) together; neither concept alone explains why a cost-saving swap backfired specifically because of which product line it hit.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Resource Substitution Decisions, Allocative Efficiency. Deleting substitution removes the scenario's trigger event entirely. Deleting allocative efficiency leaves only 'the substitute lowered quality,' which fails to explain why the SAME quality drop mattered for one product but not another, that distinction only makes sense through the allocative lens. Both concepts are load-bearing.

questions.question: A small clothing workshop wants to increase output. It has plenty of fabric and floor space, and its two sewing machines run non-stop while workers wait for a free machine. The owner is considering either hiring two more workers or leasing one additional sewing machine. Which choice best fits the situation, and why?

options.text: Switch to a cheaper fabric supplier, since lowering material costs frees up money to expand in either direction later.
options.rationale: Misidentifies the constraint entirely; fabric and space are already abundant, so a fabric substitution doesn't address the actual bottleneck of limited machine capacity.

options.text: Hire more workers and lease a machine at the same time, since adding both factors together guarantees the biggest possible output gain.
options.rationale: Ignores that workers are already idle; adding more labor on top of the fix wastes money on a factor that isn't scarce, so this isn't the best-fit choice.

options.text: Hire more workers, since labor is the factor that always drives higher output regardless of what else is limited.
options.rationale: Wrongly assumes labor is universally the driver of output; here workers are already idle waiting on machines, so more labor alone wouldn't raise output.

options.text: Lease another machine, since capital is the bottleneck and adding it lets the idle labor actually produce more.
options.rationale: Correct: capital (machines) is the constraining factor; substituting more capital into the mix relieves the bottleneck and lets existing labor become productive, matching both the factor-identification and substitution logic.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires first identifying which factor of production is the true bottleneck, then reasoning about whether substituting more of that factor (capital) versus another (labor) actually resolves it; neither concept alone determines the right call.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Factors of Production, Resource Substitution Decisions. Deleting factors of production removes the ability to diagnose WHICH resource is scarce, leaving no basis to judge the substitution options. Deleting resource substitution leaves only 'capital is the bottleneck' with no decision to make about what to do about it. Both are necessary for the question to function.

questions.question: A workshop has more labour than it needs, materials in stock and one bottleneck machine that everything must pass through. It runs that machine mostly on its slowest selling line. What is wrong?

options.text: Materials that cost more than they should
options.rationale: Materials are plentiful, not costly.

options.text: The scarce factor on the wrong output
options.rationale: One input is the binding constraint, so the mix it produces is what decides whether the workshop is making what people want.

options.text: A machine that is far too fast here
options.rationale: Its speed is the limit, not a surplus.

options.text: Too little labour for the workload
options.rationale: Labour is in surplus.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: identifying which factor is actually scarce is what makes the efficiency question answerable.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Factors of production, Allocative efficiency. Without knowing which factor binds every line looks equally cheap to run. Without the efficiency question the bottleneck is just a machine. Both are needed.

questions.question: Which behavior best shows true adaptability and openness at work?

options.text: Adjusting your plan once a coworker shows you solid new information.
options.rationale: This matches the core definition: changing course when new facts arrive instead of clinging to the original idea.

options.text: Waiting for someone else to decide so you avoid picking a side.
options.rationale: This describes avoidance, not the active adjustment openness requires.

options.text: Agreeing out loud with new ideas but quietly keeping your old plan.
options.rationale: This is the common mistake of claiming flexibility without actually adjusting behavior.

options.text: Sticking with your original plan since you thought of it first.
options.rationale: This is the stubbornness the concept warns against, not openness.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of one concept, adaptability and openness, through a single reasoning step about what counts as genuinely adjusting versus merely appearing to.

questions.question: A manager doesn't know if a key contract will be renewed, but the team needs direction now. What does tolerating ambiguity look like here?

options.text: Setting a clear checkpoint date and making a reasonable call before then.
options.rationale: Acting sensibly on what is known, with a date to revisit it, is what keeps a team moving when the answer has not arrived.

options.text: Picking whichever option is easiest without weighing the situation.
options.rationale: Incomplete information is not a licence to stop thinking.

options.text: Holding every task until the contract news has been confirmed.
options.rationale: Freezes the team on something outside its control.

options.text: Asking each department for more reports before anything is decided.
options.rationale: Buys paper, not the missing fact, and the team still waits.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, tolerating ambiguity, applied to a single fresh scenario requiring one reasoning step about acting despite unclear information.

questions.question: Which response to a sudden business disruption best demonstrates embracing change?

options.text: Treating the disruption as a chance to test a new approach and move forward.
options.rationale: This matches the definition of actively adjusting and looking for what's useful instead of resisting.

options.text: Blaming the disruption publicly instead of adjusting any plans.
options.rationale: This focuses on assigning fault rather than adapting, which does not fit the concept.

options.text: Continuing operations exactly as before while quietly hoping things return to normal.
options.rationale: This is passive tolerance, not the active adjustment embracing change requires.

options.text: Pausing all activity until the old conditions are fully restored.
options.rationale: This is resistance disguised as caution, the opposite of moving forward.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, embracing change, tested at the recognition level by distinguishing genuine active adjustment from passive or resistant reactions.
