questions.question: A gym manager launched a new 6am spin class three weeks ago and attendance has been low every single session. Which response best shows flexibility in problem solving?

options.text: Keep the same 6am spin class running indefinitely, trusting that word of mouth will eventually build attendance.
options.rationale: This is forcing the same solution harder rather than adapting, the opposite of the concept.

options.text: Let the 6am trial finish its planned three weeks, then use the attendance data to try a different time slot or format.
options.rationale: This tests the plan fairly, then switches approach based on results, matching the concept's balance of giving something a fair shot before adapting.

options.text: Cancel the class after a single low session and avoid scheduling any new class formats for the rest of the year.
options.rationale: This overcorrects by abandoning experimentation entirely rather than adjusting the approach.

options.text: Lower the price of the same 6am class again without changing the time or format.
options.rationale: This repeats the same core approach with a minor tweak rather than genuinely trying a different approach.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept applied to a new scenario requiring the student to distinguish genuine approach-switching from stubbornness or premature abandonment.

questions.question: A store manager learns a major highway near her shop will close for repairs sometime in the next month, but the exact date is still unknown. Which action best shows tolerating ambiguity?

options.text: Set a review point in two weeks, prepare a backup staffing and marketing plan now, and adjust it once more details emerge.
options.rationale: This keeps acting reasonably despite incomplete information while building in a checkpoint, matching the concept's core behavior.

options.text: Escalate the issue to corporate and wait for a directive before taking any local action.
options.rationale: This delays decision making until someone else removes the uncertainty, rather than acting reasonably within it.

options.text: Assume the closure will happen on the earliest possible date and commit fully to that assumption without a backup plan.
options.rationale: This treats a guess as certainty rather than genuinely working with the unknown.

options.text: Refuse to plan any promotions or staffing changes until the highway department confirms an exact closure date.
options.rationale: This freezes action while waiting for certainty, which trades ambiguity for missed timing instead of managing it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept applied to a new situation requiring the student to identify action-under-uncertainty rather than certainty-seeking or freezing.

questions.question: A small print shop's biggest client suddenly moves all their business online and stops ordering physical materials. The shop owner starts researching how to offer design services for digital ads within the week. What does this show?

options.text: Flexibility in problem solving, because the owner abandoned a failing approach after giving it a fair trial period.
options.rationale: There was no prior approach being tested and dropped after a trial, this is a reaction to an external shift, not a swap of one tried solution for another.

options.text: Tolerating ambiguity, because the owner accepted not knowing exactly how the new service would perform.
options.rationale: The scenario centers on responding to a shift by adjusting the business direction, not on acting despite unclear information.

options.text: Adaptability and openness, because the owner changed their opinion after someone presented new evidence.
options.rationale: No one presented a competing opinion or new evidence to update a belief, the owner is reacting to a changed circumstance, not revising a stance.

options.text: Embracing change, because the owner treated the client's shift as an opening to actively move the business in a new direction.
options.rationale: This matches actively adjusting plans and looking for what's useful in a shift rather than resisting or just tolerating it quietly.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept applied to a scenario, but distractors use the other three adaptability-domain concepts in plausible-sounding but mismatched ways, requiring precise recognition of what embracing change specifically involves versus its neighbors.
review_flags: Distractors reference sibling concepts by name for discrimination purposes; this still tests only Embracing Change since only one concept's mechanism actually fits the scenario.

questions.question: A retailer's new checkout app has been glitching for three weeks and nobody knows when a fix is coming. The manager sets a 48-hour checkpoint to decide on a backup system, then when that checkpoint arrives, actually swaps to the backup and retrains staff on it. Which combination of behaviors does this show?

options.text: Switching systems immediately on day one before giving the app any chance to stabilize
options.rationale: This shows readiness to change but skips tolerating ambiguity entirely, since there was no attempt to function under the uncertainty first.

options.text: Keeping the same broken app running while telling staff the situation is temporary
options.rationale: This is quiet tolerance without real adjustment, which misses the flexibility piece since no new approach was ever tried.

options.text: Waiting for complete data before making any move on the checkout system
options.rationale: This describes the opposite of tolerating ambiguity; the manager acted before certainty arrived rather than stalling for clean information.

options.text: Acting under uncertainty, then genuinely switching approach once the checkpoint passed
options.rationale: Setting a checkpoint and acting without full information shows tolerating ambiguity, and actually switching to the backup instead of repeating the same broken plan shows real flexibility in problem solving.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding two mechanisms together: acting reasonably without full information, and abandoning a non-working approach for a new one after a fair test. Neither concept alone accounts for both the checkpoint-setting and the actual switch.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Tolerating Ambiguity, Flexibility in Problem Solving. Deleting Tolerating Ambiguity leaves only 'switched to a new system,' which fits Flexibility alone but drops the reasoning about acting without full information; deleting Flexibility leaves only the checkpoint-setting, which fits Tolerating Ambiguity alone but drops the actual switch. Both are needed to explain the full scenario, so the pairing holds.

questions.question: Two shop owners both lose their main supplier overnight. Owner A says 'I'm fine with change' but quietly keeps calling the old supplier hoping they'll come back, changing nothing else. Owner B immediately updates the recipe with a new ingredient source and tells customers about the improvement. What is the key difference between them?

options.text: Both owners are equally adaptable since they both accepted that the supplier situation had changed
options.rationale: Accepting a fact isn't the same as acting on it; only Owner B translated acceptance into an actual adjustment, so the two are not equivalent.

options.text: Owner A shows openness to new information while Owner B merely tolerates the disruption without adjusting anything
options.rationale: This reverses the actual behaviors; Owner A is the one not adjusting, and Owner B is the one making the real change.

options.text: Owner B actively adjusts the business to the new situation while Owner A only claims flexibility without changing behavior
options.rationale: Owner B demonstrates embracing change by actively reworking the recipe and messaging, while Owner A shows the common mistake of stating openness without adjusting plans, habits, or actions to fit reality.

options.text: Owner A is more adaptable because waiting for the old supplier avoids the risk of an untested new ingredient
options.rationale: Waiting on the old supplier is stalling rather than adapting, and the card frames genuine adaptability as adjusting to new information, not resisting it while hoping the situation reverses.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests two closely related concepts that could be conflated: claiming openness versus actually embracing change through action. The question requires distinguishing stated attitude from demonstrated behavior across two paired scenarios, which single-concept recall cannot resolve.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Adaptability and Openness, Embracing Change. Deleting Adaptability and Openness removes the 'says vs does' contrast that defines Owner A, leaving only a simple 'who reacted better' question answerable by Embracing Change alone; deleting Embracing Change removes the active-adjustment detail that defines Owner B, leaving no clear resolution. Both concepts are needed to justify why B is correct and A is the trap, so the pairing survives the break test.
review_flags: Adaptability and Openness and Embracing Change are closely related on these cards, so the distinction relies on the 'common mistake' beats (claiming openness vs. quiet tolerance vs. active adjustment); flagging in case a reviewer sees this as one concept split into two labels rather than a genuine interaction.

questions.question: A team's third attempt at the same fix has failed, and fresh test data points clearly at a different cause. The lead schedules a fourth attempt at the original fix, with more people on it. What is wrong?

options.text: Too few people on the original fix
options.rationale: Staffing is not why it fails.

options.text: Test data that cannot be trusted
options.rationale: Dismisses the evidence.

options.text: A team unwilling to work harder
options.rationale: They have tried three times.

options.text: New evidence and the same approach
options.rationale: Openness means letting new information change the plan, and flexibility means dropping an approach that has stopped working rather than pushing it harder.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: new information has arrived and the approach has not moved, and the failure needs both halves to describe it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Adaptability and openness, Flexibility in problem solving. Without the new data there is no reason to change course. Without the repeated approach the data is simply noted. Both are needed.

questions.question: A manager tells a new hire, 'try to make your emails a bit better.' What does this request lack?

options.text: Assertiveness, since the manager should have set a firm deadline for the change.
options.rationale: The issue here is vagueness, not a lack of firmness or respect.

options.text: Nothing, since managers are allowed to give general feedback without specifics.
options.rationale: This ignores that vague feedback causes guessing and rework, the core problem clarity addresses.

options.text: Clarity, since the listener has no specific idea what change is actually being asked for.
options.rationale: The request is vague and leaves the listener guessing, which is exactly what clarity in expression is meant to prevent.

options.text: Tailoring, since the manager should have used different words for a different department.
options.rationale: The problem isn't about matching the audience, it's about the message itself being unclear to anyone.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of what clarity in expression requires by identifying its absence in one plain scenario.

questions.question: What does tailoring a message to your audience mean?

options.text: Reusing one slide deck for every group so the message stays consistent.
options.rationale: Consistency of material, at the cost of reaching anyone.

options.text: Stating your view the same firm way whoever happens to be in the room.
options.rationale: The thing tailoring replaces.

options.text: Adjusting wording and detail for each listener while the core stays accurate.
options.rationale: What changes is the framing and the depth; the substance has to survive the translation intact.

options.text: Softening a direct request into a suggestion so it feels less demanding.
options.rationale: Changes what is being asked, not how it is pitched.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of a single concept's core mechanism against confusable adjacent behaviors, one reasoning step.

questions.question: An employee needs Friday off for a family commitment and tells his manager: I mean, it is probably fine either way, whatever works for you. What is missing?

options.text: An explanation of why he needs it
options.rationale: Reasons help and the request itself is missing.

options.text: A written request sent in advance
options.rationale: Format does not supply the ask.

options.text: A clear statement of what he needs
options.rationale: Being assertive means saying the need plainly and respectfully, which is exactly what the hedging removes.

options.text: A more forceful tone with the boss
options.rationale: Force is the other failure mode.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what the hedging removed.

questions.question: A manager notices a peer keeps taking credit for her ideas in meetings. She wants to address it assertively. Which response fits that approach?

options.text: She mentions it to colleagues so word gets back to him indirectly
options.rationale: Routes a direct conversation through the team.

options.text: She says calmly that the idea was hers and asks to be named next time
options.rationale: Clear about what happened and what she wants, without attacking him, which is what makes it assertive rather than passive or hostile.

options.text: She stays quiet and hopes the peer notices and stops on his own
options.rationale: Passive, and nothing signals the problem to him.

options.text: She tells him his behaviour is selfish and demands that he stop at once
options.rationale: States the need aggressively, which is the other failure mode.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, applied to a new workplace scenario requiring the student to distinguish assertive behavior from passive and aggressive alternatives rather than just define it.

questions.question: A supervisor tells an intern, 'try to make your emails sound more professional going forward.' The intern still isn't sure what to change. What is the clearest fix to this instruction?

options.text: Repeat the same phrase but say it more firmly so the intern takes it seriously this time.
options.rationale: Repeating a vague request louder doesn't add the missing specifics.

options.text: Suggest the intern ask a coworker what 'professional' generally tends to mean in most offices.
options.rationale: This outsources the clarification instead of the supervisor stating the actual expectation directly.

options.text: Tell the intern to use greetings and sign-offs, avoid slang, and keep each email under five sentences.
options.rationale: This replaces vague hinting with specific, actionable details the intern can follow exactly.

options.text: Say nothing further and let the intern figure it out by reading other employees' emails.
options.rationale: This leaves the request unclear and forces guessing, the opposite of clarity.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, applied by requiring the student to recognize which revised instruction actually removes ambiguity in a specific workplace exchange.

questions.question: A product manager needs to announce a delayed launch. Engineers already know the technical cause, but investors only care about the business impact. How should she handle these two updates?

options.text: Give investors the revised timeline and financial impact, and give engineers the specific technical cause and next steps.
options.rationale: This shapes the same core update differently for each audience based on what they need to know.

options.text: Tell investors about the new timeline and revenue impact, while giving engineers a summary of the delay without technical specifics.
options.rationale: This reverses the appropriate depth for each group, engineers need technical detail and investors need business impact.

options.text: Send investors the same detailed technical writeup the engineers received, since consistency avoids confusion later.
options.rationale: Using identical content regardless of listener ignores what each audience actually needs.

options.text: Wait until both groups can be gathered in one meeting so the exact same message reaches everyone at once.
options.rationale: Delivering one uniform message to a mixed audience doesn't adjust for what each group actually needs.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, applied by requiring the student to correctly match message depth and content to two distinct audiences in a new situation, not just recall the definition.

questions.question: A manager needs to tell both her peer and her own boss that a vendor missed a deadline and the launch must slip. To her peer she says, 'This delay affects my timeline too, so let's agree on a new date today.' To her boss she says, 'I want to flag that we need to move the launch date, and here's the plan to recover it.' What is she doing by varying the second message from the first?

options.text: Softening her request into a suggestion so her boss does not feel pressured
options.rationale: This describes losing clarity by hedging, but her boss message still states a clear ask, it just fits a different audience.

options.text: Staying assertive while adjusting framing for a different audience and power dynamic
options.rationale: Both messages are direct and respectful (assertive), but the wording and framing shift based on who she's addressing, which is tailoring on top of assertiveness.

options.text: Dropping assertiveness with her boss to avoid seeming confrontational
options.rationale: She still clearly states the issue and a plan to her boss, which is assertive, not passive.

options.text: Using one identical script for both conversations to stay consistent
options.rationale: The two messages are worded differently, so this contradicts what's described in the scenario.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding assertiveness and audience-tailoring together: the student must see that the same underlying assertive stance is expressed through two different framings, not confuse a framing change for a loss of assertiveness.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Assertive Communication, Tailoring Message to Audience. Deleting assertiveness: the question could become 'why did she word it differently' with no way to check the message stayed direct and respectful. Deleting tailoring: the question would just ask if she was assertive, with no audience contrast to reason about. Both are needed, so this passes the break test.

questions.question: A team member tells his manager, 'I really think we might want to maybe reconsider the timeline at some point, if that's okay,' hoping she'll realize the deadline is unworkable without him having to say so outright. Which combination of problems best describes this message?

options.text: It is both vague and passive, hiding the actual concern behind hedging instead of stating it directly
options.rationale: The wording is full of hedges ('maybe,' 'at some point,' 'if that's okay') that obscure the real ask, and it avoids directly naming the concern, combining unclear language with a passive stance.

options.text: It is assertive but poorly tailored to a manager audience
options.rationale: The message is not assertive at all; it avoids stating the concern directly, which is the opposite of the calm, clear stance assertiveness requires.

options.text: It is clear and assertive but too blunt for a workplace setting
options.rationale: The message is neither clear nor blunt; it hedges so much that the actual concern is barely stated.

options.text: It is clear but overly aggressive, since it pressures the manager into an immediate decision
options.rationale: The message contains no pressure or ultimatum; if anything it applies too little pressure, so aggression is not the issue.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires distinguishing two failures at once, vague language and a passive (non-assertive) stance, and recognizing they compound each other rather than being interchangeable, which a single-concept question could not test.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Assertive Communication, Clarity in Expression. Deleting assertiveness: the question could still flag vague wording alone, but couldn't explain why the person avoided stating the concern outright. Deleting clarity: the question could flag passivity alone, but couldn't explain why the wording itself ('maybe,' 'at some point') fails. Both concepts are needed to fully diagnose the message, so it passes the break test.

questions.question: An engineer explains a launch delay to the board in precise, unambiguous sentences, built on six terms that only her own team uses. Every word means exactly one thing. What is the position?

options.text: A message pitched too simply here
options.rationale: It is pitched far too technically.

options.text: Vague wording that hides the delay
options.rationale: The wording is the opposite of vague.

options.text: A delay that needed no explanation
options.rationale: The board needs to understand it.

options.text: Exact wording the room cannot decode
options.rationale: Precision is a property of the words and clarity is a property of what reaches the listener, which is why the audience has to shape the vocabulary.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the expression is genuinely clear and untailored, so the precision buys nothing with this audience.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Clarity in expression, Tailoring message to audience. Without the precision this is ordinary waffle. Without the audience mismatch the precision serves. Both are needed.

questions.question: What is the main goal of de-escalating tension in a heated moment?

options.text: Get both sides to agree on a permanent solution immediately
options.rationale: This confuses de-escalation with problem-solving, which the card says should come after the heat is lowered.

options.text: Lower the emotional heat so people can actually listen
options.rationale: Correct: the card defines de-escalation as calming emotion first so real listening becomes possible.

options.text: Prove to the other person that their reaction is unreasonable
options.rationale: This would increase defensiveness rather than reduce it, the opposite of the concept.

options.text: Explain the correct policy as clearly as possible right away
options.rationale: This is the common mistake the card warns against: defending the policy before the person feels heard fuels the anger.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of a single concept's definition with one reasoning step, no application to a novel scenario required.

questions.question: When someone is mediating between two coworkers who disagree, what role are they supposed to take?

options.text: A supervisor who assigns punishment for the disagreement
options.rationale: Mediating is about understanding and common ground, not enforcing consequences.

options.text: An advocate who argues for the side they personally agree with
options.rationale: This directly violates the 'without taking sides' part of the definition.

options.text: A judge who decides which coworker is right
options.rationale: Taking a side or ruling on who is correct contradicts the neutral, non-siding role described in the card.

options.text: A neutral helper guiding both sides toward mutual understanding
options.rationale: Correct: the card defines mediating as helping both sides understand each other without taking sides.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, straightforward recognition of what the role of a mediator is, one logical step from the definition.

questions.question: A negotiation that results in a true win-win outcome is best described as one where:

options.text: The stronger party sets the terms and the weaker party accepts them
options.rationale: This describes a power imbalance outcome, not a mutually beneficial one as defined by the concept.

options.text: Both sides split every term exactly down the middle
options.rationale: The card explicitly calls out splitting the difference as a misconception, not the real goal.

options.text: Both sides end up better off based on what they actually need
options.rationale: Correct: the card defines win-win as finding a solution that leaves each party better off by understanding their real needs.

options.text: One side gives in fully so the deal can close quickly
options.rationale: This describes a one-sided outcome, which the card says tends to poison trust or fall apart later.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept recognition question testing the core definition, requiring one step of reasoning to reject the common splitting-the-difference misconception.

questions.question: A gym member storms up to the front desk yelling because their membership was accidentally charged twice this month. What should the staff member do first?

options.text: Immediately process a refund without saying anything to the member
options.rationale: Skips addressing the emotion entirely, treating this purely as a transactional fix rather than lowering tension first.

options.text: Ask the member to lower their voice or step outside to discuss it
options.rationale: This escalates by making demands of an already angry person instead of calming the moment.

options.text: Explain the billing system's error rate to show this rarely happens
options.rationale: Defending the system before the person feels heard just adds fuel, matching the card's common mistake.

options.text: Lower your voice and acknowledge the frustration before working on the refund
options.rationale: This matches the mechanism of de-escalating: calm the emotional heat first so the person can actually hear the fix.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept applied to a new, specific scenario requiring the student to predict the correct first move rather than define de-escalation.

questions.question: Two warehouse employees keep arguing over who gets to use the forklift first each morning, and their supervisor is asked to step in. What should the supervisor do first, according to good mediation practice?

options.text: Assign forklift priority based on seniority and announce the decision to both
options.rationale: This imposes a solution immediately instead of first helping each side feel heard, skipping the mediation step.

options.text: Side with whichever employee has been with the company longer to end the dispute quickly
options.rationale: Taking sides is exactly what mediation is supposed to avoid, since it ignores the other person's concern entirely.

options.text: Tell both employees to work it out between themselves without supervisor involvement
options.rationale: This avoids mediating altogether, leaving the conflict to fester rather than stepping in to help them understand each other.

options.text: Meet with each employee separately to hear their concerns before bringing them together
options.rationale: This mirrors the mediation mechanism of hearing each side out and reflecting concerns back before proposing any fix.

notes.difficulty_justification: Applies the mediation mechanism, hearing both sides before proposing solutions, to a fresh workplace scenario rather than testing recall of the definition.

questions.question: Two colleagues who have to work together every day are openly disagreeing about who owns a weekly report. Their manager decides to let it settle by itself. What is the risk?

options.text: It hardens and the work suffers
options.rationale: An unaddressed disagreement between people who cannot avoid each other tends to set rather than fade.

options.text: One of them will simply resign
options.rationale: Jumps to the extreme outcome.

options.text: The report gets written twice
options.rationale: A possible symptom, not the risk.

options.text: It resolves faster without help
options.rationale: Nothing in the case suggests that.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: name the cost of avoidance.

questions.question: Two kitchen coworkers start yelling at each other over a mistaken order, right as a lunch rush hits. The manager steps in. What should happen first, and why does order matter here?

options.text: Ask both cooks to sit down together immediately and hash out who was at fault while tempers are still high.
options.rationale: Jumping straight to joint problem-solving before anyone calms down is the trap both cards warn against; nobody can hear the other side while still defending themselves.

options.text: Calm the emotional heat first, then help both sides hear each other's side once they can actually listen.
options.rationale: Correct: de-escalating lowers the temperature so people stop defending themselves, which is the precondition mediation needs to work at all.

options.text: Propose splitting the blame evenly between them so the rush isn't delayed any further.
options.rationale: This is the Managing Conflict mistake of a vague compromise to end tension fast, not the de-escalate-then-mediate sequence the scenario calls for.

options.text: Restate each side's complaint back to them, since reflecting concerns builds the trust needed before any calming can work.
options.rationale: This is a mediation technique from the card, but it assumes both sides can already listen; skipping the calming step first means the reflection just gets shouted over.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding two concepts, de-escalating tension and mediating between others, and reasoning about their correct sequence, not just defining either one.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: De-escalating Tension, Mediating Between Others. Deleting mediation leaves only 'calm the person down,' which is a state question. Deleting de-escalation leaves only 'help them talk it out,' losing the ordering problem. Both are needed for the question to work.

questions.question: A business partner keeps missing shared deadlines, which is forcing you to redo scheduling last minute. You decide to raise it directly and also propose a new deadline system. Why does naming the problem directly need to come before proposing the fix?

options.text: Because without naming the real issue first, any proposed system just papers over the friction instead of fixing what's actually needed.
options.rationale: Correct: a win-win solution requires understanding what's truly wrong, and that only surfaces once the difficult conversation is actually had, not hedged around.

options.text: Because proposing a system change without addressing the missed deadlines directly is a faster way to get a workable deal on the table.
options.rationale: This treats skipping the direct conversation as more efficient, but the cards suggest the opposite: avoided issues fester and derail deals later.

options.text: Because splitting the scheduling responsibility evenly between both partners resolves the tension without needing to discuss the missed deadlines at all.
options.rationale: This is the vague-compromise mistake, an even split that skips figuring out what actually caused the missed deadlines.

options.text: Because softening the message about missed deadlines makes the partner more open to negotiating the new system afterward.
options.rationale: This is the addressing-difficult-conversations mistake of over-cushioning, which risks the partner never realizing there's a real problem to solve.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interact: the conversation must expose the real need before a win-win trade can be built on it, which is a synthesis a single concept can't answer.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Addressing Difficult Conversations, Negotiating Win-Win Outcomes. Deleting the negotiation concept leaves only 'why speak up honestly,' a state question. Deleting the difficult-conversation concept leaves only 'why understand needs,' losing the sequencing reasoning. Both are required.

questions.question: A manager walks into a shouting match over the delivery rota, immediately proposes a sensible split and asks both sides to sign it. They sign. The atmosphere between them stays poisonous for weeks. What was skipped?

options.text: Cooling the heat before the fix
options.rationale: A solution reached while both people are still furious settles the rota and leaves the relationship exactly where it was.

options.text: A rota that both sides could accept
options.rationale: They accepted this one.

options.text: A written record of the agreement
options.rationale: It was signed.

options.text: Sending one of them home early
options.rationale: Separation is not resolution.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the substantive conflict is solved and the emotional temperature was never brought down, so the relationship stays broken.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Managing conflict, De-escalating tension. Without the rota fix the dispute continues openly. Without the cooling step the fix cannot repair the working relationship. Both are needed.

questions.question: An employee ships the wrong item to a customer. Which response best shows accountability?

options.text: Say the warehouse team must have grabbed the wrong box during packing.
options.rationale: Shifts blame onto another team instead of owning the mistake.

options.text: Tell the customer sorry that happened without explaining what went wrong.
options.rationale: A vague apology with no ownership of the specific error, the common mistake the card warns about.

options.text: Admit the mix-up was their error and arrange to send the correct item right away.
options.rationale: Names the personal mistake and takes concrete action to fix it, matching the definition.

options.text: Wait to see if the customer notices before saying anything.
options.rationale: Avoids disclosure entirely, the opposite of owning up.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of the single concept of accountability by asking which action fits its definition; one concept, one reasoning step.

questions.question: Which decision best demonstrates social responsibility in a business?

options.text: Switching suppliers quietly so customers do not notice the change.
options.rationale: Concealment runs against the openness the practice needs.

options.text: Choosing the cheapest supplier on the list whatever its environmental record.
options.rationale: Price as the single criterion is the posture being contrasted.

options.text: Raising prices to lift shareholder returns with no explanation offered.
options.rationale: A return decision with no community or environmental dimension.

options.text: Paying more for a supplier with sustainable practices and telling customers why.
options.rationale: It costs the business something, it changes a real impact, and saying so lets customers hold it to the claim.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, direct recognition of which action reflects weighing broader impact against pure profit.

questions.question: A colleague asks you what was said in a private HR meeting about another employee. You were in the room. What should you do?

options.text: Decline, and say why you cannot
options.rationale: Keeping the confidence and being open about the reason is what makes you someone people can rely on.

options.text: Say nothing and walk away
options.rationale: Protects the information and damages the relationship.

options.text: Share only the harmless parts
options.rationale: A partial breach is still a breach.

options.text: Ask what he already knows
options.rationale: Invites the leak from the other direction.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: apply the confidentiality duty to a direct request.

questions.question: A supervisor grants a schedule change to the colleague he eats lunch with and refuses an identical request from someone he barely knows. What rule is he breaking?

options.text: Consulting his own manager
options.rationale: Escalation is not the principle.

options.text: Documenting every decision
options.rationale: A record of a biased call is still biased.

options.text: One standard, applied to everyone
options.rationale: Fairness means the same clear test for each person, rather than a different answer by how close they are.

options.text: Keeping requests confidential
options.rationale: Privacy is not what failed.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the standard breached.

questions.question: A project will be three weeks late. The lead tells the client it is on track and plans to explain nearer the deadline. What is wrong?

options.text: A project that needs more staff
options.rationale: A fix, not the ethical fault.

options.text: A deadline set far too early
options.rationale: The date is not the issue.

options.text: A client who asks for too much
options.rationale: Blames the client for the silence.

options.text: A fact hidden to avoid friction
options.rationale: Honesty means sharing the uncomfortable information when you have it, not when it can no longer be avoided.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the breach.

questions.question: A manager is allocating a bonus pool among six people. What makes the allocation fair?

options.text: An equal share for each person
options.rationale: Equal is not the same as fair.

options.text: The same measure for each person
options.rationale: Fairness is one clear standard applied consistently, which is what makes the result defensible.

options.text: More for the longest serving
options.rationale: One factor, chosen arbitrarily.

options.text: More for whoever asks for it
options.rationale: Rewards assertiveness.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what makes a split fair.

questions.question: A warehouse clerk mislabels a batch of boxes, causing a client's shipment to arrive at the wrong site. When the client calls upset, the clerk says, 'These things happen sometimes with shipping, I'm sorry for the trouble,' then moves on to the next call. What is missing from this response?

options.text: A clear admission of the specific error and a plan to fix it.
options.rationale: Correct: accountability requires naming your own mistake and taking concrete corrective action, not a vague apology.

options.text: A promise that the company will never make a shipping error again.
options.rationale: Overpromising isn't the missing piece; accountability is about this specific fix, not a blanket guarantee.

options.text: A discount offered to the client for their next unrelated order.
options.rationale: A discount might be a goodwill gesture but doesn't substitute for admitting the specific error and correcting it.

options.text: An explanation of which department is really responsible for the mix-up.
options.rationale: This shifts blame elsewhere, which is the opposite of accountability.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (accountability) applied to a new scenario requiring the student to distinguish a vague apology from true ownership and correction.

questions.question: A payroll assistant learns during a routine audit that one employee's salary is far higher than a coworker's for the same role. A friend on the team later asks the assistant to 'just confirm' a rumor about who earns more. What should the assistant do?

options.text: Neither confirm nor deny, but hint enough that the friend can work it out.
options.rationale: A hint is a disclosure with deniability attached.

options.text: Confirm it once the friend has promised to keep it to herself.
options.rationale: A promise from the listener is not the assistant's to accept.

options.text: Decline to discuss any salary details learned through the audit.
options.rationale: The information came from the role, and nothing about the friendship changes who it belongs to.

options.text: Confirm it privately, since it goes no further than one trusted friend.
options.rationale: The duty does not scale with the size of the audience.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (confidentiality) applied to a fresh workplace situation testing whether the student understands that any disclosure, even to one person, counts as a breach.

questions.question: A small clothing brand can cut production costs by switching to a factory that pays workers less but still meets legal minimums in its country. The switch would boost quarterly profit noticeably. Applying social responsibility to this decision means the owner should primarily consider what?

options.text: Whether the switch is technically legal in the factory's home country.
options.rationale: Legal compliance alone ignores the broader impact on workers that social responsibility asks about.

options.text: How the change affects workers and the brand's reputation, beyond the profit gain.
options.rationale: Correct: social responsibility means weighing effects on people and community, not just the profit line.

options.text: How quickly competitors would copy the same cost-cutting move.
options.rationale: Competitor behavior is a market concern, not a measure of social impact on workers or community.

options.text: Whether the profit increase is large enough to justify the risk of getting caught.
options.rationale: This treats the issue as one of avoiding detection rather than genuinely weighing the human impact.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (social responsibility) applied to a new sourcing decision, requiring the student to weigh broader impact against profit rather than just define the term.

questions.question: An analyst's own recommendation looks weaker once a late data set arrives. The meeting is tomorrow and nobody else has seen the data. What does honesty require?

options.text: Put the new data in the room
options.rationale: The duty bites exactly when the truth is inconvenient and nobody would catch its absence.

options.text: Ask to postpone the whole meeting
options.rationale: Delays rather than discloses.

options.text: Mention it only if asked directly
options.rationale: Technically truthful and misleading.

options.text: Present as planned, revise later
options.rationale: Lets a decision be made on less.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: hold the duty when it costs.

questions.question: Two staff ask for the same training budget. One is a strong performer the manager likes; the other is quieter and would gain more from it. What does a fair process need?

options.text: A stated test both are judged on
options.rationale: Fairness comes from deciding the standard first and applying it to both, rather than choosing and then explaining.

options.text: The quieter one, to be balanced
options.rationale: Also an outcome chosen first.

options.text: A split of the budget in half
options.rationale: Avoids the decision rather than making it.

options.text: The stronger performer, on merit
options.rationale: Picks an outcome before a standard.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: build the process, not the outcome.

questions.question: A manager must tell a team member his promotion was declined. She is tempted to say the decision is still pending. What should she do?

options.text: Suggest he look at other roles
options.rationale: Hints without telling him.

options.text: Say it is still being considered
options.rationale: A false account of a closed decision.

options.text: Tell him plainly, and why
options.rationale: Softening a settled answer into a pending one buys comfort now by misleading him about where he stands.

options.text: Say nothing until he asks again
options.rationale: Silence as a form of the same thing.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: deliver an uncomfortable fact straight.

questions.question: A furniture shop owner can switch to a cheaper wood supplier that clear-cuts forests, freeing up cash to give her three employees a raise they've been asking for. Choosing to keep the pricier, sustainable supplier instead protects the environment but means the raise gets delayed. What does this decision actually require the owner to do?

options.text: Give the employees the raise immediately since paying staff fairly always outweighs environmental concerns.
options.rationale: Ignores the environmental/community stakeholder side entirely, favoring one group without weighing the tradeoff.

options.text: Split the cost difference evenly between a small raise and a partially sustainable supplier to please both sides equally.
options.rationale: Mistakes balancing for literally averaging the two options, which the card explicitly says isn't what real balancing means.

options.text: Choose the sustainable supplier since social responsibility always outweighs internal business costs.
options.rationale: Misconception that social responsibility is an unlimited moral upgrade that should override every other stakeholder need, which the card warns against.

options.text: Weigh the environmental impact against the employees' financial needs rather than assuming one side automatically wins.
options.rationale: Correct: this pits community/environmental impact against staff interests, requiring the owner to genuinely weigh both rather than defaulting to either.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding two concepts, stakeholder balancing and social responsibility, at once since the conflict is between an internal stakeholder (employees) and an external one (environment/community), and neither concept alone resolves it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Balancing Stakeholder Interests, Social Responsibility. Deleting stakeholder balancing leaves only 'is this environmentally responsible,' losing the employee-raise conflict. Deleting social responsibility leaves only an internal pay dispute with no external impact angle. Both are needed, so it passes the break test.

questions.question: A salon owner discovers that a batch of hair dye sold last week was mislabeled with the wrong chemical warnings due to a supplier error, though no customer has complained yet. She emails every affected client, explains the mix-up plainly, and offers free corrective treatment for anyone who had a reaction. Which pair of concepts does this response demonstrate together?

options.text: Keeping the supplier's mistake confidential while quietly correcting the label for future batches.
options.rationale: Describes the opposite: hiding the issue rather than disclosing it, which is the common mistake integrity warns against.

options.text: Considering the community impact of the dye while avoiding any direct admission of the error to customers.
options.rationale: Describes social responsibility without accountability, but the scenario shows a direct admission was made, so this contradicts the facts given.

options.text: Weighing the interests of the supplier against the interests of customers before deciding what to say.
options.rationale: Misapplies stakeholder balancing; the scenario is about disclosure and ownership, not a genuine conflict between two parties' competing needs.

options.text: Proactively disclosing a hidden problem before being caught, and owning the fix instead of just apologizing in words.
options.rationale: Correct: disclosing before anyone asks is integrity's proactive disclosure, and offering the concrete fix (free treatment) is accountability beyond a vague apology.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts must be held together: integrity's proactive disclosure and accountability's concrete ownership/fix, since the scenario only fully makes sense as both acting at once, not either alone.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Personal Integrity and Ethics, Showing Accountability. Deleting integrity leaves only 'she fixed her own mistake,' but she didn't cause the mistake, the supplier did, so the proactive disclosure piece (integrity) is essential to explain why she still spoke up unprompted. Deleting accountability leaves only 'she told people,' missing the concrete corrective action. Both needed, passes break test.

questions.question: A manager knows in confidence why a colleague needs lighter shifts. The rota change would be far easier to justify to the rest of the team if she explained the reason. What should she weigh?

options.text: Whether the rota can be explained
options.rationale: Ease of explanation is the pressure, not the test.

options.text: Who is affected, not what is easiest
options.rationale: The convenient path and the right one part company here, and the confidence belongs to the colleague rather than to the manager's explanation.

options.text: Whether the illness is serious
options.rationale: Severity does not change the duty.

options.text: How many staff already suspect it
options.rationale: Suspicion does not release a confidence.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the ethical weighing and the confidentiality duty pull against the easiest available action.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Ethical decision making, Confidentiality and trustworthiness. Without the confidence there is nothing to protect. Without the pressure to explain there is no decision to make. Both are needed.

questions.question: A manager scores every candidate on the same written rubric and picks the top one. Asked by an unsuccessful internal applicant why he lost, she says the field was simply very strong, rather than naming the two criteria he scored lowest on. What is the position?

options.text: A candidate not entitled to reasons
options.rationale: He asked and she answered evasively.

options.text: A rubric that was too rigid to use
options.rationale: It produced a defensible result.

options.text: An unfair process, honestly described
options.rationale: The rubric was applied to everyone.

options.text: A fair decision explained dishonestly
options.rationale: The standard was applied evenly and the account of it was not, which denies him the one thing the process could have given him.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: a fair decision and an honest account of it are separate duties, and only one was met.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Fairness in decision making, Honesty in communication. Without the fair rubric the evasion hides a real wrong. Without the evasion the fairness is visible to him. Both are needed.

questions.question: A consultant answers every client question confidently and truthfully as far as she knows. On two topics she is well outside her expertise and does not realise it. The client acts on both. What went wrong?

options.text: Topics that nobody in the field could answer well
options.rationale: Others have that expertise.

options.text: A client who asked the wrong things
options.rationale: Asking is reasonable.

options.text: Truthful answers past the edge of what she knows
options.rationale: She never said anything she believed to be false, and honesty includes being clear about where your knowledge stops, which takes knowing it yourself.

options.text: A consultant who lied to the client
options.rationale: She said what she believed.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: sincerity alone is not honesty, because the limits of what you know are part of what has to be communicated.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Honesty in communication, Self-awareness. Without the honest intent this is simple deception. Without the blind spot she would have flagged the limit. Both are needed.

questions.question: A manager designs a promotion standard weighted heavily toward presenting to senior leaders, which happens to be the skill he is strongest in and values most. He applies it to everyone identically. What should he examine?

options.text: Whether he applied the standard to everyone equally
options.rationale: He plainly did.

options.text: Whether to weight tenure instead
options.rationale: Swaps one unexamined choice for another.

options.text: Whether the standard itself is his preference
options.rationale: Applying a test evenly is only half of fairness, and recognising that he chose a test built around his own strength is what the other half requires.

options.text: Whether presenting matters at all
options.rationale: It may well matter.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: even application is visible and the self-knowledge needed to question the criterion is the part that catches the bias.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Fairness in decision making, Self-awareness. Without the even application this is ordinary favouritism. Without the self-examination the standard looks neutral. Both are needed.

questions.question: An employee receives criticism about a report and immediately explains why the critique is wrong before considering it. This behavior shows a lack of what?

options.text: Reflective practice
options.rationale: This concept is about looking back on past actions afterward, not about the immediate reaction to being criticized.

options.text: Continuous self-improvement
options.rationale: This concept is about tracking progress on a specific weakness over time, not about how someone reacts in the moment to criticism.

options.text: Seeking mentorship
options.rationale: This concept is about actively asking a more experienced person for input, not about how one responds when criticism is given.

options.text: Openness to feedback
options.rationale: Correct: reacting with defensiveness instead of first weighing the criticism is the core failure this concept describes.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of a single concept, distinguishing defensiveness as the direct opposite of openness to feedback, one reasoning step.

questions.question: A new supervisor regularly asks a retired manager with decades of experience to review her decisions and offer honest input. This practice is best described as what?

options.text: Continuous self-improvement
options.rationale: This concept centers on self-assessment and tracking one's own weaknesses, not on relying on another person's outside experience.

options.text: Reflective practice
options.rationale: This concept is about the supervisor analyzing her own past actions alone, not about consulting someone else with more experience.

options.text: Openness to feedback
options.rationale: This concept describes how criticism is received once it is offered, not the act of seeking out an experienced advisor in the first place.

options.text: Seeking mentorship
options.rationale: Correct: actively finding a more experienced person and asking for honest input to grow faster is exactly this concept.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, direct recognition of the definition applied to a simple example, one reasoning step.

questions.question: After every competition round, a student writes down what worked, what did not, and one specific thing she will do differently next time. What is she practising?

options.text: Comparing herself with rivals
options.rationale: She is reviewing her own round.

options.text: Keeping a record for the coach
options.rationale: The notes are for her own use.

options.text: Turning experience into change
options.rationale: Looking back honestly is only reflective practice when it produces a different approach next time.

options.text: Memorising her answers again
options.rationale: Repetition is not reflection.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the practice on display.

questions.question: After missing a big deadline, a project lead tells her team the failure was just bad luck with vendors and moves on to the next task without changing anything. What is the clearest problem with this response?

options.text: She blamed an outcome instead of examining what specific actions led to it.
options.rationale: Correct: she stopped at 'we failed' without analyzing specific behaviors, so nothing changes next time.

options.text: She should have set a 90-day target before starting the project.
options.rationale: Goal-setting timelines relate to tracking improvement over time, not to the immediate failure to reflect on causes.

options.text: She failed to accept criticism from her team about the missed deadline.
options.rationale: There's no indication anyone gave her feedback to accept or reject; the problem is her own lack of reflection.

options.text: She should have asked a mentor to review the vendor contracts first.
options.rationale: Mentorship is a different concept entirely; the issue here is the missing self-analysis, not a lack of outside guidance.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept (reflective practice) applied to judge a specific workplace scenario, requiring the student to spot the difference between outcome-blaming and action-level analysis.

questions.question: A junior analyst is told her spreadsheet formulas are error-prone and confusing to other teams. She replies 'got it, thanks' and turns in the exact same formatting the next week. What does this show about her?

options.text: She should have found a mentor instead of listening to a coworker's comment.
options.rationale: The feedback came from a legitimate source already; seeking a separate mentor isn't the missing step here.

options.text: She is tracking her progress but hasn't hit her target yet.
options.rationale: There's no tracking happening at all here; she made no attempt to measure or change her formulas.

options.text: She is reflecting on outcomes rather than specific actions in her work.
options.rationale: Reflective practice is about analyzing past actions on your own, not about how you respond when someone hands you criticism.

options.text: She accepted the feedback in words but did not actually use it to change anything.
options.rationale: Correct: she avoided visible defensiveness but the underlying behavior stayed the same, which is the surface-agreement trap.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied to a new situation: the student must recognize the surface-agreement pattern in a fresh scenario, not just recall its definition.

questions.question: A new marketing hire emails a senior colleague saying 'you've done great work, any tips for me in general?' and gets a vague reply back. What would most likely produce a more useful answer?

options.text: Sending the same general request to several more senior employees at once.
options.rationale: Broadening a vague ask to more people doesn't fix the vagueness; it just spreads the same weak question further.

options.text: Asking the colleague to confirm that her current campaign ideas are already strong.
options.rationale: This seeks validation rather than honest critique, which feels good but doesn't actually improve her work.

options.text: Waiting until her next formal performance review to bring up any questions.
options.rationale: Delaying the request removes the point of proactively seeking outside input while it's still useful.

options.text: Bringing two actual campaign drafts and specific questions about what's weak in each.
options.rationale: Correct: a focused, concrete ask respects the mentor's limited time and produces specific, usable input.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied to a new interpersonal scenario, requiring the student to distinguish a focused mentorship request from vague or validation-seeking alternatives.

questions.question: A team lead tells Marcus his client emails come across as pushy. Marcus thanks her, says he'll work on it, then sends the same kind of emails for another month with no change. What is the clearest gap in his response?

options.text: He set a vague long-term goal instead of tracking measurable progress monthly.
options.rationale: This describes a self-improvement tracking problem, but he never even got to setting a goal; he didn't act on the feedback at all.

options.text: He got defensive and argued that his emails were fine as written.
options.rationale: The scenario shows him agreeing and thanking her, not arguing, so defensiveness isn't what happened.

options.text: He sought mentorship instead of asking his manager directly for the critique.
options.rationale: Mentorship isn't the missing piece here; his manager already gave the feedback directly.

options.text: He accepted the feedback but never reflected on specific actions to actually change.
options.rationale: He was open to hearing it but skipped the reflective step of analyzing what he does and adjusting it, so nothing changed.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding two concepts at once: recognizing surface-level openness versus the deeper reflective step needed to change behavior, then diagnosing which one failed.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Openness to Feedback, Reflective Practice. Deleting Reflective Practice leaves only 'he agreed but didn't change,' which no longer explains why nothing changed; deleting Openness to Feedback removes the setup that he wasn't defensive, making the distractor about arguing implausible to rule out. Both concepts are needed to identify the specific gap.

questions.question: A supervisor tracks her own weak spots honestly and works on them on her own, month after month. She has never asked anyone more experienced to watch how she handles them. Progress is slow. What would speed it up?

options.text: A written plan for each month
options.rationale: She already works to a plan.

options.text: Someone who has solved it before
options.rationale: Honest self-assessment finds the right target and an experienced outside view shortens the time it takes to hit it.

options.text: A longer list of weak spots
options.rationale: Breadth is not the constraint.

options.text: More hours spent on practice
options.rationale: More of the slow route.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the self-improvement discipline is in place and the outside input that accelerates it is missing.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Continuous self-improvement, Seeking mentorship. Without the self-assessment a mentor has nothing to aim at. Without the mentor the work stays slow. Both are needed.

questions.question: An associate welcomes every piece of criticism, writes it all down and starts work on whichever item arrived most recently. Two years on, not one of the original weaknesses has been closed out. What is missing?

options.text: Feedback that is specific enough to use
options.rationale: He records it in detail.

options.text: A deliberate choice of what to work on
options.rationale: Taking feedback well is the entry ticket, and improvement needs someone to pick the two things that matter and stay on them.

options.text: A manager who gives more feedback
options.rationale: He already has more than he uses.

options.text: A willingness to hear criticism at all
options.rationale: That is the part he has.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the openness is exemplary and the deliberate, sustained work that turns it into improvement never happens.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Openness to feedback, Continuous self-improvement. Without the openness there is nothing coming in. Without the deliberate focus the intake never becomes progress. Both are needed.

questions.question: Which approach best reflects the idea of interpersonal influence?

options.text: Waiting for the other person to bring up the topic themselves before saying anything.
options.rationale: This is passive avoidance, not influence, since no framing or persuasion is happening at all.

options.text: Finding out what the other person cares about and framing your idea around that.
options.rationale: This matches the card's definition of influence as connecting to what actually matters to the other person.

options.text: Offering a bigger reward each time the person hesitates to agree.
options.rationale: This is bargaining with incentives, not understanding what the person genuinely values.

options.text: Repeating your original request more firmly until the other person agrees.
options.rationale: This is pushing your own agenda harder, the exact behavior the card says backfires.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of a single concept's definition with no applied scenario required.

questions.question: According to the concept of building credibility, what is the most reliable way to earn someone's trust?

options.text: Following through on a small, verifiable commitment and being honest about limits.
options.rationale: This matches the card's definition of credibility built through real expertise, follow-through, and honesty.

options.text: Agreeing with whatever the other person already believes to avoid conflict.
options.rationale: This is people-pleasing, not demonstrating competence or honesty.

options.text: Promising a large result quickly so people feel confident right away.
options.rationale: This is over-promising, which the card says risks damaging credibility if it isn't met.

options.text: Listing your past achievements and credentials at the start of the conversation.
options.rationale: The card explicitly warns this is the common mistake, credentials instead of demonstrated action.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, direct recall of what the definition requires versus common misconceptions named in the card.

questions.question: A student wants the school board to fund a food bank partnership. She already has strong figures on need in the area. What would make the point stick?

options.text: A second set of supporting figures
options.rationale: More of what she already has.

options.text: A louder delivery of the numbers
options.rationale: Volume is not memorability.

options.text: A longer slide on the methodology
options.rationale: Depth that nobody asked for.

options.text: One real family the scheme helped
options.rationale: A short concrete story turns a statistic into something the listener feels and remembers.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: pick what makes a point land.

questions.question: A sales rep wants a client to switch to a subscription plan. The client has mentioned twice that unpredictable monthly costs stress out her budgeting. The rep keeps repeating that the subscription plan is 'more advanced' with extra features. Following persuasive communication, what should the rep do instead?

options.text: List more of the plan's advanced features in greater detail.
options.rationale: This is repeating the same argument with more data, which the card explicitly names as the common mistake.

options.text: Lead with how the subscription plan locks in a flat, predictable monthly cost.
options.rationale: Correct: reframes the pitch around the client's stated concern (budget predictability) rather than repeating the rep's own priority.

options.text: Explain the plan's advanced features again but more slowly and clearly.
options.rationale: Same content delivered differently is still not reframed around what the client cares about.

options.text: Offer a discount to make the advanced features easier to justify.
options.rationale: Still centers the pitch on features/price rather than the client's actual concern about unpredictability.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept (persuasive communication) applied to a new scenario requiring the student to identify the correct reframe, not just define the term.

questions.question: A team lead is presenting a new attendance policy. Midway through, several team members start glancing at their phones and one mutters something to a neighbor. The team lead notices but keeps reading through the remaining slides exactly as planned. What does this show?

options.text: The team lead failed to notice the team's disengagement at all.
options.rationale: Contradicts the scenario, which states the team lead noticed the reaction.

options.text: The team lead is using storytelling to connect by keeping the presentation structured.
options.rationale: No story is involved; this is about noticing and reacting to mood, not narrative technique.

options.text: The team lead is building credibility by staying consistent with the original plan.
options.rationale: Consistency here isn't credibility; credibility involves competence and follow-through, not ignoring audience disengagement.

options.text: The team lead is reading the room but failing to adjust based on what they noticed.
options.rationale: Matches the card's common mistake exactly: noticing the shift but sticking to the script instead of changing course.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept applied to a specific, novel workplace moment, requiring the student to distinguish noticing from acting on it.

questions.question: Five minutes into a proposal, both decision makers have stopped taking notes and one has started answering email. There are twelve slides left. What should the presenter do?

options.text: Carry on to the last slide
options.rationale: Ignores the signal entirely.

options.text: Ask them to put phones away
options.rationale: Corrects the audience rather than the pitch.

options.text: Go back and cover it again
options.rationale: Repeats what lost them.

options.text: Cut to the decision they need
options.rationale: Reading the room means changing what you do with the time you have left, not pushing the plan through it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: adjust in the moment to what the room is showing.

questions.question: A junior analyst wants a department head to adopt a new reporting template. The department head is wary because a past consultant promised a similar tool would save hours and it never worked. The analyst knows the head's real worry is wasted time, not the template's features. Which approach best addresses both the trust problem and what the head actually cares about?

options.text: Offer to test the template on just one weekly report first, showing the time saved before asking for full adoption.
options.rationale: This targets the head's actual concern about wasted time while also rebuilding trust through a small, verifiable proof rather than a repeated big promise.

options.text: Point out that the previous consultant is no longer with the company, so this recommendation can be trusted instead.
options.rationale: This tries to borrow credibility by distancing from the past failure rather than demonstrating new competence through action, which doesn't address the head's real concern about time.

options.text: Assure the head that this template is different and ask them to commit to using it company-wide starting next month.
options.rationale: This repeats the same pattern that already broke trust, a big promise with no verifiable proof, and ignores the head's specific worry about wasted time.

options.text: Explain in detail how the new template's design is technically superior to the one that failed before.
options.rationale: This addresses features, not the head's underlying worry about wasted time, and does nothing to rebuild trust after a past broken promise.

notes.difficulty_justification: Answering requires simultaneously reasoning about what the department head values (interpersonal influence) and how to overcome a specific trust deficit through a small verifiable action (building credibility); a question testing either concept alone would not need both the past failure and the specific concern about time.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Interpersonal Influence, Building Credibility. Deleting Interpersonal Influence removes the reason the pilot must target 'wasted time' specifically, reducing it to a generic 'start small' credibility question. Deleting Building Credibility removes the reason a small pilot beats a bigger promise, reducing it to a generic 'find what they care about' influence question. Both are required for the correct answer to be uniquely right.

questions.question: A representative built his whole case around cost savings, which the buyer had named as her priority. In the meeting she keeps returning to how the change will land with her staff. What should he do?

options.text: Stop and rebook for another day
options.rationale: The information he needs is in the room.

options.text: Stay on cost, which she named first
options.rationale: Holds to a stated priority over a live one.

options.text: Add a discount to close it today
options.rationale: More of the argument she is leaving.

options.text: Shift the case onto the staff impact
options.rationale: The pitch was built on the right priority at the time, and what she keeps raising now is the one he has to answer.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the persuasive case was correctly built and reading the room is what tells him it has to move.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Persuasive communication, Reading the room. Without the prepared case there is nothing to redirect. Without reading the room the prepared case looks right. Both are needed.

questions.question: A consultant tells a vivid, well shaped story about a client turnaround she led. Asked afterwards, she cannot name the client, the year or a single figure from it. What is the effect?

options.text: A story too dull to hold attention
options.rationale: It held attention well.

options.text: Figures that got in the story's way
options.rationale: There were no figures.

options.text: A memorable story that is not believed
options.rationale: The story does its job on attention and, with nothing verifiable behind it, the listener has no reason to treat it as true.

options.text: A client whose privacy was breached
options.rationale: Nothing identifying was said.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the storytelling succeeds and the credibility it needs to convert into persuasion is missing.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Storytelling to connect, Building credibility. Without the story nothing is remembered. Without the verifiable detail the story persuades nobody. Both are needed.

questions.question: A manager hands an employee a new task but still requires her to get sign-off on every small choice she makes about it. What is this manager actually doing?

options.text: Mentoring the employee through hands-on coaching
options.rationale: Mentoring involves building skill and confidence over time, not approving every small decision on a handoff.

options.text: Empowering the employee by giving her a real task to complete
options.rationale: Handing over the task alone without authority is not true empowerment, this misses that piece.

options.text: Building trust by staying closely involved in the outcome
options.rationale: Trust comes from consistency and follow-through, not from requiring constant approval on someone else's task.

options.text: Micromanaging while pretending to delegate the work
options.rationale: Delegating the task without the authority to decide is really just close control with extra steps, matching the card's common mistake.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of what delegating and empowering actually requires, using one concept and one reasoning step to spot the common mistake pattern.

questions.question: At a team meeting, a manager says 'great job this month, everyone' without mentioning any names or specific actions. Why does this fall short as recognition?

options.text: It skips naming who did what, so the credit lands on no one in particular
options.rationale: The card's common mistake is generic praise that could apply to anyone instead of naming the person and their specific contribution.

options.text: It delegates the credit-giving task to the wrong person entirely
options.rationale: No delegation is happening in this scenario, this option misapplies an unrelated concept.

options.text: It rewards the whole group instead of picking favorites unfairly
options.rationale: Fairness across the group is not the issue here, the card's concern is specificity, not favoritism.

options.text: It focuses on results instead of motivating people through purpose
options.rationale: This confuses recognition with the separate concept of connecting work to purpose, which is not what the scenario is testing.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, direct recognition of why vague praise fails to meet the definition given in the card, one reasoning step from stem to answer.

questions.question: A new team lead tells the group 'everyone just help out where needed' during a busy shift instead of assigning specific roles. What is the most likely first result?

options.text: The team moves faster since nobody is boxed into one narrow job
options.rationale: This assumes flexibility helps, but the card explains vague direction usually causes stalling, not speed.

options.text: Team members feel more trusted and become more loyal to the lead
options.rationale: This confuses vague instruction with trust-building, which the cards tie to consistency and follow-through, not ambiguity.

options.text: Employees seek out mentoring since no one knows what to do
options.rationale: Confusion about tasks is not the same as a mentoring need, this misapplies an unrelated concept to the situation.

options.text: People duplicate work or wait around because no one owns a clear task
options.rationale: The card states directly that teams stall under vague leadership because people double up or wait for someone else to decide.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one direct consequence to predict from a single action, matching district-level recognition of a first-order effect.

questions.question: A manager tells the team punctuality matters and arrives late to most meetings himself. What is the team learning?

options.text: What he does, not what he says
options.rationale: A standard is set by the leader's own conduct, which is why the instruction cannot outrank it.

options.text: That the rule applies to everyone
options.rationale: It visibly does not.

options.text: That punctuality is very important
options.rationale: The behaviour says otherwise.

options.text: That meetings start whenever he says
options.rationale: A scheduling reading, not the lesson.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what carries the standard.

questions.question: A launch misses its date. In front of the client, the team lead says a junior developer fell behind. What has he failed to do?

options.text: Own what his team produced
options.rationale: Accountability means carrying the result, including the failures, rather than passing it down.

options.text: Hire a more senior developer
options.rationale: Staffing is not the response.

options.text: Set a realistic launch date
options.rationale: May be true and is not the failure shown.

options.text: Explain the delay in detail
options.rationale: He explained it; that is the problem.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the duty breached.

questions.question: A team can list this week's tasks precisely and cannot say what the project is ultimately for. What is the leader missing?

options.text: A picture of where this ends up
options.rationale: A vision is what makes today's task legible as part of something larger.

options.text: A clearer list of weekly tasks
