options.rationale: This removes the feedback conversation entirely and shifts extra work onto other already-exhausted teammates, worsening morale for the group instead of managing it.

notes.difficulty_justification: The question forces a trade-off between two mechanisms operating in the same moment: delivering specific, honest feedback while also being sensitive to a team's depleted energy. A correct answer must satisfy both conditions simultaneously, not just one.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Managing Team Morale, Constructive Feedback Exchange. Deleting Managing Team Morale turns this into a plain feedback-delivery question with no reason to reject option b's public callout. Deleting Constructive Feedback Exchange turns it into a plain morale question with no reason to reject option a's avoidance. Both concepts are load-bearing, so it passes the break test.

questions.question: Two team leads each finish a group project ahead of schedule. Lead A assigns the financial model to the numbers-strong teammate and the client pitch to the persuasive teammate, then tells the manager 'here's what we each built.' Lead B does the financial model and the pitch personally overnight because it was faster than explaining the work to teammates, then tells the manager 'we finished early.' Which statement correctly evaluates these two approaches?

options.text: Lead A practiced both matching strengths to tasks and genuine collaboration, while Lead B only used team language without team practice
options.rationale: Lead A both identified teammates' distinct strengths and used them, then credited them by name, satisfying both concepts; Lead B did the opposite of collaboration despite the plural language, which is exactly the surface-versus-practice gap the cards describe.

options.text: Neither lead showed real collaboration, since true teamwork requires every member to contribute to every task equally
options.rationale: This misapplies the concept; contributing diverse strengths specifically means people do different tasks based on what they're good at, not that everyone does the same work equally.

options.text: Both leads demonstrated teamwork equally well, since both projects were finished ahead of schedule with a team credited
options.rationale: Speed of completion isn't the standard; Lead B's use of 'we' while doing the work solo is teamwork in language only, which the cards specifically flag as a common mistake.

options.text: Lead B was more effective because finishing overnight without coordination avoided the scheduling delays that come with dividing work by strength
options.rationale: This treats speed as the goal, but doing everything solo is the definition of taking over rather than collaborating, regardless of how fast it was.

notes.difficulty_justification: The scenario requires distinguishing genuine strength-matching plus real collaboration from surface-level team language covering solo work, which needs both concepts held together to separate Lead A from Lead B rather than judging by outcome alone.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Contributing Diverse Strengths, Teamwork and Collaboration. Deleting Contributing Diverse Strengths leaves only 'did they work together or alone,' which still distinguishes the leads but loses the reasoning about why Lead A's task assignment mattered. Deleting Teamwork and Collaboration removes the basis for catching Lead B's 'we' language as false credit-sharing. Both concepts are necessary to fully justify option b over the distractors, so it passes the break test.

questions.question: What does entrepreneurial integrity mean for a business owner?

options.text: Advertising honest values while quietly cutting corners customers can't verify.
options.rationale: This is the named common mistake, treating integrity as a marketing claim rather than actual behavior.

options.text: Offering the lowest possible price no matter what quality suffers.
options.rationale: Confuses integrity with price competition, which isn't part of the concept at all.

options.text: Keeping promises to customers even when breaking them would be easier or cheaper.
options.rationale: Matches the core definition: honoring commitments even under short-term pressure to cut corners.

options.text: Following every government regulation that applies to the industry.
options.rationale: Confuses legal compliance with the separate idea of keeping personal and business promises.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, straight recognition of the definition with no applied scenario.

questions.question: What must a true social entrepreneurship venture do, beyond addressing a social problem?

options.text: Keep the mission separate from daily operations to protect profit margins.
options.rationale: This is the named common mistake of bolting a slogan onto an unchanged business model.

options.text: Generate enough revenue on its own to keep operating and growing.
options.rationale: Matches the definition directly: the mission only survives if the business stays financially self-sustaining.

options.text: Rely mainly on donations so all profit can go toward the cause.
options.rationale: Contradicts the card, which stresses the business must sustain itself rather than depend on outside giving running out.

options.text: Focus entirely on growth speed and worry about the mission later.
options.rationale: Reverses the concept, treating mission as optional rather than built into the model from the start.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, recognition of the definitional requirement without needing to apply it to a new case.

questions.question: A printer switches to recycled stock and a lower energy press, having first checked that the change still leaves the shop profitable. What is it doing?

options.text: Spending on image rather than value
options.rationale: The change is operational, not cosmetic.

options.text: Choosing the cheapest option going
options.rationale: Cost was a constraint, not the driver.

options.text: Ignoring cost to look responsible
options.rationale: Cost was checked first.

options.text: Cutting harm within sound economics
options.rationale: Sustainable practice means reducing the environmental cost while the business still makes financial sense.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what the change represents.

questions.question: A furniture maker promised a client solid oak dining chairs, but the oak shipment is delayed a month past the client's deadline. The maker considers finishing the order early using a cheaper oak veneer that looks nearly identical, without telling the client. What would acting with entrepreneurial integrity look like instead?

options.text: Advertise the shop as built on honesty and transparency to reassure the client while still substituting the veneer
options.rationale: This mirrors the common mistake of treating integrity as a marketing claim rather than an actual kept promise.

options.text: Cancel the order quietly and stop responding to the client's messages to avoid conflict
options.rationale: Avoiding the client abandons the relationship entirely rather than honoring or honestly renegotiating the commitment.

options.text: Contact the client, explain the delay, and offer a discount or the choice to wait for real solid oak
options.rationale: This keeps the promise or is honest about not being able to, matching the card's example of disclosing shortages rather than hiding them.

options.text: Ship the veneer chairs on time since the client likely won't notice the difference in materials
options.rationale: This is the exact corner-cutting the card warns against, betting on the customer not being able to verify quality.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, entrepreneurial integrity, applied to a new supply-shortage scenario requiring the student to identify which response actually keeps trust rather than defining the term.

questions.question: A founder wants to start a company selling low-cost eyeglasses to low-income communities that lack access to vision care. She has two funding options: rely entirely on annual grants that may not be renewed, or sell glasses at an affordable markup to cover costs while offering free exams through partner clinics. Which choice best reflects social entrepreneurship purpose?

options.text: Price the glasses at an affordable markup so the business funds its own mission over time
options.rationale: This matches the card's emphasis on designing revenue into the model so the social mission can keep running without depending on outside funding.

options.text: Depend on the grants since the mission is charitable and shouldn't be tied to sales revenue
options.rationale: This ignores that grants can dry up, leaving the mission unable to sustain itself, which the card treats as a real risk.

options.text: Focus on maximizing profit first and add a small optional donation feature later once the company is established
options.rationale: This treats the social mission as an afterthought rather than something baked into the core business model from the start.

options.text: Give away glasses for free indefinitely and cover losses by cutting product quality
options.rationale: Cutting quality to sustain free giving trades away the ability to keep serving the community reliably, undermining long-term impact.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, social entrepreneurship purpose, applied to a new funding decision requiring the student to judge which option sustains both mission and finances rather than recite the definition.

questions.question: A bakery owner wants to reduce plastic waste. She considers switching from plastic clamshell containers to compostable paper boxes, which cost slightly more per unit but qualify her for a local retailer's eco-friendly vendor program. What does this decision represent?

options.text: A poor decision, since any increase in per-unit cost automatically makes an operational change financially unsound
options.rationale: This ignores the card's point that higher material costs can be offset by other financial gains like new client access.

options.text: An example of social entrepreneurship purpose, since the bakery is helping the environment as its main goal
options.rationale: The bakery's core purpose is still selling baked goods; this is an operational sustainability change, not a mission built around solving a social problem.

options.text: Pure marketing, since the boxes cost more and the switch is really just about appearing eco-conscious
options.rationale: This misapplies the common mistake warning: here the operations and materials actually change, it isn't a label slapped on the same process.

options.text: A sustainable business practice, since the material change reduces waste and the added cost is offset by new business access
options.rationale: This mirrors the card's logic that switching materials to reduce environmental harm can still make financial sense through new opportunities that offset the cost.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, sustainable business practices, applied to a new packaging decision requiring the student to weigh whether the change reflects real sustainable practice rather than just defining the term.

questions.question: A founder launches a company selling reusable water bottles, pledging that profits fund clean-water wells overseas. To keep prices low enough to compete, the company sources bottles from the cheapest overseas plastic factory, which dumps untreated wastewater into a nearby river. Sales are strong and well funding grows every quarter. What is the core problem with this business?

options.text: The mission is funding real social good, so the manufacturing method the company chooses does not affect whether the business is doing good overall
options.rationale: This is the trap: it assumes strong financial results and a funded mission automatically validate the whole operation, ignoring the environmental harm baked into production.

options.text: The company is pursuing a genuine social mission while running operations that cause the kind of environmental harm sustainable practice is meant to prevent
options.rationale: This names the actual tension: a real, funded social purpose can still coexist with unsustainable operations, and one doesn't cancel out the other.

options.text: The wells being funded overseas are unrelated to the bottle factory's own local environment
options.rationale: This treats geographic mismatch as the flaw, but the real issue is the operations themselves causing harm, not where the social benefit lands.

options.text: The company should stop funding wells and instead lower prices further to sell more bottles
options.rationale: This suggests abandoning the mission entirely, which misreads the problem as the mission being wasteful rather than the sourcing being harmful.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding two concepts at once: a genuinely funded social mission versus operational sustainability, and recognizing that success in one doesn't guarantee soundness in the other. Neither concept alone resolves the scenario.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Social Entrepreneurship Purpose and Sustainable Business Practices. Deleting Social Entrepreneurship Purpose leaves only a pollution problem, a state-level sustainability question. Deleting Sustainable Business Practices leaves only 'is the mission real,' which the scenario already answers yes to, making the question trivial. Both are needed for the tension to exist, so it holds as icdc.

questions.question: A founder promises on every product page that orders ship completely plastic free. In the December rush the paper tape runs out and she quietly uses plastic tape for three weeks, telling nobody. What is the position?

options.text: A promise that was never realistic
options.rationale: She kept it for the rest of the year.

options.text: A sustainability gain either way
options.rationale: Ignores what was promised.

options.text: A quiet break in a public promise
options.rationale: The environmental slip is small and the silence about it is what damages the thing customers were actually buying.

options.text: A sensible response to a shortage
options.rationale: The substitution may be; the silence is not.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the sustainability commitment and the integrity of keeping a public promise come apart, and the second is the greater breach.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Sustainable business practices, Entrepreneurial integrity and trust. Without the public pledge the tape is a minor matter. Without the quiet substitution the pledge holds. Both are needed.

questions.question: A venture set up to train and employ care leavers has run at a loss for three years on donor top-ups, tells every applicant the jobs are permanent, and has no route to covering its own costs. What is the issue?

options.text: A social aim that is not worth having
options.rationale: The aim is not in question.

options.text: Training that costs more than it should
options.rationale: Cost per trainee is not given.

options.text: Donors who should give much more
options.rationale: Deeper dependence is not a fix.

options.text: A mission with no way to fund itself
options.rationale: A social venture has to earn enough to keep running, and promising permanence on money that may stop is a promise it cannot back.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the social purpose is real and the promise made on the back of it is only as good as the venture's ability to fund itself.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Social entrepreneurship purpose, Entrepreneurial integrity and trust. Without the funding gap the promise is safe. Without the promise the shortfall is a planning problem. Both are needed.

questions.question: A founder notices strong evidence that customers want something different from the original plan. What does pivoting mean in this situation?

options.text: Repeating the same strategy but with a bigger marketing budget.
options.rationale: This ignores the evidence instead of responding to it.

options.text: Waiting quietly until the market eventually comes around to the original idea.
options.rationale: This is stubbornness, the opposite of pivoting.

options.text: Shutting the business down entirely and starting over from scratch.
options.rationale: Misconception: treats a pivot as total abandonment rather than a targeted change.

options.text: Adjusting the specific part of the plan that the evidence says isn't working.
options.rationale: Matches the card's definition: changing course based on evidence, not scrapping everything.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, direct recognition of what pivoting means, one reasoning step from definition to correct behavior.

questions.question: Why might a business owner choose franchising instead of opening every new location with their own money?

options.text: It removes the need for a proven and consistent system first.
options.rationale: A system is exactly what a franchisee is buying.

options.text: It gives the owner tight control of daily operations at each site.
options.rationale: Franchising trades some of that control away.

options.text: It lets the owner expand quickly on other people's capital.
options.rationale: Each operator funds their own site, so the brand grows faster than the owner's own balance sheet would allow.

options.text: It lets the owner keep every dollar of profit from the new locations.
options.rationale: The franchisee keeps most of it; that is the trade.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, recognition of the core tradeoff franchising offers, one reasoning step.

questions.question: A bakery's new weekend pop-up event loses money for a month. The owner reviews the sales data, finds the problem, and changes the event's format before trying again. What does this response show?

options.text: Pivoting, because the owner abandoned the bakery business for a new venture.
options.rationale: The bakery kept operating and only adjusted one event, so this isn't a pivot away from the core business.

options.text: Scaling, because the owner is preparing systems for higher future volume.
options.rationale: Nothing here involves preparing for growth in volume or staffing, just fixing a losing event.

options.text: Stubbornness, because the owner kept running events despite losing money.
options.rationale: The owner changed the format based on data, which is the opposite of stubbornly repeating the same thing.

options.text: Resilience, because the setback was treated as data and led to a specific change.
options.rationale: Matches the card's definition: reviewing data and adjusting approach rather than quitting or repeating blindly.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, applying the definition of resilience to identify it correctly in a short scenario, one reasoning step.

questions.question: A boutique gym has one owner who personally designs every client's workout plan. Bookings have tripled after a viral video, and the waitlist keeps growing. What is the best next step to actually support this growth?

options.text: Create a standard plan template and train other coaches to deliver it consistently.
options.rationale: This builds a repeatable system so the business can handle more clients without the owner personally being the constraint, which is the core of scaling.

options.text: Raise session prices so fewer new clients try to join each month.
options.rationale: This limits demand rather than building the system needed to serve more clients, so it avoids the scaling problem instead of solving it.

options.text: Keep taking every new client personally to protect the quality clients are used to.
options.rationale: This is the exact bottleneck the card warns about, one person's capacity does not stretch to match higher volume.

options.text: Run more ads to bring in even more new clients before making any other changes.
options.rationale: Adding more demand on top of an already strained one-person system makes the bottleneck worse, not better.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (Growth and Scaling) applied to a new scenario, requiring the student to identify what internal capacity needs to change rather than just recognizing the term.

questions.question: A founder launched an app to help college students split rent and utility bills. After six months, almost no students sign up, but customer support keeps getting messages from small landlords asking if the app can track late fees and lease renewals too. What is the clearest example of pivoting here?

options.text: Redesigning the app's features around landlord needs like late fees and lease tracking.
options.rationale: This changes the specific part of the plan that the evidence shows isn't working, the target user and features, while keeping the core business alive, matching the definition of a pivot.

options.text: Waiting another six months to see if student sign-ups pick up on their own.
options.rationale: This is passively hoping rather than acting on the evidence, which does not change course at all.

options.text: Running more ads aimed at college students to try to boost the original sign-up numbers.
options.rationale: This ignores the evidence and doubles down on the plan that isn't working, the opposite of pivoting.

options.text: Shutting the app down completely since students never adopted it.
options.rationale: This treats the setback as a reason to quit entirely rather than redirecting toward the audience evidence points to, which is not what pivoting means.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (Pivoting When Needed) applied to a new business situation, requiring the student to distinguish a true evidence-based pivot from quitting or ignoring the signal.

questions.question: A founder's first product launch flops badly, selling eleven units against a forecast of four hundred. What response fits the skill?

options.text: Close the business and move on
options.rationale: Abandons on one data point.

options.text: Blame the market for not being ready
options.rationale: Learns nothing from the result.

options.text: Relaunch the same product louder
options.rationale: Repeats the attempt unchanged.

options.text: Work out what the flop taught her
options.rationale: A setback is information about the assumptions, and using it is what separates resilience from stubbornness.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: pick the response that converts failure into information.

questions.question: A taco shop owner wants to franchise to new operators, but every sale so far has closed only because the owner personally charms each customer with no set script or steps. What should happen before franchising moves forward?

options.text: Franchise only to operators who already ran a food truck somewhere else.
options.rationale: Outside experience doesn't fix the core issue: there's still no documented sales process for any operator to follow, experienced or not.

options.text: Skip franchising and license the taco recipe to a food manufacturer instead.
options.rationale: Licensing solves a different problem, production and distribution reach, not the missing sales process that franchising would expose.

options.text: Document the sales approach into repeatable steps first, then franchise the proven system.
options.rationale: Franchising spreads a system to independent owners, so the underlying process must be repeatable and documented before it can be handed off successfully.

options.text: Franchise now, since new owners will naturally develop their own charm and style over time.
options.rationale: Assumes personal charm transfers without a system, ignoring that franchising multiplies whatever process already exists, good or bad.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding two concepts at once: franchising depends on having a repeatable process, and the student must judge that the sales side isn't yet systematized, a single-concept question could not test this dependency.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Franchising as a Growth Path, Building Repeatable Sales Processes. Deleting franchising leaves just 'should you document your sales process,' which loses the reason why it matters right now. Deleting repeatable sales processes leaves 'should you franchise,' with no reason to say no. Both are needed, question holds.

questions.question: A consultancy's founder has closed every deal herself, through long relationships and instinct. She hires four salespeople to grow faster, and revenue per head collapses within two quarters. What was missing?

options.text: Fewer hires in the first year
options.rationale: One hire would fail the same way.

options.text: A larger marketing budget to help
options.rationale: Leads are not the described failure.

options.text: Salespeople with more experience
options.rationale: Experience cannot guess her method.

options.text: Her instinct written down as steps
options.rationale: Growing past the founder means the thing she does well has to exist as a process someone else can follow.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: scaling requires knowing what has to change, and the answer here is that the sales method had to become repeatable first.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Growth and scaling, Building repeatable sales processes. Without the hiring push nothing exposes the gap. Without the missing process the new hires could sell. Both are needed.

questions.question: A sauce maker wants her recipe on shelves nationwide. She has no wish to fund new sites and no interest in supervising how anybody else runs a business. Which path fits?

options.text: Hire staff to run other kitchens
options.rationale: Still her business to run.

options.text: Franchise restaurants under her name
options.rationale: Franchising commits her to supervising operators.

options.text: License the recipe to a producer
options.rationale: Licensing sells the right to use the asset and leaves the operating work with the other party, which is exactly what she is unwilling to take on.

options.text: Open kitchens in each new region
options.rationale: The funding she ruled out.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the two expansion routes differ in who funds and who supervises, and the constraints pick between them.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Licensing for expansion, Franchising as a growth path. Without the franchising option there is nothing to choose against. Without the licensing option her constraints rule everything out. Both are needed.

questions.question: What is the main reason a business builds a rough prototype before making the final version of a product?

options.text: It lets the team catch flaws cheaply before spending big money on the finished version.
options.rationale: This matches the core purpose of prototyping: cheap testing before heavy investment.

options.text: It lets the team skip customer feedback since the design is already mostly finished.
options.rationale: This inverts the point; prototypes exist to gather feedback, not avoid it.

options.text: It lets the team impress investors with a polished, market-ready item.
options.rationale: A prototype is meant to be rough and testable, not polished for show.

options.text: It lets the team lock in a factory contract before the design is tested.
options.rationale: Locking in production early is the opposite of what a rough test version is meant to prevent.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of a single concept's core purpose with one reasoning step, no application to a novel scenario required.

questions.question: In the design thinking process, what should a business do before building any solution?

options.text: Select the cheapest materials so the launch costs stay as low as possible.
options.rationale: Cost of materials isn't the focus of design thinking; understanding the customer's pain is.

options.text: Finalize the product features based on what competitors already offer.
options.rationale: This skips customer research entirely and just copies rivals.

options.text: Build the full, finished version to see how customers react to it.
options.rationale: This is the mistake of jumping to a final build instead of testing cheap and rough first.

options.text: Gather deep understanding of the customer's real problem through direct contact.
options.rationale: Design thinking starts with empathizing to find the true underlying pain point.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, direct recall of the process's starting step, requiring only plain logic about sequence.

questions.question: Which move best fits the idea of disruptive innovation thinking?

options.text: Matching every feature of the market leader at the exact same price point.
options.rationale: Matching the leader head to head is direct competition, not the underserved-segment approach.

options.text: Offering a simpler, cheaper option that reaches customers the big players currently ignore.
options.rationale: This matches the core idea of winning by serving overlooked customers with something simpler and cheaper.

options.text: Releasing a flashy upgrade aimed at the same wealthy customers rivals already serve.
options.rationale: A flashy product for the same top customers is just a better version, not a disruptive entry.

options.text: Adding more premium features to beat rivals in the high-end market segment.
options.rationale: This describes competing head-on for high-end customers, not serving an overlooked group.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, recognition of which action fits the definition versus common look-alike moves, one reasoning step.

questions.question: A founder wants to test a new backpack design with a built-in phone charger. Before ordering factory samples, which move best fits the point of prototyping?

options.text: Hire a design firm to build a polished, retail-ready sample first
options.rationale: Polishing the sample before testing invites polite feedback instead of the blunt reactions that catch real flaws, and costs far more upfront.

options.text: Sew a rough sample by hand and let ten hikers try it on a weekend trip
options.rationale: Correct: a cheap, rough version tested with real users before investing in a factory run is exactly the prototyping mechanism.

options.text: Order a small factory batch of 50 units to sell online right away
options.rationale: Committing to a factory batch before testing skips the cheap trial step and risks the exact wasted spending prototyping is meant to avoid.

options.text: Survey hikers about what features they'd want in an ideal backpack
options.rationale: This is gathering opinions, not building and testing a physical rough version, so it skips the core prototyping action.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (prototyping) applied to a new, specific product situation requiring the student to identify the correct low-cost testing action rather than just define the term.

questions.question: A software company builds a stripped-down accounting tool priced at $10 a month for solo freelancers who currently use paper ledgers, while big competitors sell $200 a month suites to large firms. What does this move represent?

options.text: Prototyping, since it tests a rough version before building the final product
options.rationale: There's no mention of a rough test version here, only a full pricing and market strategy already being executed.

options.text: Creative problem solving, since it finds an original fix to a business complaint
options.rationale: This describes generating a fresh fix to an internal problem, not the specific pattern of undercutting incumbents by serving an ignored segment.

options.text: Disruptive innovation, since it wins an overlooked group with a simpler, cheaper option
options.rationale: Correct: targeting an ignored segment with a simpler, cheaper alternative to the incumbents' offering matches the disruption mechanism.

options.text: A design thinking approach, since it starts by deeply interviewing customers
options.rationale: No customer interviews or empathy research are described; the scenario only shows a market-segment and pricing decision.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (disruptive innovation) applied to a new pricing and market-segment scenario, requiring the student to recognize the underserved-segment pattern rather than recall a definition.

questions.question: A gym's app has low usage, and the owner is about to redesign the app's home screen layout. Following the design thinking process, what should happen first?

options.text: Interview members to find out what's actually stopping them from opening the app
options.rationale: Correct: design thinking starts by deeply understanding the customer's real pain before jumping to a solution.

options.text: Copy the layout of the most popular fitness app on the market
options.rationale: Copying a competitor's design without investigating this gym's specific members' pain point bypasses the customer-understanding step entirely.

options.text: Lower the app's monthly fee to attract more downloads
options.rationale: This addresses pricing, not the underlying usage problem, and isn't grounded in any customer research about the actual pain point.

options.text: Hire a developer to rebuild the home screen with a cleaner layout right away
options.rationale: Building a solution before confirming the real problem skips the empathize step, the classic design thinking mistake.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (design thinking) applied to a fresh product scenario, requiring the student to sequence the correct first action rather than recall the process's name or steps abstractly.

questions.question: A meal kit startup with rising cancellations plans to spend six weeks building a polished new app before speaking to anyone who left. What does the process say to do instead?

options.text: Interview churned users, then test a rough version
options.rationale: Understand the real pain first, then put the cheapest possible version in front of people before committing six weeks.

options.text: Redesign the packaging before touching the app at all
options.rationale: Picks a solution before the problem has been identified, which is the same error in a different place.

options.text: Build the polished app, then survey the users who left
options.rationale: Reverses the order, so the expensive work happens before the learning.

options.text: Run a discount to win back the cancelled subscribers
options.rationale: Buys back churn without finding out what caused it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the process sets the order of learning, prototyping sets how much to build before testing.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Design Thinking Process, Prototyping New Concepts. Without the process, a rough build is still a build aimed at a guessed problem. Without prototyping, interviews alone leave the team building the polished app anyway. The answer needs the sequence and the fidelity together.

questions.question: A dental equipment startup cannot match the imaging features that established brands sell to hospitals at $80,000. Rural clinics currently buy nothing at all. Which path fits disruption?

options.text: A simpler, cheaper unit the rural clinics can afford
options.rationale: Serves customers the leaders ignore with a good enough product, which is the foothold disruption actually describes.

options.text: A rental plan letting hospitals spread the $80,000
options.rationale: A financing idea aimed at the incumbent's customers, not an overlooked market.

options.text: A discount on the same specification as the leaders
options.rationale: Price cutting into the same segment invites a response the startup cannot survive.

options.text: A premium unit with two features the leaders lack
options.rationale: Out-featuring the leader on its own ground, which the card names as the losing battle.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: an unserved market is only an opening if the solution is reframed as simpler rather than better.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Disruptive Innovation Thinking, Creative Problem Solving. Without disruption, rural clinics are just a smaller segment and the premium unit looks reasonable. Without the reframing, the startup keeps trying to solve the hospital problem more cheaply. Each deletion makes a different wrong option defensible.

questions.question: A food truck loses about 40 percent of its revenue on rainy days. The owner's first instinct is to buy a bigger tent. What would a fresh look at the problem test first?

options.text: Selling from the office lobby next door on wet days
options.rationale: Reframes the problem from keeping customers dry outside to moving the truck's service where they already are, and it can be trialled in a day.

options.text: A larger tent that covers the whole queue area
options.rationale: The obvious first idea, scaled up. It spends money without questioning the frame.

options.text: A rain discount to pull customers out in the wet
options.rationale: Pays people to do the thing they have already shown they will not do.

options.text: Closing on forecast rain days to save staff cost
options.rationale: Accepts the lost revenue as fixed rather than treating it as a problem to solve.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: reframing produces a non-obvious option, and the process insists it be tested cheaply before commitment.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Creative Problem Solving, Design Thinking Process. Without the reframing every option is a variation on staying dry outdoors. Without the process the lobby idea is an untested leap rather than a trial. Removing either leaves the tent looking sensible.

questions.question: A founder describes a new blender by listing its motor wattage, blade material, and sleek design, but never says who needs it or why. What is missing from this pitch?

options.text: A breakdown of who pays the company and how often revenue arrives
options.rationale: This describes revenue logic, a separate concept about cash flow, not the missing customer focus.

options.text: A description of the channel used to get the blender to buyers
options.rationale: This describes distribution, which is about the path to market, not the missing pain-point framing.

options.text: A explanation of why rivals cannot easily copy the blender design
options.rationale: This describes competitive advantage, which is about defensibility, not naming the customer's problem.

options.text: A clear statement of the specific customer and the pain the product solves
options.rationale: This is exactly the value proposition gap: naming who has the pain and what pain it solves.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, direct recognition of what a value proposition requires versus a feature list; one reasoning step.

questions.question: Which statement would satisfy an investor asking about a startup's revenue logic?

options.text: Users will love the app so much that growth will follow naturally
options.rationale: Passion and expected love for the product is not a cash flow explanation, the classic mistake of substituting enthusiasm for numbers.

options.text: No other scheduling app offers this particular integration with calendars
options.rationale: This describes a competitive edge, not whether the business actually generates enough cash to survive.

options.text: Customers pay $10 monthly, and that covers hosting and support costs at current volume
options.rationale: This names who pays, how much, how often, and shows it covers costs, the exact definition of revenue logic.

options.text: The app targets busy professionals who currently have no good scheduling tool
options.rationale: This describes a customer segment and pain point, not how money actually flows into the business.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, direct recognition of what counts as an actual revenue explanation versus other adjacent claims; one reasoning step.

questions.question: A founder moves from describing her market as pet owners to describing it as owners of elderly dogs who need mobility aids. What has she done?

options.text: Cut her market too far down
options.rationale: Judges the move rather than naming it.

options.text: Priced her offer for the group
options.rationale: No price has been set.

options.text: Chosen a product to sell them
options.rationale: The product is not the change here.

options.text: Found a niche inside a market
options.rationale: She has split a broad market and picked out a smaller group with a shared, specific need.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the move.

questions.question: A founder wants to know whether anyone will pay for an app that matches dog walkers to owners. What is the smallest honest test?

options.text: A survey asking whether they would
options.rationale: Opinions, not paying customers.

options.text: A booking form she matches by hand
options.rationale: An MVP is the simplest build that still tests the core idea with real customers before the full product exists.

options.text: The finished app with every feature
options.rationale: Spends everything before the test.

options.text: A pitch deck shown to investors
options.rationale: Tests investors, not demand.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: pick the smallest real test.

questions.question: A meal kit startup's whole offer rests on one regional farm supplying its produce. What does the model have to treat that farm as?

options.text: A dependency to secure properly
options.rationale: A partner the business genuinely relies on has to be identified as such and the relationship built to hold.

options.text: One vendor among many options
options.rationale: Understates what the offer rests on.

options.text: A competitor in the same market
options.rationale: They are not competing.

options.text: A cost to be squeezed each year
options.rationale: Pressures the thing it depends on.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: classify the relationship.

questions.question: A team spends eight months polishing features before showing anyone. What does the MVP idea say they got wrong?

options.text: Building before testing the idea
options.rationale: The point is to learn from real customers early, while changing course is still cheap.

options.text: Launching the product too early
options.rationale: They launched very late.

options.text: Polishing the features too little
options.rationale: Polish is what they over-invested in.

options.text: Hiring too few engineers for it
options.rationale: Headcount is not the lesson.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the sequencing error.

questions.question: A founder launches a bubble tea shop and tells investors their edge is being the first bubble tea shop in a growing suburb. Why is this a weak competitive advantage?

options.text: The suburb's customers do not have a clear enough value proposition to respond to
options.rationale: Value proposition is a separate concept about naming customer pain, not the reason first-mover status fails as an advantage.

options.text: The shop has not picked a specific customer niche within the suburb yet
options.rationale: This confuses segmentation with defensibility; lacking a niche is a different issue from an advantage being copyable.

options.text: Bubble tea is a low-margin product so profits will always stay thin
options.rationale: Margin concerns relate to revenue logic, not to whether the advantage is defensible.

options.text: Being first is easy for a well-funded rival to match once they see the suburb is profitable
options.rationale: Matches the card's core point that first-mover status fades and offers nothing hard to replicate, letting bigger competitors copy or undercut it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept (competitive advantage) applied to a new, specific scenario to judge why a stated edge fails to hold up, requiring the mechanism rather than the definition.

questions.question: A small candle maker is deciding between selling through a national home-goods chain, which demands a big listing fee and takes a large cut, versus selling directly on her own website at a much higher margin but smaller reach. What does this situation illustrate about channel choice?

options.text: Wider reach and higher margin retention usually trade off against each other
options.rationale: The chain buys volume with a listing fee and a cut; direct keeps the margin and has to find the customers itself.

options.text: The choice mainly shapes which segment competitors think is being targeted
options.rationale: Perception is not what the decision turns on.

options.text: The channel with the broadest reach is worth its fees in most cases
options.rationale: States one side of the trade as if it settled it.

options.text: Selling direct brings in more total revenue than a retail chain does
options.rationale: Higher margin per unit, usually on far fewer units.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires applying the single concept of distribution channel trade-offs to a new product scenario, judging how reach and margin interact for this specific founder rather than defining the term.

questions.question: A founder intends her bakery to be a regional wholesale supplier within five years. This month she signs a ten year lease on a unit with no loading access and no room for a second oven. What is the problem?

options.text: Wholesale is the wrong ambition
options.rationale: The ambition is not in question.

options.text: A choice that blocks the plan
options.rationale: A long-term picture is only useful if today's commitments are checked against it before they are signed.

options.text: The lease is priced above market
options.rationale: Price is not mentioned.

options.text: Five years is too long a horizon
options.rationale: A five year view is reasonable.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: test a present decision against the stated destination.

questions.question: A subscription box depends on one printer for its custom packaging, on a handshake, with no written terms and no alternative identified. What should the founder do?

options.text: Negotiate a lower price per box
options.rationale: Price is not the exposure.

options.text: Put terms on it and find a backup
options.rationale: A dependency this central has to be made reliable, which means agreed terms and something to fall back on.

options.text: Change to plain packaging instead
options.rationale: Gives up the offer to dodge the risk.

options.text: Order a year of packaging now
options.rationale: Ties up cash and still single sources.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: secure a relationship the model depends on.

questions.question: A founder's MVP is a landing page with a buy button that takes a card and then apologises that stock has sold out. What does this test that a sign-up form would not?

options.text: Whether the product can be built
options.rationale: Feasibility is a separate question.

options.text: Whether people will actually pay
options.rationale: Reaching for a card is a far stronger signal than registering interest, which is what makes it a test of the core idea.

options.text: What the product should cost
options.rationale: One price is being shown, not tested.

options.text: How many people visit the page
options.rationale: Traffic is measured either way.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: judge what a given test actually establishes.

questions.question: A startup lists nineteen suppliers as key partners in its model, including the firm that services the office coffee machine. What is the problem?

options.text: The model should list no partners
options.rationale: Key partners belong in it.

options.text: Nineteen suppliers is far too many
options.rationale: Count is not the issue.

options.text: The coffee service is underpriced
options.rationale: Price is irrelevant here.

options.text: Nothing is marked as truly critical
options.rationale: The point of naming key partners is to separate the few the business genuinely depends on from ordinary vendors.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: distinguish dependency from vendor.

questions.question: A small-batch candle maker sells direct online at 65% margin, covering costs at current volume. A national retail chain offers shelf space but takes a 45% cut and charges a $10,000 slotting fee per store. The founder wants to accept, reasoning the retail deal will get the candles 'in front of way more people.' What is the strongest concern with that reasoning?

options.text: Retail shelf space always signals a stronger competitive advantage than direct sales ever could.
options.rationale: Confuses distribution reach with competitive advantage; shelf space alone isn't hard for competitors to copy or a source of defensibility.

options.text: Retail distribution requires abandoning the long-term vision of becoming a recognized candle brand.
options.rationale: Retail placement could actually support a brand-recognition vision; this doesn't address the actual margin math problem described.

options.text: The customer segment served by retail stores is fundamentally different from the online candle-buying niche.
options.rationale: Introduces a segmentation concern not supported by the scenario, which is about margin and fees, not customer mismatch.

options.text: Wider reach doesn't matter if the new margin and fees no longer cover the costs that made the current model work.
options.rationale: Correctly connects channel choice to revenue logic: reach is worthless if the resulting cash flow can't cover costs anymore.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding distribution channel trade-offs and revenue logic together: the student must see that a channel decision only makes sense if the resulting margin still clears costs, not just because it increases reach.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Distribution Channel Choices, Business Model and Revenue Logic. Deleting Distribution Channel Choices removes the retail-vs-direct decision entirely, leaving no scenario. Deleting Business Model and Revenue Logic removes the reason wider reach could be wrong, leaving only a reach question with no cost check. Both are needed, so the question survives the break test.

questions.question: Two founders both target 'apartment renters with small dogs' as their niche. Founder A's only pitch is that they found this niche first. Founder B has the same niche but has signed 3-year exclusive supply deals with the two largest apartment management companies in the city. Six months later, a larger competitor enters the same niche. Which founder is better protected, and why?

options.text: Founder A, because being first to identify an underserved niche is itself difficult for a competitor to replicate.
options.rationale: Treats first-mover status as durable protection, which the cards explicitly flag as easy for a competitor to match or beat.

options.text: Founder A, because niche discovery naturally leads to lower costs that a later entrant cannot match.
options.rationale: Assumes a cost advantage that was never established; nothing in the scenario ties niche discovery to lower costs.

options.text: Both are equally protected, since choosing the same underserved niche already limits how many competitors can enter it.
options.rationale: A niche identification alone doesn't block entry; the scenario shows a competitor entering the same niche regardless.

options.text: Founder B, because the exclusive contracts create a real barrier the competitor can't copy just by targeting the same niche.
options.rationale: Correctly shows that identifying a niche is not the same as defending it; only the exclusive contracts create switching costs for a rival.

notes.difficulty_justification: Forces the student to see that picking a good niche and holding a defensible advantage are separate steps; a well-chosen segment alone provides no protection without something a rival can't easily replicate.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Customer Segments and Niches, Competitive Advantage. Deleting Customer Segments and Niches removes the shared-niche setup, but the comparison of exclusive contracts vs. first-mover claims still needs a competitive advantage argument; deleting Competitive Advantage removes the reason one founder is protected, collapsing the question to just 'who found the niche,' which has no clear answer. Both concepts are load-bearing.

questions.question: A founder's offer names exactly who benefits and how, in one sentence an investor can repeat back. Every part of it could be reproduced by an established rival inside a month. What does the investor need to hear next?

options.text: How much the product will cost
options.rationale: Price does not answer defensibility.

options.text: Who the offer is actually built for
options.rationale: That is already stated clearly.

options.text: What benefit the customer receives
options.rationale: Also already covered.

options.text: Why the rival will not simply copy it
options.rationale: A clear proposition says the offer is worth having, and the separate question is why this company keeps it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: a strong value proposition and a weak competitive position are different questions, and the pitch answers only one.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Value proposition, Competitive advantage. Without the clear proposition there is nothing worth defending. Without the defensibility question the proposition looks sufficient. Both are needed.

questions.question: A founder spots a genuine gap in same-day prescription delivery and builds a stripped-down version in three weeks to test it. Her MVP leaves out the pharmacist verification step, which is the part regulators and customers care about most. What is wrong?

options.text: Three weeks is too fast to build
options.rationale: Speed is the point of an MVP.

options.text: The cut version no longer tests the gap
options.rationale: An MVP has to keep whatever makes the opportunity real, so stripping out the piece the need depends on means the test answers a different question.

options.text: An MVP with too many features in it
options.rationale: It is stripped down already.

options.text: A gap that was never actually there
options.rationale: The need is described as genuine.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: what the opportunity rests on determines what the minimum version cannot leave out.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Opportunity recognition, Minimum viable product design. Without the identified gap there is nothing the test must preserve. Without the MVP there is no cutting decision. Both are needed.

questions.question: A founder's whole opportunity is that she can deliver rare imported ingredients within a day, something nobody local does. The only courier able to do that also serves her two likely competitors and has no exclusivity with her. What is the exposure?

options.text: Ingredients that are too hard to get
options.rationale: She can get them.

options.text: A courier that charges her too much
options.rationale: Price is not what is at stake.

options.text: An opportunity nobody else can see
options.rationale: Competitors are already near it.

options.text: The edge belongs to the courier
options.rationale: When the thing that makes the opportunity real sits with a partner anyone can hire, the advantage is rented rather than owned.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the opportunity and the partner it depends on have to be read together before the real exposure is visible.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Opportunity recognition, Key partnerships and suppliers. Without the identified opportunity the courier is an ordinary vendor. Without the shared partner the edge holds. Both are needed.

questions.question: An MVP works beautifully because the founder personally hand-finishes each unit overnight. Demand is proven and no supplier has been found who can do that finishing at volume. What has the test established?

options.text: That the business cannot work at all
options.rationale: Demand is real and the gap is solvable.

options.text: Demand, and nothing about delivery
options.rationale: A minimum version is allowed to fake the back end, and what it proves is the appetite, which leaves the partner question entirely open.

options.text: That the MVP was built too well
options.rationale: Quality is not the fault.

options.text: That the founder should keep finishing
options.rationale: Does not survive volume.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the MVP proves one thing and the supplier question is the separate thing it deliberately did not test.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Minimum viable product design, Key partnerships and suppliers. Without the MVP there is no proven demand. Without the supply gap the proof carries straight into a business. Both are needed.

questions.question: A founder keeps a list of fifty impressive names she has met at conferences, but she has never scheduled a real conversation with any of them. What mistake is she making with her mentor network?

options.text: She is mistaking contacts for actual relationships
options.rationale: Correct: the card defines this exact common mistake, collecting names without setting up real recurring conversations.

options.text: She is meeting mentors too frequently
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario suggests over-meeting; she isn't meeting them at all.

options.text: She has too many mentors from the same industry
options.rationale: Distracts by referencing the 3:1:1 mix idea, but her problem is lack of contact, not the mix of mentor types.

options.text: She is only asking for help during emergencies
options.rationale: This describes the industry-contacts mistake of only reaching out when in urgent need, not the mentor-network mistake described here.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of a single defined concept, the common mistake of mistaking contacts for relationships, one step of reasoning.

questions.question: A founder attends a startup mixer and spends the evening chatting with as many attendees as possible, without a specific goal for any conversation. What is the likely result, based on the concept?

options.text: She will automatically double her response rate from follow-up emails
options.rationale: Misapplies the follow-up timing detail, which concerns responding within 24 hours, not the number of people met.

options.text: She will mostly waste the evening without gaining real leads
options.rationale: Correct: the card explains random mingling usually just burns an evening compared to targeted, intentional conversations.

options.text: She will generate the most valuable leads of anyone at the event
options.rationale: Contradicts the card, which says intentional networking, not volume, produces valuable leads.

options.text: She will secure a warm introduction to an investor's portfolio founder
options.rationale: That specific outcome came from a targeted, prepared approach in the example, not from unfocused mingling.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, predicting the first-order consequence of unfocused networking versus intentional networking, one reasoning step.

questions.question: A founder needs a reliable contract manufacturer within a month, and she already knows three people whose businesses use one. What should she do?

options.text: Attend a manufacturing trade show
options.rationale: Builds contacts she already has.

options.text: Search online and compare quotes
options.rationale: Slower, and with no track record attached.

options.text: Ask them who they use and why
options.rationale: People already in the industry can hand over a vetted answer that no amount of searching would produce as fast.

options.text: Post the requirement on her site
options.rationale: Waits for whoever happens to look.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: use the contacts already available.

questions.question: A founder is attending a fintech mixer tomorrow evening. Which preparation matches the skill?

options.text: Set a target of fifty business cards collected
options.rationale: The numbers game the card explicitly warns against.

options.text: Arrive late so the room is already warmed up
options.rationale: A tactic about comfort that serves no stated goal.

options.text: Print a long deck to hand to anyone who listens
options.rationale: Volume of material, aimed at nobody in particular.

options.text: Pick three investors to meet and prep a short pitch
options.rationale: A named target and a rehearsed ask is what turns an evening into leads rather than contacts.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose the preparation that fits an intentional approach to one event.

questions.question: A new food truck needs a wholesale produce account, but suppliers want a $500 weekly minimum it cannot meet. A former classmate buys produce for three restaurants. What is the move?

options.text: Ask her to co-sign the first supplier invoice
options.rationale: A financial guarantee far beyond what the relationship supports.

options.text: Ask her to add the truck's order to her own
options.rationale: Puts her account and her credit at risk, which is asking for a favour rather than a connection.

options.text: Ask her what she pays, then negotiate alone
options.rationale: Uses the information but leaves the leverage, the referral itself, unused.

options.text: Ask her for an introduction to her supplier
options.rationale: A warm referral is what gets a small buyer terms that a cold call would not, which is the point of the relationship.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: convert a relationship into a specific, proportionate ask.

questions.question: A founder lists eleven well known names as her mentors, but has never scheduled a conversation with any of them. What does the skill actually require?

options.text: A formal agreement signed by each mentor
options.rationale: Formality is not the missing ingredient; contact is.

options.text: A longer list covering more of the industry
options.rationale: More names deepen the collecting problem rather than fixing it.

options.text: One mentor who can introduce all the others
options.rationale: Introductions are a contacts question, not what makes someone a mentor.

options.text: A few recurring conversations, not a list
options.rationale: A mentor relationship is defined by the repeated contact, which is exactly what the impressive list lacks.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: separate a real mentor network from a list of names.

questions.question: At a mixer, a founder has a genuinely useful first conversation with an operator whose background fits her routing problem exactly, and leaves with his card. What turns him into a mentor rather than a contact?

options.text: A request for an introduction to his investors
options.rationale: Spends the relationship immediately on a different goal, before it exists.

options.text: A follow up email thanking him for his time
options.rationale: Good practice for a contact, but it ends the exchange rather than continuing it.

options.text: A standing call she schedules within the week
options.rationale: Recurring, scheduled contact is the difference between a good conversation and a mentor relationship.

options.text: An invitation to the next event in the series
options.rationale: Another one-off encounter, which is the pattern being escaped.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the event supplies the meeting, the mentor skill supplies what has to happen after it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Networking at Startup Events, Building a Mentor Network. Without the event framing there is no cold meeting to convert. Without the mentor rule, a thank you note is a perfectly good ending. The answer sits exactly where one hands off to the other.

questions.question: A founder needs a supplier introduction this week from a contact she has not spoken to in two years, and she also hopes that contact becomes a long term advisor. What does the silence cost her?

options.text: The contact has probably left the industry
options.rationale: Assumes a fact the case does not provide.

options.text: The supplier will refuse a cold referral
options.rationale: The supplier has no view of how warm the internal relationship is.

options.text: The introduction will take longer to arrange
options.rationale: Timing is a small cost next to how the request now lands.

options.text: The ask now reads as transactional, not mutual
options.rationale: Contacts maintained only at the moment of need are the trap in both skills: it weakens this ask and forecloses the ongoing relationship.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the immediate favour and the long term advisor role are damaged by the same neglect, which is what the question turns on.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Leveraging Industry Contacts, Building a Mentor Network. Without the immediate ask the silence is merely a missed friendship. Without the advisor ambition it is a one-time awkwardness with no lasting cost. Holding both is what makes the neglect expensive twice over.

questions.question: A founder can spend one evening at a 300 person startup fair or at a small dinner with four operators from her exact category. What she needs this month is supplier terms, not funding. Which is the better use?

options.text: The fair, because investors attend it in numbers
options.rationale: Optimises for the goal she explicitly does not have this month.

options.text: The dinner, because it costs less to attend
options.rationale: Right room, wrong reason: cost is not what makes it the better use.

options.text: The dinner, where the people hold what she needs
options.rationale: The goal sets the room: supplier terms come from industry relationships, so four relevant operators beat 300 mixed attendees.

options.text: The fair, since more contacts means better odds
options.rationale: The numbers game again, with no filter for relevance.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: event selection depends on the goal, and the value of the room depends on whose industry relationships are in it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Networking at Startup Events, Leveraging Industry Contacts. Without the goal-first event rule the bigger room wins on reach. Without the contacts view the four operators are just a smaller crowd. The comparison only resolves when both apply.

questions.question: A founder notices that no local bakery sells gluten-free bread, but after asking around finds almost nobody in town actually wants it. What does this show?

options.text: An absence of a product isn't automatically a real gap without demand behind it.
options.rationale: This reflects the card's point that 'nobody's doing this' doesn't equal a real opportunity unless demand actually exists.

options.text: The founder found a genuine market gap worth pursuing.
options.rationale: A gap requires real unmet demand; an absence of a product with no demand behind it isn't a genuine gap.

options.text: The town is experiencing a trend the founder should ride quickly.
options.rationale: This describes trend spotting, a different concept, and there's no evidence of a rising shift in behavior here.

options.text: The founder should open the bakery anyway since being first matters most.
options.rationale: Being first only matters if there's real demand to capture; this ignores the lack of interest found.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, one reasoning step: recognizing why an apparent gap without demand fails to qualify as a real opportunity.

questions.question: A founder says a grocery delivery service for rural villages is worth starting because broadband reached those villages for the first time this year. What has she supplied?

options.text: A budget for the first year
options.rationale: Nothing financial is offered.

options.text: A gap and a reason it is now
options.rationale: Recognising an opportunity means naming the unmet need and explaining why this moment is the one to act.

options.text: A product and its list price
options.rationale: No price is mentioned.

options.text: A rival she plans to beat
options.rationale: No competitor appears.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the two parts of the claim.

questions.question: A founder building a scheduling tool describes her customer as any business that takes appointments. What should she do?

options.text: Name the small group who buy first
options.rationale: The first customers are a specific group with a specific reason to say yes before anyone else does.

options.text: Build every feature that is asked for
options.rationale: Builds for everyone and nobody.

options.text: Widen the market description more
options.rationale: Moves further in the wrong direction.

options.text: Set a price before choosing buyers
options.rationale: Price depends on who is buying.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the narrowing step she has skipped.

questions.question: A founder wants to sell a subscription box of local snacks. Before building the website or ordering inventory, she posts a fake product page with a Buy Now button and drives friends-of-friends traffic to it, tracking how many people actually click Buy. What is she doing?

options.text: Identifying her first customers by assuming anyone who clicks represents the whole market
options.rationale: She hasn't defined a specific beachhead group yet; she's testing general demand, not naming a first-customer segment.

options.text: Spotting a market gap by checking what boxes competitors already sell nearby
options.rationale: This describes scanning competitors for an underserved need, not testing demand for her own offer.

options.text: Recognizing an opportunity by noticing a timing reason to launch the box right now
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario points to a timing argument for why now is the moment, only a test of interest.

options.text: Validating the idea by measuring real buying intent before committing money to inventory
options.rationale: A low-cost test that measures actual clicks toward payment, before full investment, is exactly validating demand before committing resources.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept (Validating the Idea) applied to a new scenario not on the card; requires recognizing the mechanism of a low-cost demand test rather than reciting its definition.

questions.question: A founder notices that every dry cleaner in her city closes by 6pm, but she can't find any evidence that nearby office workers actually want evening drop-off hours. She opens a 24-hour dry cleaner anyway, assuming the empty niche alone proves the opportunity. What has she overlooked?

options.text: That she should have targeted a narrower first group of night-shift customers instead of all office workers
options.rationale: This is a first-customer targeting issue, not the gap-validity problem the scenario is pointing at.

options.text: That an unmet gap still needs confirmed demand, since nobody serving a niche can also mean nobody wants it
options.rationale: This is the exact common mistake on the card: mistaking 'nobody's doing this' for a real gap without checking that demand actually exists.

options.text: That she needed to run repeat-purchase tests to prove problem-solution fit before opening a full location
options.rationale: Repeat-purchase proof is part of problem-solution fit, a further step; her core oversight was not checking basic demand for the gap itself.

options.text: That she should have waited for a bigger, more obvious trend before opening any new location
options.rationale: This confuses trend spotting with gap spotting; the issue here is unconfirmed demand, not poor timing on a trend.

notes.difficulty_justification: Applies the single concept of Spotting Market Gaps to a new situation, requiring the student to see that an empty niche without demand evidence isn't automatically a real opportunity.

questions.question: Fifty parents tell a founder they would like an app that organises the school run carpool. Not one of them has ever paid for anything to solve that problem. What does that suggest?

options.text: The pain may be too mild to buy
options.rationale: Fit needs the problem to hurt enough that people adopt and pay, and never having spent anything on it is evidence it does not.

options.text: Fifty is far too small a sample
options.rationale: Fifty consistent answers is informative.

options.text: Parents do not understand the app
options.rationale: They understood it well enough to like it.

options.text: The app should be built anyway
options.rationale: Ignores the signal entirely.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: read whether the problem is painful enough.

questions.question: A founder notices more renters asking about compost pickup services in her city and immediately signs a two-year lease on a truck fleet and a processing facility before running any small test. What is the biggest risk in her approach?

options.text: She committed major money before testing whether renters would actually pay for pickup.
options.rationale: Even a real trend needs a cheap test first; she skipped validation and jumped straight to a costly commitment based on a hunch.

options.text: She misjudged the market gap since other cities already have compost startups.
options.rationale: Competition elsewhere doesn't disprove a local gap; the real issue is she never tested demand, not that a gap can't exist alongside competitors.

options.text: She spotted a fad instead of a trend, since compost interest always fades by winter.
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario shows the interest is short-lived; this assumes a fad without evidence, misapplying the fad-versus-trend distinction.

options.text: She should have picked a narrower first customer group before noticing the trend at all.
options.rationale: Sequencing is off: identifying first customers happens after confirming demand exists, not as a substitute for validating the trend itself.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding trend spotting and validation together: recognizing a real trend does not remove the need to test it cheaply before heavy investment, which is a two-concept interaction, not a single definition.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Trend Spotting for Ventures, Validating the Idea. Removing trend spotting leaves a generic 'she spent money without testing' question that no longer needs the trend concept. Removing validation leaves no problem at all, since spotting a real trend alone wouldn't explain why the lease was risky. Both are needed, so it holds as icdc.

questions.question: A founder confirms that no gym in town opens before seven in the morning. The early-shift workers she then interviews say they train at home and are perfectly happy doing so. What does the pair of findings show?

options.text: A survey that asked the wrong group
options.rationale: Early workers are the target group.

options.text: A real gap with no pain behind it
options.rationale: The gap in the market is genuine and an unmet need only becomes a business when somebody actually minds it being unmet.

options.text: Competitors who will open earlier
options.rationale: Nothing suggests they will.

options.text: A gap that guarantees a customer
options.rationale: This is the error the case exposes.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: a confirmed gap and the absence of fit have to be held together to see why the idea fails.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Spotting market gaps, Problem-solution fit. Without the gap there is no idea at all. Without the fit test the gap looks like an opportunity. Both are needed.

questions.question: A founder runs a careful landing page test and collects sign-ups from everyone who arrives, students through to retirees. Conversion sits at four percent for every group alike. What is she still missing?

options.text: Proof that the test was run well
options.rationale: The test is described as careful.

options.text: Which group would actually buy first
options.rationale: The test proves general interest and tells her nothing about where to aim a launch, because no group stood out.

options.text: A higher conversion rate overall
options.rationale: Four percent is a usable signal.

options.text: A larger number of total visitors
options.rationale: More traffic gives the same flat result.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the validation is sound and it was not designed to answer the first-customer question, so the founder is no closer to a launch.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Validating the idea, Identifying the first customers. Without the test there is no evidence at all. Without the first-customer question the flat result looks like success. Both are needed.

questions.question: A founder writes a detailed description of what her bakery will look like once it has three locations and a loyal following, but never lists the steps or resources needed to open the first store. What is missing from her business plan?

options.text: A more exciting description of the finished brand
options.rationale: She already has this; more vivid description doesn't fix the missing sequence.

options.text: A prediction of how many customers will visit daily
options.rationale: This describes demand forecasting, useful but not what's missing from the planning gap described.

options.text: A clear sequence of steps and resources to reach that future
options.rationale: Correct: business planning requires mapping the actual path, not just describing the eventual outcome.

options.text: A plan for how she'll eventually sell the bakery chain
options.rationale: This describes exit strategy planning, a different concept, not the missing steps to open the first store.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept (Business Planning), tests recognition of the common mistake of describing the outcome instead of the path.

questions.question: A founder's launch plan says only 'Grand opening: September 1.' What key element of a timeline is missing?

options.text: Intermediate checkpoints with dates before the final deadline
options.rationale: Correct: milestones break the goal into smaller dated steps so delays show up early, not just at the end.

options.text: A longer overall deadline for the launch
options.rationale: The length of the deadline isn't the issue; the missing structure is checkpoints along the way.

options.text: A backup plan for closing the business if it fails
options.rationale: This describes exit strategy planning, unrelated to the missing checkpoints in a timeline.

options.text: A forecast of how many customers will attend opening day
options.rationale: This describes demand forecasting, a separate concept from timeline structure.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept (Setting Milestones and Timelines), tests recognition of the card's common mistake at a single reasoning step.
