questions.question: A founder's plan says the new juice bar will do well because the area is busy. What should replace that line?

options.text: A number built from real counts
options.rationale: A demand forecast has to be an estimate of customers, grounded in something countable.

options.text: A stronger claim about the area
options.rationale: More conviction, no more evidence.

options.text: A photograph of the busy street
options.rationale: An image is not a forecast.

options.text: A longer opening hours schedule
options.rationale: Hours do not estimate demand.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what a forecast requires.

questions.question: A new bakery owner near an office park counts 800 workers walking past daily, sees a nearby sandwich shop with similar foot traffic capture 5% of passersby, and uses that rate to estimate 40 bakery sales a day. What is the strength of this approach?

options.text: It should be replaced with a national industry-wide average instead
options.rationale: A vague national average is actually the weaker method the concept warns against; local comparable data is stronger, not weaker.

options.text: It guarantees the bakery will hit 40 sales because the math is precise
options.rationale: Precision of the calculation doesn't guarantee the outcome; forecasts are estimates, not guarantees, and a single-point figure hides risk.

options.text: It grounds the estimate in comparable local data instead of a guess
options.rationale: Correct: using a nearby comparable business's actual capture rate against real foot traffic is exactly the evidence-based approach the concept calls for.

options.text: It works only because the owner wants to sell exactly 40 units a day
options.rationale: This reverses the logic: the mistake pattern is basing a forecast on desired sales, but this estimate is built from external data, not desire.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept (forecasting demand) applied to a new, specific bakery scenario requiring the student to judge whether the method used counts as evidence-based forecasting.

questions.question: A founder planning a September product launch writes down only one date on her calendar: 'September 1: launch day.' Based on the purpose of milestones, what is the main risk of this plan?

options.text: She will spend too much money because timelines always increase costs
options.rationale: Timelines are a scheduling tool, not a cost driver; this misattributes a budgeting concern to the milestone concept.

options.text: She will need to hire more staff since a single date requires more workers
options.rationale: Staffing needs stem from workload, not from how many dates are on a calendar; this isn't a consequence of missing checkpoints.

options.text: She will lose investor interest because exit plans require multiple dates
options.rationale: This confuses milestones with exit strategy planning, a different concept about ownership and eventual sale, not launch scheduling.

options.text: She will not know she is falling behind until it is too late to adjust
options.rationale: Correct: without intermediate checkpoints, there's no early warning system, so problems surface only when the final deadline is already missed.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept (milestones as early-warning checkpoints) applied to a fresh single-deadline scenario, requiring the student to predict the consequence rather than just define the term.

questions.question: A founder of a small logistics software company wants to eventually sell to a larger tech firm. From day one, she keeps audited financial statements, avoids letting any single client generate more than 20% of revenue, and documents all internal processes so the company doesn't depend on her personally. What does this behavior reflect?

options.text: She is setting milestones by creating dated checkpoints for each task
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario involves scheduled dates or checkpoints; it's about structuring the business for a future sale, not sequencing steps.

options.text: She is shaping current decisions around a planned future sale of the business
options.rationale: Correct: keeping clean records, diversifying clients, and documenting processes are early decisions made specifically to prepare the business as an attractive acquisition target later.

options.text: She is mapping the sequence of steps needed to open the business
options.rationale: This describes business planning for launching, but the company is already running; her actions are about a future exit, not startup sequencing.

options.text: She is forecasting demand by tracking client concentration data
options.rationale: Client diversification here is about acquisition readiness, not estimating how many customers will buy the product.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept (exit strategy shaping present-day decisions) applied to a new company and industry, requiring the student to recognize the mechanism in action rather than recall its definition.

questions.question: A founder forecasts that a new juice bar will hit 80 daily sales by its third month, based on foot traffic near a gym. She then sets a single milestone: 'reach 80 daily sales by month three.' Six weeks in, sales are at 30 a day with no earlier checkpoint to flag the gap. What is the clearest flaw in how she used these two tools together?

options.text: She should have skipped the forecast entirely and only used milestones, since milestones alone can predict customer demand.
options.rationale: Milestones track progress toward a goal; they don't generate demand estimates, so dropping the forecast removes a needed tool rather than fixing the problem.

options.text: Her foot traffic data was too specific to a gym location to ever produce a valid demand estimate.
options.rationale: Grounding a forecast in local traffic data is exactly the right method the card recommends; the flaw is not the data source.

options.text: She forecast the milestone well and set no earlier checkpoints that would catch a slip
options.rationale: This names the actual gap: a demand number without intermediate checkpoints removes the early warning system milestones are meant to provide, letting the shortfall run six weeks before detection.

options.text: The real problem is that month three was too soon to expect any meaningful sales volume at all.
options.rationale: This isn't supported by the scenario and ignores the actual issue, which is the absence of checkpoints, not the timing of the target itself.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding both forecasting mechanics and milestone structure at once: the student must see that a valid forecast can still fail operationally if it isn't broken into checkpoints, which needs both concepts interacting, not either alone.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Forecasting Startup Demand, Setting Milestones and Timelines. Deleting forecasting leaves a question purely about missing checkpoints (a state question). Deleting milestones leaves a question purely about forecast validity (also state). The question only works when both are present: a sound forecast plus a poorly structured milestone plan, so it passes the break test.

questions.question: A founder is drafting his step-by-step plan for a new tutoring center, including when to lease a second room and hire a third tutor. He sets the hiring trigger at 'when revenue covers costs,' based only on his own hope that enrollment will be steady. He has not looked at comparable tutoring centers, local student population, or run a pilot. What is the most likely consequence of building the plan this way?

options.text: The forecast does not touch the plan, since planning is about the order of the steps.
options.rationale: The steps are ordered well; what fires them is the forecast.

options.text: The plan fails whatever the trigger says, since numeric triggers do not belong in a plan.
options.rationale: Triggers are good planning; the question is what sits behind the number.

options.text: He should drop numeric triggers and move the second room and third tutor to fixed dates.
options.rationale: A calendar date rests on the same guess with less information in it.

options.text: The sequence is sound, but the triggers rest on hope rather than evidence of demand.
options.rationale: Good planning puts the steps in the right order and the point at which each one fires is only as good as the demand estimate underneath it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests the interaction between having a well-structured plan and the reliability of the demand data feeding its triggers; a student must recognize that structural soundness and numeric accuracy are separate failure points that combine here.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Business Planning, Forecasting Startup Demand. Removing forecasting leaves a question about whether numeric triggers are good practice, a state-level point. Removing business planning leaves a question purely about forecast quality, also state-level. The question requires seeing that a staged plan can be structurally correct yet functionally broken because its inputs are ungrounded, so it passes the break test.

questions.question: Two partners write a thorough plan covering steps, order, resources and dated milestones for the first three years. It says nothing about what happens if one of them wants out in year five. What is missing?

options.text: A clearer order for the early steps
options.rationale: The order is already set out.

options.text: Milestones for the second year
options.rationale: Three years of milestones exist.

options.text: A budget for the first six months
options.rationale: Resources are covered.

options.text: How either of them leaves with value
options.rationale: The operating plan is complete and the plan for getting value out at the end is a separate piece that is easiest to write early.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the plan for running the business is complete and the plan for leaving it has not been started.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Business planning, Exit strategy planning. Without the operating plan there is no venture to exit. Without the exit question the plan looks finished. Both are needed.

questions.question: What is the core idea behind smart risk-taking in a business decision?

options.text: Avoiding uncertain decisions until the outcome is guaranteed
options.rationale: This describes playing it totally safe, which the card explicitly contrasts with smart risk-taking.

options.text: Doing extensive research before making the same all-in commitment
options.rationale: This is the common mistake named in the card: more research isn't the same as limiting the size of the bet.

options.text: Structuring a decision so a bad outcome can't sink the whole business
options.rationale: This matches the card's definition: taking a chance on purpose while capping potential loss.

options.text: Committing fully to one idea once you feel confident in it
options.rationale: This describes gambling everything on one move, the opposite extreme the card warns against.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests recognition of a single concept's core definition with one reasoning step distinguishing it from two named extremes.

questions.question: A business owner writes down a specific event that could hurt sales and a specific action they'd take if it happens. What is this an example of?

options.text: Testing a risky assumption with a small experiment
options.rationale: Testing assumptions is about checking a guess before spending money, not preparing a response to a future disruption.

options.text: Limiting how much money is committed to a new idea
options.rationale: This describes smart risk-taking's focus on capping exposure, not planning for a specific disruption.

options.text: Weighing the potential gain of a decision against its potential loss
options.rationale: Weighing risk versus reward is about evaluating a choice's upside and downside, not planning a reaction to an event.

options.text: Preparing a specific response to a specific risk before it occurs
options.rationale: This matches the card's definition of thinking ahead about what could go wrong and deciding the response in advance.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, recognition of the definition applied to a described behavior, one reasoning step.

questions.question: Why does the card say asking friends if they'd buy a product is a weak way to test an assumption?

options.text: Because friends are legally not allowed to be counted as customers
options.rationale: No such rule exists in the card; this is a fabricated technicality.

options.text: Because it costs more money than building the full product
options.rationale: Asking friends costs little to nothing; cost isn't the issue the card raises.

options.text: Because it takes too long to get an answer from them
options.rationale: Speed isn't the problem identified in the card; the weakness is the lack of real commitment.

options.text: Because it doesn't require people to actually pay or commit something real
options.rationale: The card's common mistake states the test must involve real commitment, not just an easy opinion.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, direct recall of the card's stated common mistake, one reasoning step to identify why it's weak.

questions.question: A boutique owner wants to expand into a second city. Instead of signing a five-year lease on a full storefront, she rents a small kiosk for three months to see if local demand holds up before committing further. This choice best demonstrates which approach?

options.text: Gathering more research before repeating the same full commitment
options.rationale: This is the common mistake of equating smart risk with extra research rather than actually shrinking the bet itself.

options.text: Playing it totally safe by avoiding expansion
options.rationale: She is still taking a chance on a new city, not avoiding the risk entirely.

options.text: Gambling everything on one unproven move
options.rationale: This describes an all-in bet, the opposite of what she did by capping her exposure first.

options.text: Limiting the size of the bet while still testing the opportunity
options.rationale: She deliberately capped how much she could lose with the kiosk while still learning if the city works, which is the core mechanism of smart risk-taking.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept (smart risk-taking) applied to a new scenario, requiring the student to recognize the mechanism of capped exposure rather than recall a definition.

questions.question: A wedding photographer knows that rain often cancels outdoor shoots, so she already has a standing deal with two indoor event halls she can book on short notice whenever weather turns bad. What does this arrangement represent?

options.text: A test of whether customers would pay before she built the service
options.rationale: This describes checking an assumption with a cheap experiment, not preparing a backup for a known risk.

options.text: A vague worry about the business climate with no real action attached
options.rationale: This describes the common mistake of naming a generic fear, but she has a specific trigger and a specific backup action.

options.text: A prearranged response tied to a specific risk she identified in advance
options.rationale: She named the exact trigger, rain, and set up a specific action, the indoor halls, ahead of time, which is the core of contingency thinking.

options.text: A calculation of potential loss against potential gain for the whole business
options.rationale: This describes comparing upside and downside on a decision, not preparing a specific fallback for a specific problem.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept (contingency thinking) applied to a fresh venture scenario, requiring the student to distinguish a real trigger-and-plan from a vague worry.

questions.question: A founder can spend her last $8,000 on a trade show stand that might win two wholesale accounts worth $30,000, or keep it as three months of runway. What does weighing this properly involve?

options.text: Sizing the upside against being broke
options.rationale: A deliberate choice needs both what could be won and what it would cost to lose, held next to each other.

options.text: Doing both by borrowing the money
options.rationale: Adds a third risk to avoid the choice.

options.text: Picking whichever feels more exciting
options.rationale: Feeling is not weighing.

options.text: Trusting that trade shows always pay
options.rationale: Assumes the upside is certain.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: name what a deliberate weighing includes.

questions.question: A candle maker believes local gift shops will stock her products at $18 a unit. She convinces herself the guess is solid by spending three weeks reading articles about candle market trends, then signs a $12,000 contract for a full production run before approaching a single shop. What is the real flaw in her approach?

options.text: She needed a backup plan for what to do if the shops reject the candles after the run is produced.
options.rationale: This describes contingency thinking for a risk already taken, not the core problem of never testing the assumption before committing the money.

options.text: She should have weighed the reward of gift shop sales against the cost of the production run before deciding.
options.rationale: Sounds relevant but misses the point: even a careful risk versus reward calculation built on an untested guess about shop demand is still built on sand.

options.text: She researched trends instead of getting real shops to commit to an order before spending the big money.
options.rationale: Correct: she gathered information but never cheaply checked the actual risky guess (that shops will buy), then made the full-size bet anyway, which is the exact confusion both cards warn against.

options.text: She should have picked a completely safe idea with no uncertainty instead of trying something new.
options.rationale: Misapplies smart risk-taking as avoiding risk entirely, when the concept is about limiting exposure while still trying something uncertain.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding both testing assumptions and smart risk-taking at once: the student must see that research alone isn't testing, and that the failure is committing full-size money without a small proof step, which blends both mechanisms rather than either alone.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Smart Risk-Taking, Testing Assumptions Before Committing. Deleting Testing Assumptions leaves only 'she made a big risky bet,' which loses the specific flaw that research isn't the same as a real cheap test; deleting Smart Risk-Taking leaves only 'she didn't test her guess,' which loses the sizing/commitment angle. Both are needed, so the question holds.

questions.question: Two food truck owners each face the risk of a major supplier suddenly raising prices. Owner A signs a smaller, month-to-month contract with the supplier instead of a locked-in year-long deal, so a bad price hike only hurts for a month. Owner B keeps the same year-long contract but arranges in advance with a second supplier who can step in within a week if prices spike unreasonably. Which statement best describes what each owner did?

options.text: Both owners did the same thing, since having a shorter contract and having a backup supplier both reduce risk equally.
options.rationale: Flattens two distinct mechanisms into one, missing that limiting bet size and planning a reactive backup are different moves even though both reduce risk.

options.text: Owner A limited the size of the bet itself, while Owner B kept the same bet but built a specific backup plan for if it goes wrong.
options.rationale: Correct: Owner A reduced exposure by shrinking commitment length (smart risk-taking), while Owner B kept full commitment but pre-arranged a specific response to a named trigger (contingency thinking), matching each concept's mechanism precisely.

options.text: Owner A used contingency thinking by preparing a backup, while Owner B used smart risk-taking by shrinking the deal size.
options.rationale: Swaps the two concepts: this describes Owner A's move as contingency and Owner B's as sizing, which is backwards from what each actually did.

options.text: Owner A tested his assumption about the supplier, while Owner B weighed the reward of a long contract against its risk.
options.rationale: Misapplies two other concepts that don't fit: neither owner ran a cheap experiment to check a guess, and Owner B's move is about reacting to a bad outcome, not a reward calculation.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires distinguishing two mechanisms that both reduce risk but work differently, sizing down the commitment versus planning a specific reaction, which cannot be resolved by knowing only one concept.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Smart Risk-Taking, Contingency Thinking for Ventures. Deleting Contingency Thinking removes the reason Owner B's move needs a separate label, collapsing the question into 'what did Owner A do,' a single-concept question; deleting Smart Risk-Taking does the same for Owner A. The question only works when both are held and correctly told apart, so it passes the break test.

questions.question: A founder works through a $20,000 equipment purchase carefully and the numbers support it. Those numbers rest on two anchor customers, and she has no answer at all for what she does if either one leaves. What is incomplete?

options.text: A sound bet with no plan B behind it
options.rationale: The weighing is honest about the expected case, and a venture also needs a decided response for the realistic bad one.

options.text: Customers who should be replaced
options.rationale: They are the reason the case works.

options.text: Equipment that costs far too much
options.rationale: The cost is justified by the numbers.

options.text: A bet the numbers do not support
options.rationale: They do support it as stated.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the risk and reward are weighed properly and the contingency for the named downside was never decided.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Weighing risk versus reward, Contingency thinking for ventures. Without the weighing there is no case to complete. Without the contingency the case is only good while nothing changes. Both are needed.

questions.question: A founder with no budget yet wants to test her idea. Which action best shows resourcefulness and bootstrapping?

options.text: She waits for a bank loan before making any samples at all.
options.rationale: Waiting on outside funding is the common mistake the card warns against, not bootstrapping.

options.text: She delays launch until a sponsor agrees to cover early costs.
options.rationale: Building the plan around a future sponsor that isn't secured yet is the exact common mistake described.

options.text: She hires a full design team to make the first prototype look polished.
options.rationale: Hiring a team before validating demand assumes a budget she doesn't have, the opposite of bootstrapping.

options.text: She uses free software and her own time to build a working sample this week.
options.rationale: This matches the core definition: moving forward with what's already on hand instead of waiting for a budget.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests one concept, recognizing what bootstrapping actually looks like versus waiting for outside help, with a single reasoning step.

questions.question: A sole proprietor gets sued after a customer is injured by her product. What is the direct consequence of staying a sole proprietorship instead of forming an LLC?

options.text: Her personal savings and property can be taken to cover the lawsuit.
options.rationale: Sole proprietorships carry unlimited personal liability, so personal assets are exposed exactly as the card describes.

options.text: Her business automatically converts into a corporation to protect her.
options.rationale: Legal structures don't change automatically during a lawsuit; this misunderstands how structure works.

options.text: Her tax filing becomes more complex than it would under an LLC.
options.rationale: The card highlights liability exposure as the key risk here, not filing complexity, which is a separate issue.

options.text: Her profits get taxed twice because there's no legal entity involved.
options.rationale: Double taxation applies to certain corporations, not to sole proprietorships, which use simple pass-through taxation.

notes.difficulty_justification: Single concept, direct first-order consequence of one structural choice under one specific event, requiring no combination with other concepts.

questions.question: A founder spends her elevator pitch listing every feature and financial projection in detail. What is the most likely result?

options.text: The listener assumes the business has no real customer in mind.
options.rationale: The problem isn't a missing customer, it's that too much detail crowds out the message, which is a different failure mode.

options.text: The listener asks for a formal investment agreement on the spot.
options.rationale: This is an unrealistic overcorrection; the card describes losing the listener, not immediately gaining a deal.

options.text: The listener loses interest and forgets the message before she finishes talking.
options.rationale: This is the exact common mistake described: cramming in details instead of leading with the problem causes the audience to tune out.

options.text: The listener remembers the core problem clearly because of all the detail given.
options.rationale: This reverses the actual outcome the card warns about; extra detail buries the message rather than clarifying it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests one concept, the direct consequence of overloading a pitch with details, requiring a single logical step from the card's stated mistake.

questions.question: A founder's investor pitch covers the product in detail and never says how many people have this problem. What is missing?

options.text: A demonstration of the app
options.rationale: More product.

options.text: The founder's own background
options.rationale: Useful and not the named gap.

options.text: The size of the market
options.rationale: A pitch has to show the problem, the solution, how big the market is, and why the money pays off; the market is the piece left out.

options.text: More detail on the product
options.rationale: That is the covered part.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the missing element.

questions.question: Three founders split ownership in equal thirds on day one without discussing who does what. What have they not settled?

options.text: When to raise outside money
options.rationale: A funding decision.

options.text: How much the company is worth
options.rationale: Valuation is a later question.

options.text: Which bank holds the account
options.rationale: Administrative.

options.text: Who does which job, and for what
options.rationale: Roles and the contribution behind each share are the substance; an even split postpones the conversation rather than having it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what the split skipped.

questions.question: A four person startup pays market rates and the team is flat and disengaged. The founder has never explained what the work is for. What would help most?

options.text: Raise everyone's salary again
options.rationale: Pay is already at market.

options.text: Connect the work to something
options.rationale: A small team runs on seeing why the daily work matters, which pay alone does not supply.

options.text: Track hours more closely
options.rationale: Monitors the symptom.

options.text: Add two more people to help
options.rationale: More people, same disengagement.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the lever that fits.

questions.question: A new tutoring business needs $10,000 and the owner takes the full amount from an investor who wants 30% ownership in exchange. What has this owner actually given up?

options.text: Nothing, since no interest payments are required on equity money.
options.rationale: Ignores that giving up ownership is itself a cost, even without interest.

options.text: A share of future profits and some control over business decisions.
options.rationale: Equity funding trades ownership and decision-making power for cash, which is the real cost of this source.

options.text: The right to keep operating without ever answering to anyone else.
options.rationale: Backwards: taking equity investment means answering to a new part-owner, not gaining independence.

options.text: A fixed monthly payment that must be repaid regardless of profit.
options.rationale: Describes loan repayment terms, not what happens with an equity investment.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, funding and capital, applied to a new situation where the student must reason through what equity funding actually costs the founder beyond just the cash received.

questions.question: A carpenter runs a furniture business as a sole proprietorship. A client's shelf collapses and the client sues for damages far above what the business owns. What is the direct consequence of staying a sole proprietorship?

options.text: He has to incorporate now so the company can meet the claim.
options.rationale: A structure formed today does nothing about a shelf that already collapsed.

options.text: His personal savings and home could be used to pay the judgment.
options.rationale: A sole proprietor and the business are one legal person, so there is nothing standing between the judgment and what he owns.

options.text: The claim is shared out among any partners he takes on afterwards.
options.rationale: Partners joining later do not inherit this liability.

options.text: The claim stops at the business account, leaving his own property alone.
options.rationale: That separation is what a company structure buys, and he has not formed one.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, legal structure, applied to a specific liability scenario requiring the student to predict the consequence of an unincorporated structure rather than just define it.

questions.question: Asked in a lift what her company does, a founder spends two minutes on the technology behind it. Which opening would have worked better?

options.text: We are a fast growing health startup
options.rationale: Says nothing about what it does.

options.text: We cut no-shows for small clinics
options.rationale: It says what the business does, for whom, and why it matters, in one line.

options.text: We use a modern cloud based stack
options.rationale: Repeats the mistake in fewer words.

options.text: We have raised two rounds already
options.rationale: Funding is not the offer.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: pick the line that carries who, what and why.

questions.question: A founder must commit to a manufacturing slot this week. She has solid cost figures, no reliable demand data, and no way to get any in time. What does sound practice look like?

options.text: Reason from what she has, then commit
options.rationale: Deciding under uncertainty means making a defensible call on incomplete information rather than waiting for certainty that will not arrive.

options.text: Hand the choice to her supplier
options.rationale: Gives the decision to the seller.

options.text: Pick whichever option feels right
options.rationale: Incomplete is not the same as arbitrary.

options.text: Wait until demand data exists
options.rationale: The slot is gone by then.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: act well without complete information.

questions.question: An investor asks what the money will be spent on. The founder answers that it will fund growth. What does a good pitch answer instead?

options.text: What it buys and what that returns
options.rationale: The pitch has to show why the money pays off, which means naming what it is spent on and what comes back.

options.text: How little the founders take
options.rationale: Frugality is not a return.

options.text: How much the round is raising
options.rationale: The amount, not its use.

options.text: How fast the market is growing
options.rationale: Market size, already a separate beat.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: answer the use-of-funds question properly.

questions.question: Two founders split equity evenly. One works full time and builds the product; the other kept his job and advises occasionally. A year in, the builder is resentful. What should the split have reflected?

options.text: Who has the better job title
options.rationale: Titles are not contribution.

options.text: Who had the original idea
options.rationale: Ideas are the cheap part.

options.text: What each actually contributes
options.rationale: Ownership is meant to track the real contribution of work, money and risk, which an even split assumes rather than establishes.

options.text: Who invested the most cash
options.rationale: One input among several.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: tie ownership to contribution.

questions.question: A founder is taking on a $40,000 bank loan to open a small bakery and is nervous that if the bakery fails, the bank or an injured customer could come after her house. She's currently planning to operate as a sole proprietorship because it's the cheapest and fastest to set up. Which change best addresses her actual risk?

options.text: Stay a sole proprietorship but keep detailed financial records to prove the business and personal finances are separate.
options.rationale: Good bookkeeping doesn't create legal separation; a sole proprietorship still leaves personal assets exposed no matter how clean the records are.

options.text: Negotiate a lower interest rate on the loan so the monthly payments are easier to cover.
options.rationale: Addresses the cost of capital, not the personal liability exposure she's actually worried about.

options.text: Form an LLC before taking on the loan, so her personal assets are separated from business debts and lawsuits.
options.rationale: Correctly matches the legal structure decision to the liability concern, keeping her house and car protected regardless of how the loan or a lawsuit turns out.

options.text: Replace the bank loan with an equity investment from family so there's no debt to repay.
options.rationale: Swaps one funding cost (interest) for another (ownership given up) but does nothing to protect her personal assets from lawsuits.

notes.difficulty_justification: Requires holding two concepts at once: recognizing that a funding decision (loan) creates risk exposure, and that only a legal structure choice (not a funding tweak) actually resolves that exposure. A student who knows only one concept could be pulled toward a funding-side fix.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Funding and Capital, Choosing a Legal Structure. Delete legal structure: the question collapses into 'how do you reduce loan risk' with no liability angle, answerable by funding concept alone. Delete funding and capital: there's no reason to worry about personal assets since no debt is on the table. Both are load-bearing, so this holds as icdc.

questions.question: A founder pitching her subscription plant-care box to investors says: 'We ship easy-care plants monthly to busy renters who kill every plant they own, and we've got a horticulture expert and a supply-chain manager already on board to handle sourcing and logistics.' An investor says the pitch is actually weaker for including that last detail this early. Why might that critique be fair?

options.text: Naming members makes it too technical for a pitch of under sixty words
options.rationale: Invents a word count as the rule.

options.text: The team described fills no real gap, since horticulture is beside the point
options.rationale: Those are exactly the skills this business needs; the issue is where they sit.

options.text: Credentials crowd out the problem, the solution and the ask
options.rationale: The window is short, so whatever fills it displaces something, and what got displaced is the part that explains the business.

options.text: Naming the team is a mistake, since a pitch covers product and customer
options.rationale: A team can belong in a pitch when there is room for it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Cannot be resolved by the pitch concept alone (the team detail is factually relevant, not a bad hire) or the team concept alone (the hires are legitimate skill-gap fills); the tension only appears when you weigh good team-building against the pitch's structural time constraint.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Building the Founding Team, Crafting the Elevator Pitch. Delete founding team: no reason to include team details at all, so there's nothing to critique about crowding. Delete elevator pitch: a team description is simply good news with no downside. The critique only exists at the intersection, confirming icdc.

questions.question: A founder bootstrapped her handmade candle business by making candles in her kitchen and selling through free social media posts, keeping her true production cost at $3.50 per candle. She's now deciding on a launch price and is tempted to sell at $4 just to move inventory fast. Similar boutique candles at local shops sell for $12-$14. What's the strongest reasoning for rejecting the $4 price?

options.text: Having bootstrapped cheaply, she should undercut as a thank you to buyers
options.rationale: Prices on her costs rather than on what the candle is worth.

options.text: She should match the shop price of $12 to $14 exactly, to prove she belongs
options.rationale: Copies a number instead of reasoning to one.

options.text: With no investor money at stake she can price however she likes
options.rationale: Margin matters whoever funded the business.

options.text: A $4 price leaves almost no margin, whatever her own costs are
options.rationale: Low overheads are a reason she can survive on less, not a reason the candle is worth less than the shop ones beside it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Tests whether the student can keep bootstrapping (why her costs are low) and pricing strategy (how a launch price should actually be set) as separate mechanisms that interact, rather than assuming low-cost production justifies a low price.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Resourcefulness and Bootstrapping, Pricing a New Venture. Delete bootstrapping: the question becomes a plain pricing-floor question with no reason to mention her production method. Delete pricing: there's no pricing decision to reason through, just a bootstrapping success story. The interaction (low-cost production tempting her toward underpricing) is what the question actually tests, confirming icdc.

questions.question: A founder pitches a five year forecast to the decimal place for a market that does not exist yet. Investors press her on how she arrived at year four and she has no answer beyond the model. What is the real problem?

options.text: Investors who want too much detail
options.rationale: Testing the basis is their job.

options.text: A market that is not worth entering
options.rationale: Novelty is not disqualifying.

options.text: A forecast that runs for far too many years
options.rationale: Five years is a normal horizon.

options.text: Certainty claimed where none is available
options.rationale: Deciding under uncertainty is expected of a founder, and presenting a guess as precision tells an investor she cannot tell which parts of her case are solid.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the uncertainty is unavoidable and the pitch has to represent it honestly, so the fault is in how the two were reconciled.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Entrepreneurial decision-making under uncertainty, Pitching to investors. Without the uncertainty the precision would be fine. Without the pitch nobody is misled. Both are needed.

questions.question: A founder inspires her four employees with a mission they genuinely believe in, and holds 98 percent of the equity with no option pool. Two years of long hours later, the two best leave for salaried roles. What does the case show?

options.text: A founder who should hold less
options.rationale: States a remedy, not the mechanism.

options.text: Employees who were not committed
options.rationale: Two years of long hours says otherwise.

options.text: Belief asked to do the work of a stake
options.rationale: Purpose is what gets a small team to care, and over years of below-market effort the question of who owns what they are building does not stay quiet.

options.text: A mission the team never really believed in
options.rationale: They believed it for two years.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the motivation works and the ownership structure quietly undercuts it over time, so neither alone explains the departures.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Motivating a small team, Founder roles and equity splits. Without the mission nobody stays two years. Without the ownership gap the mission holds them. Both are needed.

questions.question: A founder changes direction every few weeks as new information arrives, each change defensible on its own. Her team has stopped finishing anything, saying there is no point. What is the tension?

options.text: A founder who should stop deciding so often
options.rationale: Deciding is the job.

options.text: Information that should be ignored
options.rationale: Ignoring evidence is worse.

options.text: Sound pivots read as having no direction
options.rationale: Acting on new information is correct, and a small team's engagement depends on seeing the work connect to something, which constant redirection destroys even when each turn is justified.

options.text: A team unwilling to adapt at all
options.rationale: They adapted repeatedly.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: each decision is individually right and their accumulation breaks the thing that keeps a small team pulling, which only both concepts together expose.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Entrepreneurial decision-making under uncertainty, Motivating a small team. Without the pivots there is nothing destabilising. Without the motivation question the pivots look purely rational. Both are needed.

questions.question: Store A earned $50,000 on $1,000,000 of sales. Store B earned $40,000 on $400,000. Which store is more profitable per sales dollar?

options.text: Store B, at a 10 percent margin
options.rationale: B keeps 10 cents per sales dollar against A's 5, which is what the ratio reveals and the raw profit hides.

options.text: Equal, since both are profitable
options.rationale: Being profitable is not the same as being equally profitable.

options.text: Store A, since $50,000 is larger
options.rationale: Compares raw profit, the error the card names.

options.text: Store A, since its sales are larger
options.rationale: Sales volume says nothing about what is kept.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: compare margins rather than totals.

questions.question: A $600 Instagram spend returned $3,500 of sales; a $400 radio spend returned $1,200. Which had the better return on investment?

options.text: Instagram, at about 5.8 times spend
options.rationale: 3,500 over 600 beats 1,200 over 400, and the ratio is what makes different spend sizes comparable.

options.text: Equal, since both returned more than spent
options.rationale: Both being positive does not make them equal.

options.text: Instagram, since $3,500 is the larger sum
options.rationale: Right answer from the wrong comparison, which fails when budgets differ.

options.text: Radio, since it cost less to run
options.rationale: Lower cost does not mean better return.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: compute and compare returns.

questions.question: A student argues that new packaging is more affordable. What turns that into financial evidence?

options.text: The per-unit saving and the annual total
options.rationale: A claim becomes evidence when it carries a number that can be checked.

options.text: A stronger word than more affordable
options.rationale: Emphasis is not evidence.

options.text: A supplier's assurance of lower prices
options.rationale: A promise without a figure.

options.text: A comparison of the two package designs
options.rationale: Aesthetics rather than cost.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify what quantification requires.

questions.question: A cafe owner is pleased with a 9 percent profit margin and has never looked at what other cafes make. What would benchmarking tell her?

options.text: What her costs were last year
options.rationale: That is her own history.

options.text: Whether 9 percent is good here
options.rationale: A number means little alone; comparing it to typical results for the industry is what turns it into a judgement.

options.text: How to raise the margin itself
options.rationale: Comparison diagnoses, it does not fix.

options.text: Which menu items sell the best
options.rationale: A product mix question.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: say what the comparison supplies.

questions.question: A shop budgeted $4,000 for packaging and spent $6,200. The manager notes the difference and moves on. What has he skipped?

options.text: Working out why the gap happened
options.rationale: The number is only the start; variance analysis is the hunt for the cause that tells you what to do next.

options.text: Raising next year's budget to match
options.rationale: Budgets to the overspend without knowing it.

options.text: Comparing it with another shop's spend
options.rationale: That is benchmarking.

options.text: Checking the packaging supplier's bill
options.rationale: One possible cause, not the step.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the half of variance analysis that was missed.

questions.question: A manager judges the business by this month's sales figure alone, every month. What does trend analysis add?

options.text: Whether the line is rising or falling
options.rationale: Several periods side by side show direction, which a single figure can never reveal.

options.text: The industry's typical sales level
options.rationale: That is a benchmark.

options.text: A more accurate figure for the month
options.rationale: The month's number is not in doubt.

options.text: The reason last month was better
options.rationale: Cause comes after the pattern.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what multiple periods reveal.

questions.question: A skate shop's revenue falls 15 percent in March. Records show March dips every year after the December gift-card rush. What should the owner do?

options.text: Cut the marketing budget immediately
options.rationale: Reacting to one month in isolation, the trap the card names.

options.text: Reduce staff hours until April arrives
options.rationale: A cut based on a misread of the same data.

options.text: Discount stock to recover the shortfall
options.rationale: Spends margin to fight a predictable cycle.

options.text: Treat it as the usual seasonal dip
options.rationale: A pattern repeated across years explains the number, so reacting as if it were new would be reacting to nothing.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: interpret a figure against its history.

questions.question: A bakery can sell 2,000 wholesale cupcakes monthly at $1.50 with $0.90 of cost, or 800 retail at $3.50 with $0.90 of cost. Which comparison settles it?

options.text: Retail wins, since its price is higher
options.rationale: Right answer from a comparison that ignores volume.

options.text: Wholesale wins, since 2,000 units is more
options.rationale: Units sold is the comparison the card warns against.

options.text: Wholesale wins, at $3,000 of revenue
options.rationale: Revenue without costs, another surface comparison.

options.text: Wholesale keeps $1,200, retail keeps $2,080
options.rationale: Contribution per unit times volume is what decides: 0.60 times 2,000 against 2.60 times 800.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: compare two options on profit.

questions.question: Given a statement where revenue is up 10 percent and net profit is down 5 percent, which response reads the numbers rather than repeating them?

options.text: The statement should be audited again
options.rationale: Questions the data instead of reading it.

options.text: Revenue was up 10 percent this period
options.rationale: Restates one number verbatim.

options.text: Profit fell, so the year was disappointing
options.rationale: A judgement without the mechanism.

options.text: Cost of goods rose faster than revenue did
options.rationale: It uses the two figures together to say what happened between them, which is what reading the information means.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: interpret rather than restate.

questions.question: A manager argues for a $14,000 system because it will save the team a lot of frustration. What does a cost-benefit case require him to add?

options.text: A second quote from another vendor
options.rationale: Prices the cost side again.

options.text: The saving, in the same terms as cost
options.rationale: A comparison only works when both sides are expressed the same way, so the benefit has to be put in money or hours.

options.text: The date the system could go live
options.rationale: Scheduling, not value.

options.text: How frustrated the team currently is
options.rationale: Deepens the unquantified half.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: name what makes the two sides comparable.

concepts: Impact of Interest Rates on Business
questions.question: A firm planned to borrow $200,000 next year for an expansion. Rates have risen from 5 to 9 percent since the plan was written. What should it reconsider?

options.text: Whether to expand somewhere cheaper
options.rationale: Changes the project, not the test.

options.text: Whether the return still beats the cost
options.rationale: A rate rise raises the hurdle the project has to clear, so a plan that cleared it at 5 percent may not at 9.

options.text: Whether to borrow a larger sum now
options.rationale: More borrowing at the higher rate.

options.text: Whether the bank will still lend at all
options.rationale: Availability is not what changed.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: trace a rate change through to the decision.

questions.question: An analyst wants to know whether rent is eating a bigger share of sales than it used to. Which reading does that?

options.text: This year's rent against the budget
options.rationale: That is variance analysis.

options.text: The rent figure on its own each year
options.rationale: Rising rent with rising sales may be fine.

options.text: Total costs as a percent of sales
options.rationale: Hides rent inside the total.

options.text: Rent as a percent of sales, year on year
options.rationale: Expressing the line as a share of sales is the vertical step, and setting those shares beside earlier years is the horizontal one.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: pick the reading that answers the question asked.

questions.question: A $600 Instagram spend returns $3,500 of sales at a 30 percent margin. A $400 radio spend returns $1,200 at the same margin. The bakery has $1,000 to spend and each channel saturates at its current level. What does the analysis support?

options.text: Fund neither, since a 30 percent margin is too thin
options.rationale: Both returns clear their cost at that margin.

options.text: Fund both, since each clears its own cost
options.rationale: Instagram returns $1,050 of margin on $600 and radio $360 on $400, so one is clearly profitable and the other is close enough to keep while both are capped.

options.text: Put the whole $1,000 into Instagram this month
options.rationale: Instagram saturates at its current level, so the extra spend has nowhere to go.

options.text: Fund radio only, since it costs less to run
options.rationale: Cheaper and the weaker return of the two.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: returns are computed per channel and then compared as profit against a budget constraint.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Return on Investment, Comparing Options by Profitability. Without ROI the channels cannot be compared at different spend levels. Without the profit comparison the saturation and budget do not enter. Both are needed.

questions.question: Store B's margin has slipped from 10 percent to 8 percent over three years while its sales grew steadily. Store A holds 5 percent flat. A manager says B is still the better store. What does the trend add?

options.text: B is better, since its margin is higher
options.rationale: True today and blind to the movement.

options.text: A is better, since its margin is stable
options.rationale: Stability at half the margin is not superiority.

options.text: Neither, since sales growth settles it
options.rationale: Growth without margin is the surface reading.

options.text: B leads now, on a path that is closing
options.rationale: The ratio still favours B today, and the direction across years is the part a single snapshot cannot show.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the ratio gives the current position and the trend gives the direction, and the judgement needs both.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Financial Ratios and Health, Interpreting Sales and Revenue Data. Without the ratio there is no comparison. Without the trend the slippage is invisible. Both are needed.

questions.question: A presenter is handed a one page cost sheet, leaves it face down, and tells the panel the new kiosk is clearly worth it. What is the double fault?

options.text: She skipped the figures and gave no number
options.rationale: She neither read what she was given nor put a value on the claim, so the recommendation rests on nothing the panel can check.

options.text: The kiosk decision needed board approval
options.rationale: Invents a governance issue the case does not raise.

options.text: She should have rehearsed the pitch more
options.rationale: Delivery is not what the panel cannot verify.

options.text: Cost sheets rarely help a live decision
options.rationale: The sheet is exactly what the decision turns on.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the evidence was supplied and unread, and the claim was made without a figure of its own.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Reading Financial Information, Quantifying with Financial Evidence. Without the unread sheet she might have had no numbers to use. Without the vague claim the omission would not matter. Both are needed.

questions.question: A distributor's margin sits at 11 percent against an industry norm of 8, which the board finds reassuring. Across four years its own margin has fallen from 17 to 11. What should the board take from this?

options.text: An industry norm that must be wrong
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the norm is bad.

options.text: Ahead of the field and sliding toward it
options.rationale: The benchmark says where the business stands today and the trend says where it is heading, and a comfortable position losing six points in four years is not reassuring.

options.text: A margin that is far too high already
options.rationale: Above average is not a fault.

options.text: A healthy business by both measures
options.rationale: Reads only the comparison.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: position and direction answer different questions, and the case is only legible with both.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Benchmarking against industry standards, Trend analysis over time. Without the benchmark the fall has no context. Without the trend the lead looks durable. Both are needed.

questions.question: A project came in $30,000 over budget. The variance traces cleanly to extra automation nobody planned for, which now saves about $40,000 a year. The finance lead wants it recorded as a failure. What is the better reading?

options.text: A variance too small to investigate
options.rationale: Thirty thousand was investigated.

options.text: A failure, because the budget was broken
options.rationale: Treats the gap as the whole answer.

options.text: A success, so the budget did not matter
options.rationale: The overrun is still unapproved spend.

options.text: A real overrun that bought more than it cost
options.rationale: Finding the cause is what variance analysis is for, and once the cause is known the overrun has to be judged against what it returned rather than by its sign.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the variance locates the cause and the cost-benefit test decides what the cause was worth, and neither alone settles it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Variance analysis, Cost-benefit analysis. Without the variance nobody knows what the money bought. Without the benefit test the overrun reads as pure loss. Both are needed.

concepts: Impact of Interest Rates on Business
questions.question: An importer pays overseas suppliers by letter of credit, which ties up a deposit with its bank for ninety days per shipment. Rates have doubled. The treasurer says payment terms are a legal matter, not a financial one. What is he missing?

options.text: That letters of credit are no longer valid
options.rationale: They remain a standard instrument.

options.text: The method now costs real money to hold
options.rationale: How the two sides exchange money is a financing decision as much as a protection one, and the cost of the cash it immobilises moves with the rate.

options.text: That the supplier should bear the deposit
options.rationale: Shifts the cost rather than seeing it.

options.text: That rates do not affect trade at all
options.rationale: States the error, not the correction.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the payment method determines how much cash is tied up and the rate determines what that costs, so the choice stops being purely legal.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: International trade payment methods, Impact of interest rates on business. Without the payment method no cash is immobilised. Without the rate rise holding it is nearly free. Both are needed.

questions.question: A closing print shop is valued by adding its presses, van and stock, then subtracting its debts. Which figure should the assets use?

options.text: What they originally cost to buy
options.rationale: The purchase price trap the card names.

options.text: What they would fetch today
options.rationale: Asset valuation works from current market value, since original cost says nothing about what a buyer would pay now.

options.text: What they would cost to replace new
options.rationale: Replacement cost overstates used equipment.

options.text: What the owner believes they are worth
options.rationale: Opinion is not a valuation basis.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: choose the right asset figure.

questions.question: A bakery netting $80,000 a year is valued using an earnings multiple, and the buyer treats that single figure as the answer. What is the weakness?

options.text: Asset value is the sounder basis here
options.rationale: Another single method, presented as the answer.

options.text: One method gives one view, not the value
options.rationale: A multiple is a single lens on a business, and a buyer treating it as the answer has not tested it against assets or cash flow.

options.text: Net income is the wrong earnings measure
options.rationale: A real debate, and not what the buyer got wrong.

options.text: Earnings multiples suit larger businesses
options.rationale: Multiples apply at this scale too.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify single-method risk.

questions.question: A roastery's owner says its 12-year brand and 40 wholesale relationships are worth $400,000 because they feel that valuable. What is needed instead?

options.text: Evidence tied to the cash they generate
options.rationale: Intangibles are valued from the income or retention they can be shown to produce, not from the owner's estimate.

options.text: An insurance policy covering the brand
options.rationale: Insurance is not a valuation method.

options.text: Removal of intangibles from the valuation
options.rationale: They are often the largest component.

options.text: A higher figure reflecting brand age
options.rationale: Age alone does not establish value.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: ground an intangible valuation.

questions.question: A bakery nets $80,000 a year, holds $120,000 of equipment and has a loyal customer base. Which approach gives the buyer the most complete picture?

options.text: Run earnings, assets and intangibles together
options.rationale: Each method captures something the others miss, and the spread between them is itself informative.

options.text: Use the earnings multiple and stop there
options.rationale: Single-method valuation, which the card warns against.

options.text: Use the equipment value as the floor price
options.rationale: A useful reference presented as the whole answer.

options.text: Ask the seller what price they will accept
options.rationale: Negotiation rather than valuation.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose a valuation approach.

questions.question: A print shop's presses cost $200,000 new eight years ago, would sell used for about $55,000, and the shop owes $30,000. What does asset-based valuation give?

options.text: About $170,000, original cost less debt
options.rationale: Uses purchase price rather than market value.

options.text: About $200,000, the presses as bought
options.rationale: Ignores both depreciation and debt.

options.text: About $55,000, the resale value alone
options.rationale: Forgets to subtract what the business owes.

options.text: About $25,000, market value less debt
options.rationale: 55,000 of current value less the 30,000 owed leaves 25,000 of net asset value.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: compute net asset value.

questions.question: A roastery supplies 40 cafes under contracts averaging three years with a 90 percent renewal rate. How should that be valued?

options.text: By excluding them, since they are intangible
options.rationale: Omits what may be the most valuable asset.

options.text: By counting the cafes and setting a rate
options.rationale: A per-customer figure with no basis in cash.

options.text: By the cost of the sales effort to win them
options.rationale: Historic cost does not establish current worth.

options.text: From the contracted revenue likely to continue
options.rationale: A retention rate and contract length convert relationships into a cash stream that can be valued.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: value a relationship base.

questions.question: A bakery's asset valuation gives $140,000 while a three times earnings multiple on $80,000 gives $240,000. The seller quotes the higher figure and the buyer quotes the lower. What does the gap tell them?

options.text: Earnings multiples overstate small bakeries
options.rationale: A general claim rather than a reading of this gap.

options.text: One of the two valuations must be wrong
options.rationale: Both can be correct under their own assumptions.

options.text: The midpoint of $190,000 is the true value
options.rationale: Splitting the difference is arithmetic, not valuation.

options.text: The business is worth more running than sold
options.rationale: The spread between going-concern earnings and break-up asset value is exactly the information multiple methods are meant to produce.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the asset figure and the earnings figure only mean something when the difference between them is interpreted.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Asset-Based Valuation Approach, Methods of Valuing a Business. Without the asset view there is one number and no gap. Without multiple methods the spread never appears. Both are needed.

questions.question: A roastery's assets total $90,000 and its earnings multiple gives $310,000. The buyer asks what explains the difference. What is the answer?

options.text: The equipment has been undervalued badly
options.rationale: Equipment undervaluation would not account for that size of gap.

options.text: The asset valuation was calculated wrongly
options.rationale: Both figures can be right; they measure different things.

options.text: The brand and wholesale relationships earn it
options.rationale: Earnings capture the cash that intangibles generate, which is precisely what the asset schedule leaves out.

options.text: The earnings multiple used is too generous
options.rationale: Possible in general, but it does not explain the structure of the gap.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the methods produce the gap and intangibles explain what sits inside it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Methods of Valuing a Business, Valuing Intangible Assets. Without multiple methods there is no gap to explain. Without intangibles the gap has no content. Both are needed.

questions.question: A print shop is closing permanently and its customer list will not transfer, since the work follows the retiring owner personally. Which valuation basis fits?

options.text: Assets plus the full value of the client list
options.rationale: Values something the buyer cannot acquire.

options.text: An earnings multiple on the last three years
options.rationale: Earnings will not continue after the owner leaves.

options.text: Original equipment cost plus goodwill
options.rationale: Two errors: historic cost and untransferable goodwill.

options.text: Assets at market value, intangibles at little
options.rationale: Relationships that cannot transfer carry almost no value to a buyer, which leaves the realisable assets as the basis.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the asset basis is chosen because the intangible analysis shows the relationships do not transfer.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Valuing Intangible Assets, Asset-Based Valuation Approach. Without the intangible test the client list gets valued. Without the asset approach there is no alternative basis. Both are needed.

questions.question: A kiosk costs about $2,000 a month to run and nets roughly $4 per drink after ingredients. What is its monthly break-even volume?

options.text: 500 drinks, covering the fixed costs
options.rationale: 2,000 divided by 4 of contribution per drink gives the 500 units that cover the monthly base.

options.text: 8,000 drinks, cost multiplied by four
options.rationale: Multiplies where the calculation divides.

options.text: 2,000 drinks, matching the cost figure
options.rationale: Confuses dollars of cost with units sold.

options.text: 250 drinks, at $8 of revenue each
options.rationale: Uses a price rather than the contribution left after variable costs.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: compute a break-even volume.

questions.question: A candle costs $6 to make and sells for $15. What is the margin percentage?

options.text: 60 percent, the $9 over the price
options.rationale: Margin divides the 9 of profit by the 15 selling price, giving 60 percent.

options.text: 90 percent, the profit stated directly
options.rationale: Turns a dollar figure into a percentage with no division.

options.text: 40 percent, the $6 over the price
options.rationale: Computes the cost share rather than the margin.

options.text: 150 percent, the $9 over the cost
options.rationale: That is markup, which the card warns is a different number.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: compute margin correctly.

questions.question: A company has spent $40,000 on buggy custom software and needs $25,000 more to finish it. A working alternative costs $15,000. What does sunk cost reasoning say?

options.text: Compare $25,000 against $15,000 only
options.rationale: The 40,000 is gone either way, so only the remaining spend belongs in the decision.

options.text: Finish it, since $40,000 is already in
options.rationale: The classic sunk cost error the card describes.

options.text: Compare $65,000 against $15,000 instead
options.rationale: Adds the unrecoverable spend back into the comparison.

options.text: Finish it, because switching wastes the work
options.rationale: Same error, phrased as regret about effort.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: apply sunk cost reasoning.

questions.question: A food truck pays $900 a month for propane and its lease, and about $1.80 per plate for tortillas and filling. Which statement uses the structure correctly?

options.text: Each extra plate adds its share of $900
options.rationale: Fixed costs do not rise with the next plate sold.

options.text: The lease becomes variable at high volume
options.rationale: The lease is fixed regardless of plates sold.

options.text: Total expenses rise evenly with each sale
options.rationale: Lumping both together is the trap the card names.

options.text: Each extra plate adds $1.80 of cost
options.rationale: Variable costs move with volume while the 900 stays put, which is what separating them makes visible.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: reason from a split cost structure.

questions.question: A sandwich shop's packaging cost jumped because every order, including those eaten in, goes in a heavy branded box. Which cut is the right one?

options.text: Switch to a cheaper bread supplier
options.rationale: Another quality cut when the waste is identified elsewhere.

options.text: Reduce the meat portion in each sandwich
options.rationale: Cuts the thing customers actually came for.

options.text: Cut one staff shift from every weekday
options.rationale: Attacks service quality over a packaging problem.

options.text: Use the boxes for takeaway orders only
options.rationale: It removes spending customers never valued while leaving the experience they do value untouched.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: cut cost without cutting what customers value.

questions.question: For one custom cake, which of these is an indirect cost?

options.text: The box that this cake leaves in
options.rationale: Attaches to this order specifically.

options.text: The flour and sugar used in it
options.rationale: Consumed by this specific cake, so it is direct.

options.text: The baker's hours spent decorating it
options.rationale: Traceable to the single order, so also direct.

options.text: The shop rent covering all orders
options.rationale: Rent supports every order rather than attaching to this cake, which makes it indirect.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: classify costs for one job.

questions.question: A kiosk covering $2,000 of monthly costs nets $4 a drink and sells about 650. A supplier price rise cuts the net to $3.20. What happens to break-even?

options.text: It rises to 800, at $2.50 per drink
options.rationale: Uses a contribution figure the case does not give.

options.text: It stays at 500, since costs are unchanged
options.rationale: Fixed costs are unchanged but contribution per unit fell, which moves break-even.

options.text: It rises to 625, close to current sales
options.rationale: 2,000 divided by 3.20 gives 625, so the margin squeeze pushes break-even from 500 to within 25 units of actual volume.

options.text: It falls, because each drink now costs less
options.rationale: Reverses the direction of the supplier increase.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: a margin change has to be carried into the break-even calculation to see the real exposure.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Margins and Markup, Break-even Thinking. Without the margin change nothing moves. Without break-even the smaller margin has no operational meaning. Both are needed.

questions.question: A truck signed a two-year $900 monthly lease six months ago and is considering closing a slow location. The lease cannot be cancelled. Variable costs there run $1.80 per plate against $4 of revenue. It sells 300 plates monthly. What follows?

options.text: Close it, since $900 exceeds the contribution
options.rationale: Compares a committed cost with contribution as if closing removed the lease.

options.text: Close it, because six months are already spent
options.rationale: Treats past payments as a reason to act, which is the sunk cost error.

options.text: Keep it, because the lease may be renegotiated
options.rationale: Speculation rather than the reasoning the numbers support.

options.text: Keep selling, since each plate helps the lease
options.rationale: The lease is committed either way, and 660 of contribution a month is 660 less lost than closing, which is the structure question rather than the sunk one.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the committed cost is irrelevant to the decision and the variable contribution is what decides it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Sunk Cost Recognition, Cost Structure. Without sunk cost reasoning the lease drags the decision. Without the cost split there is no contribution to weigh. Both are needed.

questions.question: A cake shop wants to cut costs. Its direct costs per cake are already lean, while indirect spending includes an unused second storage unit and a premium delivery contract customers never notice. Where should it cut?

options.text: The decorating hours on each order
options.rationale: Reduces the craft the product is sold on.

options.text: Both direct and indirect, evenly across
options.rationale: An across-the-board cut that ignores where the waste is.

options.text: The indirect items customers never see
options.rationale: Cost control targets spending that does not reach the customer, and the indirect line is where that slack sits here.

options.text: The ingredients, since they are the largest
options.rationale: Cuts the direct cost customers taste.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the direct and indirect split locates the slack and cost control decides what may be cut.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Direct Versus Indirect Costs, Cost Control. Without the classification the largest line looks like the target. Without cost control principles the indirect cuts have no justification. Both are needed.

questions.question: A chief financial officer wants January pre-orders booked as December revenue to smooth a soft quarter, arguing it evens out next month. What is wrong?

options.text: The adjustment is too small to matter
options.rationale: Size is the excuse, not the principle.

options.text: January will then look artificially weak
options.rationale: A consequence, but December's misstatement is the fault.

options.text: The period's numbers become untrue
options.rationale: Timing revenue to flatter a quarter misstates that period regardless of what later months show.

options.text: Pre-orders can never be counted at all
options.rationale: They can, in the period they are earned.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the reporting fault.

concepts: Conflicts of Interest in Financial Decisions
questions.question: A procurement manager's brother-in-law owns a vendor bidding for a contract. The manager discloses this and keeps deciding. Is that sufficient?

options.text: Yes, provided the bid is the cheapest
options.rationale: Outcome does not cure the process.

options.text: Yes, since disclosure was made openly
options.rationale: The trap the card names directly.

options.text: No, the vendor should be disqualified
options.rationale: Punishes a bidder rather than fixing the decision process.

options.text: No, he should step out of the decision
options.rationale: Disclosure names the conflict, and removing the conflicted person from the decision is what resolves it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify what resolves a conflict.

questions.question: A lending startup gets legal sign-off at launch and never revisits it as the product changes. What does that miss?

options.text: Regulators must approve every launch
options.rationale: Overstates the requirement.

options.text: Legal advice is expensive to repeat
options.rationale: Cost is not the principle at stake.

options.text: Rules apply to the product as it evolves
options.rationale: Compliance is continuous, since changes to terms and features can move a product into different regulation.

options.text: Startups are exempt while they are small
options.rationale: No such general exemption exists.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: state why compliance is ongoing.

concepts: Conflicts of Interest in Financial Decisions
questions.question: A supply contract decision involves a manager whose relative owns one bidder. What arrangement handles it properly?

options.text: He decides, with the conflict on record
options.rationale: Disclosure without recusal leaves the influence intact.

options.text: Another manager scores and awards the bids
options.rationale: Moving the decision to someone unconflicted is what protects both the outcome and the manager.

options.text: The relative's bid is rejected automatically
options.rationale: May cost the company the best bid for no good reason.

options.text: He decides, after promising impartiality
options.rationale: A promise is not a control.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: design a conflict-free process.

questions.question: A manager argues a small revenue shift is harmless because the next quarter will wash it out. What is the answer?

options.text: It is acceptable if the auditors agree
options.rationale: Outsources a judgement the company must make.

options.text: A knowing misstatement is still a false report
options.rationale: The temporary framing is the standard justification, and the figures for the period reported are wrong either way.

options.text: It is a problem only for listed companies
options.rationale: Accuracy is not limited by ownership structure.

options.text: It is acceptable below a set percentage
options.rationale: Thresholds do not make a deliberate misstatement honest.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: answer the temporary misstatement argument.

questions.question: A cash advance product cleared compliance at launch. Six months later the team adds a fee structure and extends repayment terms. What should happen?

options.text: A customer notice describing the changes
options.rationale: Disclosure does not establish compliance.

options.text: A fresh review before the change ships
options.rationale: New terms can change which rules apply, so the review belongs with the change rather than the original launch.

options.text: Nothing, since the product was approved
options.rationale: Approval covered a different product.

options.text: A review at the next annual audit
options.rationale: Ships a possibly non-compliant product for months.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: apply compliance to a product change.
