options.rationale: Nothing here is timed to a season.

options.text: Purchases decided right at the register
options.rationale: Point of purchase targets the decision made in the last few feet, for items nobody came in for.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what a checkout display is for.

questions.question: A pet store places grooming kits and treats along the right hand path from the entrance, because most shoppers turn right on the way in. What is that?

options.text: Seasonal planning by weather
options.rationale: Nothing here changes with the calendar.

options.text: Category management by margin
options.rationale: Category work decides each group's role, not where feet go.

options.text: Layout planning around traffic
options.rationale: Arranging the space so customers meet chosen products on the path they already walk is exactly this skill.

options.text: Point of purchase at checkout
options.rationale: The decision point here is the entry path, not the register.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the practice from the described arrangement.

questions.question: A hardware store treats paint as a destination people plan trips around and fasteners as a fill in purchase, giving each different space, pricing and stock depth. What is that practice?

options.text: Visual merchandising
options.rationale: That is how a display looks and pulls attention, not what role a group plays.

options.text: Category management
options.rationale: Running each product group as its own small business with its own role is the definition.

options.text: Channel management
options.rationale: Channels are about partners who sell for you, not aisles inside your own store.

options.text: Seasonal planning
options.rationale: Neither paint nor fasteners is being timed to a season here.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: match the described approach to its name.

questions.question: A garden center swaps holiday clearance for seeds and soil on March 1 every year. This year a hard frost is forecast through mid March. What does the skill say?

options.text: Hold the date, since customers expect it
options.rationale: Planning to the calendar rather than the conditions is the error the card names.

options.text: Move with the weather, not the date
options.rationale: Seasonal timing follows demand signals, and nobody plants during a frost no matter what the calendar says.

options.text: Discount the seeds until demand appears
options.rationale: Pays away margin to fight the weather rather than waiting out a two week delay.

options.text: Skip seeds this year and start with patio
options.rationale: Abandons the window that carries most of the year's revenue.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: time a seasonal switch against real demand signals.

questions.question: A sporting goods store wants to move one specific new running shoe this month. Which display does the work?

options.text: A back aisle display next to the treadmills
options.rationale: A relevant neighbour, but well off the traffic the launch needs.

options.text: An entrance end cap with the shoe raised and lit
options.rationale: High traffic position plus a presentation built around one product, which is what ties display to a sales target.

options.text: A tidy wall of every running shoe in stock
options.rationale: Organised, but it singles out nothing and so sells nothing in particular.

options.text: A seasonal banner about the store's history
options.rationale: Decoration with no product attached, the trap the card describes.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: build a display against a specific selling goal.

questions.question: A new shop puts its strongest promotional display in the first six feet inside the door, and shoppers walk straight past it. What explains that?

options.text: Shoppers prefer displays near the checkout
options.rationale: Checkout works for small impulse items, which is a different job.

options.text: Shoppers are still adjusting at the entrance
options.rationale: The first few feet are a transition zone where people orient rather than shop, so merchandise there is routinely missed.

options.text: The display was priced above the market
options.rationale: Price cannot explain a display nobody registers.

options.text: The store's signage font was hard to read
options.rationale: A detail that would matter only if people were looking.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: diagnose a placement failure from how shoppers move.

questions.question: A hardware store's paint category pulls planned trips, while small impulse goods carry the best margin. A manager wants the high margin items moved onto the paint wall. What is wrong with that?

options.text: Impulse items should never appear on a wall
options.rationale: An absolute rule that the case does not need and the practice does not hold.

options.text: The store should raise paint prices instead
options.rationale: Attacks the margin gap and damages the reason the trips happen.

options.text: The wall's job is to pull the trip, not the margin
options.rationale: Categories have different roles, and the destination category earns its space by bringing people in, which the layout is built to serve.

options.text: Paint earns less margin than the impulse goods
options.rationale: True and stated, which is why it is the manager's argument rather than the objection to it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: category roles say what a group is for, layout says where that role gets executed.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Category Management, Store Layout Planning. Without category roles the highest margin item obviously belongs in the best spot. Without the layout there is no contested wall. The objection only holds when a destination role meets a traffic decision.

questions.question: A garden center earns roughly 40 percent of annual revenue in the spring window. Grills sell steadily all summer at a better margin but draw no planned trips. How should March floor space be allocated?

options.text: Split evenly so neither category is favored
options.rationale: Neutral allocation wastes the only weeks that matter most.

options.text: To clearance, to clear last season's stock
options.rationale: Spends peak traffic on goods the season has already passed.

options.text: To the spring category that brings people in
options.rationale: The season concentrates the traffic and this category is the one people make the trip for, so it earns the space in that window.

options.text: To grills, since their margin is the highest
options.rationale: Optimises every category for the same goal, which the card warns against.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the calendar concentrates demand, the category roles decide who gets the space while it lasts.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Seasonal Merchandising Planning, Category Management. Without the season, margin is a fair way to allocate space year round. Without category roles, the spring goods have no special claim beyond timing. Both are needed to rule out the margin answer.

questions.question: A store adds eleven different small products to its checkout counter. Impulse sales fall rather than rise. What went wrong?

options.text: Checkout buyers only respond to discounts
options.rationale: Impulse items sell on visibility and convenience, not only on price.

options.text: The products were priced too low to notice
options.rationale: Low price is what makes checkout items easy to add.

options.text: Crowding removed the focus a display needs
options.rationale: The position was right but the presentation stopped working: with eleven competing items nothing catches the eye in the seconds available.

options.text: Impulse buying happens mostly in the aisles
options.rationale: Reverses the premise the store was right about.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the location is correct by one rule and the execution fails by the other, so only holding both explains a fall.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Point-of-Purchase Marketing, Visual Merchandising and Display. Without the point of purchase idea the checkout is not obviously the right place and option d looks plausible. Without display principles, more products at a good spot should mean more sales. The fall needs both to make sense.

questions.question: A $3,000 ad push drove $9,000 in extra sales at a 40 percent margin. Which figure is the return the business should report?

options.text: The $3,600 profit, against $3,000 spent
options.rationale: Return compares profit generated with the cost of generating it, not headline revenue.

options.text: The 40 percent margin on those sales
options.rationale: A rate, not a return, and it says nothing about the spend.

options.text: The $9,000 in sales the campaign drove
options.rationale: Reporting revenue as the return is the error the card names.

options.text: The $6,000 difference between the two
options.rationale: Subtracts cost from revenue while ignoring margin entirely.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: pick the correct return figure from given numbers.

questions.question: An online store had 20,000 visits and 200 orders last month. What is the conversion rate, and what does it describe?

options.text: 1 percent, the share who took the action
options.rationale: Conversion is the fraction of people who did what you wanted, which locates where the funnel leaks.

options.text: 20,000 visits, the reach of the site
options.rationale: Traffic is the denominator, not the conversion.

options.text: 200 orders, the monthly sales total
options.rationale: A count rather than a rate, so it cannot be compared.

options.text: 1 percent, the share of revenue from ads
options.rationale: Right arithmetic attached to the wrong meaning.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: compute and interpret a conversion rate.

questions.question: A bakery writes its campaign goal as increase brand awareness. What is missing from it?

options.text: A second social platform to post on
options.rationale: Adds a channel to a goal that remains unfalsifiable.

options.text: A number and a way to track it
options.rationale: Without a target figure and a measurement method, nobody can say afterwards whether the campaign worked.

options.text: A longer campaign period to run
options.rationale: More time spent measuring nothing still measures nothing.

options.text: A bigger creative production budget
options.rationale: Spends more against the same unmeasurable aim.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify what makes a goal measurable.

questions.question: A meal kit service grew sales 15 percent last year. The metro meal kit market grew 30 percent over the same period. How should the team read that?

options.text: Growing, while losing ground to rivals
options.rationale: Share is relative: growing slower than the market means competitors took the difference.

options.text: Performing well, since sales rose 15 percent
options.rationale: Own-sales growth without the market comparison, exactly the trap on the card.

options.text: Losing money, since costs rose with sales
options.rationale: Nothing about costs appears in the figures.

options.text: Leading the market it competes in
options.rationale: The numbers argue the opposite.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: interpret growth against market growth in a fresh case.

questions.question: A cold brew brand wants to know whether its city launch is registering. Which measurement fits the skill?

options.text: A one time survey after the launch week
options.rationale: A snapshot with nothing to compare it against.

options.text: Follower count on the brand's accounts
options.rationale: Counts an audience that opted in, not the target market's recall.

options.text: Total cans sold in the launch month
options.rationale: Sales, which mixes awareness with price, placement and everything else.

options.text: The same monthly survey question, repeated
options.rationale: Awareness is a trend, so the same measure over repeated periods is what shows movement.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose a measurement design that can show change.

questions.question: A store converts 1 percent of visitors against an industry norm near 3 percent. The owner's plan is to double the ad budget. What should come first?

options.text: Switch the ads to a different platform
options.rationale: Changes the source of traffic that converts poorly either way.

options.text: Double the ads, since traffic drives sales
options.rationale: Treats a conversion problem as a traffic problem, which the card names directly.

options.text: Raise prices to earn more per order
options.rationale: Fewer, dearer orders on a funnel that is already leaking.

options.text: Find where visitors drop before checkout
options.rationale: A conversion gap says the site loses people it already has, so buying more traffic multiplies the leak.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: diagnose a rate against a benchmark before spending.

questions.question: A campaign spent $5,000, brought 10,000 visits and 100 orders at $80 with a 30 percent margin. The manager calls it a success because traffic doubled. What does the analysis actually show?

options.text: A traffic problem needing a larger budget
options.rationale: More visits at the same rate deepen the loss.

options.text: A success, since ten thousand visits arrived
options.rationale: Counts the input as the result.

options.text: A profit of $8,000 on the campaign spend
options.rationale: Reports revenue as return and ignores both margin and cost.

options.text: A 1 percent rate and a loss on the spend
options.rationale: Profit generated is $2,400 against $5,000 spent, and the low conversion explains why the traffic never became money.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the rate explains the mechanism and the return decides the verdict, and either alone gives the wrong answer.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Conversion Rate Analysis, Return on Marketing Investment. Without the return the 1 percent rate is a diagnostic with no verdict attached. Without the conversion view the loss has no explanation and option d looks reasonable. Both are needed.

questions.question: A team's annual goal is grow sales 15 percent. It hits the number in a market that grew 30 percent. What should the goal have been?

options.text: An awareness goal instead of a sales goal
options.rationale: Swaps the outcome measure for an upstream one.

options.text: A larger sales number, such as 25 percent
options.rationale: A bigger version of a measure that still ignores what rivals did.

options.text: A share target, measured against the market
options.rationale: A goal is only useful if hitting it means winning, and a raw sales target can be met while losing position.

options.text: A revenue goal with no percentage at all
options.rationale: Removes the comparability the goal needs.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: goal setting supplies the form, share analysis supplies the standard that makes the goal meaningful.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Marketing Goals and Metrics, Market Share Analysis. Without the share view a met sales target is a clean success. Without the goals view the share data is an observation with nothing to change. The lesson lives in rewriting the goal, which needs both.

questions.question: A sponsorship costs $20,000 and drives almost no direct sales, but unaided recall in the target city rises from 4 percent to 11 percent over six months. How should it be judged?

options.text: A failure, since sales did not move at all
options.rationale: Applies a direct response standard to a brand objective.

options.text: A success, since any recall gain is worth it
options.rationale: Waves away the $20,000 rather than weighing it.

options.text: Unmeasurable, since brand effects never show
options.rationale: The tracked recall figures are exactly the measurement.

options.text: On the recall it bought, with the sales lag noted
options.rationale: Awareness work is measured by the awareness measure, while the return question stays open until later sales can be attributed.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the tracking supplies the evidence of effect, the return framework insists the cost still has to be answered for.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Brand Awareness Tracking, Return on Marketing Investment. Without the tracking there is no evidence and the spend looks wasted. Without the return view the recall gain justifies any price. Holding both is what produces a judgment with the sales lag stated rather than hidden.

questions.question: A coffee roaster that sells bags through grocery stores launches a subscription website selling the same bags itself. What has it added?

options.text: A direct channel to the end customer
options.rationale: Selling through its own storefront, with no wholesaler or retailer between, is the definition.

options.text: A co-op advertising agreement
options.rationale: That is shared ad spending with a partner, not a sales channel.

options.text: A wholesale account with a distributor
options.rationale: That is the arrangement it already has through grocery.

options.text: A licensing deal with a retail chain
options.rationale: No other company is paying to use the name.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the channel being described.

questions.question: A furniture company ships flat packed rather than assembled, cutting the cubic volume of each item by roughly 70 percent. Which cost does that mainly attack?

options.text: Freight, which is priced by volume
options.rationale: Carriers charge on dimensional weight, so shrinking the box is a direct cut to shipping cost.

options.text: Warehouse rent at the factory site
options.rationale: Storage benefits too, but freight is where volume pricing bites.

options.text: The retailer's margin on each unit
options.rationale: A direct shipper's packing choice does not move a retailer's cut.

options.text: Materials used in each cabinet
options.rationale: The same parts are in the box either way.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: connect a packing decision to the cost it moves.

questions.question: A granola brand gives a grocery chain's managers a better margin on end cap displays and trains their staff on the product. Why does that matter?

options.text: The retailer pushes what pays it best
options.rationale: The partner has its own economics, and the brand that supports them gets the shelf position.

options.text: The retailer sets the brand's list price
options.rationale: Pricing control is a separate question from partner support.

options.text: The brand cannot advertise on its own
options.rationale: Nothing prevents the brand from advertising.

options.text: The chain owns the granola inventory
options.rationale: Ownership of stock does not explain why support changes placement.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: state why partner incentives matter.

questions.question: A small batch hot sauce brand is offered national grocery placement carrying slotting fees near $20,000 per item. It holds about eleven weeks of cash. What does channel strategy say?

options.text: Take the placement, since reach decides success
options.rationale: Chasing the bigger channel regardless of fit and funding is the trap the card names.

options.text: Offer the chain a lower wholesale price instead
options.rationale: Worsens the economics of a channel it cannot afford to enter.

options.text: Borrow the fee against next year's revenue
options.rationale: Finances a channel decision that has not been justified yet.

options.text: Start direct and at markets, where cash allows
options.rationale: Picks the path this business can actually fund and where its buyers already shop, rather than the most impressive one.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose a channel against real constraints in a fresh case.

questions.question: A handmade candle brand with no audience yet is deciding where to sell online. Which mix fits the skill?

options.text: A single listing on the highest fee marketplace
options.rationale: Picks the costliest option without asking what the fee buys.

options.text: A custom built site launched before anything else
options.rationale: Pays for a storefront with no one walking past it.

options.text: Every major marketplace and platform at once
options.rationale: The everything list, with fees and fulfillment demands nobody has weighed.

options.text: A marketplace for discovery plus a social shop
options.rationale: Borrows an existing stream of browsers while keeping a channel it controls, which is what a brand without traffic needs.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: select an online channel mix for a brand with no traffic.

questions.question: A cold pressed juice line needs refrigerated space and buyers who care about health claims. Which retail format fits first?

options.text: Discount clubs selling in bulk packs
options.rationale: A format built on low price per unit, which contradicts a premium fresh product.

options.text: Big box grocery chains nationwide
options.rationale: Volume the line cannot supply, and the product disappears among cheaper drinks.

options.text: Vending machines in office lobbies
options.rationale: Convenient, but the buyer is choosing on thirst and price rather than health claims.

options.text: Boutique gyms and health food stores
options.rationale: Matches both constraints at once: refrigerated space and an audience that already screens for what the product sells.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: match a format to a product's requirements and buyer.

questions.question: A small jam maker considers cutting out its wholesaler to keep that margin. The wholesaler currently warehouses stock, breaks pallets into shop-sized cases and bills 300 small retailers. What does the maker have to replace?

options.text: The work the margin was paying for
options.rationale: An intermediary earns its cut by doing something, and removing it moves the storing, splitting and billing onto the maker.

options.text: Nothing, since the shops order direct
options.rationale: Someone still has to do the work.

options.text: The retailers, who will need replacing
options.rationale: The customers stay.

options.text: The recipe, to justify a higher price
options.rationale: Unrelated to distribution.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: identify the value an intermediary adds.

questions.question: A roaster nets about $4 a bag through grocery and could charge $16 selling directly. A founder calls the difference pure upside. What does the physical side force into that comparison?

options.text: Roasting capacity limits how much can be sold
options.rationale: A production ceiling, separate from the cost of moving goods.

options.text: Grocery buyers will drop the wholesale account
options.rationale: A channel conflict worth watching, but it is not what the logistics view adds.

options.text: Shipping, returns and service eat into the gap
options.rationale: Going direct moves the fulfilment burden onto the roaster, so the headline margin is gross rather than what lands.

options.text: Direct customers order smaller bags on average
options.rationale: Invents a demand difference the case does not describe.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the channel sets the price captured, the logistics set the cost of capturing it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Direct-to-Consumer Distribution, Physical Distribution and Logistics Awareness. Without the direct channel there is no $16 and no gap to examine. Without the logistics the gap really does look like pure upside. The correction exists only where both apply.

questions.question: A brand wins shelf space in a regional chain and then leaves the retailer to sell it. A rival funds end caps and trains the staff. Six months later the brand sits on a bottom shelf. What happened?

options.text: The chain's shoppers preferred the rival's flavor
options.rationale: Shoppers cannot prefer what they are no longer shown at eye level.

options.text: The brand's wholesale price was set too high
options.rationale: Price is not what the rival changed; support was.

options.text: The retailer breached the placement agreement
options.rationale: Shelf position is normally the retailer's to move, so nothing was breached.

options.text: The channel was won and then never managed
options.rationale: Winning placement is the start of the relationship, and the partner's own incentives decide what happens to it after that.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: choosing the channel and sustaining it are different jobs, and the failure sits in the gap between them.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Distribution and Channel Strategy, Managing Channel Partners. Without the channel decision there is no shelf to lose. Without the partner management view, losing position looks like a product or price problem. Both are needed to name the actual cause.

questions.question: A premium skincare line sells well in boutiques. To grow online it is weighing a large marketplace known for price led shoppers and heavy discounting. What is the risk?

options.text: Boutique buyers will demand the same low price
options.rationale: A real channel conflict, but it follows from the pricing rather than the format itself.

options.text: Online sales always carry higher return rates
options.rationale: A general claim that says nothing about this format choice.

options.text: The format's shoppers judge it against cheap rivals
options.rationale: A channel carries its own buying context, and a premium product placed in a bargain context is compared on the one dimension it loses.

options.text: The marketplace will not accept a small brand
options.rationale: Access is rarely the constraint on these platforms.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: format decides the context a product is judged in, and the online mix decides which contexts it enters.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Retail Format Selection, E-commerce Channel Strategy. Without format thinking a marketplace is just another storefront with fees. Without the online channel decision there is nothing to place. The risk appears only when the format's shopper is carried into the online choice.

questions.question: A taco truck expecting $180,000 in first year revenue sets marketing at 6 percent of that figure. What has the owner done?

options.text: Matched what a competitor spends
options.rationale: No competitor figure appears in the decision.

options.text: Tied the budget to expected revenue
options.rationale: Sizing spend as a share of what the business expects to earn is what makes the number defensible.

options.text: Picked a round number that felt right
options.rationale: That is the guess this approach replaces.

options.text: Spent whatever cash was left over
options.rationale: Leftover funding is not a budget method.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name how a marketing budget was set.

questions.question: A food truck's summer launch depends on a park festival, and rain would kill the foot traffic. Which line is a real contingency plan?

options.text: If it rains, shift to the brewery lot that day
options.rationale: Names the specific risk and the specific alternative, decided before the day arrives.

options.text: If sales are low, we will advertise more
options.rationale: The generic filler the card calls out: no named risk and no named action.

options.text: If the festival is cancelled, we will refund
options.rationale: Handles a different event and does nothing for the launch.

options.text: If it rains, we will reassess our options
options.rationale: Names the risk and then defers the decision it was supposed to make.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: distinguish a real contingency from a placeholder.

questions.question: A bakery lists social posts, a flyer drop and a discount with no target and no order. What does the list lack to be a plan?

options.text: A goal, a sequence and a budget
options.rationale: Tactics become a plan when a measurable goal, an order of steps and money are attached.

options.text: A social platform for each post
options.rationale: Channel detail on a list that still has no aim.

options.text: A larger number of tactics
options.rationale: More activity without direction is the same problem, scaled.

options.text: A designer to produce the flyer
options.rationale: Execution help for an undirected list.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify what turns tactics into a plan.

questions.question: A cold pressed juice line is positioned as premium, priced at $7.50, and promoted around craft and freshness. The founder then adds a discount club listing. What breaks?

options.text: The price becomes too low to sustain
options.rationale: The price has not changed in the scenario.

options.text: The channel contradicts the other three
options.rationale: Product, price and promotion all say premium while the place says bargain, and the mix stops supporting itself.

options.text: The product needs a longer shelf life
options.rationale: A real operational issue, but not the coordination failure described.

options.text: The promotion reaches too small a group
options.rationale: Reach is not what the new listing damages.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: find the element that contradicts the rest of the mix.

questions.question: A local bakery facing a new grocery store bakery counter writes good location under strengths and the economy under threats. Why is that SWOT weak?

options.text: Threats should always come before strengths
options.rationale: Order carries no meaning in the tool.

options.text: Nothing in it points to an actual decision
options.rationale: A SWOT earns its place by producing moves, and generic entries connect to no plan at all.

options.text: Location belongs under opportunities instead
options.rationale: Reshuffling a vague item leaves it just as vague.

options.text: It should list four items under each letter
options.rationale: Quantity is not what makes the entries useful.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: judge a filled-in SWOT against what it is for.

questions.question: A bakery wants 200 brunch orders in its first month. Which plan shape fits the goal?

options.text: A plan that starts once the first orders land
options.rationale: Waits for the result the plan is supposed to create.

options.text: Every tactic launched together on day one
options.rationale: Spends the budget at once with nothing built to receive the attention.

options.text: A single discount code run for four weeks
options.rationale: One tactic with no build-up and no follow through.

options.text: Teasers first, then a launch push, then reviews
options.rationale: A sequence where each step feeds the next, aimed at a stated number.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: sequence tactics toward a measurable goal.

questions.question: A taco truck has $10,800 for the year and a goal of 200 orders a week by month three. A vendor offers a $9,000 billboard package for month one. What does sound planning say?

options.text: Take it and raise the budget to 20 percent
options.rationale: Rewrites the budget to fit a tactic rather than the reverse.

options.text: Refuse it, since one step would eat the year
options.rationale: The budget is sized to the whole sequence, so a single tactic consuming it leaves the plan with no later steps.

options.text: Refuse it because billboards never work
options.rationale: Right call, wrong reason: the medium is not the problem.

options.text: Take it, since awareness has to come first
options.rationale: True about sequence, but it ignores what the spend leaves for everything after.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the budget sets the ceiling, the plan's sequence decides how much of it any one step may take.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Marketing Budgeting, Marketing Planning. Remove the budget and the billboard is simply one tactic among many. Remove the plan and $9,000 of a $10,800 budget is just a large purchase with nothing it starves. Both are needed for a.

questions.question: A premium juice brand's rain plan is to dump unsold stock into a discount club at half price. The brand is positioned on craft and freshness. What is wrong with the fallback?

options.text: Half price is not a deep enough cut
options.rationale: Deepening the cut worsens the actual problem.

options.text: The fallback names no specific trigger
options.rationale: Rain is named, so the trigger is not the flaw here.

options.text: Discount clubs will refuse fresh juice
options.rationale: Invents a constraint the case does not state.

options.text: The rescue undoes the position it protects
options.rationale: A contingency has to fit the mix, and a bargain channel at half price teaches the market the opposite of the positioning.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the contingency is well formed by one rule and destructive by the other.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Contingency Planning in Marketing, Marketing Mix Coordination. Without the contingency there is no fallback to judge. Without the mix view a specific, triggered plan looks textbook correct. The fault appears only where a sound plan collides with the position.

questions.question: A bakery's SWOT names scratch made recipes and loyal regulars as strengths, and a new grocery bakery counter undercutting on price as a threat. Which plan follows from that?

options.text: Match the counter's prices for three months
options.rationale: Fights on the dimension where the threat is strongest and the strength is irrelevant.

options.text: Lead on what the counter cannot copy quickly
options.rationale: Builds the plan on a real strength aimed at a named threat, which is what the analysis exists to produce.

options.text: Run the same plan as last year, unchanged
options.rationale: Treats the analysis as paperwork with no consequence.

options.text: Add packaged bread to compete on assortment
options.rationale: Moves toward the competitor's ground and away from the strength named.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the analysis supplies the honest inputs, the plan is what converts them into moves.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: SWOT Analysis for Marketing, Marketing Planning. Without the SWOT there is no strength or threat to build from and price matching is an ordinary response. Without the planning step the SWOT is a list nobody acts on. Both are needed to reject option b.

questions.question: A meal prep service tells customers it is the 20 minute option, against national kits that take 35 to 40 minutes. What has the service defined?

options.text: Its distribution plan for the region
options.rationale: Distribution is how the product reaches people, a separate decision.

options.text: Its target market's age and income
options.rationale: That is a profile of who buys, not a claim about where the product stands.

options.text: Its position against a named alternative
options.rationale: Positioning is where you stand relative to a specific competitor, stated so customers can hold it in mind.

options.text: Its pricing tier within the category
options.rationale: No price appears; the claim is about time.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: recognize a positioning claim from its shape.

questions.question: A new grooming shop lists friendly staff and quality service as the reasons to choose it. Why does that fail as a unique selling point?

options.text: It costs too much to deliver reliably
options.rationale: Cost of delivery is not what makes the claim weak here.

options.text: It appeals to the wrong customer group
options.rationale: The audience is fine; the claim would be empty for any audience.

options.text: It cannot be measured by the customer
options.rationale: Closer, but plenty of good differentiators are qualitative. The fault is that it is not distinctive.

options.text: Every competitor claims the same thing
options.rationale: A claim the whole category makes cannot be the reason to pick one member of it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: test a stated difference against the bar for a real one.

questions.question: A brand plots itself and four rivals on a chart with price on one axis and natural ingredients on the other. What is that chart for?

options.text: Setting the price for the next quarter
options.rationale: Price appears as an attribute, but the map does not produce a price decision by itself.

options.text: Tracking sales growth over four years
options.rationale: A perceptual map is a snapshot of standing, not a time series.

options.text: Finding the open space on the map
options.rationale: The point of the exercise is to see which positions are crowded and which are free to own.

options.text: Ranking rivals by total market share
options.rationale: Share is not an axis here, and the map is about perception rather than size.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: state the purpose of a described tool.

questions.question: A granola brand's draft line reads: our bars contain oats, honey, almonds and no preservatives. To turn that into a positioning statement, what has to change?

options.text: Name the retailer that will stock it
options.rationale: Where it sells is distribution, not position.

options.text: Name the price and the pack size
options.rationale: More specification, same problem: still no comparison and no buyer.

options.text: Name the factory standards it meets
options.rationale: Credentials support a claim but do not make one.

options.text: Name the buyer and the rival it beats
options.rationale: A positioning statement says who it is for and what it beats, which is exactly what a spec list leaves out.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: repair a real statement against the definition of the form.

questions.question: A minivan brand known as the boring family hauler rewrites its ads around adventure and cargo space, while trims, dealer pitch and showroom stay exactly as they were. What follows?

options.text: The brand loses its existing loyal buyers
options.rationale: Possible over time, but the immediate, certain effect is the mismatch.

options.text: The new message reaches too few buyers
options.rationale: Reach is not the issue described; the ads are running.

options.text: The experience contradicts the new message
options.rationale: Repositioning fails when only the advertising moves, because the buyer's actual encounter still teaches the old position.

options.text: The ads cost more than the trims would
options.rationale: Invents a cost comparison the scenario does not support.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: predict the outcome of a partial repositioning.

questions.question: A team builds a perceptual map from its own view of the product and finds a wide open position. Customer surveys later place the brand somewhere else entirely. What went wrong?

options.text: The map used two attributes instead of three
options.rationale: Two axes is the standard form; adding one would not have fixed the source of the data.

options.text: The map used opinion, not buyer perception
options.rationale: A map is only useful when built from how customers actually rate the brand, which is the input that was skipped.

options.text: The map was drawn before the price was set
options.rationale: Sequence with pricing is unrelated to the perception gap.

options.text: The map included too few rival brands
options.rationale: Coverage matters, but the brand's own placement is what turned out wrong.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: identify the input error behind a failed map in a new case.

questions.question: Two groomers share a block: one is cheap with a two week wait, the other is fast but premium with no loyalty program. A third shop is opening between them. Which plan does the most work?

options.text: The lowest price on the block, advertised heavily
options.rationale: Attacks the cheap rival where it is strongest, and price is the one position that invites a race.

options.text: 48 hour turnaround at mid price, with a loyalty card
options.rationale: Takes an unclaimed position between the two and backs it with a difference neither rival offers.

options.text: Friendly staff and quality grooming, priced to match
options.rationale: A category claim and a copied price: no position and no difference.

options.text: Premium service positioned against the cheap rival
options.rationale: Picks a clear position, but lands on top of the premium rival and offers nothing it lacks.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: where you stand relative to rivals, and what specific thing makes that stand true.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Market Positioning, Differentiation and Unique Selling Point. Remove positioning and option d competes fine. Remove differentiation and option c is a perfectly good answer, since it takes a clear spot. Only holding both rules out three of the four.

questions.question: Brand trackers still place a snack brand at processed and cheap, though its recipe changed two years ago. Leadership wants a new tagline next month and expects perception to follow. What is the flaw in that plan?

options.text: Repositioning needs a higher price to be believed
options.rationale: Price can support a position, but no rule makes it the requirement.

options.text: Perception moves with sustained proof, not one tagline
options.rationale: The map records what buyers believe, and shifting a belief takes consistent evidence over many months, not a single campaign.

options.text: The tracker data is too old to act on this year
options.rationale: The data is current; it is the recipe change that is two years old and still unnoticed.

options.text: A tagline cannot mention ingredients at all
options.rationale: Invents a restriction. Taglines can absolutely carry an ingredient claim.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the map says where perception sits and who owns it, repositioning says what it costs to move.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Perceptual Mapping, Repositioning Strategy. Without the map there is no evidence the old perception persists, so the tagline plan looks reasonable. Without the repositioning knowledge the persistence is a fact with no implied timeline. The flaw only appears when both are held.

questions.question: A bar brand's positioning statement claims it beats rivals by being gluten free, in a category where very few buyers screen for gluten. The claim is entirely true. Why is the statement still weak?

options.text: It states a benefit the product cannot prove
options.rationale: Gluten free is provable; it just is not wanted.

options.text: It differentiates on something buyers do not weigh
options.rationale: A real difference nobody is shopping on is not a position, because the thing that makes it distinctive does not enter the decision.

options.text: It names a category that is already crowded
options.rationale: Crowding is a reason to differentiate, not a flaw.

options.text: It compares the brand against a single named rival
options.rationale: Naming one rival is a fine way to position.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the statement is well formed, so only the test for a real differentiator exposes the fault.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Competitive Positioning Statements, Differentiation and Unique Selling Point. Without the statement form the question is a plain definition of a weak differentiator. Without the differentiation test the statement passes every structural check it has, since it names a buyer, a category and a rival. The weakness lives in the gap between the two.

questions.question: An artisan dog bakery prices a box of cookies at $14 while grocery treats sit at $4. Beyond covering costs, what is the $14 communicating?

options.text: The number of boxes the shop can make
options.rationale: Capacity is an operations fact that price does not announce.

options.text: The exact cost of making the cookies
options.rationale: Cost sets a floor, but the gap to $14 is the positioning choice.

options.text: The discount available to repeat buyers
options.rationale: No discount is mentioned, and a list price is not a loyalty offer.

options.text: Who the product is for and its worth
options.rationale: Price is a signal: it tells shoppers which shelf this belongs on and which buyer it expects.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: read what a price communicates.

questions.question: A candle is listed at $19.99 beside a crossed out $26 launch price. Which lever is being used?

options.text: The break-even volume for the line
options.rationale: Break-even is an internal calculation, not a display tactic.

options.text: The cost of the wax and jar per unit
options.rationale: Unit cost is invisible to the shopper and unchanged by presentation.

options.text: How the price reads, not just what it is
options.rationale: Charm endings and a reference price change the feel of a number without changing the money.

options.text: The elasticity of candle demand
options.rationale: Elasticity may explain the result, but the lever pulled here is presentation.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the pricing lever in a described display.

questions.question: A cold brew can costs $0.90 to make, the co-packer bills $3,000 a month whatever the volume, and each can nets $1.60 wholesale. What does the $3,000 decide?

options.text: How much each can costs to produce
options.rationale: That is the $0.90 variable cost, which does not move with the monthly fee.

options.text: How many cans must sell to cover it
options.rationale: A fixed cost is what the contribution per unit has to pay off, which is the break-even volume.

options.text: How large the launch discount is
options.rationale: Nothing about a fixed fee determines a promotional cut.

options.text: How much shelf space to ask for
options.rationale: Shelf space is a constraint on volume, not something the fee sets.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: state what a fixed cost determines.

questions.question: A food truck raises its $9 burrito by a dollar. A cheaper truck parks two spaces away, and regulars have been price sensitive all year. What should the owner expect?

options.text: Revenue rises because each sale earns more
options.rationale: The arithmetic that ignores lost units, which is the error this skill exists to prevent.

options.text: Volume may fall enough to lower revenue
options.rationale: With a close substitute and price sensitive buyers, demand can drop faster than the price rises.

options.text: The cheaper truck will raise its price too
options.rationale: Assumes a competitor response that helps, with nothing to support it.

options.text: Demand is unaffected by a one dollar move
options.rationale: An eleven percent increase in a price sensitive market is not invisible.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: predict the revenue effect of a price move in specific market conditions.

questions.question: A landscaping supplier wants contractors to pay faster and to order in bigger loads. Which structure does both?

options.text: An end of season clearance on remaining mulch
options.rationale: Clears inventory, which is a different goal from cash timing and order size.

options.text: 2 percent off within 10 days, 5 percent over 50 bags
options.rationale: Two conditions, each tied to a behavior the business wants, so the margin given up buys something specific.

options.text: A flat 10 percent off every order this quarter
options.rationale: An unconditional giveaway: buyers who would have paid full price take it too.

options.text: A free delivery offer on all orders this month
options.rationale: Pleasant, but attached to no behavior change the supplier asked for.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: design a discount against two stated behavioral goals.

questions.question: A juice bar is quiet between 2pm and 4pm and busy the rest of the day. Rather than discounting everything, which tactic targets that specific gap?

options.text: A punch card that rewards a tenth drink
options.rationale: Rewards frequency at any hour, so the quiet window stays quiet.

options.text: A tiered happy hour bundle for those hours
options.rationale: Aims the offer at the hours that need traffic and raises the ticket rather than only cutting it.

options.text: A 20 percent price cut across the menu
options.rationale: Pays away margin during the busy hours that needed no help.

options.text: A higher price on the busiest morning items
options.rationale: Taxes the strongest part of the day without giving anyone a reason to come at 3pm.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: match a tactic to a specific business goal in a new case.

questions.question: Break-even math says a cold brew can needs 1,900 units a month at $2.50, but launch shelf space realistically caps sales near 1,200. Moving the price to $2.90 closes the gap on paper. What has to be checked first?

options.text: Whether the co-packer can produce 1,900 cans
options.rationale: Capacity is not the binding constraint; shelf space and demand are.

options.text: Whether a competitor sells a similar can nearby
options.rationale: Useful context that still does not test this product's own volume at $2.90.

options.text: Whether demand holds at the higher shelf price
options.rationale: The higher price only works if the units survive it, and a break-even sheet assumes volume it cannot promise.

options.text: Whether the ingredient cost can fall below $0.90
options.rationale: A real lever, but it answers the cost side while the question is whether the price sticks.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: break-even produces the required price, elasticity decides whether that price survives contact with buyers.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Break-even Pricing Analysis, Price Elasticity Awareness. Without the break-even there is no reason to raise the price at all. Without elasticity the new price is simply the answer and nothing needs checking. The trap only exists where one feeds the other.

questions.question: A luxury candle brand prices at $200 to signal craftsmanship. A junior marketer proposes listing it at $199.99 with a crossed out $260. What is the objection?

options.text: Crossed out prices are not allowed in retail
options.rationale: Reference pricing is ordinary practice when the original price was real.

options.text: A $260 anchor is lower than buyers expect
options.rationale: Invents an expectation the case does not describe.

options.text: Charm pricing undercuts the premium signal
options.rationale: The cue works on bargain reading, which is the opposite of what a price chosen to say luxury is doing.

options.text: The discount is too small to notice at all
options.rationale: Size of the cut is not the issue; the register it speaks in is.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the price carries a position, and the cue carries a contradictory message about the same number.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Pricing and Value Positioning, Psychological Pricing Cues. Without the positioning, .99 and a reference price are a sound tactic worth using. Without the cue there is nothing to contradict the position. The objection is the collision of the two.

questions.question: A shop answers every slow week with a blanket 15 percent off. Margin is sliding and regulars have started waiting for the sale before buying. Which change addresses both problems?

options.text: Deepen the cut to 25 percent for one week
options.rationale: Trains the waiting behavior harder and costs more margin doing it.

options.text: Run the same sale on a fixed monthly date
options.rationale: Makes the wait predictable, which is worse for full price sales, not better.

options.text: Tie the cut to a behavior the shop wants
options.rationale: A condition stops the unconditional margin leak and stops teaching customers that waiting always pays.

options.text: Raise list prices so the cut costs less
options.rationale: Hides the discount in the list price and risks the position the shop holds.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the tactic has to serve a goal, and the discount has to carry a condition, or the same leak continues.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Pricing Tactics, Discount and Allowance Structures. Without the tactic rule, a blanket sale is a legitimate response to a slow week. Without the structure rule, any targeted promotion looks equivalent. Both are needed to rule out options b and c.

questions.question: A snack brand's classic bar has had flat sales for three years while its new protein line grows quickly. Which life cycle stage describes the classic bar?

options.text: Introduction
options.rationale: Introduction is a product's first months on sale, not its fourth year.

options.text: Mature
options.rationale: Flat sales over a long stretch, with the growth happening elsewhere, is the mature stage.

options.text: Growth
options.rationale: Growth means rising sales; that describes the protein line, not the classic bar.

options.text: Development
options.rationale: Development happens before launch, and this bar has been selling for years.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: place a product on the life cycle from its sales pattern.

questions.question: A small batch hot sauce moves from a plastic squeeze bottle to a matte labeled glass bottle with a wax dipped cap, aimed at gift shoppers. What is the packaging doing?

options.text: Signaling quality to gift buyers
options.rationale: Packaging is a visual cue about worth, read before the product is ever tasted.

options.text: Lowering the cost per unit sold
options.rationale: Glass and wax raise unit cost; the return comes from price, not savings.

options.text: Widening the distribution network
options.rationale: Where it sells is a separate decision from how it presents.

options.text: Extending the sauce's shelf life
options.rationale: A preservation benefit is not what the described change is for.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what a packaging change accomplishes.

questions.question: A coffee shop's pastry case holds six items and two of them barely sell. Deciding what to drop, add and feature across the whole case is a question about what?

options.text: The product mix
options.rationale: Judging items as a lineup rather than one at a time is precisely the mix decision.

options.text: The supply chain
options.rationale: Sourcing follows the assortment decision rather than making it.

options.text: The unit price
options.rationale: Nothing here is being repriced; the question is which items exist.

options.text: The store layout
options.rationale: Where the case sits is display, not what goes in it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the decision type from its description.

questions.question: A camera shop sells a body, a lens and a bag together for less than the three cost separately. What is it doing?

options.text: Designing a service standard
options.rationale: No service is involved.

options.text: Eliminating a slow product
options.rationale: Nothing is being discontinued.

options.text: Offering a longer warranty
options.rationale: No promise is made.

options.text: Bundling to lift the basket
options.rationale: Packaging items as one deal makes the whole look better value and moves more than item-by-item buying would.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the tactic.

questions.question: A tool brand is deciding between a one year and a lifetime guarantee. What is the trade-off?

options.text: Bundle size against margin
options.rationale: Bundling is a different decision.

options.text: Shelf space against unit price
options.rationale: Neither is at stake.

options.text: Trust gained against claims paid
options.rationale: A more generous promise buys confidence at the counter and commits the business to more repairs and refunds later.

options.text: Supplier terms against demand
options.rationale: Supply is not involved.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name both sides of the policy choice.

questions.question: A line has lost money for three years and stays on the list because it was the founder's first product. What should drive the decision?

options.text: How long it has been sold
options.rationale: Age is not performance.

options.text: How it is actually performing
options.rationale: The call is made on the product's real results, not on what it meant historically.

options.text: Whether rivals still sell one
options.rationale: Their results are not these.

options.text: What the founder prefers
options.rationale: That is the reason being questioned.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the criterion.

questions.question: A meal prep company sells a flexible pick any ten meals plan, and busy parents keep lapsing after a month. The food rates well and the price matches rivals. What should change first?

options.text: The price, with a discount on the ten meal plan
options.rationale: Discounting a plan people find effortful buys a cheaper version of the same friction.

options.text: The offer's shape, into a set family bundle
options.rationale: When the product and price are fine, the offer is the lever: a preset bundle removes the weekly choosing that is costing these customers.

options.text: The ingredients, toward cheaper family staples
options.rationale: The food is already rated well, so the problem is not what is in the box.

options.text: The promotion, with more ads aimed at parents
options.rationale: More parents entering the same plan will lapse the same way.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: isolate the offer from the product and price in a fresh case.

questions.question: Regulars at a juice bar keep asking for something to grab before a 7am class that is not a full smoothie. Which development path fits the skill?

options.text: A breakfast sandwich menu tested next spring
options.rationale: Drifts from the stated need and delays it past the demand that exists now.

options.text: A grab and go protein shot using current equipment
options.rationale: Starts from a confirmed customer problem and takes the route to market the shop can actually fund.

options.text: A loyalty app that rewards early morning visits
options.rationale: Rewards a visit for a product the shop still does not sell.

options.text: A full smoothie line with new blenders and staff
options.rationale: Answers the request with the exact thing customers said they did not want, at the highest cost.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose the development path that matches a stated need and a realistic launch.

questions.question: A granola brand known for clean, simple ingredients weighs two launches under its own name: new bar flavors, or an energy drink. What does fit predict?

options.text: Neither should launch under the existing name
options.rationale: Overcorrects: a close line extension is the textbook good use of an existing name.

options.text: Both stretch the name equally, so cost decides
options.rationale: Treats fit as neutral when fit is the whole variable.

options.text: The drink wins because the category grows faster
options.rationale: Category growth is real but it does not fix a mismatch with what the name means.

options.text: New flavors ride the trust; the drink strains it
options.rationale: A near neighbour inherits the brand's meaning, while a category that contradicts it spends the trust instead of using it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: judge two candidate launches against the fit test.

questions.question: A software team is redesigning a workflow its warehouse customers use daily. The product lead proposes building it from the team's own notes and demoing at the end. What would co-creation change?

options.text: Survey the users after it ships
options.rationale: Feedback after the fact, which is the current plan.

options.text: Bring those users in while it is built
options.rationale: Co-creation means the people who will use it shape the thing during design, not just react to a finished version.

options.text: Let the engineers decide the design
options.rationale: Moves it further from the user.

options.text: Demo to more customers at the end
options.rationale: A wider audience for the same reveal.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: say what co-creation changes about the process.

questions.question: A dental practice gets glowing reviews on days one hygienist works and lukewarm ones otherwise. The owner wants every visit to feel like the good days. What does she need to build?

options.text: A survey after every appointment
options.rationale: Measures the gap she already sees.

options.text: The steps and checks, written down
options.rationale: Designing the service means the standard lives in the process rather than in whoever happens to be rostered.

options.text: A bonus for the best hygienist
options.rationale: Rewards the person, spreads nothing.

options.text: More appointments on her days
options.rationale: Concentrates the dependency.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: move quality from a person into a process.

questions.question: A gym bundles membership with personal training and nutrition coaching at one price. Most members use only the gym, and the bundle costs more than membership alone. What is the risk?

options.text: Coaching capacity sitting unused
options.rationale: An operations consequence, not the risk to the offer.

options.text: Paying for what they will not use
options.rationale: A bundle has to read as more value, and one that forces unwanted items on most buyers reads as a price rise.

options.text: Members using all three services
options.rationale: That would be the bundle working.

options.text: A price that is clearly too low
options.rationale: It is higher than membership alone.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: test a bundle against what buyers actually want.

questions.question: A bakery's muffin sales are declining, but muffins still pull the morning crowd that buys the coffee alongside them. A manager wants to cut muffins and move the budget to a growing cookie line. What is the risk?

options.text: Muffins can be revived with launch level ad spending
options.rationale: Spending new-launch money on a declining item is the error the life cycle warns against.

options.text: Cutting a declining item can remove traffic others need
options.rationale: The life cycle says harvest, and the mix says the item's value includes what it sells alongside it, so the decline is not the whole picture.

options.text: The savings will not cover the cookie line's costs
options.rationale: A budgeting guess that sidesteps the reason muffins earn their slot.

options.text: Cookies will decline at the same rate within a year
options.rationale: Invents a life cycle for the cookie line that nothing in the case supports.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the stage says retire it, the lineup says it carries other sales, and the tension is the question.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Product Life Cycle Awareness, Product Mix and Assortment. Without the life cycle there is no case for cutting muffins at all. Without the mix view the decline settles it and the manager is simply right. The risk exists only where the two disagree.

questions.question: A craft hot sauce aimed at gift shoppers upgrades to glass bottles with a story card, but still sells single bottles only. Gift buyers browse and leave. What is missing?

options.text: A second label design tested against the first
options.rationale: Keeps iterating on the half that is already working.

options.text: A lower price to match the grocery shelf options
options.rationale: Undoes the premium signal the packaging was bought to create.

options.text: A wider range of heat levels in the same bottle
options.rationale: More variants of the same single bottle leave the gift problem untouched.

options.text: A gift ready offer, such as a boxed three bottle set
options.rationale: The presentation now signals gift, but the unit being sold is still a pantry item, so the offer has to change too.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: packaging sets the expectation, offer design decides what is actually purchasable, and a mismatch between them is the fault.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Packaging and Presentation, Product and Offer Design. Without the packaging upgrade the brand simply is not a gift item and price would be the story. Without offer design the bottles look right and nothing explains the walkaway. Both are needed to locate the gap.

questions.question: A juice bar whose lineup already includes full smoothies can add a protein shot line on existing equipment, or a second smoothie line needing $6,000 of new gear. Both answer requests it has heard. What settles it?

options.text: The smoothie line will always earn more per order
options.rationale: A higher ticket on a product the lineup already sells is not new revenue, it is a split.

options.text: The shot line adds what the lineup lacks, at lower cost
options.rationale: It fills a gap rather than duplicating a slot, and it reaches market on equipment the shop already owns.

options.text: Whichever line the current staff prefers to make
options.rationale: Preference is not a development criterion; demand and route to market are.

options.text: The smoothie line, because the request came first
options.rationale: Order of arrival says nothing about fit or feasibility.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: development weighs the route to market, the mix weighs whether the lineup needs the slot.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: New Product and Service Development, Product Mix and Assortment. Remove the development view and cost and equipment stop mattering. Remove the mix view and the duplicate smoothie slot looks like a fine idea. Only together do they eliminate option b.

questions.question: A repair chain advertises a bold no-questions guarantee to win trust, and each branch handles repairs its own way with no shared checks. Claims run at four times the forecast. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: A guarantee that is simply too generous
options.rationale: It would be affordable over a consistent service.

options.text: Customers claiming dishonestly
options.rationale: Nothing points at the customers.

options.text: A generous promise over an uneven service
options.rationale: What a guarantee costs is set by how reliably the service performs, so the promise and the process have to be designed against each other.

options.text: Branches that need more technicians
options.rationale: Headcount is not the described gap.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the promise sets the exposure and the service design sets how often it is triggered, and only together do they explain the claims rate.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Warranty and guarantee policy, Service quality design. Without the bold guarantee uneven repairs annoy people cheaply. Without the uneven service the guarantee is affordable. Both are needed.

questions.question: A product was designed hand in hand with a dozen enthusiastic customers who still love it. Across the wider market it has lost money for two years. The team argues it cannot be cut because customers helped build it. What is the error?

options.text: Two years is too short a run to judge it on
options.rationale: Two years of losses is a signal.

options.text: A product that should never have been launched
options.rationale: Its users value it; the question is whether it earns its place.

options.text: Treating involvement as a reason to keep it
options.rationale: Co-creation makes a product fit the people who shaped it and says nothing about whether the range can afford to carry it.

options.text: A dozen customers is too small a design group
options.rationale: A dozen engaged users is a reasonable design input.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the co-creation was done properly and the elimination decision runs on performance, so one cannot be used to answer the other.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Co-creation with customers, Product elimination decisions. Without the co-creation there is no loyalty argument. Without the performance test the losses go unexamined. Both are needed.

questions.question: A weak accessory looks profitable because it is sold inside a popular bundle. Standalone it sells almost nothing. A manager cites the bundle revenue to keep it. What should the review establish?

options.text: Whether the bundle price is too low
options.rationale: Prices the pack, not the item.

options.text: Whether to bundle it more widely
options.rationale: Hides the item in more packs.

options.text: Whether the bundle sells without it
options.rationale: Bundle revenue is credited to every item in the pack, so the elimination question is whether this one adds anything buyers are actually there for.

options.text: Whether standalone sales can grow
options.rationale: A separate project, not the test.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the bundle is what makes the item look healthy, so the elimination test has to isolate its own contribution.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Product bundling, Product elimination decisions. Without the bundle the weak sales are plain. Without the elimination question nobody looks. Both are needed.

questions.question: A grooming shop's ad reads: family owned since 2009, full service grooming, certified staff. What is missing from it?

options.text: The address and opening hours
options.rationale: Useful detail, but its absence is not what makes the message weak.

options.text: What the customer personally gets
options.rationale: An ad has to answer what is in it for me; this one only describes the business.

options.text: The shop's years of experience
options.rationale: That is already there, and it is part of the problem rather than the fix.

options.text: The names of the groomers
options.rationale: More company facts, which is the category the ad is already full of.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: spot the missing benefit in a single ad.

questions.question: A bakery invites the local paper to cover its Friday bread donation to a shelter, and the paper runs the story. What has the bakery earned?

options.text: Coverage it did not pay for
options.rationale: Publicity is attention earned through something newsworthy rather than bought as ad space.

options.text: A discount on future ads
options.rationale: Editorial coverage and ad rates are separate transactions.

options.text: Control over the final story
options.rationale: Backwards: giving up control is the trade earned media makes.

options.text: A guaranteed sales increase
options.rationale: Coverage creates attention, never a guaranteed result.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what earned coverage provides.

questions.question: A studio texts every client a review link right after their appointment, every single time. What makes that a referral system rather than a hope?

options.text: It fires at the same moment every time
options.rationale: A repeatable trigger tied to a specific point in the visit is what turns goodwill into a channel.

options.text: It reaches the widest possible audience
options.rationale: It reaches only existing clients, which is the point rather than a flaw.

options.text: It offers the largest possible discount
options.rationale: No discount is involved, and size of reward is not what makes it systematic.

options.text: It runs only when business is slowest
options.rationale: Occasional asking is exactly the habit the skill replaces.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify what makes a referral mechanism repeatable.

questions.question: A shop runs twenty percent off every time the week feels slow, with no end date and no particular goal. What is missing from the promotion?

options.text: A longer run so shoppers notice it
options.rationale: Length makes a permanent markdown, not a promotion.

options.text: A purpose the deal is meant to serve
options.rationale: A promotion is a short-term tool aimed at something specific, clearing stock or winning trial, and without that it is just a lower price.

options.text: A deeper discount to draw people in
options.rationale: More of the thing that is not working.

options.text: A sign in the window announcing it
options.rationale: Visibility does not supply a reason.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what separates a promotion from a markdown.

questions.question: A brand wants to pull in price-sensitive buyers without lowering the price everyone else pays. Which tool fits?

options.text: A coupon only some shoppers redeem
options.rationale: A coupon discounts for the people who bother to use it while the shelf price, and the margin from everyone else, stays where it was.

options.text: A permanent cut to the shelf price
options.rationale: Gives the discount to every buyer.

options.text: A loyalty card with no reward yet
options.rationale: Offers nothing to act on now.

options.text: A higher price with a free gift
options.rationale: Raises the barrier it meant to lower.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: match the tool to the stated constraint.

questions.question: A new juice bar has almost no budget and chalks a trail of fruit footprints along the pavement leading to its door. What is this?

options.text: Low cost attention, won by being odd
options.rationale: Guerrilla tactics buy notice with invention rather than with media spend.

options.text: A sponsorship of a local attraction
options.rationale: No third party is involved.

options.text: A loyalty scheme for repeat buyers
options.rationale: Nothing rewards a second visit.

options.text: A discount aimed at new customers
options.rationale: No price is changed.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the tactic.

questions.question: A skincare brand pays a dermatologist with a large following to use and discuss its cleanser. What is the brand buying?

options.text: Trust the audience already has
options.rationale: The value is that the audience's existing confidence in that person carries over to the product.

options.text: A place on a retailer's shelf
options.rationale: Distribution is a different matter.

options.text: A cheaper way to run adverts
options.rationale: Cost is not the mechanism.

options.text: Rights to use a medical claim
options.rationale: No claim is licensed here.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what transfers in an influencer deal.

questions.question: A coffee roaster is confident that anyone who tastes its blend will prefer it, but shoppers will not pay premium for an unknown bag. What should it do?

options.text: Give the taste away at the shelf
options.rationale: When the product itself is the best argument, a trial lets the customer's own experience do the persuading.

options.text: Buy adverts in a food magazine
options.rationale: Another claim, more expensively.

options.text: Lower the price to match the others
options.rationale: Gives up the premium it believes in.

options.text: Describe the roast on the packaging
options.rationale: A claim is what they already distrust.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: pick the tool for a product that sells itself on contact.

questions.question: A bank pays to put its name on a town's much loved summer festival. Beyond the exposure, what is it hoping for?

options.text: Some of the goodwill people feel
options.rationale: Sponsorship borrows the audience's existing warmth toward the thing being sponsored.

options.text: Ownership of the festival itself
options.rationale: Sponsoring is not owning.

options.text: A discount on its own costs
options.rationale: Sponsorship is a cost.

options.text: Control of who may attend
options.rationale: Access is not what is bought.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the second thing sponsorship buys.

questions.question: A skate shop is launching a board line aimed at 14 to 17 year olds. Which plan shows the skill rather than a channel list?

options.text: Posts on Instagram, TikTok and Facebook at once
options.rationale: Three platforms with no reason given for any of them, which the card calls out.

options.text: Short trick clips on TikTok tagged to local spots
options.rationale: Names one platform, matched to where this age group actually spends attention, with a format that suits the product.

options.text: A weekly email newsletter to the shop's list
options.rationale: A channel this audience rarely opens, and the list predates the new line.

options.text: A printed flyer drop in the surrounding blocks
options.rationale: Reaches households rather than the teenagers who choose the board.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: match channel to audience and goal in a specific launch.

questions.question: A bike shop's discount posts are being scrolled past. It wants people to stop and follow. Which content plan fits the skill?

options.text: A story about the owner's discount philosophy
options.rationale: A sales pitch wearing a story, the disguise the card warns about.

options.text: A weekly five minute repair tip video series
options.rationale: Useful on its own terms, which is what earns attention and makes the shop the place to come when something breaks.

options.text: A countdown to the next clearance weekend
options.rationale: Urgency without usefulness, which still asks rather than gives.

options.text: A daily post listing this week's sale prices
options.rationale: More of the message people are already scrolling past.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose content that earns attention rather than demands it.

questions.question: A dog bakery sells to owners aged 30 to 45 within one suburb. Which promotional mix reflects a strategy rather than a list of tools?

options.text: A national podcast sponsorship for six months
options.rationale: Pays for an audience that cannot visit a single suburban shop.

options.text: TV, radio, print, social and email, all at once
options.rationale: More tools is not a strategy, and most of these reach far outside one suburb.

options.text: Billboards on the two main routes into town
options.rationale: Broad reach aimed at drivers rather than at dog owners.

options.text: Farmers market booth and vet clinic referral cards
