options.rationale: Two channels chosen because this audience already passes through them, one for discovery and one carrying borrowed trust.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: build a mix around one audience's habits.

questions.question: A bike shop knows which customers bought a road bike last spring and wants to sell them a winter service. What does direct marketing look like here?

options.text: The same offer sent to every address
options.rationale: A blast is the thing direct marketing replaces.

options.text: A note naming the bike they bought
options.rationale: Direct marketing earns its cost by using what you already know about that person, which is what makes the message worth opening.

options.text: A poster in the shop window all winter
options.rationale: Only reaches people already walking past.

options.text: A banner advert on a cycling website
options.rationale: Reaches strangers, not these customers.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: shape a message around what is known about the recipient.

questions.question: A paint brand books a stand at a home show and hands out leaflets. Footfall is good and nobody stops. What would make it experiential?

options.text: Hiring a larger stand next to the door
options.rationale: More traffic past the same offer.

options.text: Letting visitors paint a sample board
options.rationale: The point of an experience is that the customer does something with the product, which a leaflet cannot deliver.

options.text: Adding a discount code to the leaflet
options.rationale: A price tool, not an experience.

options.text: Printing the leaflets in full colour
options.rationale: A better leaflet is still a leaflet.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: turn attendance into interaction.

questions.question: A cinema sends every subscriber the full week's listings each Monday at 9am. Open rates are falling. What should change?

options.text: Adding every showing time to the mail
options.rationale: More to wade through.

options.text: Sending the same listings twice weekly
options.rationale: Doubles what is already being ignored.

options.text: Moving the send to Monday evening
options.rationale: Changes the hour, not the ask.

options.text: One film, timed to when they book
options.rationale: These channels work on a specific, timely action, and a full catalogue at a fixed hour asks the reader to do the sorting.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: aim the message at one timely action.

concepts: Search Engine and Search Ad Marketing
questions.question: A plumber gets most of his work from people with a burst pipe who need someone now. Where should his promotional money go?

options.text: Into a glossy brochure through doors
options.rationale: Arrives long before the pipe bursts.

options.text: Into a monthly newsletter by email
options.rationale: Reaches past customers on his schedule.

options.text: Into a billboard on the ring road
options.rationale: Broad reach, no intent behind it.

options.text: Where people search for a plumber
options.rationale: Search reaches someone at the moment they have the problem, which is the whole advantage over interrupting people who do not.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: match the channel to a demand that arrives suddenly.

questions.question: A brand splits its promotional budget evenly across five channels every year because that feels fair. Two of the five produce almost all the tracked sales. What should it do?

options.text: Add a sixth channel to the same split
options.rationale: Thins every share further.

options.text: Keep the split and spend more overall
options.rationale: Scales the waste along with the gain.

options.text: Drop the budget to the two that work
options.rationale: Cuts total spend rather than reallocating it.

options.text: Move money toward what sells
options.rationale: Budgeting across channels is a judgement about where spend converts, not a division into equal shares.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: allocate by effect rather than by habit.

questions.question: A components maker sells to engineers at perhaps forty firms nationwide, and those engineers all attend one annual industry show. What does the show offer that its other channels do not?

options.text: Permanent presence through the year
options.rationale: A show is a burst, not a presence.

options.text: The lowest cost per person reached
options.rationale: Stands are rarely the cheapest reach.

options.text: A way to avoid talking to buyers
options.rationale: The contact is the point.

options.text: Its whole market in one room
options.rationale: A trade show concentrates a small, specific buying audience into a short window of face-to-face time.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: name what the format is uniquely good for.

questions.question: A bakery sends reporters a press release announcing a 10 percent off week. No outlet runs it. What does that failure show?

options.text: The release should have gone to more outlets
options.rationale: Wider distribution of the same non-story changes nothing.

options.text: A sales message is not a story a reporter can use
options.rationale: Earned coverage needs news value for the outlet's readers, which a promotion aimed at the bakery's customers does not have.

options.text: Reporters prefer to cover established bakeries
options.rationale: Blames the outlet rather than the pitch.

options.text: The discount was too small to interest readers
options.rationale: A bigger discount is still an ad, so the size was never the obstacle.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the message is built for a customer audience while the channel serves an editorial one, and the mismatch is the point.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Public Relations and Publicity, Advertising and Messaging. Without the publicity rules a promotional message is perfectly well formed. Without the advertising view there is nothing to contrast the pitch against. Remove either and the failure looks like bad luck rather than a category error.

questions.question: A grooming studio has $400 a month for promotion. Clients who arrive by referral stay far longer than clients from paid social, but referrals arrive more slowly. How should the mix be set?

options.text: Pause promotion until referrals grow on their own
options.rationale: Referrals are engineered rather than awaited, which is the whole idea.

options.text: Split the budget evenly across both channels
options.rationale: Even splits ignore what the two channels actually return.

options.text: Move everything into paid social for reach
options.rationale: Buys the faster but weaker channel with the whole budget.

options.text: Fund the referral rewards before the ad spend
options.rationale: The mix follows the audience and the economics: referral clients cost less and last longer, so they get first claim on a small budget.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: referral economics set the value of one channel, promotional strategy decides how a limited budget is divided.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Word-of-Mouth and Referral Marketing, Promotional Strategy. Without the referral view both channels look interchangeable and an even split is fine. Without the strategy view there is no budget pressure forcing a choice. Both are needed for a to beat b.

questions.question: A bike shop films a genuinely useful repair tip series, then publishes it as short clips on a professional network where its riders do not spend time. Views stay flat. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Wrong content, since tips do not sell bicycles
options.rationale: Judges content by immediate sales, which is the standard this approach rejects.

options.text: Right content, wrong platform for this audience
options.rationale: The content passes the usefulness test, so the failure is in the channel choice rather than the material.

options.text: Too few posts to build any following at all
options.rationale: Volume on the wrong platform does not fix placement.

options.text: The clips should have carried a discount code
options.rationale: Turns useful content back into an ad.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: one judges whether the material earns attention, the other judges whether it was placed where attention lives.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Content and Storytelling Marketing, Digital and Social Media Marketing. Without the content standard, option b is a reasonable read. Without the channel rule the flat views have no explanation but the material itself. Separating a good asset from a bad placement needs both.

questions.question: A retailer's goal is to clear last season's stock before the new range lands. It issues a coupon good on anything in the shop, and the coupons are mostly spent on new arrivals. What went wrong?

options.text: The discount was not deep enough
options.rationale: Depth would subsidise the same wrong goods.

options.text: A clear goal and a tool that ignores it
options.rationale: The promotion had a real purpose and the coupon was not restricted to the stock that purpose named, so the discount landed on goods that were selling anyway.

options.text: Old stock cannot be sold at a discount
options.rationale: Clearing it is the standard use.

options.text: Coupons are the wrong tool to clear stock
options.rationale: They work well when scoped to the stock.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the promotional purpose and the mechanics of the coupon have to agree, and here only one of them was set.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Sales promotion and incentives, Coupon and rebate programs. Without the stated goal the coupon is simply a discount. Without the unrestricted coupon the goal is met. Both are needed.

questions.question: A salon has detailed records of what each client books and when, and sends one identical text to the whole list every Friday at 5pm. Bookings do not move. What is the fault?

options.text: The client records are too detailed
options.rationale: The detail is the unused asset.

options.text: Text is the wrong channel for a salon
options.rationale: It is the right channel, badly used.

options.text: Friday at 5pm is too late to book
options.rationale: Timing is not what the records would fix.

options.text: A personal channel used impersonally
options.rationale: A text reaches the person directly, which is exactly why a message that could have been addressed to anyone wastes the one advantage the channel has.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the channel is immediate and personal, and the message was never made personal, so the two work against each other.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Email and mobile marketing, Direct and personal marketing. Without the direct channel a generic message is unremarkable. Without the records there is nothing to personalise with. Both are needed.

questions.question: A startup sets up a free arcade machine on a busy corner for a day. Crowds gather and film it, and nothing on or near the machine says who put it there. What is the result?

options.text: A stunt too expensive for a startup
options.rationale: One machine for a day is the cheap route.

options.text: Attention that attaches to nobody
options.rationale: The stunt and the experience both worked, and an experience only markets anything if the brand is attached to what people remember.

options.text: An experience nobody wanted to try
options.rationale: Crowds gathered.

options.text: A crowd that should have been smaller
options.rationale: Reach was the easy part.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the guerrilla tactic bought the crowd and the experience held it, and neither does any marketing without the brand attached.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Guerrilla marketing tactics, Event and experiential marketing. Without the unconventional stunt nobody stops. Without the hands-on experience nobody stays. Both are needed, and both are wasted here.

questions.question: A brand's adverts, packaging and email all say the product is for serious athletes. Its paid influencers, chosen for reach alone, present it as an easy everyday treat. Both halves perform well on their own measures. What is the problem?

options.text: A message too narrow for athletes
options.rationale: Narrow is a choice, not the fault.

options.text: Influencers that reach too few people
options.rationale: Reach is what they were picked for.

options.text: Two campaigns teaching different things
options.rationale: Every tool is meant to carry the same core message, and borrowed credibility is worth nothing if it vouches for a different product than the one the brand is building.

options.text: Packaging that contradicts the advert
options.rationale: Those two already agree.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the influencer work succeeds by its own metric and fails the coordination rule that governs every channel together.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Integrated marketing communications, Influencer marketing. Without the influencer strand the message is already consistent. Without the coordination rule each strand looks fine alone. Both are needed.

questions.question: A supplier can spend its whole annual promotional budget on one industry show where most of its buyers go, or split it across a show stand at half size and twelve months of search ads. Its sales cycle runs nine months. What does the split argue for?

options.text: Everything on the show, where buyers are
options.rationale: Buys one burst and ten silent months.

options.text: Everything on search, which runs all year
options.rationale: Gives up the one room holding the market.

options.text: Holding the budget until the cycle ends
options.rationale: Spends nothing during the deciding.

options.text: A presence for the months between shows
options.rationale: The show concentrates the audience and a nine month cycle means most of the deciding happens long after the hall empties, which is what the rest of the budget has to cover.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: what the show format is good for and how the budget is split across time have to be decided against each other.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Trade show and exhibition marketing, Promotional budgeting. Without the show there is no concentrated audience to weigh. Without the allocation question the show simply wins. Both are needed.

concepts: Search Engine and Search Ad Marketing
questions.question: A software firm's free trial converts well once people start it, and its search ads send clicks to a page that explains the product and asks for a sales call. Trial starts are low. What should change?

options.text: Shorten the free trial to a week
options.rationale: Trims what is already working.

options.text: Explain the product more thoroughly
options.rationale: More of the weaker argument.

options.text: Send the search click into the trial
options.rationale: The trial is the thing that persuades and the search click is someone already looking, so putting a sales call between them spends the intent on the weaker argument.

options.text: Raise the budget on the search ads
options.rationale: More clicks into the same bottleneck.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the trial is the persuasive tool and search supplies the intent, and the case turns on what sits between them.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Sampling and product trial offers, Search engine and search ad marketing. Without the trial there is nothing better to send the click to. Without the search traffic the trial has no one to convince. Both are needed.

questions.question: A grooming shop texts customers six weeks after a visit saying their dog is probably due. What is that text for?

options.text: Bringing an existing customer back
options.rationale: Retention work aims at the people who have already bought, at the moment they are likely to need you again.

options.text: Collecting reviews from recent clients
options.rationale: Reviews serve reputation; this text asks for a booking.

options.text: Finding customers who never visited
options.rationale: The message goes only to people with a visit history.

options.text: Raising the price of a standard groom
options.rationale: No pricing change is involved.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the purpose of a retention message.

questions.question: A packaging company earns 40 percent of its orders from one client and assigns that client a dedicated manager and quarterly reviews. Why?

options.text: Losing it would hurt more than losing many
options.rationale: Concentrated revenue makes one relationship a business risk, which is what justifies the extra attention.

options.text: Regulations require a named account contact
options.rationale: Invents a rule that does not exist here.

options.text: Smaller clients do not need any support
options.rationale: Overstates the case and is not why key accounts get managers.

options.text: Large clients always pay their invoices first
options.rationale: Payment behaviour is unrelated to account size.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: explain why concentrated revenue changes service levels.

questions.question: A grooming shop replaces its $60 per visit pricing with a $50 monthly membership that includes one groom plus add on discounts. What does the shop gain?

options.text: Revenue it can predict each month
options.rationale: The point of a subscription is recurring, forecastable income and a stickier relationship.

options.text: A higher price on every single groom
options.rationale: The per groom figure actually drops from $60 to $50.

options.text: Freedom from tracking customer visits
options.rationale: Memberships require more usage tracking, not less.

options.text: An end to competing on service quality
options.rationale: Subscribers judge quality every month, so the pressure rises.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify what a subscription structure changes.

questions.question: A regular's custom cake arrives in the wrong flavor an hour before her party. What recovery leaves her more loyal than before?

options.text: Apologize and offer 20 percent off next time
options.rationale: A generic credit that leaves tonight's party unfixed.

options.text: Refund the order and close the ticket
options.rationale: Returns her money and leaves her without a dessert.

options.text: Explain how the flavor mix up happened
options.rationale: Context she did not ask for, and it repairs nothing.

options.text: Apologize, send a free backup dessert now
options.rationale: Solves the problem inside the window that matters to her, which is what turns a complaint into loyalty.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose the recovery that fixes the real problem in time.

questions.question: A home cleaning service could not finish the oven on one visit because a part was missing. Which action builds trust?

options.text: Mention it only if the client complains
options.rationale: Makes honesty conditional on being caught.

options.text: Say nothing, since the client rarely checks
options.rationale: Trades a small silence for the relationship if it is ever noticed.

options.text: Discount the visit without saying why
options.rationale: Pays for the shortfall while hiding it, which teaches nothing about reliability.

options.text: Flag it in the photo recap and book a return
options.rationale: Proactive honesty about a gap, with a fix attached, is what makes reliability visible over time.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: pick the action that reinforces reliability in a specific incident.

questions.question: A pet grooming shop keeps running first visit discount ads and keeps seeing those customers once. Which change reflects relationship marketing?

options.text: A referral bonus paid to brand new customers
options.rationale: Still aimed at strangers rather than the clients already served.

options.text: A deeper first visit discount to pull more in
options.rationale: Doubles down on acquisition, which is the leak rather than the fix.

options.text: A rebrand of the same discount as a loyalty offer
options.rationale: Renaming a one time cut without building repeat contact, the trap named on the card.

options.text: A punch card plus a birthday email for each pet
options.rationale: Builds a reason and a rhythm for repeat contact rather than buying another first visit.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose the mechanism that creates an ongoing relationship.

questions.question: A grooming shop's $50 membership is popular, but the heaviest users book twice a month and now cost more to serve than they pay. Cancelling the plan would anger the loyal customers it attracted. What is the sound move?

options.text: Raise add on prices for members only
options.rationale: Punishes the same customers in a way they will read as a penalty for joining.

options.text: End the membership and return to per visit
options.rationale: Solves the math by discarding the loyalty the plan created.

options.text: Reprice or cap the plan before renewals land
options.rationale: Keeps the retention benefit while fixing the unit economics, which is the only way both halves survive.

options.text: Keep it as is, since retention is what matters
options.rationale: Retention bought below cost is a growing loss, not a win.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the subscription math and the retention value pull in opposite directions, and the answer has to hold both.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Membership and Subscription Models, Loyalty and Retention Marketing. Without the subscription economics there is no problem to solve. Without the retention value, cancelling is obviously right. The tension between them is the question.

questions.question: A cleaning service fixes a botched visit generously, and the client is delighted. Two months later a similar miss happens and is fixed just as generously. The client leaves anyway. Why?

options.text: The second recovery was not generous enough
options.rationale: The case says it matched the first, so generosity was not the variable.

options.text: Clients always leave after two complaints
options.rationale: A rule of thumb standing in for the actual mechanism.

options.text: The recoveries should have been discounts
options.rationale: Changes the currency of the apology and still ignores the pattern.

options.text: Recovery cannot substitute for being reliable
options.rationale: A good save repairs one incident, but trust is built by consistency, and a repeated miss is evidence about the norm.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: recovery handles the incident, trust tracks the pattern, and only together do they explain a departure after two good saves.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Customer Complaint Recovery, Building Customer Trust. Without recovery the departure is ordinary bad service. Without the trust view two excellent saves should have held her. The puzzle exists only where a well handled incident still damages a pattern.

questions.question: A packaging firm's largest client takes 40 percent of orders and now asks for deeper discounts and rush handling each quarter. Margin on the account has gone slightly negative. What does sound account management say?

options.text: Drop the client and pursue smaller accounts
options.rationale: Discards 40 percent of orders before trying to fix the terms.

options.text: Cut service quietly until the margin recovers
options.rationale: Damages the relationship without ever discussing the economics.

options.text: Measure the account, then renegotiate the terms
options.rationale: The relationship is worth protecting, but attention has to be checked against profitability rather than assumed.

options.text: Keep granting requests, since the account is vital
options.rationale: Treats size as a reason to stop measuring, the exact trap the card names.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the relationship justifies investment, key account discipline requires that investment to be tested.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Managing Key Accounts, Relationship Marketing. Without the key account view this is any customer asking for a discount. Without the relationship view the negative margin simply ends the deal. Both are needed to land on renegotiation rather than compliance or exit.

questions.question: Before opening a dog grooming shop, an owner visits the two nearby groomers and records their prices, wait times and loyalty offers. What is she doing?

options.text: Focus group research
options.rationale: A focus group gathers customer reactions in a guided session; nobody is being interviewed here.

options.text: Competitive analysis
options.rationale: Examining what rivals already offer, in order to find where you can beat them, is exactly this skill.

options.text: Feedback analysis
options.rationale: Feedback analysis reads what your own customers said, and this shop has none yet.

options.text: Trend forecasting
options.rationale: Forecasting looks at where demand is heading, not at what two specific rivals charge today.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: match an activity to its name.

questions.question: A support team notices that 40 of the last 150 tickets and reviews say the same thing: portions feel small for the price. What makes this worth acting on?

options.text: The complaint was the loudest one received
options.rationale: Volume of one voice is exactly what the skill warns against reacting to.

options.text: The complaint came from the newest customers
options.rationale: Who complained is secondary; the strength here is how often it recurs.

options.text: The complaint arrived most recently of all
options.rationale: Recency is the trap: the newest complaint is not automatically the important one.

options.text: The complaint repeats across many customers
options.rationale: A pattern across many voices is what separates a signal from a one-off, which is the test this skill applies.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify why a set of feedback qualifies as evidence.

questions.question: Weekend dinner sales at a taco shop have risen about 8 percent in each of the last three months. Why does that read as a trend rather than a blip?

options.text: It is the largest single month on record
options.rationale: One record month is the definition of a blip until it repeats.

options.text: It holds across several periods in a row
options.rationale: Repetition over consecutive periods rules out a single event driving the number.

options.text: It matches what the owner expected to see
options.rationale: Matching an expectation is confirmation, not evidence.

options.text: It came after a new item was advertised
options.rationale: A plausible cause, but a cause is not what makes the pattern trustworthy.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: apply the repeated-periods test to a single figure.

questions.question: Before commissioning a survey, a founder checks census figures and a published industry report. What is she using?

options.text: Interviews with her customers
options.rationale: Also primary.

options.text: A live test in the market
options.rationale: That is test marketing.

options.text: Data that already exists
options.rationale: Secondary research draws on information someone else has already gathered.

options.text: A survey she ran herself
options.rationale: That would be primary.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: classify the source.

questions.question: Which survey question is written neutrally?

options.text: Do you agree our delivery is excellent?
options.rationale: Invites agreement.

options.text: How much did you love our fast delivery?
options.rationale: Assumes the answer twice over.

options.text: Was our delivery as slow as you feared?
options.rationale: Leads in the other direction.

options.text: How would you rate our delivery speed?
options.rationale: It asks for a judgement without suggesting which one, which is what keeps the answers usable.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: spot the neutral wording.

questions.question: A snack brand sells a new flavour in twelve stores for six weeks before deciding on a national rollout. What is this?

options.text: A survey of likely buyers
options.rationale: Nobody is being asked.

options.text: A small live trial before committing
options.rationale: Test marketing puts the real thing in front of real customers on a small scale first.

options.text: A national launch that has already begun
options.rationale: Twelve stores is the point.

options.text: A review of published reports
options.rationale: That is secondary data.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the method.

questions.question: In a snack taste test, one participant answers first every time and the rest have started agreeing with him. What should the facilitator do next?

options.text: Ask a quiet member to react before he speaks
options.rationale: Changes who speaks first, which is what recovers the independent opinions the session exists to collect.

options.text: Ask him to explain his reasoning in more depth
options.rationale: Gives the dominant voice more airtime, deepening the imbalance.

options.text: Ask the group whether they all agree with him
options.rationale: Invites the agreement that is already the problem, and makes dissent socially costly.

options.text: End the session and recruit a new group later
options.rationale: Throws away recruiting cost over a problem that facilitation can fix in the room.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose the facilitation move that fixes a live group dynamic.

questions.question: A student testing a new boba flavor surveys her friends and the school club she runs. Every response is enthusiastic. Why is that weak evidence for the launch?

options.text: She sampled people likely to agree with her
options.rationale: A friendly sample confirms the idea instead of testing it, the failure this skill is defined against.

options.text: She ran the survey before checking rivals
options.rationale: Competitor work is a separate input; order is not what invalidates this.

options.text: She asked about flavor instead of pricing
options.rationale: Flavor is the right question for a flavor decision.

options.text: She surveyed too few people to be certain
options.rationale: Sample size is a real limit, but doubling a biased sample would not fix the result.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: diagnose why a specific piece of research fails to inform a decision.

questions.question: A smoothie shop owner hears regulars ask for oat milk and protein add-ins more often each month, and national plant-based sales are climbing. What move treats this as a trend?

options.text: Pilot three oat milk drinks as a standing menu
options.rationale: A small, real commitment made early is how this skill converts an observed shift into a position.

options.text: Wait until competitors add oat milk, then match
options.rationale: Moving after rivals is the catch-up position the skill exists to avoid.

options.text: Ask the supplier whether oat milk costs more
options.rationale: A sensible operational check, but it answers nothing about demand and defers the decision.

options.text: Replace the classic blends with oat milk versions
options.rationale: Overcommits on an early signal and drops customers the shop already has.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: size the right response to an emerging signal in a new setting.

questions.question: A founder has two weeks and no budget to size the market for pet grooming in her county. What should she do first?

options.text: Use census and industry figures
options.rationale: Existing data is fast and free, which makes it the right first move when time and money are the constraints.

options.text: Ask ten friends what they think
options.rationale: Not a market estimate.

options.text: Open a shop and see what happens
options.rationale: The most expensive possible test.

options.text: Commission a representative survey
options.rationale: Neither affordable nor fast enough.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose the method the constraints allow.

questions.question: A survey asks: do you prefer our improved recipe and lower price, or the old version? Ninety percent pick the first. What is wrong with the result?

options.text: Two changes bundled into one choice
options.rationale: A question that moves two things at once cannot tell you which one the answer is about.

options.text: An answer that is obviously wrong
options.rationale: The answer may be sincere.

options.text: A sample that was far too small
options.rationale: Size is not given or implied.

options.text: A scale with too few points
options.rationale: It is a choice, not a scale.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: diagnose a flawed question.

questions.question: A chain tests a new menu item in its three busiest flagship stores, staffed by its best teams. It sells well and fails everywhere on rollout. What was wrong with the test?

options.text: Three stores being far too many
options.rationale: Count is not the flaw.

options.text: A test that ran for too long
options.rationale: Duration is not mentioned.

options.text: A slice that was not representative
options.rationale: A small trial only predicts the whole market if the slice resembles it, and the best stores do not.

options.text: An item that nobody ever wanted
options.rationale: It sold well where tested.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: judge whether a test slice predicts the whole.

questions.question: A boba shop's sales have been flat for three months. Reviews repeatedly mention long waits at 3pm, and the shop two doors down has just launched mobile ordering. What should the owner conclude?

options.text: The flat sales are a seasonal dip that the feedback does not explain
options.rationale: Three flat months is a pattern, not a dip, and it discards feedback that names a cause.

options.text: The feedback matters less than the sales numbers, which are flat
options.rationale: Ranks one source over another when the numbers say what is happening and the feedback says why.

options.text: The rival's mobile ordering is the only cause of the flat sales
options.rationale: The rival launched recently while sales have been flat for months, so it cannot be the whole story.

options.text: The wait is costing sales that the rival is now better placed to take
options.rationale: Reads the three signals together: a repeated complaint, a flat trend rather than a dip, and a rival whose new feature targets that exact complaint.

notes.difficulty_justification: Three concepts held together: the complaint pattern, the sales trend, and the competitor move only mean something jointly.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Customer Feedback Analysis, Sales Data Trend Interpretation, Competitive Analysis. Remove the feedback and there is no cause for flat sales. Remove the sales reading and the complaint has no business consequence. Remove the competitor and there is no urgency and no one to lose customers to. Each deletion leaves a different, easier question.

questions.question: A brand runs one focus group of eight people recruited from its own mailing list, and two enthusiastic fans dominate the discussion. The report calls the product validated. What is the problem?

options.text: Focus groups cannot validate a product at all
options.rationale: Overcorrects: a well recruited, well run session is legitimate evidence.

options.text: Eight people is too many for a single session
options.rationale: Eight sits inside the workable range; the count is not what broke this.

options.text: The session should have been run twice instead
options.rationale: Repeating a biased method with a biased list produces the same answer twice.

options.text: The recruiting and the room both favored agreement
options.rationale: Two separate faults compound: a sample selected for enthusiasm, then a session where the enthusiastic set the tone.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: who was recruited is a research question, how they were handled is a facilitation one, and only together do they explain the false validation.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Focus Group Facilitation, Marketing Research and Insight. Without the facilitation fault, a biased list still produces a warm room and the answer is about sampling alone. Without the sampling fault, good facilitation would have surfaced dissent. The answer names both, so removing either leaves a partly true option looking correct.

questions.question: A grocery chain sees its oat milk sales rise three months running while its dairy sales slide, and category data shows the same shift nationally. Which reading of both signals holds up?

options.text: A supply problem in dairy rather than a change in demand
options.rationale: A supply story would not lift oat milk nationally at the same time.

options.text: A local spike that the national data cannot confirm yet
options.rationale: Reverses the evidence: the national data is precisely what corroborates the local pattern.

options.text: A seasonal swing that will reverse once winter ends
options.rationale: Seasonality would show in both directions across prior years, and nothing here suggests it.

options.text: A lasting shift worth permanent shelf space, not a promotion
options.rationale: Internal repetition and an outside category move point the same way, which is what justifies a structural response rather than a test.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: own-sales interpretation says the pattern is real, trend spotting says it is bigger than this store.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Sales Data Trend Interpretation, Spotting Market Trends. Without the sales reading the national data could be irrelevant to this chain. Without the trend the three months could be a local quirk deserving a test, not shelf space. The size of the commitment in the correct answer depends on having both.

questions.question: Industry reports say the category is growing 12 percent a year, so a brand skips a trial and launches nationally. Sales are flat because the growth is concentrated in a price tier it does not sell into. What does the case show?

options.text: A category not worth entering at all
options.rationale: It is growing strongly.

options.text: A national launch handled badly
options.rationale: Execution is not the described fault.

options.text: Industry reports that were simply wrong about the category
options.rationale: The category did grow.

options.text: Category data that said nothing about its product
options.rationale: Existing data describes a market in aggregate, and only putting the actual product in front of actual buyers tests whether this offer shares in that growth.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the secondary data is accurate and the live test is what would have told them it did not apply to them.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Secondary data analysis, Test marketing. Without the reports there is no basis for confidence. Without the skipped trial the mismatch surfaces cheaply. Both are needed.

questions.question: A carefully neutral survey finds 70 percent would buy a reusable cup at $14. A three-store trial at that price sells almost none. The team argues the survey must have been flawed. What is the better explanation?

options.text: A price that both methods rejected
options.rationale: The survey accepted it.

options.text: A trial run in the wrong three stores
options.rationale: Possible, and not the general lesson.

options.text: Saying yes costs nothing, paying does
options.rationale: A well designed survey measures stated intention accurately, and a live trial measures behaviour, which is a different and more demanding thing.

options.text: A survey written with leading questions
options.rationale: It is described as neutral.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the survey and the trial measure different things, so a clean survey and a failed trial are not a contradiction.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Survey and questionnaire design, Test marketing. Without the sound survey the gap is a design flaw. Without the trial nobody learns what people do. Both are needed.

questions.question: A team has census data showing the local age profile and runs a survey to learn what matters to buyers. The survey goes out through its own newsletter, whose readers skew twenty years older than the county. What should it do with the results?

options.text: Discard the survey and start again
options.rationale: Throws away usable information.

options.text: Trust the census and skip the survey
options.rationale: The census says nothing about preferences.

options.text: Weight them against the known profile
options.rationale: The existing data describes who the market actually is, which is exactly what lets a skewed sample be corrected rather than discarded.

options.text: Use the results exactly as collected
options.rationale: Reports the newsletter, not the county.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the secondary data supplies the frame that makes a flawed primary sample usable.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Secondary data analysis, Survey and questionnaire design. Without the census there is nothing to weight against. Without the survey there are no preferences to weight. Both are needed.

questions.question: A store has 400 raffle entries and one salesperson. She pulls out the entrants who bought running shoes in the last year and calls those first. What is she doing?

options.text: Handling an objection about the price
options.rationale: No customer has raised a hesitation yet.

options.text: Qualifying the list before spending time
options.rationale: Ranking leads by how likely they are to buy, so limited selling hours go where they can pay off.

options.text: Closing the leads she already contacted
options.rationale: Closing happens at the end of a conversation, and none has started.

options.text: Following up after a completed sale
options.rationale: These entrants have not bought anything in this campaign.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the sales activity being described.

questions.question: A shopper says the running shoes are kind of pricey. The salesperson immediately offers 15 percent off. What has he skipped?

options.text: Finding out what is actually bothering her
options.rationale: Pricey can mean compared to what, or not worth it to me, and the discount answers only one of those.

options.text: Presenting two more features of the shoe
options.rationale: More features on an unheard objection is pushing harder, not listening.

options.text: Checking whether her size is still in stock
options.rationale: An operational detail unrelated to the objection.

options.text: Asking her to complete the purchase today
options.rationale: Closing before the hesitation is understood repeats the same error.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the missing step in an objection response.

questions.question: At a mattress store a customer lies on the same model twice and asks about delivery dates. What do those signals call for?

options.text: Asking directly to schedule the delivery
options.rationale: Repeated interest plus a logistics question is a buying signal, and the sale still has to be asked for.

options.text: Explaining the foam construction in depth
options.rationale: More product detail after the decision point stalls it.

options.text: Walking her through three more models
options.rationale: Reopens a decision the customer has effectively made.

options.text: Waiting for her to raise the purchase herself
options.rationale: Leaving the ask to the customer is exactly how ready buyers walk out.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: read a buying signal and name the response.

questions.question: A customer asks whether the software handles payroll for forty staff. It handles twenty comfortably and slows badly beyond that. What should the salesperson say?

options.text: That nobody has complained yet
options.rationale: Technically true and designed to mislead.

options.text: That it handles any team size
options.rationale: A claim he knows to be false.

options.text: That forty is unusually large
options.rationale: Dodges the question asked.

options.text: Where it stops working well
options.rationale: Telling the whole truth about what a product cannot do is the duty, even when the smaller claim would close the sale.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: apply the honesty duty to a direct question.

questions.question: Two representatives pitch together and both cover the pricing, while nobody covers implementation. What does the team need?

options.text: A longer meeting with the buyer
options.rationale: More time, same overlap.

options.text: One of them to stay home
options.rationale: Loses the second strength too.

options.text: A part each, agreed beforehand
options.rationale: Group selling works by dividing the pitch so each person covers their strength and nothing is said twice or left out.

options.text: A manager to lead the pitch
options.rationale: Adds a third person to an unassigned pitch.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what makes a joint pitch work.

questions.question: A company sets next year's target by dividing its national goal equally among eight territories. What does that ignore?

options.text: The total the company needs
options.rationale: That is the figure being divided.

options.text: What each area can actually sell
options.rationale: A territory forecast is built from that area's own market size, history and conditions, not from arithmetic on a national number.

options.text: Which products sell the best
options.rationale: A mix question, not a territory one.

options.text: How many representatives it has
options.rationale: Headcount is not the measure.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what an even split leaves out.

questions.question: A salesperson tells a parent the pushchair has an aluminium frame and a one-hand fold. Which line turns that into a benefit?

options.text: It folds using a single mechanism
options.rationale: Restates the feature.

options.text: It comes in four different colours
options.rationale: Another feature entirely.

options.text: You can close it holding the baby
options.rationale: A benefit says what the feature does for this customer, in their own situation.

options.text: The frame is aircraft grade aluminium
options.rationale: A deeper specification.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: pick the benefit among features.

questions.question: A customer buying a laptop for photo editing is shown a faster model with more memory and a card reader. What is the salesperson doing?

options.text: Discounting to close the deal
options.rationale: No price is reduced.

options.text: Padding the sale with extras
options.rationale: That is the version that does not fit.

options.text: Asking for a referral to others
options.rationale: Nobody is being referred.

options.text: Offering more that fits the need
options.rationale: Upselling is legitimate when the better version actually serves what the customer came to do.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the practice and what makes it legitimate.

questions.question: A contractor's happiest clients never send anyone his way, and he fills his diary with cold calls. What is he not doing?

options.text: Lowering his prices for them
options.rationale: They are already happy.

options.text: Cold calling a larger list
options.rationale: More of the expensive route.

options.text: Asking them who else needs this
options.rationale: Referrals rarely happen unprompted; the ask is the practice.

options.text: Advertising in the local paper
options.rationale: Paid reach, not referral.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the missing habit.

questions.question: A customer walks into a running store and says she needs new shoes. Which opening does the skill call for?

options.text: Ask what she is looking for, then start pitching
options.rationale: One surface question followed by a pitch is the trap the card names.

options.text: Ask what she trains for and her weekly mileage
options.rationale: Specific questions about use and history are what make the later recommendation fit this runner.

options.text: Ask what her budget is before anything else
options.rationale: Leads with price and frames the sale as a spending limit rather than a need.

options.text: Walk her to the most popular model in stock
options.rationale: Recommends before understanding, so the fit is luck.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose the discovery move in a fresh sales conversation.

questions.question: A family shopping for a minivan has mentioned three young children and a long daily commute. Which presentation fits?

options.text: Run the standard walkaround for every buyer
options.rationale: The same pitch for everyone, which is the error the card describes.

options.text: Lead with the vacuum, seats and fuel economy
options.rationale: Ties the features to the two things this family actually said, which is what a presentation is for.

options.text: Lead with the financing terms available today
options.rationale: Money talk before the vehicle has been connected to their life.

options.text: Lead with horsepower and towing capacity
options.rationale: Impressive specs that answer nothing they raised.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: build a pitch from stated customer facts.

questions.question: A customer training for his first backpacking trip says he is worried about blisters. The boot wall holds twelve models. What does product knowledge look like here?

options.text: Recommend thicker socks and send him home
options.rationale: Solves around the product instead of matching it.

options.text: Walk through every feature of the top seller
options.rationale: A brochure recital, which is what the card warns against.

options.text: Explain how all twelve models differ by price
options.rationale: Organises the wall by cost rather than by his problem.

options.text: Name the two boots whose fit prevents rubbing
options.rationale: Knowing the range well enough to select the few features that solve this specific worry is the skill.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: convert product knowledge into a match for one stated need.

questions.question: A rep's territory covers a city of four million with two established rivals; her colleague's covers three rural counties with none. Both are set the same number. What should the forecast reflect?

options.text: The effort each rep is willing to give
options.rationale: Effort does not change the market.

options.text: Market size and who is already there
options.rationale: A realistic territory number comes from that area's own conditions, and a city with entrenched rivals is not the same opportunity as an empty rural patch.

options.text: Whichever rep performed better last
options.rationale: Judges people, not territories.

options.text: The travel time between accounts
options.rationale: A cost factor, not the ceiling.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: build the number from the territory's own facts.

questions.question: A rep is one sale short of her quarterly bonus. The buyer in front of her would be better served by the cheaper model, which carries no bonus. What does the standard require?

options.text: Mention the bonus to the buyer
options.rationale: Makes it the buyer's problem to solve.

options.text: Recommend the one that fits
options.rationale: The duty holds precisely when telling the truth costs something, which is the only time it is tested.

options.text: Present both and stay neutral
options.rationale: Withholds the advice she was asked for.

options.text: Sell the larger one this once
options.rationale: Trades the customer's interest for the bonus.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: hold the standard where it actually costs.

questions.question: A pitch team has one person strong on technical detail and one strong on the business case. The buying room holds an IT lead and a finance director. How should the pitch be divided?

options.text: The senior one presents it all
options.rationale: Wastes the other strength.

options.text: Each takes the listener they fit
options.rationale: Dividing by strength is the point, and here the strengths map cleanly onto two different people who have to be convinced.

options.text: Both cover both halves in turn
options.rationale: Doubles the length and the overlap.

options.text: Split the time exactly in half
options.rationale: Divides the clock, not the content.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: allocate the pitch by strength against the room.

questions.question: A rep's usual pitch runs twenty minutes with a long story up front. This buyer opens by saying she has eight minutes and knows the category well. What should he do?

options.text: Deliver the usual pitch faster
options.rationale: Same content, less comprehension.

options.text: Lead with the decision she faces
options.rationale: Adapting means the pace and focus move to fit the person in front of you rather than the script you planned.

options.text: Start with the background anyway
options.rationale: Spends her time on what she knows.

options.text: Ask to rebook for a longer slot
options.rationale: Declines the eight minutes offered.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: reshape the pitch to the buyer in the room.

questions.question: A buyer asks for 20 percent off. The seller's margin cannot take it, but he has flexibility on delivery timing and payment terms. What does negotiating well look like?

options.text: Give the 20 percent to close today
options.rationale: Gives away the value entirely.

options.text: Trade the terms, hold the price
options.rationale: Both sides give something, and the giving should come from what you can afford rather than from the value you are selling.

options.text: Split it and concede 10 percent
options.rationale: Halves the damage, same mistake.

options.text: Refuse and restate the list price
options.rationale: Offers nothing, so nothing moves.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: concede on the axis you can afford.

questions.question: A first meeting with a cautious buyer opens with the rep setting out his pricing sheet before a word is exchanged. The buyer goes quiet. What was skipped?

options.text: Asking for her budget up front
options.rationale: Another demand before any connection.

options.text: The part where she decides to listen
options.rationale: Rapport is what buys you the attention the pitch needs, and a cautious buyer gives it before she gives anything else.

options.text: A discount to open the conversation
options.rationale: Price does not create trust.

options.text: A longer and clearer pricing sheet
options.rationale: More of what silenced her.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: name what has to come before the pitch.

questions.question: A salesperson asks four good discovery questions, listens well, then delivers the same standard feature walkthrough he gives everyone. The customer leaves. What failed?

options.text: He should have presented before asking
options.rationale: Reverses the order the skill requires.

options.text: What he learned never reached the pitch
options.rationale: Discovery only pays off if the presentation is built from it, and the handoff between the two steps is where this sale died.

options.text: The product was wrong for this customer
options.rationale: Nothing suggests a mismatch, only a pitch that ignored what was learned.

options.text: His discovery questions were too general
options.rationale: The case states the questions were good and the listening real.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: each step is performed correctly in isolation, so only the link between them explains the loss.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Uncovering Needs in the Sale, Making the Sales Presentation. Remove discovery and the generic pitch is all he ever had. Remove the presentation standard and good questions look like a job well done. The failure lives only in the handoff, so both are load bearing.

questions.question: A shopper hesitates on a $160 running shoe, saying a $90 pair online looks the same. The salesperson knows the $160 pair uses a different midsole rated for her mileage. What should she do?

options.text: Suggest she order the cheaper pair online
options.rationale: Concedes a comparison the salesperson knows to be false.

options.text: Match the online price to keep the sale
options.rationale: Treats a comparison objection as a price objection and gives away margin to do it.

options.text: Explain the store's return policy in detail
options.rationale: Reduces the risk of buying without addressing the reason for doubt.

options.text: Name the midsole difference her mileage needs
options.rationale: The objection is a comparison, so it is answered with the product knowledge that shows the two are not the same shoe.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the objection has to be diagnosed as a comparison, and only product knowledge can answer it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Handling Buying Objections, Understanding What You Sell. Without the objection skill the discount looks like a reasonable close. Without the product knowledge there is nothing true to say in response. Each deletion makes price matching the sensible move.

questions.question: A rep has two hours. She can call forty unscreened raffle entrants once, or call the eight buyers who asked about delivery last week and ask for the order. What should she do?

options.text: Call the forty, since more calls means more chances
options.rationale: Volume with no ranking, which is exactly how selling time evaporates.

options.text: Call the eight, who are qualified and close to buying
options.rationale: Qualification says these are the leads worth the hours, and the close says the sale still has to be asked for.

options.text: Call the forty first and the eight tomorrow
options.rationale: Spends the ready buyers' patience on a list that has not been screened.

options.text: Email all forty eight and wait for replies
options.rationale: Avoids asking anyone for the sale.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: qualification decides who is worth the hours, closing decides what the hours are spent doing.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Prospecting and Qualifying, Closing and Follow-up. Without qualification the bigger list wins on raw odds. Without the closing rule the eight could just as well get another nurture email. Both are needed to pick a.

questions.question: A manager asks each rep for a territory forecast, then pays the bonus on beating it. Reps quickly learn to submit numbers well under what their areas can do. What has the scheme produced?

options.text: Reps who cannot read their markets
options.rationale: They read them well enough to shade them.

options.text: A bonus that is too small to matter
options.rationale: It plainly changes behaviour.

options.text: Forecasts that reward understating them
options.rationale: A forecast is meant to be an honest estimate of the territory, and paying on the gap gives the person making it a reason to make it wrong.

options.text: Territories that are genuinely weaker
options.rationale: The areas did not change.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the forecast is a factual estimate and the incentive attached to it makes honesty costly, so the two cannot be designed separately.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Sales forecasting for territories, Sales ethics and honesty. Without the forecast there is nothing to shade. Without the incentive an honest number costs nothing. Both are needed.

questions.question: In a two person pitch the technical rep says the integration takes about four months. The commercial rep, closing, tells the buyer it is live in six weeks. Neither corrects the other in the room. What is the position?

options.text: A pitch that needed a third presenter
options.rationale: Headcount is not the failure.

options.text: An honest difference of estimates
options.rationale: Four months and six weeks is not a range.

options.text: A divided pitch that misled the buyer
options.rationale: Splitting the pitch does not split the duty, and a team that lets two numbers stand has told the buyer something false between them.

options.text: A disagreement for them to settle later
options.rationale: The buyer decides on what was said.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the division of roles is what let the contradiction stand, and the honesty duty is what makes it a breach rather than an oversight.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Team and group selling, Sales ethics and honesty. Without two presenters there is no contradiction. Without the honesty duty it is a tidy-up for later. Both are needed.

questions.question: Two reps share one large territory and are each forecast half of it. Both chase the same handful of big accounts, and the smaller accounts that make up most of the area go unworked. What is missing?

options.text: A larger forecast for the territory
options.rationale: A bigger number aimed nowhere.

options.text: A third rep for the small accounts
options.rationale: Adds a person to an undivided job.

options.text: A split of the work, not just the number
options.rationale: Halving the target divides the credit and leaves the coverage unassigned, which is the part a shared territory actually has to decide.

options.text: A forecast built per account instead
options.rationale: Finer numbers, same unassigned work.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the territory forecast and the division of roles across it are separate decisions, and only the first was made.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Sales forecasting for territories, Team and group selling. Without the shared territory one rep covers it all. Without the role split the forecast leaves the ground uncovered. Both are needed.

questions.question: A rep has a polished benefit line for every feature, built around saving a busy owner time. This buyer is a technician who has asked three questions about tolerances and build quality. The rep keeps returning to time saved. What is wrong?

options.text: A buyer who asked the wrong questions
options.rationale: His questions define the sale.

options.text: Benefits aimed at the wrong buyer
options.rationale: A benefit is defined by what it does for this customer, so the translation has to be redone when the person changes, not just delivered more smoothly.

options.text: Features listed with no benefit at all
options.rationale: Every feature has a benefit attached.

options.text: Too many features covered at once
options.rationale: Volume is not the failure.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the benefit translation is done well for a buyer who is not in the room, which only the adaptation step would catch.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Feature-benefit selling, Adapting the sales approach. Without the benefit work there is nothing aimed anywhere. Without adapting it is aimed at the wrong person. Both are needed.

questions.question: A rep builds warm relationships and his clients say they would recommend him. He has never asked any of them to, and his pipeline is all cold outreach. What is being wasted?

options.text: Clients who do not actually like him
options.rationale: They say the opposite.

options.text: Rapport that was built too slowly
options.rationale: Pace is not the issue.

options.text: Goodwill nobody has been asked to spend
options.rationale: The relationship is the hard part and it only becomes new business when someone makes the ask.

options.text: Cold outreach that should be stopped
options.rationale: A second channel is fine.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the rapport is genuine and the referral ask that converts it was never made.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Building rapport with buyers, Referral generation in selling. Without the rapport an ask falls flat. Without the ask the rapport stays private. Both are needed.

questions.question: A buyer pushes hard for a discount the seller cannot give. The seller instead adds a service plan the buyer does not need, to make the package look bigger at the same price. What is the fault?

options.text: A service plan priced too cheaply
options.rationale: Price is not what makes it wrong.

options.text: A buyer who negotiated too hard
options.rationale: Pushing is the buyer's job.

options.text: An add-on used as a bargaining chip
options.rationale: Trading on terms is right and the thing traded has to be something the buyer actually wants, or the concession is only the appearance of one.

options.text: A refusal to move on the price
options.rationale: Holding price is the correct instinct.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the negotiation tactic is sound and the add-on fails the fit test that makes cross-selling legitimate.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Negotiating the sale, Cross-selling and upselling. Without the negotiation there is no reason to add anything. Without the fit rule the add-on looks like a fair trade. Both are needed.

questions.question: A new cleaning company leaves a printed checklist after every visit and texts before and after photos. What problem is that solving?

options.text: Staff forget which rooms to clean
options.rationale: That would be a process tool, not customer facing evidence.

options.text: Customers prefer paper to digital records
options.rationale: The format is incidental to the purpose.

options.text: A service cannot be seen before buying
options.rationale: Physical evidence gives customers something concrete to judge an intangible service by.

options.text: Cleaning supplies cost too much per visit
options.rationale: Nothing here addresses cost.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the problem physical cues solve.

questions.question: A salon is overwhelmed on Saturday mornings and empty on Tuesday afternoons. Why can it not simply stock up in advance?

options.text: Products expire before they are used
options.rationale: Shampoo keeps; the perishable thing is the appointment slot.

options.text: Saturday customers pay a higher rate
options.rationale: Pricing is not why inventory is impossible.

options.text: Service time cannot be stored
options.rationale: An unused hour is gone, which is why services balance capacity against demand rather than holding inventory.

options.text: Stylists refuse to work Tuesdays
options.rationale: Invents a staffing conflict.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: state why service capacity is perishable.

questions.question: A tax firm finds most delays come from clients arriving with disorganised receipts. What does that illustrate?

options.text: The firm should raise its prices
options.rationale: Charges more for a delay it could reduce.

options.text: Staff training is the only lever
options.rationale: The described cause sits outside the staff entirely.

options.text: Tax work is inherently slow
options.rationale: Blames the category rather than the identified cause.

options.text: Customers help produce the service
options.rationale: In a service the customer is a participant, and their inputs shape the quality and speed of the result.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: recognise the customer's productive role.

questions.question: A hotel keeps failing at late check in. A manager maps the guest's visible steps only and finds nothing wrong. What is the map missing?

options.text: The guest's opinion of the lobby
options.rationale: Atmosphere is not where a check in breaks.

options.text: The backstage steps behind the desk
options.rationale: Failures usually live in the work guests never see, so a blueprint that stops at the counter cannot find them.

options.text: The competitor hotels nearby
options.rationale: External comparison does not map an internal process.

options.text: The price paid for the room
options.rationale: Rate has no bearing on the process failure.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: find the missing half of a service map.

questions.question: A guest with a confirmed reservation arrives to find no room ready. What recovery leaves trust higher than before?

options.text: Staff empowered to fix it on the spot
options.rationale: Speed and authority at the point of failure are what turn a bad moment into evidence that the business handles problems.

options.text: A discount code for a future stay
options.rationale: Treats recovery as a coupon, which the card names as the trap.

options.text: An apology letter mailed next week
options.rationale: Arrives long after the damage and asks nothing of the process.

options.text: A refund processed within five days
options.rationale: Money back later does nothing about the guest standing there now.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose the recovery that restores trust at the moment of failure.

questions.question: A salon is slammed on Saturday mornings and quiet midweek. The owner is about to hire two full time stylists. What should she check first?

options.text: Whether the surge is only a few hours
options.rationale: A narrow peak calls for shifting capacity or demand rather than adding permanent cost across the week.

options.text: Whether new stylists accept Tuesday shifts
options.rationale: Assumes the hire before testing whether it is needed.

options.text: Whether rivals charge more on Saturdays
options.rationale: Competitor pricing does not tell her what her own load looks like.

options.text: Whether the chairs need replacing soon
options.rationale: An equipment question unrelated to the imbalance.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: diagnose a demand pattern before adding capacity.

questions.question: A hotel's recovery for unready rooms is generous and guests leave satisfied, but the same failure recurs weekly and recovery costs are climbing. What does the situation call for?

options.text: Stop confirming reservations for late arrivals
options.rationale: Removes the promise rather than keeping it.

options.text: Make the recovery offers more generous still
options.rationale: Raises the cost of a failure nobody has diagnosed.

options.text: Blueprint the backstage steps that keep failing
options.rationale: Recovery handles the guest in front of you, while the repeating cause sits in the unseen process that only a blueprint exposes.

options.text: Train front desk staff to apologise better
options.rationale: Improves the part already working.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: recovery is succeeding by its own measure, so only the process view explains why costs keep rising.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Service Recovery Strategy, Service Blueprinting. Without recovery the guests would already be lost and the case is simple. Without blueprinting the recurring cause stays invisible and generosity looks like the answer. Both are needed.

questions.question: A tax firm blueprints its process and finds the longest delay sits at document intake, driven by how clients submit receipts. Which fix targets the real cause?

options.text: A surcharge applied to messy submissions
options.rationale: Prices the problem while leaving the delay in place.

options.text: A longer turnaround promised to clients
options.rationale: Lowers the promise rather than fixing the step.

options.text: Two extra preparers hired for the season
options.rationale: Adds capacity to absorb disorder instead of reducing it.

options.text: A guided upload tool clients use beforehand
options.rationale: The customer's input is part of the process, so the fix has to shape what they hand over rather than only what staff do with it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the blueprint locates the step, the customer's role explains why staffing it harder will not help.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Service Blueprinting, Customer Role in Service Delivery. Without the blueprint the bottleneck is unknown. Without the customer's role the obvious answer is more preparers. The fix lands on the client input only when both apply.

questions.question: A cleaning company wants midweek bookings and better proof of quality. It can fund one initiative: a discounted Tuesday slot, or photo and checklist evidence after every visit. Bookings are peaked and new customers hesitate. What reasoning holds?

options.text: Evidence wins because photos cost nothing
options.rationale: Right answer, wrong reason: cost is not the deciding factor.

options.text: Neither matters while capacity is unbalanced
options.rationale: Dismisses both levers and leaves the situation unchanged.

options.text: Evidence wins new buyers who then fill Tuesdays
options.rationale: Hesitation is the binding constraint, and evidence converts it, whereas a discount only moves customers who already trust the service.

options.text: The discount wins, since price moves demand
options.rationale: Discounts shift existing demand between days without addressing why newcomers hesitate.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the intangibility problem and the capacity problem compete for one budget, and the answer depends on which constraint binds.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Managing Service Intangibility, Service Capacity and Demand Balancing. Without intangibility the discount is the only lever on the table. Without the capacity imbalance there is no midweek goal to weigh it against. Choosing between them requires both.

questions.question: A bakery sorts its customers into weekday breakfast buyers, late night student snackers, and custom cake orderers. What has the bakery done?

options.text: Measured total demand for its goods
options.rationale: Naming groups says nothing about how many buyers exist or how much they would spend.

options.text: Split its market by buying occasion
options.rationale: Segmentation is dividing a mixed market into groups that behave differently, which is exactly what occasion-based groups are.

options.text: Picked one group of buyers to serve
options.rationale: Confuses segmentation with target market selection: finding the groups comes before choosing one.

options.text: Built a profile of one buyer's values
options.rationale: Profiling describes a single customer in depth; this describes the shape of the whole market.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: recognize the named activity from a concrete example.

questions.question: A gym stops advertising to everyone downtown and commits to one group: office workers who want a 45 minute lunch workout. It rebuilds its class schedule and ads around them. What follows directly from that choice?

options.text: Its offer and its message both get sharper
options.rationale: A defined target is what lets product, price and message align, which is the first-order effect of choosing one.

options.text: Its total addressable market gets larger
options.rationale: Backwards: focusing narrows who is being served. The gain is depth, not reach.

options.text: Its prices must fall to stay competitive
options.rationale: Assumes focus competes on price; a tailored offer usually supports price rather than cutting it.

options.text: Its need for customer research disappears
options.rationale: Choosing a target raises the need to understand that group, it does not remove it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: the direct consequence of a single decision.

questions.question: A founder pitching a dog walking app for one suburb opens with the size of the national pet industry. Why does that figure fail as a demand estimate?

options.text: It counts spending the app cannot serve
options.rationale: A top-line industry figure includes buyers and categories outside the business's actual reach, so it cannot be planned against.

options.text: It leaves out what rivals already charge
options.rationale: Competitor pricing is a separate question from how many buyers exist for this service.

options.text: It comes from an outdated industry survey
options.rationale: Treats the problem as data freshness; the figure would be just as unusable if it were current.

options.text: It states revenue instead of profit earned
options.rationale: Demand estimates are built on revenue and buyer counts; swapping in profit would not fix the scope problem.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify why a single number fails the definition of a demand estimate.

questions.question: A bootmaker builds its whole range for people who work long shifts standing on concrete, and ignores every other buyer. What is this?

options.text: Targeting two groups at once
options.rationale: There is only one.

options.text: Reaching the widest market
options.rationale: It deliberately narrows.

options.text: Competing purely on price
options.rationale: Price is not mentioned.

options.text: Serving one slice very well
options.rationale: A niche approach builds the entire offer around a small group with an unmet need.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the strategy.

questions.question: A gym runs one offer and message for retirees and a separate one for students, on purpose. What is it doing?

options.text: Choosing a single niche to serve
options.rationale: There are two.

options.text: Stretching one message over both
options.rationale: That is the thing it avoids.

options.text: Serving two groups, each its own way
options.rationale: Multi-segment targeting means picking more than one group and building a distinct offer for each.

options.text: Dropping one group entirely
options.rationale: Both are served.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the strategy.

questions.question: What does a niche approach trade away in exchange for serving its slice better than anyone?

options.text: The quality of what it can offer
options.rationale: Quality is what it buys.

options.text: The size of the market it can reach
options.rationale: Depth for one group is bought with breadth across everyone else.

options.text: The loyalty it can build up
options.rationale: Loyalty tends to be stronger.

options.text: The price it is able to charge
options.rationale: Niches often support a premium.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the trade-off.
