questions.question: A tutoring service has cut its hourly rate twice and still gets few bookings. Asked why, parents say they watch sample lessons and ask other parents before they pick a tutor. What should the owner do next?

options.text: Run a third discount with a short booking deadline
options.rationale: Repeats the move that has already failed twice, assuming price is the barrier when the stated barrier is trust.

options.text: Post sample lesson clips and a parent referral offer
options.rationale: Matches the decision process parents described: proof of teaching plus a trusted recommendation are what they act on.

options.text: Shift the whole ad budget into paid search ads
options.rationale: Buys more attention at the same broken step, since parents do not decide inside a search ad.

options.text: Widen the subject list to bring in more parents
options.rationale: Treats a conversion problem as a reach problem; more subjects still meet the same hesitation.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept deployed in a fresh scenario: map a described decision process onto the right action.

questions.question: A regional bookstore chain wants to segment its shoppers so the stores can act on it. Which split is a real segmentation rather than a label?

options.text: Men who enter the store versus women who enter
options.rationale: Same error, and gender predicts even less here about what the visit requires.

options.text: Gift buyers needing wrapping versus browsing readers
options.rationale: The two groups want different things from the same visit, so staffing, layout and promotions genuinely change between them.

options.text: Shoppers paying by card versus shoppers paying cash
options.rationale: A transaction detail recorded after the decision; it changes nothing about what the store offers.

options.text: Customers over forty versus customers under forty
options.rationale: A demographic cut with no different need attached, which is the classic segment in name only.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: judge candidate splits against the standard of differing needs.

questions.question: A food truck owner plans one lunch stop at an office park of 2,000 workers. She assumes 40 percent buy lunch out, that 15 percent of those would pick her truck, and an average ticket of 12 dollars. What has she produced?

options.text: The share of the lunch market she already holds
options.rationale: Market share describes a business with customers; she has not opened at this stop yet.

options.text: A planning estimate resting on stated assumptions
options.rationale: This is what a bottom-up sizing produces: a usable number whose reliability depends on the two rates she assumed.

options.text: The full market value of local food service
options.rationale: Confuses her reachable slice with the whole category, the top-line error sizing exists to avoid.

options.text: A daily demand figure she can staff against
options.rationale: Close, but the chain of assumptions gives a planning estimate, not a measured daily figure she can treat as fact.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: read a bottom-up calculation and name what it does and does not establish.
review_flags: Option a is deliberately close to the key: it is the right shape of answer with a false claim to certainty. Worth a reviewer's eye.

questions.question: A software firm sells to solo freelancers and to 500-person enterprises using one price, one message and one onboarding flow. Both groups churn. What does multi-segment targeting prescribe?

options.text: Picking whichever group is larger
options.rationale: That is a niche choice, not this one.

options.text: A distinct offer built for each
options.rationale: Choosing two groups on purpose means each gets an offer and message shaped for it, rather than one stretched across both.

options.text: A longer onboarding for everyone
options.rationale: One flow stretched further.

options.text: A price set midway between them
options.rationale: Suits neither.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: prescribe the fix for a stretched offer.

questions.question: A small accounting practice competes with national firms on everything and wins little. It notices that veterinary clinics have payroll and stock quirks nobody serves well. What does the niche approach suggest?

options.text: Target every professional practice
options.rationale: Widens back out again.

options.text: Build the whole practice around vets
options.rationale: A niche is served by shaping the entire offer to that group, which is how a small firm beats a large one locally.

options.text: Add vets to its list of services
options.rationale: A line item, not a strategy.

options.text: Match the national firms on price
options.rationale: Competes where it is weakest.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: turn an observed gap into a niche strategy.

questions.question: A brand decides to target four segments with four separate campaigns, on a budget that funded one campaign properly last year. What is the risk?

options.text: Campaigns that overlap too much
options.rationale: They are separate by design.

options.text: Four efforts too thin to land
options.rationale: Serving multiple segments properly means funding a real offer for each, and spreading one budget across four buys presence in none.

options.text: Four segments that do not exist
options.rationale: Their existence is not questioned.

options.text: A budget that should be cut back
options.rationale: Less money, same problem.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: test a multi-segment plan against its resources.

questions.question: A meal kit startup has three segments: time pressed parents, the largest but most price sensitive; serious home cooks, the smallest but highest spending; and students, mid sized and lowest spending. It can fund one launch. Which reasoning best supports launching to the home cooks?

options.text: Choosing the biggest segment always gives the most defensible base to grow from
options.rationale: Size-only reasoning, which is the habit sizing demand is meant to correct. It also argues for a different segment.

options.text: Their spend per order can outweigh their smaller numbers, and one offer can be built around them
options.rationale: Holds all three together: the segments exist, their value is sized rather than counted, and selection follows from the sized comparison.

options.text: Their segment needs no demand estimate because high spenders are reliable buyers
options.rationale: Treats spend per head as a substitute for total demand, so the smallest group is never actually sized.

options.text: Their group becomes the largest once the three segments are merged back into one market
options.rationale: Undoes the segmentation that made the decision possible; merging groups hides the difference being decided on.

notes.difficulty_justification: Three concepts held at once: segmentation produces the groups, demand sizing values them, selection acts on the comparison.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Market Segmentation, Estimating Market Size and Demand, Target Market Selection. Remove segmentation and there are no groups to compare. Remove the sizing and size versus spend cannot be weighed, which is the whole question. Remove selection and nothing is being decided. Each deletion breaks it.

questions.question: A trail running shoe brand profiles its buyer as 25 to 40, earning 60K or more, who treats weekend races as identity. Sales stall anyway, and runners say they wait for injury data and ask club mates before switching shoes. What should the brand change?

options.text: Drop the identity detail and market on age and income alone
options.rationale: Throws away the psychographic half of the profile, which is what identified club channels in the first place.

options.text: Raise the income floor in the profile and aim at wealthier runners
options.rationale: Adjusts demographics when the obstacle described is a decision step, so the same wait happens at a higher price.

options.text: Hold the profile steady and widen the age band to reach more buyers
options.rationale: Reach fixes a shortage of audience; this is a shortage of evidence at the moment of switching.

options.text: Move spend into club channels and publish the injury data buyers wait on
options.rationale: Uses the profile to find the channel and the decision steps to decide what to say there, which is the pairing the stall calls for.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the profile names who and where, the behavior names when and why, and the fix needs both.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Demographic and Psychographic Profiling, Understanding Buyer Behavior. Without the profile there is no club channel to move spend into. Without the behavior there is no reason to publish injury data rather than more ads. Delete either and the correct answer stops being derivable.

questions.question: A scheduling software team can pursue 300 large enterprises or 6,000 mid sized property firms in its region. Enterprise deals are worth roughly ten times more but take three procurement cycles to close. What makes the mid sized tier the sounder identification?

options.text: Larger firms always carry more risk than smaller firms do in software
options.rationale: A general rule swapped in for the specific comparison; size alone does not decide which buyer to name.

options.text: A reachable count at a shorter cycle beats a bigger deal it cannot close
options.rationale: Identifies the buyer type by how it actually buys, then sizes what that tier can realistically produce in a year.

options.text: The mid sized tier holds the higher total contract value of the two
options.rationale: Asserts a number the scenario contradicts, so the sizing step is skipped rather than done.

options.text: Enterprise buyers rarely need scheduling automation at this kind of scale
options.rationale: Dismisses the segment on invented need rather than on cycle length and reachable volume.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: naming the business buyer type and sizing what that tier yields, where the answer depends on both at once.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Business-to-Business Market Identification, Estimating Market Size and Demand. Without the identification there is no buyer type whose cycle length matters. Without the sizing, ten times the deal value simply wins. Removing either makes the comparison trivial.

questions.question: A bakery finds two groups it serves: commuters who want speed before 8am, and parents who book custom cakes weeks ahead. It can make one change to its website. Which choice answers both groups' actual problems?

options.text: A loyalty card that rewards a tenth visit with a free item
options.rationale: Rewards frequency, which neither the 8am rush nor a once-a-year cake order is about.

options.text: One order form that lists every product the bakery sells
options.rationale: Flattens two genuinely different jobs back into one, undoing the segmentation.

options.text: A homepage banner featuring the bakery's newest pastries
options.rationale: Leads with what the bakery wants to promote rather than what either group came to do.

options.text: A pre-order pickup lane and a separate cake booking form
options.rationale: Each group's different need gets the path that fits it, which is what segmenting is for once the pains are known.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: segmentation produces two different jobs, and customer-centered thinking decides what each is owed.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Market Segmentation, Customer-Centered Thinking. Without the segmentation there is one undifferentiated audience and option b is fine. Without the customer-centered rule the bakery leads with its own pastries, which option c does. Both are needed for a to be the only defensible pick.

questions.question: A gym's data splits its members cleanly into early morning commuters, midday retirees and evening students. The marketing plan still speaks to members in general. What is missing?

options.text: More data on how members behave
options.rationale: The split is already clean and usable.

options.text: Three separate gyms, one per group
options.rationale: Segmenting does not require separate businesses.

options.text: A larger advertising budget overall
options.rationale: Spend does not decide who is being addressed.

options.text: A choice of which group to build for
options.rationale: Segmentation shows the groups exist and the plan only sharpens once one of them is picked to serve.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the segmentation is done well and the selection step that makes it useful was never taken.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Market segmentation, Target market selection. Without the segmentation there is nothing to choose between. Without the choice the segments change no decision. Both are needed.

questions.question: A sauce maker owns a small niche of chilli enthusiasts who pay a premium and reorder constantly. Growth has flattened because the niche is nearly saturated. A supermarket wants a milder line for families. What does the decision turn on?

options.text: Whether the niche is worth keeping
options.rationale: It is profitable and loyal.

options.text: Whether the supermarket pays enough
options.rationale: A term, not the strategic question.

options.text: Whether it can fund two real offers
options.rationale: Leaving a saturated niche for a second segment is the standard move, and it only works if each group gets a genuine offer rather than the first one diluted.

options.text: Whether families like chilli sauce
options.rationale: The milder line answers that.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the niche's ceiling is what raises the question and the multi-segment rule is what decides whether the answer is viable.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Niche marketing approach, Multi-segment targeting strategy. Without the saturated niche there is no reason to expand. Without the multi-segment discipline the move dilutes what works. Both are needed.

questions.question: A bank builds separate campaigns for students and for retirees, with different imagery and tone. Both campaigns promote the same account, chosen because it is the one the bank most wants to sell. Neither group responds. What is wrong?

options.text: Imagery that was poorly chosen
options.rationale: Presentation is not the substance.

options.text: Two campaigns running where one would do
options.rationale: Fewer wrappers, same problem.

options.text: Two wrappers around one unwanted offer
options.rationale: Targeting separate segments means each gets an offer built from what that group needs, and changing only the imagery leaves the bank's own preference at the centre.

options.text: Segments that are too far apart
options.rationale: Distinct groups are the premise.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the segmentation work is real and the customer-centred step that should determine each offer was skipped.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Multi-segment targeting strategy, Customer-centered thinking. Without the two segments there is nothing tailored. Without starting from each group's needs the tailoring is cosmetic. Both are needed.

questions.question: A founder picks left-handed guitarists as her niche because she is one and knows the frustrations well. Interviews with thirty of them show their real complaint is price, not the design features she has built the range around. What should she do?

options.text: Abandon the niche for a wider market
options.rationale: The niche is real and underserved.

options.text: Keep the design and explain it better
options.rationale: Argues with the research.

options.text: Keep the niche, rebuild on their need
options.rationale: The group is a sound niche and the offer has to be built from what they actually struggle with rather than from what the founder assumed.

options.text: Add right-handed models to the range
options.rationale: Dilutes before fixing the offer.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: choosing the niche and building the offer from that niche's stated need are separate steps, and only the first was done well.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Niche marketing approach, Customer-centered thinking. Without the niche there is no group to study. Without the customer research the founder's own frustration stands in for theirs. Both are needed.

questions.question: A boutique's sales are down 10 percent and the owner blames the new employee. Breaking the figure down shows the drop is entirely in online orders. What does that show?

options.text: The overall decline was measured wrongly
options.rationale: The total is accurate; its composition was unknown.

options.text: The new employee needs more training
options.rationale: The breakdown clears the shop floor entirely.

options.text: Online sales should be discontinued
options.rationale: Drops the channel instead of diagnosing it.

options.text: The cause lies outside the shop floor
options.rationale: Analysing the components of a number is what replaces a hunch with a located cause.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: read a disaggregated figure.

questions.question: A pitch cites a blog claiming 60 percent of teens want more caffeine options, with no study named. What should be checked?

options.text: Whether the blog is well designed
options.rationale: Presentation says nothing about reliability.

options.text: Whether the percentage sounds plausible
options.rationale: Plausibility is not verification.

options.text: Who produced it and how recently
options.rationale: Origin, date and possible bias are what establish whether a figure can carry weight in a decision.

options.text: Whether competitors cite the same figure
options.rationale: Repetition does not establish a source.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: test a source.

questions.question: Twelve weeks of data show Thursday orders climbing steadily each week. One Tuesday last month was unusually busy. Which is a trend?

options.text: The busy Tuesday, as a new pattern
options.rationale: One data point, which the card warns against acting on.

options.text: The Thursday climb across twelve weeks
options.rationale: Repetition over time is what distinguishes a trend from a single unusual reading.

options.text: Neither, since twelve weeks is too short
options.rationale: Twelve consecutive weeks is a usable series.

options.text: Both, since each is a change in sales
options.rationale: Conflates a one-off with a pattern.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: separate trend from outlier.

questions.question: Data shows Thursday 5pm to 7pm orders are 40 percent combo platters while Thursday staffing is set for a normal evening. What completes the analysis?

options.text: Report the finding to the management team
options.rationale: Presenting without recommending, the trap the card names.

options.text: Staff and prep Thursdays for the combo rush
options.rationale: A finding becomes useful when it produces a specific change, which is the step past describing the pattern.

options.text: Add more combo options to the menu
options.rationale: A product change rather than the operational fix indicated.

options.text: Track the same figures for another month
options.rationale: Defers a decision the data supports.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: convert insight into action.

questions.question: Three Decembers show steady 20 percent lifts. This year a major employer nearby has closed. How should the holiday forecast be built?

options.text: Use last December's figure without change
options.rationale: Ignores both the trend and the closure.

options.text: Start from the pattern, adjust for the closure
options.rationale: History gives the base and known changes have to be applied, since a straight projection assumes conditions held.

options.text: Apply the 20 percent lift as in prior years
options.rationale: Straight-line projection ignoring a known change.

options.text: Forecast no lift at all this December
options.rationale: Discards a strong seasonal pattern entirely.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: adjust a historical forecast.

concepts: Weighing Costs and Benefits of Information
questions.question: A bakery weighing a gluten-free line is offered a $6,000 market study. The line would cost about $2,000 to trial for a month. What does the comparison suggest?

options.text: Do both to confirm the trial result
options.rationale: Pays for information the trial already provides.

options.text: Trial it, since the answer costs less
options.rationale: Information is worth its price only when it costs less than finding out directly, which a cheaper live test undercuts.

options.text: Commission the study for certainty
options.rationale: Assumes more research is always safer, the trap the card names.

options.text: Decide without either, using intuition
options.rationale: Discards cheap evidence that is available.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: price information against the decision.

concepts: Weighing Costs and Benefits of Information
questions.question: A team can rely on a free industry blog figure of unknown origin, or spend $4,000 and three weeks on a reliable study, for a decision worth about $15,000. What is the sound path?

options.text: Use the blog figure, since the study costs more
options.rationale: Cost cannot make an unverifiable source usable.

options.text: Decide without information to save the time
options.rationale: Abandons evidence entirely.

options.text: Seek a cheaper reliable source before either
options.rationale: The free figure fails the reliability test and the study is disproportionate, so the sensible move is to look for credible evidence at a proportionate cost.

options.text: Commission the study, since reliability matters
options.rationale: Spends over a quarter of the decision's value on information.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: reliability and cost both constrain the choice and neither option satisfies both.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Judging Source Reliability, Weighing Costs and Benefits of Information. Without reliability the free figure wins. Without the cost view the study wins. Both are needed to reject each.

questions.question: A three-year upward trend in total sales conceals that in-store sales have fallen every year while online has grown faster. A forecast projects the total forward. What is the risk?

options.text: Online growth will continue indefinitely
options.rationale: An assumption rather than the structural flaw.

options.text: Total sales are the wrong thing to track
options.rationale: Totals are worth tracking alongside components.

options.text: Two opposite movements forecast as one
options.rationale: Projecting an aggregate hides divergent components, so the forecast will miss as soon as either trend changes pace.

options.text: The three-year window is too short
options.rationale: Three years is a workable base.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the forecast rests on an aggregate that analysis shows is composed of opposing trends.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Forecasting from Historical Data, Interpreting and Analyzing Information. Without the forecast there is no projection at risk. Without the breakdown the aggregate looks sound. Both are needed.

questions.question: A cafe manager's report notes, for eleven weeks running, that Sunday pastry waste is climbing. Each week she writes the observation down and orders the same quantity again. What is incomplete?

options.text: Waste figures that must be wrong here
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the measurement is faulty.

options.text: A pattern noticed and never acted on
options.rationale: Spotting the trend is only half the work, and a finding that changes no order is indistinguishable from never having looked.

options.text: A pattern that needs more weeks of data
options.rationale: Eleven consecutive weeks is a settled pattern.

options.text: A report nobody on the team reads
options.rationale: She reads it herself and still does nothing.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the pattern work is done properly and the step that converts it into a decision never happens.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Spotting patterns and trends, Turning insight into action. Without the pattern there is nothing to act on. Without the missing action the observation pays for itself. Both are needed.

questions.question: Sales went from $98,000 to $103,000 and the draft bar chart starts its axis at $97,000, making the bars look several times different. What is wrong?

options.text: A bar chart is the wrong form for sales
options.rationale: Bars are a fine way to show two periods.

options.text: The chart should be drawn in percentages
options.rationale: Percentages on the same cut axis mislead identically.

options.text: The two periods sit too close to compare
options.rationale: Close figures can be compared honestly.

options.text: The scale exaggerates a small change
options.rationale: A five percent rise drawn from a cut axis looks like a multiple, which is the chart telling a story the numbers do not.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify a misleading scale.

questions.question: A quarterly review needs to compare four store locations on one measure. What presentation fits?

options.text: A written paragraph describing each store
options.rationale: Prose where a comparison is wanted.

options.text: One chart holding every metric tracked
options.rationale: The overloaded chart the card warns against.

options.text: A simple bar chart of the four stores
options.rationale: A visual makes the key comparison immediate, which a table of figures does not.

options.text: A spreadsheet with all quarterly detail
options.rationale: Comprehensive and slow to read.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: choose a visual form.

questions.question: An executive summary of an automation study opens by recapping each section in order. What should it open with instead?

options.text: A description of the problem background
options.rationale: Context before conclusion delays the point.

options.text: The methodology used in the study
options.rationale: Method belongs in the body.

options.text: A list of everyone who contributed
options.rationale: Credits are not the point of a summary.

options.text: The finding and what it means to decide
options.rationale: Busy readers need the conclusion and the implied decision first, with support following.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: order an executive summary.

questions.question: A survey finds 68 percent of respondents say they would visit on a slow Tuesday afternoon if there were a discount. How should that be reported to the owner?

options.text: Read the results question by question
options.rationale: The recital the card warns against.

options.text: Lead with what it means for Tuesday pricing
options.rationale: Reporting means saying what the finding implies for a decision, rather than reciting the statistics in order.

options.text: Summarise the survey's methodology first
options.rationale: Necessary support, wrong opening.

options.text: Present the raw response counts first
options.rationale: Detail before meaning.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: report a finding for decision.

questions.question: A draft slide holds sales, margin, footfall and staffing for four stores across twelve months in one chart. Nobody can read it. What is the fix?

options.text: One chart per comparison that matters
options.rationale: A visual works by making one relationship obvious, so the fix is to split rather than compress.

options.text: Removing three of the four stores
options.rationale: Discards data rather than presenting it.

options.text: A table holding the same information
options.rationale: Moves the overload into rows.

options.text: A larger version of the same chart
options.rationale: Size does not reduce the complexity.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: fix an overloaded visual.

questions.question: A 22 page supplier review lands on the owner's desk on the morning she has to pick a supplier. What should its summary do?

options.text: Name the pick and the reason for it
options.rationale: A busy reader needs the decision and the one line that supports it, which is exactly what a summary is for.

options.text: List every supplier's full scorecard
options.rationale: Reproduces the report rather than distilling it.

options.text: Highlight the three longest sections
options.rationale: Length is not a measure of importance.

options.text: Restate the method used in the review
options.rationale: Method matters to the analyst, not the decision.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: shape the summary around what the reader has to do.

questions.question: An analyst has a genuine insight that Tuesday traffic could be lifted, and presents it with a truncated axis that makes current Tuesdays look catastrophic. The owner approves a large discount programme. What is the problem?

options.text: A real insight oversold by the display
options.rationale: The finding is sound and the presentation exaggerated its scale, so the decision is sized to a distortion rather than the data.

options.text: The owner should have read the appendix
options.rationale: Places the burden on the reader for a misleading chart.

options.text: The insight itself was not supported
options.rationale: The case states the insight is genuine.

options.text: Discounting is never the right response
options.rationale: It may be right at the correct scale.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the insight is valid and the display distorts it, and only both together explain an oversized decision.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Communicating Data and Insight, Avoiding Misleading Data Displays. Without the insight there is nothing worth presenting. Without the distortion the decision matches the data. Both are needed.

questions.question: A clear bar chart comparing four stores is prepared for a board that wants direction, and for regional managers who need to know which SKUs drove each store's result. What should be produced?

options.text: A single chart holding both levels at once
options.rationale: Produces the overloaded visual that serves neither.

options.text: The chart alone, since it is clearest
options.rationale: Clear and insufficient for the operational question.

options.text: The chart for the board, detail for managers
options.rationale: The same data serves two decisions, and each audience needs the level of detail their decision requires.

options.text: The SKU detail alone, since it is complete
options.rationale: Buries the comparison the board needs.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: visual clarity and audience needs pull in different directions and the answer serves both.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Presenting Data Visually, Tailoring Reports to an Audience. Without visual principles the overloaded chart looks acceptable. Without the audience view one chart serves everyone. Both are needed.

questions.question: An analyst writes a tight one page summary naming the recommended supplier, and sends the identical page to the owner making the call and to the warehouse team that has to work the change. What is the gap?

options.text: The warehouse needs what changes for it
options.rationale: The summary is well written for the decider, and the team carrying out the decision needs different content, not a shorter version of the same content.

options.text: The recommendation should stay unnamed
options.rationale: Naming the pick is the summary's job.

options.text: The summary is too short for the owner
options.rationale: Brevity is what the owner needed.

options.text: Two summaries would duplicate the work
options.rationale: Treats the cost as a reason not to tailor.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the summary is well built and the audience question was answered only once for two different readers.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Writing clear executive summaries, Tailoring reports to an audience. Without the good summary there is nothing worth sending on. Without the audience question one page serves everyone. Both are needed.

questions.question: A customer tweets that a packaged salad made people sick. What should happen before any public recall statement?

options.text: Check the claim against batch records
options.rationale: Acting on unverified information can cause harm of its own, so confirmation comes before a public step this large.

options.text: Delete the tweet from the brand feed
options.rationale: Suppression rather than verification.

options.text: Issue the recall within the hour
options.rationale: Speed over confirmation, the trap the card names.

options.text: Reply publicly disputing the claim
options.rationale: Also acts before knowing.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: verify before acting.

questions.question: During a chemical odour scare, air testing is underway and results are hours away. What should residents be told now?

options.text: What is known, unknown and being done
options.rationale: Naming the limits of current knowledge keeps people informed without asserting what has not been established.

options.text: That the cause is under investigation only
options.rationale: True and too thin to be useful.

options.text: Nothing until the results are final
options.rationale: Silence during an odour scare invites rumour.

options.text: That there is no danger to anyone
options.rationale: An unverified reassurance, which the card warns against.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: communicate under uncertainty.

questions.question: A delivery app has confirmed that some customer emails leaked. A manager wants to wait until every detail is known before telling anyone. What is the risk?

options.text: Others fill the silence first
options.rationale: In a crisis the gap gets filled by rumour or press, so the confirmed facts have to go out early even while detail follows.

options.text: The investigation will take longer
options.rationale: Communication does not slow the inquiry.

options.text: Customers will demand compensation
options.rationale: May happen either way.

options.text: The leak will grow while they wait
options.rationale: Disclosure does not stop an existing leak.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the cost of delay.

questions.question: A payment system leaked some customer email addresses. What does sound crisis information management look like?

options.text: Wait for the full forensic report to finish
options.rationale: Leaves users uninformed while the story spreads.

options.text: Post a general security notice on the website
options.rationale: Too vague to let anyone protect themselves.

options.text: Notify only users who contact support first
options.rationale: Reactive disclosure to a fraction of those affected.

options.text: Tell affected users early, then update as known
options.rationale: Deciding who needs to know, what is confirmed and how fast is the core of the skill, with detail following.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: manage crisis information.

questions.question: Two hours into the odour scare, a manager is tempted to say the air is safe to reassure residents, though testing is incomplete. What is the objection?

options.text: Two hours is too soon for any statement
options.rationale: An early statement is right; this content is not.

options.text: Residents would not believe it anyway
options.rationale: Speculates about reception rather than the principle.

options.text: It should come from the regulator instead
options.rationale: Source does not fix an unverified claim.

options.text: It asserts what nobody yet knows
options.rationale: False confidence costs credibility permanently if the testing later contradicts it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: avoid false certainty.

questions.question: During a product scare, a manager sees a screenshot circulating that claims a second batch is affected. What should happen before she recalls that batch?

options.text: Wait for the story to die down
options.rationale: Silence lets the rumour set.

options.text: Recall the batch and check later
options.rationale: Acts on a claim nobody has stood up.

options.text: Post a denial while she looks into it
options.rationale: Denies something she has not checked either.

options.text: Trace the claim back to its source
options.rationale: A fast-moving situation is exactly where an unverified claim does the most damage, so the origin has to be checked first.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: name the verification step under time pressure.

questions.question: An unverified claim of illness is spreading online. Verification will take six hours; a recall announcement would reach customers now. What does sound practice do?

options.text: Deny the claim until evidence emerges
options.rationale: Asserts a conclusion with no more basis than the rumour.

options.text: Recall immediately, since safety comes first
options.rationale: Acts on unverified information at large cost and may misdirect attention.

options.text: Say nothing for six hours until it is clear
options.rationale: Leaves the story to spread unanswered.

options.text: Say what is confirmed now, act when verified
options.rationale: The two duties are reconciled by communicating early about the situation while reserving the operational step for confirmed facts.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: verification restrains the action while crisis communication demands early contact, and the answer separates the two.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Verifying Information Before Acting, Managing Information During a Crisis. Without verification the recall is obvious. Without crisis communication silence looks prudent. Both are needed.

questions.question: A company notifies affected users of a leak within two hours, and the notice states firmly that no passwords were exposed although that check is still running. Passwords later prove to be affected. What was the error?

options.text: Telling users about the leak at all
options.rationale: Disclosure was required.

options.text: Notifying users before the checks finished
options.rationale: Early notice is correct practice.

options.text: Fast notice carrying an unverified assurance
options.rationale: Speed was right and the content overstated what was known, which costs more credibility than the delay would have.

options.text: Using email rather than a public statement
options.rationale: Channel is not the fault.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the timing satisfies crisis management and the content fails the uncertainty standard.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Managing Information During a Crisis, Communicating Uncertainty to Stakeholders. Without the fast notice the failure is delay. Without the uncertainty standard the assurance looks helpful. Both are needed.

questions.question: Residents demand a definite answer about the odour while testing continues. A manager can give a firm all-clear, stay silent, or describe the position. What should she say?

options.text: A firm all-clear to calm the neighbourhood
options.rationale: Asserts an unverified conclusion under pressure.

options.text: Nothing further until testing concludes
options.rationale: Silence in the face of a direct question.

options.text: That the company cannot comment at all
options.rationale: Reads as evasion and invites speculation.

options.text: What testing covers, when results are due
options.rationale: Describing the verification underway answers the demand honestly without claiming a result that does not exist.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: verification limits what can be claimed and the uncertainty standard says how to speak within that limit.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Verifying Information Before Acting, Communicating Uncertainty to Stakeholders. Without verification the all-clear is available. Without the communication standard silence is defensible. Both are needed.

questions.question: A surf shop with slumping wetsuit sales pulls every report from last year and hopes something explains it. What step was skipped?

options.text: Asking staff for their own theories
options.rationale: Opinion gathering rather than question definition.

options.text: Deciding what needed to be learned first
options.rationale: A defined question tells you which data to pull, and without it the search produces volume rather than an answer.

options.text: Pulling data from the prior year too
options.rationale: More data compounds the same problem.

options.text: Checking the reports for formatting errors
options.rationale: A technical detail unrelated to the approach.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the missing first step.

questions.question: Stores with in-store bakeries show 20 percent higher grocery sales. What does that figure establish on its own?

options.text: The two move together, and nothing more
options.rationale: A relationship in the data does not establish direction or cause, which is what a build decision would require.

options.text: Bakeries cause the higher grocery sales
options.rationale: Assumes the causal direction the data cannot show.

options.text: The relationship is a statistical accident
options.rationale: Dismisses a real association without evidence.

options.text: Grocery sales cause bakeries to be built
options.rationale: Equally unsupported in the other direction.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: read what a correlation supports.

questions.question: A regional report shows a 40 percent sales jump last month. What should happen before it is presented?

options.text: Check where the figure came from
options.rationale: Accuracy, completeness and currency are tested before a number is used, since precision is not the same as reliability.

options.text: Round it down to appear conservative
options.rationale: Alters a figure rather than verifying it.

options.text: Present it, since the report is official
options.rationale: Source formality does not establish accuracy.

options.text: Add a note that results may vary
options.rationale: A disclaimer instead of a check.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: verify before using.

questions.question: A food truck is deciding whether to keep a new taco flavour. Sales were strong on one festival Saturday and modest on the other twelve days. What does using data properly look like?

options.text: Keep it, since the best day was excellent
options.rationale: The single data point the card warns about.

options.text: Judge it on the full period, not the peak
options.rationale: Selecting the flattering day is cherry-picking, and the decision needs the whole record to be honest.

options.text: Extend the trial until a clearer day appears
options.rationale: Waits for a data point that will flatter.

options.text: Drop it, since most days were modest
options.rationale: Right conclusion possible, wrong method: one end of the range again.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: use the full record.

questions.question: A bakery considering a gluten-free line has two enthusiastic customer comments. What does gathering the right information involve?

options.text: A decision based on the two comments
options.rationale: Treats the first source as sufficient.

options.text: Sales data, local demand and supply costs
options.rationale: The facts needed for this decision span demand, feasibility and cost, not just the first signals that appeared.

options.text: A competitor's gluten-free pricing alone
options.rationale: One useful input presented as the whole picture.

options.text: More comments from the same customers
options.rationale: Deepens one narrow source.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: identify what information a decision needs.

questions.question: A warehouse receives 5,000 phone cases and inspects 100. Which sampling approach gives a usable conclusion?

options.text: Inspect all 5,000 to be certain
options.rationale: Defeats the purpose of sampling.

options.text: Take the top layer of the nearest pallet
options.rationale: The easiest-to-reach sample the card warns against.

options.text: Inspect the first 100 units unpacked
options.rationale: Also convenience rather than representativeness.

options.text: Draw from across the pallets at random
options.rationale: A representative sample supports a claim about the whole shipment, which a convenient handful cannot.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: design a sample.

questions.question: A chain plans a $2 million bakery build-out in twelve stores based on the 20 percent sales association. What should precede that commitment?

options.text: Abandoning it, since correlation proves nothing
options.rationale: Overcorrects and discards a real signal worth testing.

options.text: A test in a few stores to see what changes
options.rationale: A trial converts an association into evidence about effect, which is what a spend of this size requires.

options.text: Gathering two more years of the same data
options.rationale: More of the same observational evidence.

options.text: Proceeding, since the association is strong
options.rationale: Treats a correlation as a demonstrated cause.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the causal limit of the data determines what a data-driven decision may commit to.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Distinguishing Correlation from Causation, Using Data to Decide. Without the causal distinction the build is justified. Without the decision stake the distinction is academic. Both are needed.

questions.question: An analyst asks a sharp question about which store segments drove a decline, then answers it with a regional report that double-counts online orders. What is the status of her conclusion?

options.text: Sound, provided the double counting is small
options.rationale: Size unknown, and the flaw is systematic.

options.text: Sound, since the question was well defined
options.rationale: Framing does not validate inputs.

options.text: Unsound, because the question was too narrow
options.rationale: The narrowing is what made it answerable.

options.text: The right question answered with bad data
options.rationale: A precise question does not repair a flawed source, so the conclusion inherits the error regardless of how well the analysis was framed.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: question definition and data quality are separate requirements and only one was met.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Defining the Right Question, Identifying Data Quality Issues. Without the question the analysis is unfocused as well. Without the quality check the good framing looks sufficient. Both are needed.

questions.question: A 100-unit random sample of a shipment shows a 2 percent defect rate. The warehouse logs, however, record only units that passed initial scanning. What does that do to the estimate?

options.text: Nothing, since the sample was random
options.rationale: Randomness within a biased frame does not fix the frame.

options.text: The true rate is likely higher than measured
options.rationale: A well drawn sample from an already filtered population inherits the filter, so the defect rate is understated.

options.text: The estimate becomes entirely worthless
options.rationale: It remains informative as a lower bound.

options.text: The sample should have been larger
options.rationale: Size does not correct a population problem.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: sampling method is sound and the underlying data quality undermines what it measures.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Sampling for Practical Decisions, Identifying Data Quality Issues. Without sampling there is no estimate. Without the quality issue the estimate stands. Both are needed.

questions.question: A carrier scorecard rates each option on cost, on-time rate and damage rate, with no weights applied. What can go wrong?

options.text: Carriers cannot be scored numerically
options.rationale: They routinely are.

options.text: The ratings should run one to ten
options.rationale: Scale granularity is not the flaw.

options.text: A cheap but unreliable option can win
options.rationale: Unweighted criteria treat every factor as equally important, which lets a strong score on a minor factor decide.

options.text: The scorecard has too few criteria
options.rationale: Three relevant criteria is workable.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the missing weights.

questions.question: A bakery models only its most likely delivery scenario and plans staffing from it. What does scenario planning add?

options.text: A reason to delay the decision
options.rationale: Scenarios inform rather than defer.

options.text: A more accurate single prediction
options.rationale: Accuracy of one number is not the aim.

options.text: Confirmation the likely case is right
options.rationale: Reinforces the single-scenario habit.

options.text: A range of outcomes to prepare for
options.rationale: Sketching best, likely and worst cases is what reveals which outcomes the plan can survive.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: state what scenarios provide.

questions.question: A food truck delays deciding on a second location until it has gathered every available statistic about the neighbourhood. What is the flaw?

options.text: Second locations rarely succeed
options.rationale: A claim about outcomes, not information.

options.text: Neighbourhood data is unreliable
options.rationale: Quality is not the stated issue.

options.text: Not every fact is needed to decide
options.rationale: Ranking information by what the decision turns on is what keeps the process moving.

options.text: The truck should decide without data
options.rationale: Overcorrects into guessing.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the prioritisation failure.

questions.question: A food truck weighing a second location can research foot traffic, average lunch spend, competitor count, parking rules and demographic trends. Which two come first?

options.text: Demographic trends and parking rules
options.rationale: Useful later; neither establishes viability.

options.text: Foot traffic and average lunch spend
options.rationale: Those two determine whether the site can produce revenue at all, so they rank ahead of the refinements.

options.text: All five together before deciding
options.rationale: The equal-urgency stall the card names.

options.text: Competitor count and demographic trends
options.rationale: Context before the basic revenue question.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: rank information needs.

questions.question: A delivery app wants a daily dashboard that surfaces problems early. Which design fits?

options.text: Every metric the platform can produce
options.rationale: The crammed dashboard the card warns about.

options.text: On-time rate, delivery time and refunds
options.rationale: A few measures tied to how the service performs is what lets a problem be spotted the day it appears.

options.text: Total orders placed since launch
options.rationale: A cumulative figure that hides daily movement.

options.text: Monthly revenue and app store rating
options.rationale: Too slow and too coarse for daily monitoring.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: design a monitoring dashboard.

questions.question: A bakery considering delivery models three cases from last quarter's order data. What makes the exercise useful?

options.text: Presenting the best case to the bank
options.rationale: Selective use of the modelling.

options.text: Seeing which cases the bakery can survive
options.rationale: The value of scenarios is testing the plan against a range, particularly the downside.

options.text: Choosing the scenario that looks likeliest
options.rationale: Collapses the range back to one case.

options.text: Averaging the three into one forecast
options.rationale: Discards the information the spread carries.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: use scenarios properly.

questions.question: A carrier scorecard has weighted criteria, and two of the five inputs will take three weeks to obtain while a decision is needed in one. What does the framework allow?

options.text: Drop the framework and choose on cost
options.rationale: Abandons the structure under time pressure.

options.text: Decide on the weighted criteria available now
options.rationale: Weights show which inputs actually move the result, so a decision can proceed when the heaviest are in hand.

options.text: Wait three weeks for the complete scorecard
options.rationale: Stalls on inputs that may barely affect the outcome.

options.text: Score the missing inputs by estimate
options.rationale: Invents data rather than working with what exists.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the weighting tells you which information is essential, which is how the priority call is made.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Building Decision-Making Frameworks, Prioritizing Information Needs. Without the framework nothing ranks the inputs. Without prioritisation the missing data stops everything. Both are needed.

questions.question: A weighted scorecard ranks carrier A first on likely volumes. Scenario modelling shows that if volumes fall 30 percent, carrier A's minimum-charge clause makes it the most expensive by far. What follows?

options.text: Choose carrier A, since it ranks highest
options.rationale: Ignores a downside the modelling has surfaced.

options.text: Abandon the scorecard as unreliable
options.rationale: The tool is sound; its inputs were too narrow.

options.text: Score the options across the scenarios too
options.rationale: A framework evaluated against a single assumed future hides risks that only appear when the volume changes.

options.text: Choose the cheapest option in the downside
options.rationale: Optimises for one scenario instead of balancing.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the framework produces a ranking and the scenarios test whether the ranking survives other futures.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Building Decision-Making Frameworks, Scenario Planning with Data. Without the framework there is no ranking. Without scenarios the ranking looks decisive. Both are needed.

questions.question: A manager's dashboard carries forty tiles, every one refreshed hourly, and she still missed a three week slide in on-time delivery. What does the dashboard need?

options.text: A longer history behind every tile
options.rationale: Adds depth to a screen already too full.

options.text: Fewer numbers, chosen for the decisions
options.rationale: Monitoring only works when the screen shows what actually drives action, and forty equally weighted tiles hide the one that mattered.

options.text: A second screen to show it all at once
options.rationale: Doubles the display and the noise.

options.text: Updates more often than once an hour
options.rationale: Freshness was never the failure.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the monitoring habit is in place and the prioritisation of what to monitor was never done.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Using dashboards for monitoring, Prioritizing information needs. Without the dashboard there is nothing to read daily. Without the prioritisation the dashboard buries its own signal. Both are needed.

questions.question: Churn rose from 4 percent to 7 percent, and a teammate proposes charting it from a baseline of 3 percent to soften the look. What is that?

options.text: An error in the churn calculation
options.rationale: The figures are correct; the display is not.

options.text: An acceptable simplification for slides
options.rationale: Simplification does not license distortion.

options.text: Distorting the scale to hide a rise
options.rationale: Choosing a baseline to change the visual impression misrepresents data that is otherwise accurate.

options.text: A standard charting convention
options.rationale: Convention starts axes where the comparison stays honest.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the manipulation.

questions.question: A market report paraphrases a trade association's analysis closely enough that the structure and wording remain recognisable, with no citation. What is wrong?

options.text: Trade association analysis is off limits here
options.rationale: It can be used; it has to be credited.

options.text: The report should rest on original research
options.rationale: Secondary sources are legitimate when cited.

options.text: The source's work is used without credit
options.rationale: Close paraphrase still borrows the structure and the thinking, and leaving the citation off is what makes it a breach rather than a method.

options.text: Paraphrase is weaker than quoting the source
options.rationale: Paraphrase is fine when attributed.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify uncredited use.

questions.question: A survey finds 40 percent would renew, and the report presents only the positive open comments. What does transparency require?

options.text: Removing comments from the report
options.rationale: Discards useful qualitative data.

options.text: A larger survey before reporting
options.rationale: Sample size is not the issue.

options.text: The renewal figure reported alongside
options.rationale: Findings are reported including the inconvenient parts, since selective presentation misleads by omission.

options.text: More positive comments to balance it
options.rationale: Deepens the selection problem.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: apply the transparency standard.

questions.question: Of 500 customers surveyed about a subscription box, 40 percent would renew, while open comments praise the packaging. The team supports launching. How should the findings be reported?

options.text: A summary saying feedback was mixed overall
options.rationale: Vague enough to hide the specific risk.

options.text: The packaging praise, since it supports launch
options.rationale: Selective reporting toward a preferred answer.

options.text: The renewal figure alone, as the hard number
options.rationale: Drops genuine qualitative evidence.

options.text: Both results, with the renewal risk stated
options.rationale: Reporting what was found, including the part that complicates the recommendation, is what lets the decision be made honestly.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: report findings honestly.

questions.question: A quarterly report shows flat sales. A manager proposes reporting only the final six weeks, which happen to trend upward. What is the objection?

options.text: Six weeks is too short to chart at all
options.rationale: Short periods can be legitimate when not chosen for effect.

options.text: The window was chosen for its result
options.rationale: Selecting a favourable period is manipulation even when every number inside it is accurate.

options.text: The upward trend is probably inaccurate
options.rationale: It may be real; the selection is the fault.

options.text: Quarterly reporting is the legal standard
options.rationale: No legal requirement is at issue.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: identify cherry-picked windows.

questions.question: A student needs an industry growth figure from a trade association's published report for her own analysis. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Cite the association and the publication
options.rationale: Using someone else's work is legitimate when the credit makes the source visible to the reader.

options.text: Find a blog repeating the same number
options.rationale: Launders the source rather than citing it.

options.text: Use the figure without naming a source
options.rationale: Leaves the reader unable to check it.

options.text: Reword the sentence and present it as hers
options.rationale: Close paraphrase without credit.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: cite a source properly.

questions.question: A report includes every finding, favourable and not, and charts the unfavourable ones on compressed axes so they appear minor. Is the report transparent?

options.text: Complete in content, misleading in presentation
options.rationale: Disclosure and honest display are separate duties, and a chart designed to minimise a real finding defeats the disclosure.

options.text: Yes, provided the axes are labelled
options.rationale: Labels rarely undo the visual impression.

options.text: Yes, since nothing was left out
options.rationale: Inclusion is not the whole of honesty.

options.text: No, because unfavourable data was included
options.rationale: Inclusion is the correct part.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: full disclosure and honest display are both required and only one is present.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Transparency in Reporting Findings, Avoiding Data Manipulation. Without transparency the omission is the fault. Without the display standard inclusion looks sufficient. Both are needed.

questions.question: An analyst cites every source correctly and omits the one cited study whose findings contradict her recommendation. What is the status of the work?

options.text: Sound, since one study proves little
options.rationale: Its weight is for the reader to judge.

options.text: Sound, since every source used is credited
options.rationale: Credit covers what was used, not what was hidden.

options.text: Properly credited and selectively presented
options.rationale: Attribution is satisfied and the transparency duty is not, since leaving out contrary evidence misleads the reader.

options.text: Unsound, because citation was incomplete
options.rationale: The citations present are correct.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the attribution duty is met and the transparency duty is not.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Respecting Intellectual Property in Research, Transparency in Reporting Findings. Without attribution the fault is plagiarism. Without transparency the correct citations look sufficient. Both are needed.

questions.question: A student reuses a consultancy's chart with a full and correct citation, and crops it so the declining second half of the series never appears. What is the status of the work?

options.text: Fine, as charts are often trimmed to fit
options.rationale: Trimming that removes the trend is not formatting.

options.text: Acceptable, since the source is named
options.rationale: Treats attribution as covering everything.

options.text: Plagiarism, because the chart was reused
options.rationale: Reuse with credit is not plagiarism.

options.text: Properly credited and no longer honest
options.rationale: Citing the source discharges one duty and says nothing about whether the borrowed figure still tells the truth.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the attribution duty is met and the honesty duty is broken by the same borrowed exhibit.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Respecting intellectual property in research, Avoiding data manipulation. Without the correct citation this is a plain theft case. Without the crop the citation settles it. Both are needed.

questions.question: A returns clerk notices the same sneaker coming back for sole separation, tells her own manager, and considers the matter handled. What has she assumed?

options.text: That returns are not worth recording
options.rationale: She recorded and reported it.

options.text: That one manager will pass it onward
options.rationale: Sharing means the information reaches the people who can act, which here includes buying and the supplier relationship.

options.text: That the defect affects only one pair
options.rationale: She has already spotted a pattern.

options.text: That customers will stop returning them
options.rationale: Nothing about customer behaviour is assumed.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the sharing assumption.

questions.question: A bakery starts documenting its head decorator's methods in the month before she retires after six years. What is the weakness of that timing?

options.text: Six years of know-how in four weeks
options.rationale: Capture works as an ongoing habit, since a departure notice leaves no time to record what took years to build.

options.text: Retiring staff will not cooperate
options.rationale: Cooperation is not the issue described.

options.text: Documentation is the wrong format
options.rationale: Format is secondary to timing here.

options.text: Decorating cannot be written down
options.rationale: Much of it can, given time.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the timing flaw.

questions.question: A helpdesk dumps its documents into one shared folder and calls it a knowledge base. What is missing?

options.text: A structure that makes answers findable
options.rationale: A knowledge base is defined by retrieval, so storage without organisation is just a folder.

options.text: Permission settings for each document
options.rationale: Access control is a separate concern.

options.text: More documents covering more issues
options.rationale: Volume deepens the retrieval problem.

options.text: A monthly reminder that it exists
options.rationale: Awareness does not make it usable.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what makes a knowledge base work.

questions.question: Customer service has logged hundreds of complaints about a specific chair's wobble, and the buying team has just reordered it in volume. What went wrong?

options.text: Customer service logged too much detail
options.rationale: The logging was the part that worked.

options.text: The complaint data never reached buying
options.rationale: Information existing somewhere in the company is not the same as reaching the team whose decision it should change.

options.text: The supplier concealed the defect
options.rationale: The company already held the evidence.

options.text: Buying ordered more than it needed
options.rationale: Quantity is not the failure.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: diagnose a silo.

questions.question: A plant's head machinist retires in six months and is the only person who can tune the old press. What transfer approach fits?

options.text: A video recording of the machinist working
options.rationale: Useful reference, no practised skill.

options.text: A named successor doing the work supervised
options.rationale: Knowledge transfers when the learner performs the task under guidance, rather than watching or chatting.

options.text: A written manual completed before he leaves
options.rationale: Documentation alone rarely carries tacit skill.

options.text: A series of informal conversations over lunch
options.rationale: Casual contact without practice, the trap the card names.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: design a transfer.

questions.question: Helpdesk representatives retype the same password reset fix three times a day. What would a knowledge base change?

options.text: Customers solving the problem themselves
options.rationale: That would require a customer-facing article.

options.text: Fewer password reset issues being raised
options.rationale: The underlying volume is unchanged.

options.text: Representatives needing less training
options.rationale: Training need is not the target.

options.text: One written answer everyone can find fast
options.rationale: Capturing a repeated answer once and making it searchable removes the repeated effort and keeps replies consistent.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: state the benefit of a knowledge base.

questions.question: A retiring machinist can spend his last six months writing a detailed manual, or training a successor on the press with no manual produced. The plant wants the knowledge kept. What is the sound reading?

options.text: Do neither and hire an external specialist
options.rationale: Buys the skill without retaining the plant's own knowledge.

options.text: Train the successor, capturing notes as they go
options.rationale: Tacit skill transfers through supervised practice, and documenting alongside it preserves what the successor might later forget.

options.text: Record videos of every press adjustment made
options.rationale: Another passive artefact with no practised successor.

options.text: Write the manual, since it outlasts any person
options.rationale: A manual cannot carry judgement nobody has practised.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: capture and transfer are different mechanisms and the answer has to weigh what each preserves.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Capturing Institutional Knowledge, Mentoring for Knowledge Transfer. Without capture nothing is written down. Without mentoring the tacit skill dies with the manual. Both are needed.

questions.question: A retailer builds a company-wide complaints dashboard that every team can open. Buying still reorders the defective chair, because nobody in buying has reason to look at it. What does that reveal?

options.text: Complaints data belongs only to service
options.rationale: Contradicts the purpose of sharing it.

options.text: The dashboard holds too little detail
options.rationale: Detail is not what stopped it being used.

options.text: Buying deliberately ignored the warnings
options.rationale: They had no prompt to look.

options.text: Availability is not the same as delivery
options.rationale: Breaking a silo means the information reaches the decision, which passive access does not accomplish on its own.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the silo was opened and the active sharing step was still missing.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Avoiding Information Silos, Sharing Knowledge Across the Organization. Without the dashboard the silo explanation suffices. Without the sharing duty open access looks like a solution. Both are needed.

questions.question: A helpdesk's knowledge base is well structured and searchable, and its articles were all written three years ago by staff who have since left. Representatives have stopped using it. Why?

options.text: The search function must be broken
options.rationale: The case states it is searchable.

options.text: Good structure holding knowledge that aged out
options.rationale: Retrieval works and the content is stale, so capture has to be continuous rather than a one-time exercise.

options.text: Representatives prefer asking colleagues
options.rationale: A symptom rather than the cause.

options.text: The base holds too many articles to browse
options.rationale: Search exists precisely to avoid browsing.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the retrieval system is sound and the capture practice lapsed.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Building a Searchable Knowledge Base, Capturing Institutional Knowledge. Without the base there is nothing to consult. Without ongoing capture the content decays. Both are needed.

questions.question: A firm has a careful folder structure by year and client, and the files inside are named scan1, scan2 and final_v3. What still fails?

options.text: Files should be stored by date only
options.rationale: Replaces one scheme with a weaker one.

options.text: Nobody can tell what a file holds
options.rationale: Retrieval depends on consistent naming as much as on folders, since the structure only narrows the search.

options.text: The folder structure is too detailed
options.rationale: The structure is the part that works.

options.text: Scanned documents cannot be organised
options.rationale: They can, with proper naming.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the retrieval gap.

questions.question: A clinic's system logs that a record was edited but not who did it or what changed. What is the log missing?

options.text: The user, the time and the change
options.rationale: An audit trail has to answer who, when and what, or it cannot support any later question.

options.text: A backup copy of the record
options.rationale: Backup is a different function.

options.text: A monthly summary of edit counts
options.rationale: Aggregates say nothing about individual changes.

options.text: An alert sent to the supervisor
options.rationale: Notification is not the record.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name audit trail contents.

questions.question: A firm keeps every email, invoice and draft it has ever produced, on the reasoning that deleting anything is risky. What is it missing?

options.text: A larger storage allowance each year
options.rationale: Buys room for the problem rather than solving it.

options.text: A rule for how long each type is kept
options.rationale: A retention policy sets a period per record type, which is what tells the firm when something can safely go.

options.text: A backup copy of the oldest records
options.rationale: Adds another copy of everything.

options.text: Permission from staff before deleting
options.rationale: Retention is set by policy, not by request.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the policy the firm has never written.

questions.question: A medical billing company must keep patient billing records for seven years and holds marketing email lists indefinitely. What does a sound policy do?

options.text: Set periods by type, then delete on schedule
options.rationale: Each category gets the period its rules require, and safe destruction at the end is part of the policy rather than an afterthought.

options.text: Delete all records after three years
options.rationale: Breaches the seven-year requirement.

options.text: Keep everything for seven years to be safe
options.rationale: Holds personal data longer than needed.

options.text: Keep marketing data until customers object
options.rationale: Shifts the duty onto the customer.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: build a retention schedule.

questions.question: Contractor invoices need to be findable by client and year, by anyone in the office. Which convention works?

options.text: One folder per invoice with a short code
options.rationale: Codes nobody can decode without a key.

options.text: Year and client folders, with dated file names
options.rationale: Structure plus a consistent naming rule is what lets someone who did not file it still find it.

options.text: A single archive folder with search enabled
options.rationale: Relies on search to compensate for no scheme.

options.text: Chronological folders with original file names
options.rationale: Keeps the naming problem in place.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: design a retrieval convention.

questions.question: A bike rental shop needs to settle damage disputes weeks after a hire. What record-keeping supports that?

options.text: Staff recollection supported by the shift rota
options.rationale: Recollection is not a record.

options.text: Check-out sheets with bike, renter and condition
options.rationale: Records earn their place when the business can find and trust them later, which means capturing the facts a dispute will turn on.

options.text: A daily count of how many bikes went out
options.rationale: Volume without the detail a dispute needs.

options.text: Payment receipts held by the card processor
options.rationale: Proves payment, not condition.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: design records for a known use.

questions.question: A clinic keeps complete audit logs and deletes them after 90 days under a general policy, while patient billing disputes typically surface after a year. What does that combination produce?

options.text: A breach of patient confidentiality rules
options.rationale: Deletion is not a confidentiality breach.

options.text: Good logging that is gone when needed
options.rationale: The trail is well designed and a retention period set without reference to when questions arise destroys it before use.

options.text: Excess storage cost from over-retention
options.rationale: The problem is the opposite.

options.text: Logs that are too detailed to search
options.rationale: Detail is not the described problem.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: logging quality and retention period interact, and one undoes the other.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Maintaining Audit Trails, Establishing Retention Policies. Without the trail there is nothing to lose. Without the retention error the logs survive to be used. Both are needed.

questions.question: A rental shop captures every hire in detail on paper slips kept in an unsorted box. A damage dispute takes four hours of searching and the slip is never found. What does the case show?

options.text: Disputes should be settled without records
options.rationale: Abandons the evidence entirely.

options.text: The slips held insufficient detail
options.rationale: The case states the capture was detailed.

options.text: Paper records are inherently unusable
options.rationale: Organised paper works fine.

options.text: Capture without retrieval is not a record
options.rationale: Documentation only works when the information can be found and trusted on demand, which an unsorted box prevents.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: recording and organising are separate requirements and only one was met.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Record-Keeping and Documentation, Organizing Files for Retrieval. Without capture there is nothing filed. Without organisation the capture cannot be used. Both are needed.

questions.question: A firm names and folders its files impeccably and deletes nothing, so a search for last year's signed contract returns four hundred near-identical drafts. What does the case show?

options.text: Search tools are the wrong approach here
options.rationale: Search is fine; the corpus is the problem.

options.text: Order alone cannot fix keeping everything
options.rationale: A good filing scheme narrows the search and the absence of retention rules means what it narrows to is still a heap.

options.text: Contracts should be stored outside the system
options.rationale: Moves one record type and leaves the rule missing.

options.text: The naming convention needs rebuilding
options.rationale: The naming is described as impeccable.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the retrieval system is sound and retention is absent, so the two together produce a search nobody can use.
