notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Organizing files for retrieval, Establishing retention policies. Without the filing scheme the case is ordinary chaos. Without the retention gap the folder holds one contract. Both are needed.

questions.question: A skate shop surveys the twenty regulars who hang around the counter about a new app. What is the weakness?

options.text: They do not represent the target users
options.rationale: Research needs a group that reflects who you are trying to understand, and the most loyal regulars are not that group.

options.text: The questions were asked in person
options.rationale: Mode is not the flaw identified.

options.text: Twenty responses is too small a number
options.rationale: Size matters less than whether the group fits.

options.text: Surveys cannot evaluate app ideas
options.rationale: They can, with the right respondents.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify a sampling frame problem.

questions.question: A taste test asks shoppers, do you not love the new flavour? What is wrong with the question?

options.text: It signals the answer expected
options.rationale: Leading wording pushes respondents toward one reply, which makes the result useless.

options.text: It should be asked after the purchase
options.rationale: Timing is not the defect.

options.text: It asks about flavour rather than price
options.rationale: Flavour is the right subject for a taste test.

options.text: It is too short to be informative
options.rationale: Brevity is a virtue in survey questions.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: spot a leading question.

questions.question: A bakery knows a new muffin is underperforming and wants to know why. Which kind of research fits?

options.text: Open questions about what customers think
options.rationale: Numbers show that something is happening and open responses are what explain the reason behind it.

options.text: More detailed unit sales tracking
options.rationale: Measures the symptom more precisely.

options.text: A rating scale from one to five
options.rationale: Quantifies opinion without explaining it.

options.text: A comparison of margins across products
options.rationale: Financial analysis rather than customer reasoning.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: match method to question type.

questions.question: A student cites a news article that summarises a university study. Which is the primary source?

options.text: The news article that cites it
options.rationale: That is the secondary source.

options.text: The student's summary of both
options.rationale: Third hand by then.

options.text: The journalist's own opinion
options.rationale: Further removed again.

options.text: The study the article describes
options.rationale: The primary source is the original work; the article is someone else's gathering and interpretation of it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: classify the sources.

questions.question: A bakery wants to know whether a gluten-free line will actually sell. Which method gives the most reliable answer?

options.text: A survey of in-store regulars about interest
options.rationale: Defaults to a survey and asks the wrong group.

options.text: A focus group discussing dietary preferences
options.rationale: Explores attitudes rather than purchase behaviour.

options.text: A review of national gluten-free market growth
options.rationale: Category data that says little about this shop.

options.text: A limited trial run measuring real purchases
options.rationale: Stated intentions overstate demand, so a small live test measures what people do rather than what they say.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose a method for a demand question.

questions.question: A cafe is testing a loyalty app and wants a short survey. Which design fits the skill?

options.text: One open box asking for any thoughts
options.rationale: Unstructured responses that resist comparison.

options.text: Twenty questions covering every feature
options.rationale: Length that costs completion and focus.

options.text: Three questions asking if they like it
options.rationale: Short but too vague to act on.

options.text: Five specific questions on use and value
options.rationale: Short and precisely targeted is what produces usable answers and completed responses.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: design a survey.

questions.question: A meal kit startup has a folder of competitor prices, menus and delivery times collected monthly for a year, and has never changed anything as a result. What is missing?

options.text: Sharing the folder with the whole company
options.rationale: Distribution is not the same as action.

options.text: Tracking more competitors each month
options.rationale: More collection, same absence of use.

options.text: Collecting the data more frequently
options.rationale: Cadence is not the gap.

options.text: Turning the findings into decisions
options.rationale: Intelligence is gathered to inform action, and a collection nobody acts on is an expensive archive.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: complete the intelligence cycle.

questions.question: A taste test uses neutral, carefully worded questions and recruits only shoppers who already buy the brand weekly. Results are overwhelmingly positive. What should be concluded?

options.text: The sample size should simply be increased
options.rationale: More of the same biased group.

options.text: The result is reliable, since wording was fair
options.rationale: Fair questions cannot fix an unrepresentative sample.

options.text: Good questions asked of the wrong group
options.rationale: Neutral wording removes one source of bias and the sample still guarantees a favourable answer.

options.text: The wording must have been leading after all
options.rationale: The case states it was neutral.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: bias can enter through wording or sample and only one was controlled.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Avoiding Bias in Research Design, Asking the Right People. Without the wording control the fault would be obvious. Without the sample problem the study would be sound. Both are needed.

questions.question: A shop knows from sales data that a product is failing and needs to know why before relaunching. A manager proposes a large numerical survey. What should the design be?

options.text: A rating survey of current loyal buyers
options.rationale: Numbers from the wrong group for a reason question.

options.text: A larger sample of the same sales data
options.rationale: More of the data that revealed the symptom.

options.text: A competitor price comparison study
options.rationale: One hypothesis treated as the whole answer.

options.text: Open conversations with recent non-buyers
options.rationale: The question is a why question, so the method has to gather reasons, and the people to ask are those who chose not to buy.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: method choice and the numbers-or-words decision jointly determine the design.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Choosing a Research Method, Choosing Numbers or Words. Without method choice there is no design question. Without the numbers-or-words distinction a survey looks fine. Both are needed.

questions.question: Competitor tracking shows three rivals now offer 20-minute delivery. A startup surveys its own customers asking whether they are satisfied with current delivery times. Satisfaction is high, and churn keeps rising. Why?

options.text: Customers were dishonest in the survey
options.rationale: They answered the question they were asked.

options.text: Churn is unrelated to delivery times
options.rationale: The competitive shift suggests otherwise.

options.text: The survey never asked about the alternative
options.rationale: Satisfaction with what people have says nothing about what they would switch to, which the competitive data had already flagged.

options.text: The competitor data was collected too late
options.rationale: It was available and pointed at the issue.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the competitive finding should have shaped the survey design, and the disconnect explains the contradiction.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Competitive Intelligence Gathering, Designing a Simple Survey. Without the competitor data nothing indicates the missing question. Without the survey there is no contradictory result. Both are needed.

questions.question: A boutique's loyalty app asks for date of birth, home address, income bracket and occupation, though it only ever sends a birthday offer. What is the problem?

options.text: Birthday offers are not worth sending
options.rationale: The offer is fine; the collection is not.

options.text: It collects data it does not need
options.rationale: Collecting beyond the purpose creates risk with no benefit, which is why minimisation is the starting rule.

options.text: Loyalty apps cannot store personal data
options.rationale: They can, within limits.

options.text: The app should ask for more detail
options.rationale: Reverses the principle.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: apply data minimisation.

questions.question: A clinic gives every employee full access to the patient database on their first day and never revisits it. What is wrong?

options.text: Access should be granted by the IT team
options.rationale: Who grants it is not the flaw.

options.text: Access exceeds what roles require
options.rationale: People should hold the access their job needs, and permissions have to be reviewed as roles change.

options.text: New staff should have no access at all
options.rationale: They need what their role requires.

options.text: Databases should not hold medical notes
options.rationale: That is their purpose.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify excessive access.

questions.question: A dental office backs up nightly to the cloud and has never attempted a restore. What is the exposure?

options.text: Cloud storage is unsuitable for records
options.rationale: It is a standard approach.

options.text: The backups may not restore when needed
options.rationale: An untested backup is an assumption, and the test is what turns it into a recovery capability.

options.text: Nightly backups are too infrequent
options.rationale: Nightly is reasonable for this office.

options.text: The office needs a second backup provider
options.rationale: Duplication without testing repeats the flaw.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the untested-backup risk.

concepts: Responsible and Ethical Use of Information
questions.question: A fitness app collected workout and location data to personalise training plans. A partner now offers to buy that data. What does responsible use require?

options.text: Proceeding, since users already shared it
options.rationale: The assumption the card names as the trap.

options.text: Adding a line to the terms next update
options.rationale: Quiet terms changes are not consent.

options.text: Fresh consent for a use nobody agreed to
options.rationale: Consent covers the purpose it was given for, and selling the data is a different purpose entirely.

options.text: Proceeding if the data is anonymised
options.rationale: Location traces frequently re-identify people.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: test a secondary use.

questions.question: A dental clinic is launching a patient portal. Which set of safeguards fits the skill?

options.text: An IT audit scheduled for next year
options.rationale: Delays the protection past launch.

options.text: Insurance covering breach notification costs
options.rationale: Transfers cost rather than preventing harm.

options.text: Two-factor login, encryption and ongoing review
options.rationale: Layered controls plus continuing attention is what prevention means, rather than a single setup task.

options.text: A strong password policy set at launch
options.rationale: One control treated as sufficient.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: design breach prevention.

questions.question: A fitness app is expanding into Europe. What does compliance require at launch?

options.text: A privacy policy translated into local languages
options.rationale: Translation without the underlying rights.

options.text: A legal review scheduled after launch
options.rationale: Ships first and checks later.

options.text: Explicit opt-in and deletion rights built in
options.rationale: The rules of the market have to be designed into the product rather than added after users arrive.

options.text: The same settings used in its home market
options.rationale: Assumes one regime fits every market.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: build compliance into a launch.

questions.question: A clinic encrypts its database and requires two-factor login, and every member of staff including temporary receptionists can open full medical histories. A record is leaked. What failed?

options.text: Temporary staff should never be hired
options.rationale: Staffing model rather than the access design.

options.text: Two-factor login is insufficient in clinics
options.rationale: It is a strong control, just not this one.

options.text: Strong defences around universal access
options.rationale: Technical controls protect against outsiders, and access breadth determines how much any one insider or compromised account can reach.

options.text: The encryption was incorrectly configured
options.rationale: Nothing indicates the encryption failed.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: breach prevention is strong at the perimeter and the permission design leaves the interior open.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Preventing Data Breaches, Managing Access Permissions. Without the technical controls the leak has an easier explanation. Without the access problem the controls would have held. Both are needed.

questions.question: A clinic's recovery plan keeps seven years of nightly backups of all patient data, while its regulator requires certain records to be deleted on request. A deletion request arrives. What does the clinic face?

options.text: A need to stop backing up patient records
options.rationale: Abandons recovery entirely.

options.text: No issue, since backups are not live data
options.rationale: Retained copies are still held data.

options.text: No issue, since recovery rules take priority
options.rationale: Asserts a hierarchy that does not exist.

options.text: Backups holding data it must erase
options.rationale: Recovery design and deletion duties collide, so the backup policy has to be built with erasure obligations in mind.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: sound recovery practice and a deletion obligation conflict, which only both together reveal.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Planning for Information Disaster Recovery, Complying with Data Regulations. Without recovery there are no retained copies. Without the regulation there is no erasure duty. Both are needed.

concepts: Responsible and Ethical Use of Information
questions.question: An app minimises collection and secures what it holds, then uses that small dataset to target users with ads based on inferred health conditions. What is the position?

options.text: Acceptable, since the data is fully encrypted
options.rationale: Security does not answer the ethics question.

options.text: Secure data used in a way users never expected
options.rationale: Protecting data and using it properly are different duties, and minimisation does not license any purpose.

options.text: Unacceptable, because inference is impossible
options.rationale: Inference is plainly possible and is the concern.

options.text: Acceptable, since very little data is collected
options.rationale: Volume does not determine legitimacy of use.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: privacy practice is good and the use test is failed.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Data Privacy and Security, Responsible and Ethical Use of Information. Without the security the case is a simple breach story. Without the ethics of use the minimisation looks sufficient. Both are needed.

questions.question: Three clinic staff enter phone numbers three different ways. A style guide is written and the system still accepts any format. What happens?

options.text: The guide should list more examples
options.rationale: More documentation, same enforcement gap.

options.text: The inconsistency continues as before
options.rationale: A standard holds when the system enforces it, since a document alone does not change what gets typed.

options.text: Phone numbers should not be stored
options.rationale: They are needed for the business.

options.text: Staff will adopt the guide within weeks
options.rationale: Assumes compliance the case contradicts.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the enforcement gap.

questions.question: A twelve-person landscaping company picks between two scheduling apps by counting features. What should decide it instead?

options.text: Which interface looks more modern
options.rationale: Appearance over function.

options.text: Which product has the longer feature list
options.rationale: The count the card names as the trap.

options.text: Which vendor is the larger company
options.rationale: Size is not fit.

options.text: How well each handles their actual work
options.rationale: Software is judged against what the business needs to do, since unused features are not value.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the selection criterion.

questions.question: A grooming shop's client details live on three groomers' personal phones. What is the core problem?

options.text: The groomers record too much detail
options.rationale: Volume is not the issue.

options.text: No shared system anyone can use
options.rationale: Customer information has to be organised where the business can reach it, not scattered across individual devices.

options.text: Phones are unreliable for storage
options.rationale: Device type is secondary to the fragmentation.

options.text: Clients should keep their own records
options.rationale: Shifts the business's responsibility.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the systems gap.

questions.question: A furniture retailer's website shows items in stock that the warehouse shipped out days ago. Both teams use the same software. What is missing?

options.text: The two systems updating each other
options.rationale: Shared access is not integration, and without a live connection each department works from its own picture.

options.text: A disclaimer about stock on the website
options.rationale: Warns customers instead of fixing the data.

options.text: More frequent manual stock counts
options.rationale: Manual reconciliation of a connection problem.

options.text: Training for warehouse staff on the software
options.rationale: Skill is not what breaks the sync.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: distinguish shared access from integration.

questions.question: A clinic wants every phone number stored identically from now on. What makes the standard hold?

options.text: A field format the system enforces
options.rationale: Building the rule into the entry point is what makes consistency automatic rather than voluntary.

options.text: A briefing at the next staff meeting
options.rationale: One-off instruction.

options.text: A monthly audit of recent entries
options.rationale: Finds errors after they enter the system.

options.text: A laminated card at each workstation
options.rationale: A reminder that relies on attention.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: enforce a data standard.

questions.question: One scheduling app has a flashy interface and 60 features; the other handles recurring jobs and crew assignment, which is 90 percent of the company's work. Which wins?

options.text: The one matching the daily workload
options.rationale: Fit to the actual work decides, and features outside that work add cost and training rather than value.

options.text: The one with more features for growth
options.rationale: Pays now for capability that may never be used.

options.text: Whichever the crew finds prettier
options.rationale: Appearance as the deciding factor.

options.text: Whichever offers the longer free trial
options.rationale: A sales term rather than a fit test.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: select software on fit.

questions.question: A retailer's best-fit warehouse system cannot exchange data with the online store, while a slightly weaker option connects natively. Stock accuracy is the company's main complaint. Which should it choose?

options.text: The best-fit system, since features matter most
options.rationale: Optimises one system against the company's actual complaint.

options.text: Neither, until a perfect option appears
options.rationale: Defers a decision the evidence supports.

options.text: The best-fit system plus manual reconciliation
options.rationale: Buys ongoing labour to patch a known gap.

options.text: The connecting option, since accuracy depends on it
options.rationale: Fit includes fitting the rest of the business, and the stated problem is exactly what integration solves.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: software fit and cross-department integration both bear on the choice and point different ways.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Evaluating Software Solutions, Integrating Information Across Departments. Without the fit question there is no trade. Without integration the better-featured system wins. Both are needed.

questions.question: A grooming shop moves three groomers' client lists into one shared system. Within a month the same dog appears under four spellings and appointment history is split. What was skipped?

options.text: A decision on who owns each client
options.rationale: Ownership is a commercial question.

options.text: Training on the new shared system
options.rationale: Usage is not the described failure.

options.text: A backup of the original phone lists
options.rationale: Backup does not prevent duplication.

options.text: Agreed entry rules before the merge
options.rationale: Centralising the data without a common format simply collects the inconsistencies in one place.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the system consolidation is correct and the entry standard needed to precede it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Managing Customer Data and Systems, Standardizing Data Entry Practices. Without the shared system the lists stay separate. Without standards the merge produces duplicates. Both are needed.

questions.question: Two departments' systems are connected and syncing hourly, and customer records still fail to match because each team formats names and addresses differently. What does that show?

options.text: Integration cannot reconcile inconsistent entry
options.rationale: A connection moves data faithfully, and mismatched formats mean the same customer arrives as two different records.

options.text: The hourly sync frequency is far too low
options.rationale: Hourly is frequent; matching is the problem.

options.text: Customer records should be entered only once
options.rationale: Desirable and not always possible across functions.

options.text: The two systems were connected incorrectly
options.rationale: The connection works as described.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: integration is in place and data standards are not, so the connection propagates the inconsistency.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Integrating Information Across Departments, Standardizing Data Entry Practices. Without integration the departments never compare records. Without standards the comparison fails. Both are needed.

questions.question: A repair shop's front desk texts every customer individually when a car is ready. What makes this a candidate for automation?

options.text: Texting is cheaper than telephoning
options.rationale: Cost per message is not the criterion.

options.text: Customers dislike receiving text messages
options.rationale: The channel is working; the labour is the issue.

options.text: The front desk has spare time anyway
options.rationale: Spare time argues against the investment.

options.text: It repeats identically many times daily
options.rationale: Routine, high-volume information tasks with a fixed trigger are where automation pays.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify an automation candidate.

questions.question: An online store tracks only total sales because it is the easiest figure to pull. What does that cost?

options.text: The speed of the reporting system
options.rationale: Performance is not the issue.

options.text: The accuracy of the sales figure
options.rationale: Total sales can be perfectly accurate.

options.text: No view of what drives the total
options.rationale: A few chosen measures show how the business is working, while a single convenient number hides the mechanism.

options.text: The ability to file tax returns
options.rationale: Unrelated to metric choice.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the cost of convenience metrics.

questions.question: A shop owner buys every new tool that appears in his trade magazine. What is the flaw in that approach?

options.text: Trade magazines are unreliable sources
options.rationale: The source is not the problem.

options.text: New tools are always more expensive
options.rationale: Cost varies and is not the principle.

options.text: Staff dislike learning new systems
options.rationale: A consequence rather than the flaw.

options.text: No test of whether each one helps
options.rationale: Keeping up means adopting what improves the work, which requires judging each tool against a real need.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify undisciplined adoption.

concepts: Assessing New Technology Costs and Benefits
questions.question: A repair shop is quoted $6,000 for a digital inspection tablet system, plus $150 a month in software and two days of training. What does a proper assessment include?

options.text: The monthly fee compared with rivals
options.rationale: One component compared externally.

options.text: The training days as the main cost
options.rationale: Isolates the smallest element.

options.text: Purchase, subscription and training together
options.rationale: The full cost of ownership is what the benefits have to clear, not the sticker price alone.

options.text: The $6,000 purchase price against savings
options.rationale: Ignores ongoing and setup costs, the trap named.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: cost a technology decision fully.

questions.question: Three food trucks share inventory counts through a cloud folder, and drivers download copies to edit offline and upload them later. What goes wrong?

options.text: Drivers cannot access the folder at all
options.rationale: They are accessing it.

options.text: The cloud service becomes too expensive
options.rationale: Cost is not the described failure.

options.text: Inventory counts take longer to complete
options.rationale: Speed is not what breaks.

options.text: Versions diverge and overwrite each other
options.rationale: Shared storage only works when everyone edits the live copy, since downloaded versions become separate truths.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: diagnose a shared-file failure.

questions.question: An online sneaker store wants a weekly dashboard that shows how the business is really doing. Which set fits?

options.text: Every metric the platform can export
options.rationale: Volume rather than selection.

options.text: Total sales, page views and follower count
options.rationale: Easy figures that flatter and explain little.

options.text: Cart abandonment, repeat rate and return rate
options.rationale: A few measures that each expose part of the buying process is what turns a dashboard into a diagnostic.

options.text: Monthly revenue compared with last year
options.rationale: Too coarse and too slow for weekly use.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: select operating metrics.

questions.question: A team copies figures between two systems by hand every Monday, two hours a week, although both systems already export and import the same file format. Why does it continue?

options.text: Two hours being too short to fix
options.rationale: Two hours weekly is substantial.

options.text: A format the systems cannot share
options.rationale: They share it already.

options.text: A rule requiring manual checking
options.rationale: No rule is mentioned.

options.text: Habit, where a tool already exists
options.rationale: Adoption is about using what is already available rather than defaulting to manual effort because that is how it has always been done.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: name why an available tool goes unused.

questions.question: Three trucks report daily inventory into a shared cloud sheet, and head office builds a waste metric from it. Two drivers still upload edited copies each evening. What does the metric actually measure?

options.text: Average waste across the three trucks
options.rationale: That is what it is intended to measure, not what it does.

options.text: Whichever version was uploaded last
options.rationale: A measure is only as good as the data feeding it, and overwritten files mean the metric reflects upload order rather than inventory.

options.text: Nothing at all, since cloud data is unreliable
options.rationale: Overstates: correctly used shared editing is reliable.

options.text: The waste of the most accurate truck
options.rationale: Nothing selects for accuracy.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the metric design is sound and the sharing practice corrupts its input.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Using Analytics and Metrics, Cloud-Based Information Sharing. Without the metric the file conflict is a nuisance. Without the sharing fault the metric is sound. Both are needed.

questions.question: A shop automates its ready-for-collection texts, drawing phone numbers from a shared cloud sheet that two staff still edit as downloaded copies. Some customers get no message and others get two. What is the cause?

options.text: Automation reading a file with rival versions
options.rationale: Automation executes against whatever the source says, and offline copies mean the source holds conflicting records.

options.text: Text messages are the wrong channel for this
options.rationale: The channel worked when sent manually.

options.text: The texting tool was a poor choice here
options.rationale: The tool is doing what it was told.

options.text: The front desk should check each message
options.rationale: Reintroduces the labour automation removed.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the automation is correctly targeted and the shared-file practice corrupts its input.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Automating Routine Information Tasks, Cloud-Based Information Sharing. Without automation the errors stay manual and catchable. Without the version conflict the automation works. Both are needed.

concepts: Assessing New Technology Costs and Benefits
questions.question: A trade magazine's most-hyped tool would cost $9,000 all in and save about $1,200 a year. A dull scheduling upgrade costs $1,500 and saves about $2,000 a year. What should the shop do?

options.text: Take the hyped tool, to stay current in trade
options.rationale: Chasing trends without testing value.

options.text: Take the dull one, which actually pays back
options.rationale: Keeping up means adopting what improves the work, and the full-cost comparison shows which tool does.

options.text: Take neither and keep the current methods
options.rationale: Refuses a clearly positive upgrade.

options.text: Take both, since each one offers some savings
options.rationale: One of them loses money for years.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: staying current is disciplined by the cost and benefit assessment.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Keeping Up with Technology, Assessing New Technology Costs and Benefits. Without the adoption question there is nothing to buy. Without the assessment the hyped tool wins. Both are needed.

questions.question: A bagel shop worker makes about 40 sandwiches an hour, and the 7 to 9am rush brings 100 orders an hour. What does that gap tell the manager?

options.text: Three people are needed in those hours
options.rationale: Capacity per person against demand per hour is what sets the staffing for that window.

options.text: The menu is too large for the space
options.rationale: Nothing in the figures points at menu size.

options.text: The shop should open an hour later
options.rationale: Closes during the busiest demand of the day.

options.text: Sandwich prices should rise at 7am
options.rationale: A pricing response to a staffing calculation.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: convert a capacity gap into a staffing number.

questions.question: A call center's morning shift takes 70 percent of inbound calls with 40 percent of the reps, while evening reps sit idle. What is wrong with the schedule?

options.text: Staff are split by headcount, not workload
options.rationale: Balanced shifts mean matching people to the work arriving, not dividing bodies evenly across the clock.

options.text: Customers call at unpredictable times
options.rationale: The pattern given is clear and predictable.

options.text: Evening reps are less experienced
options.rationale: Skill is not what the figures describe.

options.text: The center employs too few people overall
options.rationale: The total appears sufficient; the distribution is wrong.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the scheduling error.

questions.question: Saturday croissant sales average 180 with a record high of 210. A baker proposes making 210 every Saturday. What is the flaw?

options.text: Planning to the best day wastes most days
options.rationale: Production should track typical demand, since the record is an outlier that leaves surplus on ordinary Saturdays.

options.text: The record was probably measured wrong
options.rationale: Questions the data rather than the planning logic.

options.text: Croissants cannot be baked in batches
options.rationale: Batch size is not the issue.

options.text: Saturday demand will keep rising anyway
options.rationale: Assumes growth the figures do not show.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: distinguish typical demand from a peak.

questions.question: A bakery triples orders for six weeks each December. The default plan is time and a half for the whole crew throughout. What should be compared first?

options.text: December sales against November sales
options.rationale: Confirms the surge that is already known.

options.text: Last year's overtime against this year's
options.rationale: Compares one option with itself over time.

options.text: The crew's willingness to work extra
options.rationale: Relevant to execution, but not the cost question.

options.text: Overtime cost against temporary hires
options.rationale: Surge coverage is a cost comparison, and a six week peak is long enough that temps may beat premium hours.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: weigh surge staffing options for a known peak.

questions.question: A bakery forecasts December demand up 15 percent on last year and stops there. What has the forecast left undone?

options.text: Setting the price for holiday orders
options.rationale: Pricing is a separate decision from resourcing.

options.text: Checking whether growth will continue
options.rationale: A later question that does not make this forecast usable.

options.text: Comparing the number with competitors
options.rationale: External comparison does not size internal resources.

options.text: Turning demand into hours and materials
options.rationale: A forecast is only actionable once it is expressed in the staff, equipment and inputs needed to meet it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: complete a forecast into resource terms.

questions.question: A cafe builds one staffing level from its daily average of 300 customers. Mornings back up badly while afternoons are quiet. What should change?

options.text: Close the cafe during the afternoon lull
options.rationale: Solves the idle half by giving up its revenue.

options.text: Raise the daily average target to 350
options.rationale: Changes a number that is not the problem.

options.text: Add one more person to every shift
options.rationale: Pays for coverage in the hours that are already quiet.

options.text: Schedule against hourly demand, not the day
options.rationale: Averages hide the peaks that actually break service, so staffing has to follow the hour by hour curve.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: correct a schedule built on an average.

questions.question: A shop's overload is two hours each weekday morning. The manager proposes six weeks of overtime for the full crew. What does the pattern argue for instead?

options.text: No change, since mornings always rush
options.rationale: Accepts a known, fixable shortfall.

options.text: Full crew overtime, since demand is high
options.rationale: Pays premium rates through hours that need no help.

options.text: Short extra shifts covering those hours
options.rationale: The capacity gap is narrow and predictable, so targeted coverage beats paying a premium across whole days.

options.text: Two permanent full time hires this month
options.rationale: Permanent cost for a two hour daily peak.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the capacity analysis defines the shape of the gap, the staffing choice has to match that shape.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Capacity and Scheduling, Managing Overtime and Surge Staffing. Without the capacity view the surge looks like a whole day problem and overtime is reasonable. Without the staffing options the gap is identified with no remedy to choose between. Both are needed.

questions.question: A bakery forecasts holiday demand carefully and plans production to the typical day, but December arrives with too few trays and one oven for the volume. What went wrong?

options.text: The demand forecast was far too low
options.rationale: The case states the forecast was careful and the shortfall is in equipment.

options.text: Production should have targeted the peak day
options.rationale: Planning to the peak is the error the other card warns about.

options.text: Staff were scheduled for the wrong shifts
options.rationale: Nothing here points at the shift pattern.

options.text: The plan was never converted into equipment
options.rationale: Good demand planning still fails if the forecast is not translated into the physical resources required to produce it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: planning what to produce and resourcing the means to produce it are separate steps, and only one was done.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Demand and Production Planning, Forecasting Resource Needs. Without the production plan there is no target to resource against. Without the resource step the plan stays a number on paper. The failure sits exactly between them.

questions.question: A call center forecasts a 20 percent rise in calls next quarter and plans to hire evenly across all shifts. Mornings already carry 70 percent of volume with 40 percent of reps. What is the better plan?

options.text: Delay hiring until the rise is confirmed
options.rationale: Leaves a known imbalance in place through a rising quarter.

options.text: Move evening reps onto the morning shift
options.rationale: Helps the balance but ignores the forecast growth entirely.

options.text: Add the new hires where the volume lands
options.rationale: The forecast tells you how many, and the existing imbalance tells you where, so spreading them evenly repeats the current fault at a larger scale.

options.text: Hire evenly, to keep the shifts fair
options.rationale: Fairness by headcount is precisely what created the imbalance.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the forecast sets the quantity and the load pattern sets the placement.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Forecasting Resource Needs, Load Balancing Across Shifts. Without the forecast there is nobody to place. Without the load pattern the even split looks orderly. The answer needs the number and the distribution together.

questions.question: Sales emails a custom order to Production and marks it complete. Production never opens it and the order stalls. What went wrong at the handoff?

options.text: Production was short of staff
options.rationale: Nothing suggests capacity was the issue.

options.text: Sending was treated as receiving
options.rationale: A handoff is complete when the other team confirms it has the work, not when the message leaves.

options.text: The email contained too much detail
options.rationale: Detail is not what stalled it.

options.text: Sales should build the order itself
options.rationale: Removes the handoff instead of making it work.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the handoff failure.

questions.question: Marketing holds the spring sale launch date until the warehouse confirms stock has arrived. What is that?

options.text: Timing set across both teams
options.rationale: Coordination means the departments sequence their actions together rather than each optimising its own calendar.

options.text: A forecast of spring demand
options.rationale: No demand prediction is involved.

options.text: A scaling decision for the sale
options.rationale: Nothing is growing in capacity here.

options.text: A quality check on the stock
options.rationale: Arrival is being confirmed, not inspected.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the coordination behavior.

questions.question: A bakery expects a 40 percent sales bump over a holiday week and pre-orders extra flour while adding shifts. What is it doing?

options.text: Matching operations to the forecast
options.rationale: Staffing and inventory are being set by what sales predicts rather than by habit.

options.text: Auditing its holiday safety rules
options.rationale: Safety is not the subject.

options.text: Benchmarking against other bakeries
options.rationale: No external comparison appears.

options.text: Reducing its overhead expenses
options.rationale: Costs are rising here, deliberately.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the alignment activity.

questions.question: A bakery builds one holiday staffing and inventory plan from a single forecast number. Sales come in 20 percent under. What should the plan have included?

options.text: A higher forecast to be safe
options.rationale: Overcommits further in the direction that just failed.

options.text: A way to scale down if demand missed
options.rationale: Forecasts are estimates, so the operational plan needs adjustment points rather than one fixed commitment.

options.text: A discount to clear the surplus
options.rationale: Handles the aftermath rather than the planning fault.

options.text: A second forecast from marketing
options.rationale: Another number without flexibility changes nothing.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: build flexibility into a forecast-driven plan.

questions.question: Marketing launches a promotion built entirely around what would make its campaign strongest, and the warehouse cannot pick the volume. What was the mistake?

options.text: Choosing the wrong advertising channel
options.rationale: Channel choice is unrelated to picking capacity.

options.text: Planning from one department's view
options.rationale: Coordination fails when a team optimises its own outcome and assumes the others will absorb the consequences.

options.text: Offering too small a discount
options.rationale: A deeper discount would worsen the volume problem.

options.text: Running the promotion in a busy month
options.rationale: Timing within the year is not what broke it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: diagnose a cross-team planning failure.

questions.question: Sales closes a custom order and drops the spec into a shared folder. Production finds it four days later with two required fields blank. What should change?

options.text: Production checking the folder daily
options.rationale: Fixes the delay and not the missing fields.

options.text: A weekly meeting between the two
options.rationale: A meeting cannot carry every order.

options.text: Sales writing longer order notes
options.rationale: Length is not completeness.

options.text: A defined handoff with required fields
options.rationale: A clean transfer names who passes what, when, and in what state, which is exactly what a shared folder does not do.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: repair the gap between two teams rather than either team's own work.

questions.question: Sales forecasts a 40 percent holiday bump and tells nobody until the week before. Operations cannot secure flour or shifts in time. Both teams did their own job well. What failed?

options.text: Sales should reduce holiday promotions
options.rationale: Shrinks the business to fit a fixable process.

options.text: The forecast itself was inaccurate
options.rationale: Accuracy is not questioned in the case.

options.text: Operations should hold surplus stock
options.rationale: Carries cost all year to cover a communication gap.

options.text: The forecast reached operations too late
options.rationale: Alignment depends on the forecast arriving with enough lead time for staffing and inventory to respond, which is a coordination duty.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: a good forecast and competent operations still fail without the timing link between departments.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Aligning Operations With Sales Forecasts, Coordinating Across Teams. Without the alignment duty the late notice is merely impolite. Without coordination the forecast is an internal sales document. The failure is the interval between them.

questions.question: A furniture company's spring sale is coordinated well at the leadership level, but individual custom orders still stall between Sales and Production. What does that pattern indicate?

options.text: Production is deliberately slowing work
options.rationale: Attributes motive where a process gap explains it.

options.text: Plans align while daily transfers do not
options.rationale: Coordination at the calendar level does not create the order-by-order confirmation that keeps work moving.

options.text: Custom orders should be discontinued
options.rationale: Drops a product line over a fixable transfer.

options.text: The leadership plan was never agreed
options.rationale: The case states coordination at that level works.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: departmental alignment and individual handoffs are different mechanisms, and only one is working.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Coordinating Across Teams, Managing Handoffs Between Departments. Without coordination the stalls look like general dysfunction. Without handoffs the working leadership plan suggests nothing is wrong. The contrast requires both.

questions.question: A revised forecast cuts expected volume by a third. It is posted to a shared drive that Operations rarely opens, and pre-orders go out at the old number. What should change?

options.text: Order at the lower number by default
options.rationale: Guesses conservatively instead of transferring the information.

options.text: Freeze the forecast once it is published
options.rationale: Locks in a number already known to be wrong.

options.text: Have Operations check the drive daily
options.rationale: Puts the burden on discovery rather than delivery.

options.text: Confirmed receipt whenever a forecast moves
options.rationale: A revision is only useful when the receiving team acknowledges it, which is the handoff discipline applied to forecast changes.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: forecast alignment supplies the changing input and handoff discipline is what makes the change land.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Aligning Operations With Sales Forecasts, Managing Handoffs Between Departments. Without alignment the revision does not matter to anyone. Without handoff rules posting it looks like communication. Both are needed to name the fix.

questions.question: A manager responds to a tight quarter by ordering every department to cut 20 percent. What is wrong with that instruction?

options.text: It should have been announced earlier
options.rationale: Timing does not fix an untargeted cut.

options.text: It cuts without finding where waste is
options.rationale: Cost control means pinpointing the spend that is not earning, since an even cut takes the same slice from what works.

options.text: It asks for too small a reduction
options.rationale: Size is not the fault; the lack of targeting is.

options.text: It applies only to variable costs
options.rationale: The instruction covers everything, which is the problem.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the flaw in an across-the-board cut.

questions.question: A bakery's ingredient costs rose 18 percent, and a breakdown shows butter alone accounts for most of the increase. What has the breakdown found?

options.text: The driver behind the rise
options.rationale: A driver is the specific factor causing the movement, which is what tells you where to act.

options.text: The largest expense category
options.rationale: Being big is not the same as being the cause of the change.

options.text: The supplier's profit margin
options.rationale: Nothing here reveals what the supplier earns.

options.text: The overhead the bakery pays
options.rationale: Ingredients are variable costs, not overhead.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what a cost breakdown identified.

questions.question: A print shop pays $1,800 a month for a storage unit it barely uses. Which kind of cost is that?

options.text: Overhead, paid whatever sales do
options.rationale: Ongoing costs that do not move with output are overhead, and an underused one is the clearest trimming candidate.

options.text: A cost of goods sold line item
options.rationale: Storage is not consumed in producing a specific job.

options.text: A variable cost tied to volume
options.rationale: The rent does not change with how much is printed.

options.text: A one-time capital expenditure
options.rationale: It recurs monthly rather than being bought once.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: classify a recurring fixed cost.

questions.question: A bakery compares making its own boxes, needing a $12,000 machine plus a part-time operator, against buying them from a supplier. It compares the supplier price to raw cardboard cost only. What has it left out?

options.text: The colour options each route allows
options.rationale: A feature question that does not change the cost math.

options.text: The machine, the labor and the upkeep
options.rationale: An honest comparison includes every cost the in-house route creates, not just the material it consumes.

options.text: The cardboard price two years ago
options.rationale: Historic prices do not bear on the current decision.

options.text: The supplier's delivery schedule
options.rationale: Relevant to reliability, but not the omitted cost.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: complete a make-or-buy comparison.

questions.question: A cafe wastes about $1,800 a month on unsold afternoon pastries from morning over-baking. Which move controls the cost without hurting service?

options.text: Buy cheaper flour for all baking
options.rationale: Trades product quality for a saving elsewhere.

options.text: Bake smaller afternoon batches to demand
options.rationale: Targets the specific waste while keeping the case stocked when customers are actually there.

options.text: Discount the leftovers every evening
options.rationale: Recovers a little and teaches customers to wait.

options.text: Stop selling pastries after midday
options.rationale: Removes the waste by removing the revenue.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: cut a specific cost without cutting quality.

questions.question: Facing an overhead review, a manager proposes cutting the customer support team, which handles renewals worth a third of revenue. What is the objection?

options.text: Rent should be cut before salaries
options.rationale: A sequencing preference rather than the real objection.

options.text: Support salaries are not overhead
options.rationale: They are overhead; that is not what makes the cut wrong.

options.text: The savings would arrive too slowly
options.rationale: Timing is not the issue with cutting revenue-producing capacity.

options.text: That cost carries revenue with it
options.rationale: Overhead trimming targets spend that does not produce income, and this line is directly tied to renewals.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: distinguish trimmable overhead from revenue-bearing cost.

questions.question: Food cost is up 18 percent. Butter prices drove most of it, and the rest is waste from over-baking. A manager proposes trimming portion sizes across the menu. What does the analysis argue?

options.text: Raise menu prices by the same 18 percent
options.rationale: Passes an avoidable cost to customers.

options.text: Address butter and waste, not portions
options.rationale: The drivers are known, so the response should follow them rather than reach for a generic reduction customers will notice.

options.text: Wait a quarter to see if butter falls back
options.rationale: Ignores the waste half entirely while hoping on commodities.

options.text: Trim portions, since food cost is high
options.rationale: An untargeted cut applied to a cost whose causes are already identified.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the driver analysis names the causes and cost control decides what a proportionate response looks like.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Analyzing Cost Drivers, Controlling Operational Costs. Without the drivers, portion trimming is a defensible generic answer. Without cost control discipline the drivers are facts with no action attached. Both are needed to reject the across-the-board move.

questions.question: Bringing packaging in-house would cut the per-unit price by 30 percent but adds a machine lease, an operator and floor space the shop currently rents by the metre. Volumes are steady but modest. How should it be judged?

options.text: The floor space, which is already rented
options.rationale: Space has an alternative use, so it is not free.

options.text: The unit saving alone, since it is large
options.rationale: Ignores everything the in-house route adds.

options.text: The supplier's margin on each box
options.rationale: What the supplier earns is not the buyer's comparison.

options.text: The unit saving against new fixed cost
options.rationale: Making it converts a variable purchase into standing overhead, so modest volume may never cover the fixed base it creates.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the make-or-buy math is incomplete until the overhead it creates is counted.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Make-or-Buy Decision Making, Reducing Overhead Expenses. Without the make-or-buy frame there is no decision. Without the overhead view the 30 percent saving looks decisive. The answer lives where a variable cost becomes a fixed one.

questions.question: A shop's packaging spend rose 25 percent. The breakdown shows volume grew while the price per box held flat. A consultant recommends buying the die-cut machine. What does the driver say?

options.text: The supplier has quietly raised prices
options.rationale: Directly contradicted by the flat unit price.

options.text: Growth, not price, is moving the spend
options.rationale: Rising volume at a flat price is a different problem from an expensive supplier, and it weakens the case for a machine bought to beat that price.

options.text: The machine will cut the total by a quarter
options.rationale: Asserts a saving the analysis does not support.

options.text: Packaging should be dropped from the product
options.rationale: Removes a necessary input over a cost question.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the driver analysis reframes what the rise means, which changes whether the make-or-buy case holds.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Analyzing Cost Drivers, Make-or-Buy Decision Making. Without the driver the rising total looks like a supplier problem and the machine is attractive. Without the make-or-buy question there is no recommendation to test. Both are load bearing.

questions.question: An online retailer with a 4 percent mis-ship rate adds a barcode scan-to-verify step at packing. What is that step doing?

options.text: Reducing the cost of each parcel
options.rationale: Accuracy work is about correctness first.

options.text: Prioritising which orders ship first
options.rationale: Sequencing is a different decision.

options.text: Catching the error before it ships
options.rationale: A verification check at packing stops the wrong item reaching the customer.

options.text: Speeding up the packing process
options.rationale: A check adds a moment rather than saving one.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what a verification step does.

questions.question: A bike shop sells out of a popular commuter model and offers waiting customers a firm two week date rather than a vague soon. Why does that matter?

options.text: It guarantees the stock will arrive
options.rationale: A date is a commitment, not a certainty.

options.text: It removes the need to reorder
options.rationale: Replenishment still has to happen.

options.text: A definite date lets people decide
options.rationale: Stockout handling is judged on whether the customer can make a decision, and a firm commitment is what allows that.

options.text: It raises the price of the model
options.rationale: No pricing change is involved.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: state why a firm date helps.

questions.question: A bakery fills every order strictly in the order received, including a 9am wedding pickup that came in after several retail case orders. What is wrong with that rule?

options.text: It favours large orders over small ones
options.rationale: Strict order of arrival favours neither.

options.text: It requires more staff than available
options.rationale: Staffing is not the subject.

options.text: It ignores which deadlines are fixed
options.rationale: Sequencing should weigh deadlines and consequences, since not every order carries the same cost of lateness.

options.text: It processes too few orders per hour
options.rationale: Throughput is not what the rule gets wrong.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the flaw in pure first-in sequencing.

questions.question: A retailer fixes warehouse picking accuracy, yet customers still receive wrong items. Investigation shows many errors begin as mistyped SKUs on the web form. What does that mean for the accuracy programme?

options.text: Customers should confirm each order twice
options.rationale: Moves the checking onto the buyer.

options.text: Picking accuracy was the wrong thing to fix
options.rationale: It was a real fault and it was worth fixing.

options.text: The warehouse should re-check orders itself
options.rationale: Checks a record that was already wrong on arrival.

options.text: It has to cover the front end too
options.rationale: An order typed in wrong is picked perfectly and still arrives wrong, so accuracy has to start where the order is captured.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: extend accuracy work across the whole flow.

questions.question: A shop is out of a $2 accessory with three near-identical alternatives in stock, and also out of a $900 bike with a distinctive frame. What does good handling look like?

options.text: Backorder both, to keep the sale intact
options.rationale: Makes a customer wait for something interchangeable.

options.text: Substitute the accessory, backorder the bike
options.rationale: Stockout responses should differ by what the product means to the customer, and a commodity is not a considered purchase.

options.text: Cancel both and refund the customers
options.rationale: Discards two recoverable sales.

options.text: Substitute both, to clear the demand today
options.rationale: Offers a different bike to someone who chose that frame.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: match stockout response to product type.

questions.question: A kitchen has a 9am wedding pickup, a retail case to fill before opening at 10, and a corporate order due at noon. Which sequence fits?

options.text: Wedding, then case, then corporate
options.rationale: Sequencing follows the deadlines and the cost of missing each, which orders the day without needing a queue rule.

options.text: The retail case first, since it is routine
options.rationale: Routine work displacing a fixed-time commitment.

options.text: Whichever order arrived first that week
options.rationale: Strict arrival order ignores the clock.

options.text: Corporate first, since it is the largest
options.rationale: Size does not outrank a fixed morning deadline.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: sequence competing orders by deadline.

questions.question: Under deadline pressure a packing team skips the scan-to-verify step to get urgent orders out first. Mis-ships on those urgent orders triple. What does the case show?

options.text: Packing staff need closer supervision
options.rationale: They did what the deadline pressure asked of them.

options.text: Urgent orders should not be prioritised
options.rationale: Sequencing by urgency is correct practice.

options.text: The verification step was slowing the line
options.rationale: It was, and dropping it is what tripled the errors.

options.text: Priority was gained by removing the check
options.rationale: The sequencing decision was sound and it was paid for with the verification step, so the orders that mattered most got the least protection.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: sequencing and accuracy both operate on the same queue, and one was traded for the other.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Order Accuracy Management, Prioritizing Order Fulfillment Sequencing. Without accuracy the skipped step has no consequence. Without sequencing there is no pressure prompting the skip. Both are needed to read the failure.

questions.question: A retailer's stock system shows six units of an item that is actually sold out, because mis-shipped returns were logged as restocked. Customers keep ordering it. What is the first fix?

options.text: Remove the item from the site for now
options.rationale: Hides one item while the logging fault stands.

options.text: Backorder every unit customers request
options.rationale: Manages the symptom and keeps selling air.

options.text: Correct the returns logging that feeds stock
options.rationale: The count is wrong because mis-shipped returns are recorded as sellable, so the record keeps regenerating the error until that step changes.

options.text: Count the warehouse stock once a quarter
options.rationale: Catches the gap months after customers do.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: what looks like a stockout problem is produced by an accuracy problem, and the fix has to follow the cause.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Managing Backorders and Stockouts, Order Accuracy Management. Without the stockout there is no customer-facing symptom. Without the accuracy view the response stops at backorder handling. Tracing symptom to cause needs both.

questions.question: A supplier is three hundred units short. It ships strictly in the order requests arrived and tells no buyer anything, so a hospital contract carrying a late penalty is filled last. What went wrong?

options.text: The hospital order should be cancelled
options.rationale: Turns a late delivery into a broken contract.

options.text: The shortage should have been hidden
options.rationale: Silence is half of what caused the damage.

options.text: First come first served is always unfair
options.rationale: It is a defensible rule when nothing is at stake.

options.text: No priority rule and no word to buyers
options.rationale: A shortage needs both a sequence that reflects what each order costs to miss and a message that lets buyers plan around the gap.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the sequencing rule and the stockout communication each fail, and fixing only one still leaves a penalty or a surprise.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Prioritizing order fulfillment sequencing, Managing backorders and stockouts. Without the sequencing fault the hospital ships first. Without the silence the buyer could have covered. Both are needed.

questions.question: A bakery schedules a technician to check its walk-in freezer seals each spring rather than waiting for a summer failure. What is that?

options.text: A warranty claim on the freezer
options.rationale: No manufacturer claim is involved.

options.text: A site selection decision for storage
options.rationale: Where the bakery sits is a different question.

options.text: Planned upkeep before a breakdown
options.rationale: Maintenance planning means servicing on a schedule instead of responding to failures.

options.text: An emergency repair arrangement
options.rationale: Nothing has broken in this scenario.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the maintenance approach.

questions.question: A supply warehouse picks a pricier lot beside the highway over a cheaper one forty minutes away. What is being weighed?

options.text: The layout inside the building
options.rationale: Internal arrangement is a separate decision.

options.text: The brand image of the district
options.rationale: Image is not what a supply warehouse buys with proximity.

options.text: The maintenance schedule of the roof
options.rationale: Upkeep is not the comparison here.

options.text: Rent against daily access cost
options.rationale: Site choice balances the cost of the space against the logistics and access it provides.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the trade in a site decision.

questions.question: At a packing station, workers lift boxes to a waist-high counter and reach overhead for labels all shift. What should be adjusted?

options.text: The brand of tape used on boxes
options.rationale: Materials do not change the posture.

options.text: The number of boxes packed hourly
options.rationale: Slows output without removing the reach.

options.text: The label height, down to arm level
options.rationale: Setting up the station so tasks happen without strain is exactly what ergonomics addresses.

options.text: The lighting above the packing area
options.rationale: Visibility is not what the described strain comes from.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: apply ergonomics to a described station.

questions.question: A sandwich shop puts its ordering line and pickup counter side by side near the door. Crowds tangle at the entrance. What should change?

options.text: Widen the door to reduce the crowding
options.rationale: Admits the crowd faster into the same tangle.

options.text: Separate the two flows across the space
options.rationale: Layout has to serve how people move, and ordering and collecting are different flows that should not compete for one spot.

options.text: Repaint the interior to feel more open
options.rationale: Judges layout by appearance, the trap the card names.

options.text: Ask waiting customers to stand outside
options.rationale: Moves the problem onto the pavement.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: fix a flow conflict through layout.

questions.question: A maintenance calendar exists for every machine, but tasks keep slipping and two breakdowns happened last quarter. What is most likely missing?

options.text: More frequent service intervals
options.rationale: Schedules more work that nobody is doing.

options.text: A named owner for each task
options.rationale: A calendar without accountability is a list, and the work only happens when someone is responsible for it.

options.text: A longer warranty from the vendor
options.rationale: Covers repair cost rather than preventing failure.

options.text: A newer set of machines entirely
options.rationale: Replaces equipment to avoid fixing the process.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: diagnose why a maintenance plan fails to execute.

questions.question: A bakery picks the cheapest available storefront, which sits on a side street with little foot traffic. Sales come in below plan. What was mispriced?

options.text: The length of the lease agreement
options.rationale: Term length does not explain low traffic.

options.text: The customers the location never sees
options.rationale: Rent saved is only a saving when weighed against the access and traffic given up.

options.text: The cost of the ovens installed there
options.rationale: Equipment cost is the same at either address.

options.text: The wage rate in that neighborhood
options.rationale: Labor cost is not what the case describes.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: evaluate a site choice against its real cost.

questions.question: A packing floor is rearranged to shorten the walk between stations, which also forces workers to twist and reach for labels at every box. Throughput per trip rises, injuries rise too. How should it be judged?

options.text: Ergonomics matters only in offices
options.rationale: A false limit on where strain occurs.

options.text: The flow gain is paid for in strain
options.rationale: Layout and ergonomics are the same physical decision, so a movement saving bought with awkward posture is not a net gain.

options.text: The layout is correct, injuries aside
options.rationale: Separates two things the same arrangement decides.

options.text: Workers should be rotated more often
options.rationale: Spreads the strain instead of removing it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the same layout change improves flow and harms posture, so both have to be weighed together.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Facilities and Layout, Ergonomics in Workspace Design. Without layout there is no flow gain to weigh. Without ergonomics the injuries are unexplained and the change looks purely good. The judgment needs both.

questions.question: A bakery is choosing between a high traffic corner with an awkward narrow floor plan and a quiet street unit with an ideal layout. Its revenue depends on walk-in customers. Which fits better?

options.text: The quiet unit, since the layout works
options.rationale: Optimises the fixable factor and accepts the unfixable one.

options.text: Either one, since both can be adapted
options.rationale: Foot traffic cannot be adapted into existence.

options.text: The corner, with the floor plan reworked
options.rationale: Traffic is hard to create and layout is something you can redesign, so the constraint that cannot be changed should decide.

options.text: The quiet unit, because rent is lower
options.rationale: Repeats the cheapest-space error for a walk-in business.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: what the site provides and what the interior can be made to do are different kinds of constraint.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Site Selection Decisions, Facilities and Layout. Without site selection the layout decides and the quiet unit wins. Without layout knowledge the awkward floor looks disqualifying. Knowing which factor is changeable requires both.

questions.question: A new kitchen layout boxes the walk-in freezer's compressor into a tight alcove. Service visits now take three times as long and get postponed. What does the case show?

options.text: The technician should work faster
options.rationale: Blames the person for an access problem.

options.text: The freezer needs replacing with a newer unit
options.rationale: New equipment in the same alcove has the same problem.

options.text: Layout decided whether upkeep gets done
options.rationale: Access is part of the physical design, and a plan that makes servicing hard quietly converts scheduled maintenance into deferred maintenance.

options.text: The maintenance schedule was too frequent
options.rationale: Frequency is not why visits are being postponed.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: a layout decision determines whether the maintenance plan can actually be executed.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Facilities and Layout, Equipment Maintenance Planning. Without the layout the postponements have no cause. Without the maintenance plan the alcove is merely tight. The connection between them is the point.

questions.question: A chain tests a new tablet ordering system in one store for six weeks before deciding on a full rollout. What is the purpose?

options.text: Training staff at every location
options.rationale: Only one store is involved.

options.text: Proving the system to the supplier
options.rationale: The vendor is not the audience for the test.

options.text: Delaying a decision already made
options.rationale: A pilot exists to inform the decision, not stall it.

options.text: Finding problems before full commitment
options.rationale: A pilot buys learning in a limited setting, where a fault costs one store instead of the whole chain.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: state what a pilot is for.

questions.question: A bakery takes 48 hours to move a custom order into production and checks what two regional chains take. What is it doing?

options.text: Auditing its own order records
options.rationale: An internal audit would not look outward.

options.text: Piloting a new intake method
options.rationale: Nothing new is being tested yet.

options.text: Comparing its practice with others
options.rationale: Benchmarking judges your own performance against how comparable operations do the same thing.

options.text: Forecasting next quarter's orders
options.rationale: No demand projection is involved.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the activity.

questions.question: A manager proposes replacing paper tickets with a tablet because the system feels outdated, without naming a problem it would solve. What is missing?

options.text: The brand of tablet to purchase
options.rationale: A detail that follows the decision.

options.text: The specific problem being fixed
options.rationale: Change is justified by the fault it removes, not by novelty.

options.text: The month the change would start
options.rationale: Timing is not what makes the case.

options.text: The number of staff to train
options.rationale: Also downstream of the justification.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify what justifies a change.

questions.question: A chain runs its tablet pilot in its strongest store, staffed by its most experienced team, and changes the workflow twice midway. What does that pilot prove?

options.text: That the system works across the chain
options.rationale: The best store is precisely the wrong evidence for average ones.

options.text: Little, since conditions were not typical
options.rationale: A pilot has to run a stable method in a representative setting, or the result cannot be read as a forecast for the rollout.

options.text: That six weeks was too short a window
options.rationale: Length is not what compromised it.

options.text: That the workflow changes were correct
options.rationale: Mid-flight changes make the result unattributable.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: evaluate pilot design.

questions.question: A three-person bakery benchmarks its order intake against a national chain with a dedicated intake team and concludes it is failing badly. What is wrong with that conclusion?

options.text: National chains never publish figures
options.rationale: The scenario assumes the figures were obtained.

options.text: The comparison is to a different model
options.rationale: A benchmark is only informative against operations of comparable size and structure.

options.text: Intake speed is not worth measuring
options.rationale: It is a reasonable thing to measure.

options.text: Two comparisons are better than one
options.rationale: Count is not the flaw; comparability is.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: test whether a benchmark is comparable.

questions.question: A print shop still collates brochures by hand because that is how it has always been done, though a folding machine would free about two hours a day. What does the skill call for?

options.text: Testing the better method on its merits
options.rationale: Improvement means the familiar process has to justify itself against the alternative rather than win by default.

options.text: Asking the machine supplier to decide
options.rationale: Hands the judgement to the seller.

options.text: Hiring a second person to collate them
options.rationale: Adds cost to an unchanged process.

options.text: Keeping the method the team knows well
options.rationale: Familiarity is the reason being questioned.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: act on the case where habit is standing in for a reason.

questions.question: Benchmarking shows comparable bakeries move custom orders into production in 12 hours against this bakery's 48. The owner wants to copy their intake system chain-wide next month. What should come first?

options.text: A second benchmark against larger chains
options.rationale: More comparison where a trial is the missing evidence.

options.text: A limited run in one shift or store
options.rationale: The benchmark establishes that a gap exists, and the pilot establishes whether this method closes it here before everything depends on it.

options.text: A full rollout, since the gap is proven
options.rationale: A proven gap is not a proven remedy.

options.text: A decision to accept the 48 hour figure
options.rationale: Discards a validated improvement opportunity.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: benchmarking motivates the change and piloting tests it before commitment.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Benchmarking Against Industry Practice, Piloting New Operational Methods. Without the benchmark there is no reason to change anything. Without the pilot the comparison alone drives a chain-wide bet. Both are needed for the measured step.
