questions.question: A team proposes three changes at once to the weekend order process and runs them together for two weeks. Mix-ups fall by half. What can they conclude?

options.text: All three changes should be kept
options.rationale: Keeps cost and complexity that may be doing nothing.

options.text: The result is meaningless and should be redone
options.rationale: Overcorrects: a halved error rate is real information.

options.text: Something worked, but not which change
options.rationale: The improvement is real and unattributable, so the pilot cannot tell them what to keep when they scale.

options.text: The digital screen caused the whole gain
options.rationale: Picks a favourite with no evidence separating it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the improvement is genuine and the pilot design limits what can be concluded from it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Innovation and Improvement, Piloting New Operational Methods. Without the improvement there is no result to interpret. Without pilot discipline the halved errors justify keeping everything. The careful conclusion needs both.

questions.question: A bakery matches the industry benchmark on intake speed exactly. A supervisor argues there is therefore nothing to improve in intake. What is the flaw?

options.text: Intake speed is the wrong thing to measure
options.rationale: Rejects a measure the case treats as relevant.

options.text: The industry will slow down next year
options.rationale: Speculates about others rather than examining the process.

options.text: A benchmark is a reference, not a ceiling
options.rationale: Matching typical practice says you are not behind, and improvement work asks whether the process itself can be better regardless.

options.text: The benchmark figure is probably wrong
options.rationale: Doubts the data rather than the reasoning.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the benchmark settles the comparison while the improvement mindset denies that comparison is the limit.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Benchmarking Against Industry Practice, Innovation and Improvement. Without the benchmark there is no claim of parity. Without the improvement view parity genuinely would close the question. The flaw sits between them.

questions.question: A warehouse arranges its shelves alphabetically so everything is tidy. Pickers walk the full aisle for the most common items. What should drive slotting instead?

options.text: The price of each product held
options.rationale: Value does not predict pick frequency.

options.text: How often each item is picked
options.rationale: Fast movers belong closest to hand, since slotting exists to cut walking rather than to look orderly.

options.text: The alphabetical order of names
options.rationale: That is the tidy arrangement causing the walking.

options.text: The supplier each item came from
options.rationale: Grouping by source suits receiving, not picking.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the basis for slotting.

questions.question: A furniture maker ships bulky dining tables 300 miles and rules out parcel carriers. What is the main reason?

options.text: The goods do not suit that network
options.rationale: Carrier choice follows the nature of the freight, and parcel systems are built for small, handleable boxes.

options.text: Parcel carriers charge by weight only
options.rationale: Pricing method is not what disqualifies them.

options.text: Parcel carriers do not insure goods
options.rationale: They do, within limits.

options.text: The distance is too short for parcel
options.rationale: Parcel handles 300 miles routinely.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: match freight type to carrier.

questions.question: A bakery dispatches its delivery van in the order the orders were received, crossing the city repeatedly. What would clustering stops achieve?

options.text: More stops in less driving time
options.rationale: Grouping nearby deliveries is what cuts mileage and lets one run cover more customers.

options.text: Fewer orders needing delivery
options.rationale: Demand is unchanged by routing.

options.text: A larger vehicle for the run
options.rationale: Routing does not change the van.

options.text: A lower price per delivery charged
options.rationale: Pricing is a separate decision.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: state the gain from routing.

questions.question: A planner builds the shortest possible route for the morning van, and three cafes that must receive stock before opening at 7am are served at 9. What was ignored?

options.text: The fuel cost of the shorter route
options.rationale: The short route already minimises fuel.

options.text: The delivery windows each stop has
options.rationale: Optimising distance alone breaks commitments, since a route has to satisfy time constraints as well as mileage.

options.text: The driver's preferred starting point
options.rationale: Preference is not a delivery requirement.

options.text: The number of cafes on the run
options.rationale: Count is not the constraint being broken.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: balance distance against time windows.

questions.question: A shipper picks the cheapest carrier per shipment. Damage claims on fragile goods now consume more than the savings. What does carrier selection require?

options.text: Shipping fragile goods less often
options.rationale: Reduces the business to avoid the decision.

options.text: Weighing damage risk with the rate
options.rationale: The true cost of a carrier includes what arrives broken, so reliability belongs in the comparison.

options.text: Passing claim costs to customers
options.rationale: Charges buyers for an avoidable choice.

options.text: Choosing the most expensive option
options.rationale: Overcorrects into the same single-factor error.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: cost a carrier decision properly.

questions.question: A pet supply warehouse finds 20 percent of its items account for most picks, and those items sit on high shelves at the back. What is the move?

options.text: Buy taller ladders for the back shelves
options.rationale: Makes the hardest picks slightly less hard.

options.text: Add a second picker to that aisle
options.rationale: Staffs the walking instead of removing it.

options.text: Reorder the aisles by product category
options.rationale: Tidiness again, rather than pick frequency.

options.text: Slot them at ground level near packing
options.rationale: Putting the highest-frequency items where they are easiest to reach is the largest single gain slotting offers.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: reslot by demand.

questions.question: Vans leave 40 minutes late every morning because pickers walk the back aisles for the highest volume items. The routes themselves are well planned. Where does the delay actually originate?

options.text: With the drivers, who start too slowly
options.rationale: Drivers are waiting on the pick.

options.text: Inside the warehouse, before loading
options.rationale: A perfect route cannot recover time lost before departure, so the slotting layout is what sets the start of every run.

options.text: In the carrier contract terms
options.rationale: These are own-fleet deliveries.

options.text: In the route plan, which needs rebuilding
options.rationale: The case states routing is sound.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: routing is correct so only the layout explains the late departures.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Warehouse Layout and Slotting, Route and Delivery Optimization. Without routing quality the delay looks like a driving problem. Without slotting there is no cause inside the building. Locating it needs both.

questions.question: A furniture maker can run its own van on an optimised regional route three days a week, or hand every delivery to a freight carrier. Volumes are clustered in one metro area and items are bulky. How should it decide?

options.text: By the van, since control is always better
options.rationale: Control does not pay for an underfilled run.

options.text: By whichever quotes the lower rate
options.rationale: Ignores that the two options have different cost structures.

options.text: By the carrier, since bulky goods need one
options.rationale: Bulk rules out parcel, not an own van.

options.text: By whether the cluster fills the van
options.rationale: Own-fleet routing pays when stops are dense enough to fill a run, and a carrier makes sense when they are scattered.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: carrier choice and route density determine each other in this decision.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Freight and Carrier Selection, Route and Delivery Optimization. Without carrier selection there is only one option. Without route density the van looks equally good anywhere. The deciding test requires both.

questions.question: Fragile glassware is slotted at the far end of the warehouse and handled three times before it reaches packing. Damage claims are rising with the current carrier. What should be checked first?

options.text: Whether a pricier carrier reduces claims
options.rationale: Pays more without knowing where damage occurs.

options.text: Whether breakage starts before dispatch
options.rationale: Extra internal handling can break goods the carrier is then blamed for, so the source has to be located before switching freight.

options.text: Whether glassware should be discontinued
options.rationale: Drops a product over an unlocated fault.

options.text: Whether customers are mishandling parcels
options.rationale: Blames the end of the chain first.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the layout and the carrier are competing explanations and the answer orders the investigation.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Warehouse Layout and Slotting, Freight and Carrier Selection. Without slotting the carrier is the only suspect. Without carrier knowledge the internal handling has no downstream consequence. Both are needed to sequence the check.

questions.question: A print shop promises a client work that is fastest, cheapest and highest quality all at once. What is missing from that promise?

options.text: A delivery date for the order
options.rationale: Fastest implies urgency; the missing piece is the trade.

options.text: A list of the paper stocks used
options.rationale: A specification detail, not the flaw.

options.text: A discount for the inconvenience
options.rationale: Nothing has gone wrong yet.

options.text: A statement of what gives way
options.rationale: The three rarely maximise together, so a credible plan names which one is being traded.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the missing trade-off.

questions.question: A delivery kitchen tracks order-to-door time, order accuracy and prep time per ticket. What makes these good indicators?

options.text: They cover every part of the business
options.rationale: Coverage is not the goal; decision relevance is.

options.text: They match what competitors publish
options.rationale: Comparability is a benchmarking question.

options.text: Each one can change a decision
options.rationale: A useful indicator is small in number and tied to an action somebody actually takes.

options.text: They are the easiest numbers to gather
options.rationale: Ease of measurement is the trap, not the standard.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: state what makes a KPI good.

questions.question: A print shop logs the time from order placed to ready for pickup on every custom shirt. What is it measuring?

options.text: The cost of producing each shirt
options.rationale: No money is being tracked.

options.text: The shop's total monthly output
options.rationale: Volume is a different measure.

options.text: The accuracy of each completed order
options.rationale: Correctness is not what a timestamp records.

options.text: Cycle time for one unit of work
options.rationale: Start to finish for a single job is exactly what cycle time captures.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the measure.

questions.question: A shop's average cycle time looks healthy at 26 hours, yet complaints about late orders keep arriving. What should the manager look at?

options.text: A longer averaging window than a week
options.rationale: Smooths the outliers further out of view.

options.text: The fastest orders, for best practice
options.rationale: Studying the wins does not locate the failures.

options.text: The slowest orders behind the average
options.rationale: A few extreme delays can sit inside a good average, and those are the orders customers complain about.

options.text: The total number of orders taken
options.rationale: Volume does not explain lateness.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: read beyond an average cycle time.

questions.question: A warehouse ships in 38 hours on average and assumed that was fine until a comparable regional operator was found to ship in 20. What does the comparison provide?

options.text: Proof that 38 hours breaks a standard
options.rationale: There is no external rule being violated.

options.text: Evidence that the gap is closable
options.rationale: A comparable operation achieving better numbers turns an internal assumption into a measurable target.

options.text: A guarantee the same methods will work
options.rationale: A benchmark shows what is possible, not how to copy it.

options.text: A reason to stop tracking cycle time
options.rationale: Tracking is how any improvement gets verified.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: interpret what a benchmark establishes.

questions.question: A client needs 500 flyers by tomorrow morning. The shop can run overtime on premium stock, or use its cheapest process and miss the deadline. What is the defensible plan?

options.text: Promise all three and sort it out later
options.rationale: Defers a trade that will surface as a failure.

options.text: Take speed and quality, accept higher cost
options.rationale: Naming which of the three gives way, and why, is what a real plan does when all three cannot be maximised.

options.text: Split the run across two processes
options.rationale: Produces an inconsistent order for one client.

options.text: Take cost and quality, deliver next week
options.rationale: Discards the deadline the client came with.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose and justify a trade-off.

questions.question: A kitchen's dashboard reports average cycle time as its headline indicator. Complaints concentrate in the worst 5 percent of orders. How should the indicator change?

options.text: Report the average weekly rather than daily
options.rationale: Changes cadence without changing what is measured.

options.text: Track the slowest orders as the indicator
options.rationale: The measure should follow the decision it supports, and the decision here concerns the tail that generates complaints.

options.text: Add five more averages to the dashboard
options.rationale: More averages hide the same tail.

options.text: Stop tracking cycle time entirely
options.rationale: Discards the measure that contains the answer.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the KPI standard says measures must drive decisions, and the cycle time detail says which cut of the data does.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Setting Operational Key Performance Indicators, Tracking Cycle Time. Without the KPI rule the average is a perfectly normal metric. Without cycle time knowledge there is no better cut to propose. Both are needed.

questions.question: A benchmark shows a rival shipping in 20 hours against this warehouse's 38. Matching it would require a night shift that raises cost per order by 30 percent. What is the sound reading?

options.text: Ignore it, since the rival is different
options.rationale: The case establishes the operation is comparable.

options.text: The gap is real and buying it has a price
options.rationale: A benchmark proves the speed is achievable without proving it is worth what this operation would pay for it.

options.text: Match the rival, since the benchmark is clear
options.rationale: Treats a comparison as an instruction and ignores the cost side.

options.text: Match it and absorb the cost quietly
options.rationale: Same commitment with the trade hidden rather than decided.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the benchmark sets the target and the trade-off frame prices it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Benchmarking Operational Performance, Balancing Cost, Quality, and Speed. Without the benchmark there is no target. Without the trade-off the target is simply a goal to adopt. The judgement lives between them.

questions.question: A warehouse picks indicators that are easy to pull from its software: total shipments, hours worked and fuel spend. A benchmark comparison against a rival proves impossible. Why?

options.text: The rival refuses to share its figures
options.rationale: Access is not the problem described.

options.text: Benchmarking requires audited financials
options.rationale: Operational benchmarking uses operating measures.

options.text: None of them measure how well it performs
options.rationale: Convenience-driven metrics describe activity rather than performance, so there is nothing meaningful to line up against another operation.

options.text: The warehouse is larger than the rival
options.rationale: Size would affect comparability, but the metrics are the fault.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: weak indicator selection is what makes the benchmarking exercise impossible.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Setting Operational Key Performance Indicators, Benchmarking Operational Performance. Without the KPI failure there would be figures to compare. Without the benchmarking attempt the weak metrics would go unnoticed. The pairing exposes the fault.

questions.question: At a sandwich shop the register and prep stations have idle time, while orders pile up at a toaster that holds one sandwich for 90 seconds. Which step should be fixed first?

options.text: The prep line, which handles the most items
options.rationale: Volume is not the same as constraint, and prep is not backing up.

options.text: The toaster, where the work backs up
options.rationale: The constraint sets the pace of the whole line, so improving anything else leaves total output unchanged.

options.text: The register, since it starts the order
options.rationale: Speeding a station with idle time only makes it wait longer.

options.text: All three at once, to be thorough
options.rationale: Spreads effort across steps that are not limiting output.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: pick the constraint from a described line.

questions.question: A smoothie shop writes its new standard as blend until smooth. Why is that a weak standard?

options.text: Two people can follow it differently
options.rationale: A standard exists to remove variation, and wording open to interpretation leaves the variation in place.

options.text: It was written by a single barista
options.rationale: Who drafted it does not determine whether it works.

options.text: It is too short to post on the wall
options.rationale: Brevity is a virtue when the instruction is precise.

options.text: It does not mention the ice supplier
options.rationale: Sourcing is outside what this standard covers.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: judge a standard against its purpose.

questions.question: A bakery keeps sending out cakes in the wrong flavor and responds by adding a final inspector before pickup. What is the limitation of that fix?

options.text: The error still gets made every time
options.rationale: Inspection catches defects after the cost is incurred, while first-time quality prevents them from happening.

options.text: Customers dislike waiting at pickup
options.rationale: A side effect rather than the structural flaw.

options.text: Inspectors are expensive to recruit
options.rationale: Cost is secondary to the fact that the cake is already wrong.

options.text: Cakes cannot be inspected reliably
options.rationale: Flavor can be checked; the point is that it should not need to be.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify why inspection is not prevention.

questions.question: At a sandwich shop, every order is walked from the register to the sandwich line and then walked again to the drink station. Which change addresses the design?

options.text: Add a second person to carry the tickets
options.rationale: Staffs the wasted motion instead of removing it.

options.text: Reorder the stations along the order path
options.rationale: The waste is in the movement the layout forces, so the fix is the sequence rather than the speed of any one station.

options.text: Reduce the menu until the walking stops
options.rationale: Cuts revenue to avoid solving the flow problem.

options.text: Ask staff to walk faster during the rush
options.rationale: Pushes people harder inside a flawed layout.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: fix a flow problem at the design level.

questions.question: A shop pre-portions meat and cheese each night, and about half dries out and is discarded. What is the first move?

options.text: Buy cheaper meat so waste costs less
options.rationale: Reduces the price of the waste rather than the waste.

options.text: Portion closer to the volume actually used
options.rationale: Matching the prep quantity to real demand removes the waste without removing the prep benefit.

options.text: Discount sandwiches to use up the excess
options.rationale: Sells margin away to consume an avoidable surplus.

options.text: Stop pre-portioning entirely from tonight
options.rationale: Cuts a step that is protecting speed during the rush.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: cut waste without cutting a protective step.

questions.question: A bakery maps its custom cake process and records only the working steps: sketch, bake, decorate, box. Lead time still looks unexplained. What is missing?

options.text: The customer's design preferences
options.rationale: An input to the work, not a source of hidden time.

options.text: The cost of ingredients at each step
options.rationale: Material cost does not account for elapsed time.

options.text: The names of the staff at each step
options.rationale: Assignment detail does not locate delay.

options.text: The waits and handoffs between steps
options.rationale: Most elapsed time in a value stream sits between the value-adding steps, so a map without them cannot explain the delay.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: complete a value stream map correctly.

questions.question: A shop's toaster is the constraint. A manager proposes cutting the nightly pre-portioning step to save labor, though pre-portioning is what keeps the prep line ahead of the toaster. What is the risk?

options.text: The toaster will need replacing sooner
options.rationale: Equipment life is unrelated to prep timing.

options.text: The saving may starve the constraint
options.rationale: Waste cuts are only gains if they do not slow the step that sets total output, and this one protects the constraint's feed.

options.text: Customers will notice fresher ingredients
options.rationale: Names a benefit, not the risk being asked about.

options.text: Labor cost will rise on the prep line
options.rationale: The proposal reduces prep labor, not raises it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: a legitimate waste cut collides with the constraint that governs output.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Managing Bottlenecks, Efficiency and Waste Reduction. Without the bottleneck the saving is simply good housekeeping. Without the waste view there is no proposal on the table. The risk exists only where a saving touches the constraint.

questions.question: Cakes come out with wrong flavors during rush hours because bakers work from memory. The owner posts a sign reading double check the order. Errors continue. What would actually work?

options.text: A bonus for bakers with no flavor errors
options.rationale: Incentivises accuracy without changing what makes it hard.

options.text: A larger sign placed above the ovens
options.rationale: More reminder aimed at the same memory dependence.

options.text: A weekly meeting reviewing recent errors
options.rationale: Discusses defects after they reach customers.

options.text: A printed ticket at the station, checked off
options.rationale: A written standard embedded in the work removes the memory step that causes the defect, which is prevention rather than reminder.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the defect has to be designed out, and the standard is the mechanism that does it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Designing for First-Time Quality, Standardizing How Work Is Done. Without first-time quality a reminder sign looks like a reasonable answer. Without standardization there is no concrete way to build prevention into the station. Both are needed.

questions.question: A value stream map shows a cake order spends 40 minutes in work and 26 hours waiting, most of it between decorating and boxing. A manager wants to speed up decorating. What does the map argue?

options.text: Speed decorating, since it is the longest task
options.rationale: Optimises the small share of total time.

options.text: Attack the wait, not the working step
options.rationale: The elapsed time lives in the handoff, so redesigning that transition returns far more than accelerating a 40 minute task.

options.text: Add decorators until the backlog clears
options.rationale: Adds capacity to a step that is not the delay.

options.text: Quote customers a longer lead time instead
options.rationale: Accepts the delay rather than removing it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the map exposes where time sits, workflow design decides what to do about a handoff.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Mapping the Value Stream, Process and Workflow Design. Without the map the longest visible task looks like the target. Without workflow design the wait is a fact with no remedy. The answer depends on both.

questions.question: A display project's plan lists every task but never says what is excluded. What does that omission invite?

options.text: The budget being approved faster
options.rationale: Vagueness tends to slow approval, not speed it.

options.text: Extra work creeping into the project
options.rationale: Scope is defined as much by what is out as by what is in, and without the boundary additions arrive unchallenged.

options.text: Tasks being finished ahead of time
options.rationale: An undefined boundary does not accelerate anything.

options.text: Fewer people being needed overall
options.rationale: Unbounded scope usually pulls in more help, not less.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the consequence of undefined scope.

questions.question: In an office renovation, permits must clear before rewiring, which must finish before drywall, then flooring. Painting the lobby can happen any time. What is the critical path?

options.text: Permits, rewiring, drywall, flooring
options.rationale: The critical path is the chain of dependent tasks that sets the shortest possible finish, and the lobby work floats outside it.

options.text: The lobby painting, which takes longest
options.rationale: Duration alone does not make a task critical when nothing waits on it.

options.text: Permits alone, since they come first
options.rationale: A path is a sequence, not a single step.

options.text: Every task in the renovation plan
options.rationale: Independent tasks are not on the path.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: read a critical path from dependencies.

questions.question: A renovation budgeted at $60,000 over eight weeks has spent $30,000. Why is that figure alone not enough to judge?

options.text: It says nothing about progress so far
options.rationale: Spend has to be compared with the work completed at this stage, or half the money can hide a quarter of the job.

options.text: It should be measured weekly instead
options.rationale: Frequency does not fix a missing comparison.

options.text: It excludes the cost of the permits
options.rationale: Nothing suggests permits sit outside the budget.

options.text: It counts labor and materials together
options.rationale: Combining them is normal and not the flaw.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify what spend-to-date omits.

questions.question: A website estimate adds one week discovery, two design, three build and one testing, and promises seven weeks. Client approvals take about three days each at two points. What is wrong?

options.text: The build phase is far too short
options.rationale: Nothing indicates the build estimate itself is wrong.

options.text: Waiting time was never counted
options.rationale: Realistic estimates include the gaps between work, since approvals and handoffs consume calendar time nobody is working.

options.text: The phases should run in parallel
options.rationale: Dependent phases cannot simply overlap.

options.text: Testing should come before build
options.rationale: Reverses a sensible order.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: correct an estimate that counts only working time.

questions.question: A remodel has a detailed task list and a launch date, but nobody has scheduled any check-ins. Shelving arrives before the electrical work finishes. What was missing?

options.text: A larger budget for the remodel
options.rationale: Money would not have ordered the trades correctly.

options.text: Ongoing sequencing once work began
options.rationale: Execution means steering the order of work and catching conflicts as they form, which a static plan cannot do by itself.

options.text: A different shelving supplier
options.rationale: The supplier delivered as asked; the timing was unmanaged.

options.text: A longer planning phase up front
options.rationale: The plan existed and was detailed; the steering did not.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: identify the execution gap behind a sequencing failure.

questions.question: A warehouse software rollout finishes when the last station goes live. The team moves straight onto the next project. What did skipping close-out cost?

options.text: The users' training on the system
options.rationale: Training belongs to the rollout itself.

options.text: The final station's configuration
options.rationale: All twelve stations are described as live.

options.text: The budget approval for the project
options.rationale: Approval happened at the start.

options.text: The lessons the next rollout needed
options.rationale: Close-out captures what was learned and releases resources formally, and without it the same mistakes get repaid next time.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: state what close-out provides.

questions.question: A renovation is a week behind. The team can shorten lobby painting by four days or permit-to-rewiring turnaround by two. Painting sits off the dependent chain. Which saves calendar time?

options.text: Both equally, since days are days
options.rationale: Treats float and critical time as interchangeable.

options.text: The two days on the dependent chain
options.rationale: Only compression on the critical path moves the finish date, so a smaller saving there beats a larger one on a task with float.

options.text: Neither, since the delay is already fixed
options.rationale: Gives up on a schedule that can still be compressed.

options.text: The four days on lobby painting
options.rationale: The bigger number, on work nothing is waiting for.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the path decides which savings count and the estimate supplies the durations to compare.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Identifying the Critical Path, Estimating Project Timelines. Without the path the larger saving obviously wins. Without the timeline estimates there are no durations to weigh. Both are needed to prefer two days over four.

questions.question: At week four of eight, a renovation has spent half its $60,000 budget and completed roughly a quarter of the work. What should the manager do?

options.text: Reassure the client that spend is on plan
options.rationale: Spend is on plan only against the calendar, not the work.

options.text: Wait for the next milestone report
options.rationale: Burns the remaining room to act.

options.text: Request a budget increase immediately
options.rationale: Funds the overrun before diagnosing it.

options.text: Act now, while four weeks remain
options.rationale: Comparing spend with progress is what surfaces an overrun early, and execution means adjusting while there is still schedule left to adjust.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: budget tracking detects the problem and execution is what converts detection into a correction.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Managing Project Budgets, Project Execution and Coordination. Without the budget comparison the overrun is invisible. Without execution the finding has no response while time remains. Both are needed.

questions.question: A team's projects keep absorbing extra requests mid-flight. Each one ends when the work stops, with no review. What breaks the pattern?

options.text: A longer list of tasks at the start
options.rationale: More tasks without a boundary invites the same creep.

options.text: A written scope plus a close-out review
options.rationale: The boundary prevents the additions and the review records why they happened, so the next project starts better defended.

options.text: A rule refusing all mid-project requests
options.rationale: Rigidity where a defined change process is what is needed.

options.text: A larger contingency in each budget
options.rationale: Pays for the creep rather than stopping it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: scoping prevents the pattern and close-out is what makes the prevention improve over time.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Project Planning and Scoping, Closing Out a Project. Without scoping there is no defence against the next request. Without close-out the same lesson is relearned every project. Breaking a repeating pattern needs both.

questions.question: A bakery's display glass fogs every morning and staff wipe it every twenty minutes. What does the wiping represent?

options.text: A quality tolerance set too tightly
options.rationale: No tolerance range is described here.

options.text: A standard written for the morning shift
options.rationale: A routine is not the same as a standard, and neither addresses the cause.

options.text: A bottleneck slowing the morning rush
options.rationale: Wiping is not the step limiting output.

options.text: Treating the symptom, not the cause
options.rationale: The fogging has a source, and repeated wiping manages its appearance without touching it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: label a symptomatic fix.

questions.question: An inspector always pulls the first 50 bottles off the line each shift. Why is that sample unreliable?

options.text: Bottles should be tested individually
options.rationale: Full inspection is what sampling exists to avoid.

options.text: Fifty bottles is too small a number
options.rationale: Sample size can be fine; the selection method is the fault.

options.text: It is not representative of the run
options.rationale: A convenient slice can miss drift that develops later, so the conclusion about the batch does not hold.

options.text: The first bottles are always defective
options.rationale: Asserts a pattern rather than the sampling principle.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify a sampling flaw.

questions.question: Two inspectors reject different loaves off the same line, because each one decides for himself how dark is too dark. What is missing?

options.text: A third inspector to break the tie
options.rationale: Adds a third opinion to two.

options.text: An agreed limit on how much may vary
options.rationale: A written tolerance turns a matter of opinion into a check two people can apply the same way.

options.text: More training for the newer inspector
options.rationale: Neither is wrong without a standard to be wrong about.

options.text: A slower line so checks are easier
options.rationale: Speed is not what makes the calls differ.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what turns judgement into a consistent check.

questions.question: A bakery launching a cupcake line says the team will just be careful and rely on its most experienced baker. What should replace that?

options.text: A rule that only that baker makes them
options.rationale: Builds the line around one person's availability.

options.text: A checklist with weights, times and a photo
options.rationale: Written, checkable standards are what make output consistent when the experienced person is not on shift.

options.text: A note asking staff to report mistakes
options.rationale: Relies on self report with no definition of correct.

options.text: A tasting session at the end of each day
options.rationale: Catches problems after a day of production.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: replace informal care with a real standard.

questions.question: A manager adds a second register once, the morning queue shortens, and the issue is declared solved. What does continuous improvement add?

options.text: Add a third register to be safe
options.rationale: More capacity without evidence it is needed.

options.text: Keep measuring and adjust as it drifts
options.rationale: Processes are never finished, so the fix needs a way to notice when conditions change again.

options.text: Reverse the change to test the effect
options.rationale: Removes a working fix to run an experiment on customers.

options.text: Document the fix and move to other work
options.rationale: Documentation is useful but it closes the loop too early.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: extend a one-off fix into a practice.

questions.question: A central kitchen catches defects only at a final inspection desk. Which change builds quality into the work?

options.text: Monthly awards for the cleanest station
options.rationale: Rewards tidiness rather than defect prevention.

options.text: Each station signs off before passing on
options.rationale: Spreading responsibility to everyone who touches the work is what a quality culture actually means in practice.

options.text: A poster campaign about caring for quality
options.rationale: Slogans without any change in who checks, the trap the card names.

options.text: A second inspector added at the same desk
options.rationale: Doubles the end-of-line check rather than moving it upstream.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: move quality responsibility into the line.

questions.question: A team fixes the fogging display by adjusting the cooler vent. Two months later it returns after a shelf is moved. What does the recurrence show about the first fix?

options.text: The vent was never the real problem
options.rationale: Contradicted by the fix having held until something else moved.

options.text: It solved the cause but watched nothing after
options.rationale: The diagnosis was right, and without ongoing measurement the process drifted back when conditions changed.

options.text: It treated a symptom rather than a cause
options.rationale: The vent was the actual cause, which is why it worked for two months.

options.text: Staff stopped following the wiping routine
options.rationale: The wiping was the symptom management the fix replaced.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: correct diagnosis and ongoing monitoring are different requirements, and this case separates them.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Getting to the Root Cause, Continuous Improvement. Without root cause thinking the two good months have no explanation. Without continuous improvement the return looks like a wrong diagnosis. Both are needed to read it correctly.

questions.question: A plant tightens its fill tolerance to 11.99 to 12.01 ounces and keeps pulling samples from the first units of each run. Rejects soar while customer complaints stay flat. What is happening?

options.text: The sample is catching real quality loss
options.rationale: Flat complaints argue against a genuine quality change.

options.text: Inspectors are measuring the wrong units
options.rationale: Nothing suggests a measurement error.

options.text: Normal variation is being flagged as defect
options.rationale: The tolerance is now narrower than the process can hold, so the checks condemn ordinary drift that no customer notices.

options.text: The machines have begun to wear out
options.rationale: Wear would show in complaints and across the whole run.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the tolerance decides what counts as a defect and the sampling decides what gets seen, and both shape the reject rate.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Setting Acceptable Tolerance Levels, Statistical Sampling for Inspection. Without tolerances the reject spike has no definition behind it. Without sampling there is no mechanism producing the readings. The pairing is what explains rejects rising while complaints do not.

questions.question: A kitchen asks every station to own quality, but no station has a written definition of correct for its step. Defects fall at first, then return. Why?

options.text: Ownership without a standard drifts apart
options.rationale: Six people each deciding what correct means produce six standards, so the culture needs something written to hold the stations to the same line.

options.text: A final inspector to catch what stations miss
options.rationale: Puts quality back at the end, which is what owning it at each step replaces.

options.text: A smaller team so the culture holds together
options.rationale: Size is not why the definitions drifted.

options.text: Stronger incentives for the station staff
options.rationale: They are already motivated; they disagree about the target.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: culture supplies the willingness and standards supply the definition, and one without the other decays.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Building a Quality Culture, Quality Standards and Control. Without the culture nobody is checking at the station. Without the standard there is nothing consistent to check against. The initial improvement and the later drift each need one of them.

questions.question: A bakery's entire online ordering flow depends on one employee who alone knows the software. What is that employee?

options.text: An operational cost driver
options.rationale: This is about dependency, not what moves expenses.

options.text: A well trained specialist
options.rationale: True and beside the point, since the risk is the concentration.

options.text: A compliance requirement
options.rationale: No rule requires a single operator.

options.text: A single point of failure
options.rationale: Everything routing through one person means one absence stops the operation, and people count as failure points.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the dependency.

questions.question: A plan lists eight things that could go wrong with the festival stall and says nothing about what to do for any of them. What is that list?

options.text: A safety audit of the stall
options.rationale: An audit inspects conditions rather than forecasting problems.

options.text: A complete contingency plan
options.rationale: Contingency means the fallback, which is exactly what is absent.

options.text: A worry list, not a risk plan
options.rationale: Risk management attaches a specific response to each risk, otherwise the naming accomplishes nothing.

options.text: An incident report from last year
options.rationale: Nothing has happened yet.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: distinguish a risk list from a risk plan.

questions.question: A customer has an allergic reaction to an unlabelled ingredient in a smoothie. What comes first?

options.text: A statement protecting the brand
options.rationale: Downplaying to protect image is the trap and it usually backfires.

options.text: The person's medical safety
options.rationale: Incident response protects people before anything else, including the business's position.

options.text: A refund issued for the drink
options.rationale: A trivial gesture while someone is unwell.

options.text: An internal review of the recipe
options.rationale: Necessary later, not in the first minute.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: order the first response.

questions.question: One overseas mill supplies 90 percent of a furniture shop's oak with a ten week lead time and no qualified backup. Quality and price are both excellent. How should the exposure be read?

options.text: Low, since quality and price are strong
options.rationale: Judges a supplier on performance while ignoring concentration.

options.text: High, because recovery would take months
options.rationale: Exposure is concentration multiplied by how long replacement takes, and a ten week lead time with no qualified alternative is severe.

options.text: High, because overseas shipping is slow
options.rationale: Distance matters only through the replacement problem.

options.text: Low, because one supplier is simpler
options.rationale: Simplicity of administration is not a risk measure.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: assess concentration exposure in a specific case.

questions.question: A food truck's plan for a big Saturday festival says the propane could run out. What turns that into continuity planning?

options.text: A decision to sell cold items only
options.rationale: Abandons the menu rather than securing the fuel.

options.text: A spare tank on board and a neighbour deal
options.rationale: A named fallback arranged in advance is what keeps service running when the risk lands.

options.text: A note to monitor the propane gauge
options.rationale: Watching the problem arrive is not a fallback.

options.text: A sign apologising if the grill stops
options.rationale: Communicates the failure instead of preventing it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: convert a named risk into a fallback.

questions.question: A team audits its systems for single points of failure and lists servers, the payment gateway and the delivery van. Two weeks later the only trained scheduler quits and dispatch stops. What did the audit miss?

options.text: Servers should have been excluded
options.rationale: Systems belong on the list; the list was incomplete, not wrong.

options.text: People can be single points too
options.rationale: Looking only at equipment and systems is the standard blind spot, and knowledge held by one person is the same risk.

options.text: The van needed a backup vehicle
options.rationale: The van was already on the list and is not what failed.

options.text: The audit ran two weeks too early
options.rationale: Timing would not have surfaced a category it does not consider.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: extend the failure-point analysis to people.

questions.question: A shop depends on one mill for 90 percent of its oak. Qualifying a second supplier costs about $8,000 in samples and testing, and the board calls that money spent on nothing. What is the counterargument?

options.text: The second mill will beat the first on price
options.rationale: Promises a saving the case does not support.

options.text: The first mill will improve once challenged
options.rationale: A negotiating side effect, not the reason to qualify.

options.text: It buys the fallback the exposure demands
options.rationale: The assessment establishes how costly a failure would be, and qualification is what converts that finding into an actual continuity option.

options.text: Two suppliers always produce better quality
options.rationale: A general claim rather than the risk argument.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the exposure assessment justifies the spend and continuity planning is what the spend produces.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Assessing Supplier Risk Exposure, Contingency and Continuity Planning. Without the exposure the $8,000 really is unjustified. Without continuity planning the exposure is a number with no remedy attached. The argument requires both.

questions.question: A smoothie bar handles an allergic reaction well: staff call for help, stay with the customer and inform the family clearly. The same labelling gap caused a near miss a month earlier and no change was made. What does the case show?

options.text: Near misses are unrelated to real incidents
options.rationale: The earlier near miss involved the identical gap.

options.text: Labelling rules are impossible to enforce
options.rationale: Gives up on the control rather than applying it.

options.text: Good response cannot replace prevention
options.rationale: Handling the incident correctly limits harm once it starts, while the risk work that would have stopped it was never done.

options.text: The response should have been faster still
options.rationale: The response is described as handled well.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: response quality and risk prevention are separate obligations, and this case satisfies one while failing the other.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Crisis and Incident Response, Operational Risk Management. Without the response the case is simply a harm story. Without the risk view the good handling closes the matter. The lesson sits in the contrast between them.

questions.question: A bakery knows one employee is the only person trained on its ordering system and lists that on its risk register each quarter. Nothing else happens. The employee books a month of leave. What should have followed the listing?

options.text: A policy limiting that employee's leave
options.rationale: Manages the symptom by constraining a person.

options.text: A note on the register marked reviewed
options.rationale: Repeats the documentation that changed nothing.

options.text: A second trained operator, months ago
options.rationale: Naming the dependency is only the first half; risk work means attaching a response, and cross-training is the obvious one.

options.text: A software change to a simpler system
options.rationale: A large project where training solves it directly.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the failure point is correctly identified and the risk discipline of attaching a response is what was skipped.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Identifying Single Points of Failure, Operational Risk Management. Without the failure point there is nothing on the register. Without the risk discipline the register entry looks like the job done. The gap between naming and acting needs both.

questions.question: A smoothie shop's floor behind the blender gets slippery with spilled ice and juice. Which response fits the skill?

options.text: Rubber mats and a set wipe-down routine
options.rationale: Removing the hazard and building an ongoing habit is what workplace safety means in practice.

options.text: An incident form kept beside the blender
options.rationale: Records the fall after it happens.

options.text: A poster reminding staff to be careful
options.rationale: A one-time notice that leaves the hazard in place.

options.text: A rule that only seniors work the station
options.rationale: Restricts who slips rather than stopping the slipping.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: choose the hazard response.

questions.question: A warehouse logs only incidents that caused injury or damage. What does that policy hide?

options.text: Near misses that warn of the next one
options.rationale: Close calls are the cheapest data a safety system gets, and a log that ignores them only records failures already paid for.

options.text: The training each employee completed
options.rationale: Training records are not what an incident log captures.

options.text: The names of staff on each shift
options.rationale: Staffing records are a separate system.

options.text: The cost of repairs after each event
options.rationale: Damage events are exactly what does get logged.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify what a narrow log misses.

questions.question: A food truck logs fridge temperatures every four hours and stores raw chicken below ready-to-eat items every day, not just before inspections. What does that represent?

options.text: Compliance built into daily work
options.rationale: Standards are met by how the operation runs routinely, rather than by a scramble when an inspector is due.

options.text: A safety audit of the whole truck
options.rationale: An audit is a periodic inspection, not the daily routine.

options.text: An incident report for a temperature
options.rationale: Nothing has gone wrong in this description.

options.text: A training programme for new hires
options.rationale: The scenario describes practice, not instruction.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: recognise operational compliance.

questions.question: A warehouse runs a quarterly audit, files the completed checklist, and finds the same blocked fire exit noted three quarters running. What is the audit missing?

options.text: A more detailed inspection checklist
options.rationale: The hazard is already being found, so detection is not the gap.

options.text: An external inspector to run the walk
options.rationale: Who walks the floor is not why the exit stays blocked.

options.text: More frequent quarterly inspections
options.rationale: Finding it more often without fixing it changes nothing.

options.text: Tracking each finding to a closed fix
options.rationale: An audit produces value only when findings are followed to resolution, otherwise it documents the same hazard repeatedly.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: complete the audit loop.

questions.question: A warehouse adds a new conveyor line. Staff were trained on safety at hire, some of them years ago. What should happen before the line runs?

options.text: A note added to the employee handbook
options.rationale: Documentation nobody is required to read before operating.

options.text: A reminder email about general safety
options.rationale: Generic content for a specific new hazard.

options.text: A sign posted at the conveyor switch
options.rationale: Signage is not instruction in lockout steps.

options.text: Hands-on training on this equipment
options.rationale: Training has to match the hazards that exist now, and a new machine introduces procedures nobody has been taught.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: match training to a new hazard.

questions.question: A warehouse wants dock staff to actually report incidents. Its current form is a paper packet kept in the supervisor's office. What change fits the skill?

options.text: A longer form capturing more detail
options.rationale: More friction on a system already going unused.

options.text: A monthly meeting to recall what happened
options.rationale: Relies on memory weeks after the event.

options.text: A rule requiring supervisors to file reports
options.rationale: Adds a gatekeeper between the event and the record.

options.text: A QR code at each dock opening a short form
options.rationale: Reporting has to be quick and available where events happen, or the data never gets captured.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: design reporting that gets used.

questions.question: A warehouse's audits come back clean, yet a serious injury occurs at a dock where staff had been reporting near misses for months. What does the pair of systems reveal?

options.text: Near miss reports are inherently unreliable
options.rationale: They proved accurate, which is the point of the case.

options.text: The audit checklist was fundamentally wrong
options.rationale: Possible in general, but the evidence points at the data never reaching it.

options.text: Reports were collected and never fed the audit
options.rationale: The near miss data existed and the audit did not use it, so two working systems produced a blind spot between them.

options.text: Staff should have stopped work themselves
options.rationale: Shifts responsibility to the people who did report.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: both systems function individually and the failure is the missing link between them.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Conducting Safety Audits, Incident Reporting Systems. Without the audit there is nothing that should have caught it. Without the reports there was no warning to miss. The gap only exists when both are present and disconnected.

questions.question: A food operation passes every inspection but relies on a scramble the night before each one. Training happened at hire only. What does that combination predict?

options.text: The operation is meeting its obligations
options.rationale: Passing on inspection day says nothing about the other days.

options.text: Inspections are scheduled too frequently
options.rationale: Frequency is not what creates the gap.

options.text: New hires need less training than veterans
options.rationale: Reverses the refresher principle entirely.

options.text: Standards will slip between inspections
options.rationale: Compliance is a daily practice, and without ongoing training there is nothing holding the standard up on the days nobody is watching.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: compliance defines the standard and training is what sustains it between checks.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Compliance and Standards in Operations, Employee Safety Training Programs. Without compliance there is no standard to slip. Without the training gap the scramble might still hold. Predicting the slide requires both.

questions.question: An audit flags the same slippery blender area each quarter. Staff mop it when they remember. Management wants the finding closed for good. What closes it?

options.text: An extra audit each month at that station
options.rationale: Observes more often without changing anything.

options.text: A warning letter to the shift supervisor
options.rationale: Assigns blame where a physical fix is available.

options.text: Mats plus a scheduled wipe-down with an owner
options.rationale: Closing a finding means removing the hazard and assigning the routine that keeps it gone, not repeating the observation.

options.text: A note in the audit that staff were reminded
options.rationale: Documents the same hazard for a fourth quarter.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the audit identifies the recurrence and the safety practice supplies what actually resolves it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Safety and Workplace Health, Conducting Safety Audits. Without the audit the recurrence is invisible. Without the safety practice the finding has no remedy beyond reminders. Both are needed to close it.

questions.question: A food truck jumps from 80 to 250 orders a day. The owner's plan is to hire two more staff around the same single grill. What is the flaw?

options.text: Two staff is too many to hire at once
options.rationale: Headcount size is not the issue.

options.text: The grill limits output, not staffing
options.rationale: Scaling means finding which resource actually caps throughput, and more hands at one grill cannot cook more food.

options.text: The truck should raise its prices
options.rationale: A demand lever applied to a capacity problem.

options.text: The menu is too small for the volume
options.rationale: Nothing points at menu breadth.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: locate the scaling constraint.

questions.question: A taco chain opening a third site writes a prep manual with exact portion weights and photos of each finished plate. What does that support?

options.text: The same experience at every site
options.rationale: Standards are what let a customer get the same product regardless of which location they visit.

options.text: A marketing campaign for the opening
options.rationale: Nothing about promotion is involved.

options.text: A lower food cost per plate
options.rationale: Consistency may help cost, but that is not its purpose here.

options.text: A faster hiring process for cooks
options.rationale: Recruitment is a separate activity.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: state what standards deliver.

questions.question: A franchisor issues a detailed operations manual and assumes consistency is now guaranteed. What does that assumption miss?

options.text: Regular checks that it is followed
options.rationale: A manual sets the standard; visits and audits are what keep practice attached to it.

options.text: A separate manual for each city
options.rationale: Local versions dilute the standard.

options.text: A different supplier for each site
options.rationale: Varying suppliers works against consistency.

options.text: A longer manual with more detail
options.rationale: More pages without verification changes nothing.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify what a manual alone lacks.

questions.question: Orders have tripled after a blog feature. Prep space, the till and the grill are all near their limits, and the grill backs up first every service. Where does the first investment go?

options.text: A second grill, the first limit to bind
options.rationale: Scaling proceeds by relieving whichever resource caps output now, then re-checking what binds next.

options.text: All three at once, to be ready
options.rationale: Spends on limits that are not yet binding.

options.text: A second till, since orders start there
options.rationale: Taking orders faster feeds a grill that cannot keep up.

options.text: More prep space, since it is tight
options.rationale: Tight is not the same as binding first.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: sequence scaling investment.

questions.question: A chain wrote its prep standards three years ago and never revisited them. Two sites now use different portion sizes than the manual. What is the gap?

options.text: The original standards were too strict
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the standards were unworkable.

options.text: The manual should be digital, not paper
options.rationale: Format is not what caused the drift.

options.text: The sites should set their own portions
options.rationale: Abandons the consistency being sought.

options.text: No auditing or updating since launch
options.rationale: Standards drift unless they are checked and refreshed, so a document written once is only a starting point.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: explain standards drift.

questions.question: A taco franchise expanding to a new city wants its salsa to taste identical. Which measure does the most?

options.text: A taste test at the opening week only
options.rationale: One check at launch cannot hold a standard over time.

options.text: A written recipe sent to the new owner
options.rationale: A recipe without specified ingredients or training leaves room to vary.

options.text: A requirement to buy locally where possible
options.rationale: Local sourcing directly threatens the consistency goal.

options.text: Exact supplier specs plus training on prep
options.rationale: Consistency needs both the inputs and the method pinned down, since either alone still allows the flavour to move.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose the measure that secures consistency.

questions.question: A franchisor audits every site quarterly against a manual last updated four years ago. Sites pass the audits, yet customers say the food differs by location. How is that possible?

options.text: Franchisees are deliberately cutting corners
options.rationale: They are passing audits, so the fault is upstream.

options.text: The auditors are not visiting often enough
options.rationale: Quarterly visits are happening and sites pass.

options.text: Customers cannot detect real differences
options.rationale: Dismisses the evidence the case provides.

options.text: The standard itself has gone stale
options.rationale: Auditing enforces whatever the document says, so an outdated standard produces compliant sites that still differ in practice.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: enforcement is working while the thing being enforced is out of date.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Franchise Operations Consistency, Standardizing Operations Across Locations. Without the audits the divergence is unsurprising. Without the standards view a passing audit means everything is fine. The paradox needs both.

questions.question: A franchisor can fund either two more support visits per site per year or a second commissary that removes the biggest prep constraint at every location. Sites are both inconsistent and capacity-bound. How should it choose?

options.text: Neither, until franchisees fund it themselves
options.rationale: Defers a decision the franchisor owns.

options.text: The commissary, since capacity always wins
options.rationale: A rule of thumb standing in for the diagnosis.

options.text: By which constraint is costing customers now
options.rationale: Both problems are real, so the decision turns on which one is actively losing business rather than on which is easier to fund.

options.text: The visits, since consistency defines a brand
options.rationale: Also a slogan rather than a reading of this situation.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: scaling capacity and franchise consistency compete for one budget and the answer requires weighing both.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Scaling Operations, Franchise Operations Consistency. Without scaling there is no commissary option. Without consistency there is no case for support visits. Choosing between them requires holding both.

questions.question: A salad chain goes from four sites to eight on the same central kitchen and the same written prep standards. Audits confirm the standards are being followed and food now arrives late at every site. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Late food means the recipes are wrong
options.rationale: Timing is not a recipe fault.

options.text: The prep standards were never followed
options.rationale: The audits say otherwise.

options.text: Eight sites is too many to standardise
options.rationale: Consistency is the part still working.

options.text: Standards held while capacity did not
options.rationale: Standardisation keeps the product identical across sites and says nothing about whether the kitchen behind it can produce twice as much.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: consistency and capacity are separate scaling problems, and solving one leaves the other untouched.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Standardizing operations across locations, Scaling operations. Without the standards the lateness could be site by site drift. Without the capacity question the doubling looks harmless. Both are needed.

questions.question: Hotel check in takes 90 seconds with one clerk and eight minutes with another. What does that spread indicate?

options.text: No defined process behind the desk
options.rationale: Consistent service comes from a designed sequence, not from whoever happens to be working.

options.text: Guests arrive with incomplete bookings
options.rationale: That would slow both clerks equally.

options.text: One clerk is unfriendly to guests
options.rationale: Speed variation is not evidence about manner.

options.text: The hotel is understaffed at night
options.rationale: Staffing levels are not what the comparison shows.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: read variation as a process signal.

questions.question: Register data shows a sandwich shop gets triple its normal line from 11:30 to 1:00 on Tuesday through Thursday. What should that drive?

options.text: Extra staff in exactly those hours
options.rationale: Predictable peaks are matched with capacity aimed at the window, not spread across the week.

options.text: A shorter menu for the whole week
options.rationale: Reduces the offer instead of the wait.

options.text: Higher prices on Tuesday lunches
options.rationale: A pricing lever applied to a staffing finding.

options.text: A uniform schedule for every day
options.rationale: The average day schedule is what misses these peaks.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: convert a demand pattern into coverage.

questions.question: When an order arrives wrong at a diner, each server improvises a different response, anywhere from a free dessert to a shrug. What does the diner need?

options.text: A set plan for putting mistakes right
options.rationale: Recovery works when every server knows the same steps, so a bad plate ends the same way whoever is on shift.

options.text: A rule against giving anything free
options.rationale: Removes a tool instead of directing it.

options.text: Servers who make fewer order errors
options.rationale: Fewer errors still leaves the response undefined.

options.text: A manager called to every complaint
options.rationale: Slows recovery and does not scale.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the procedure the inconsistency reveals is missing.

questions.question: A hotel's written recovery plan says to offer a refund when a room is not ready. Guests still leave angry. What is the plan missing?

options.text: Steps staff take in the moment
options.rationale: A recovery procedure has to say what happens at the desk, not only what money changes hands afterwards.

options.text: A larger refund for longer delays
options.rationale: More of the element that is already failing.

options.text: A manager's signature on each case
options.rationale: Adds approval friction at the worst moment.

options.text: A survey sent the following week
options.rationale: Measures the anger rather than preventing it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: complete a recovery procedure.

questions.question: A hotel owner's plan for consistent service is to hire friendlier people. Check in times still swing widely. What would fix it?

options.text: A friendliness score in each review
options.rationale: Measures the trait that was never the constraint.

options.text: A second desk opened during evenings
options.rationale: Adds capacity while the variation remains.

options.text: Higher pay for the fastest clerks
options.rationale: Rewards speed without teaching the method.

options.text: A defined sequence every clerk follows
options.rationale: Consistency is built into the process, since warmth does not standardise how long a task takes.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: fix service variation at the process level.

questions.question: A counter cuts its average wait from 14 to 11 minutes, but customers still complain because there is no line order and latecomers get served first. What should be added?

options.text: A sign apologising for busy periods
options.rationale: Acknowledges the problem without ordering the queue.

options.text: Another two minutes cut from the wait
options.rationale: Keeps optimising the clock that is not the complaint.

options.text: A free drink for anyone who waits
options.rationale: Pays compensation for a fixable design flaw.

options.text: A visible order, so the wait feels fair
options.rationale: Fairness is the part of waiting people react to most, and a shorter but disordered queue still feels unjust.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: address the perceived side of a wait.

questions.question: A lunch counter cannot add staff for its 90 minute peak this quarter. Waits run 15 minutes and customers walk out. What is the best available move?

options.text: Accept the walkouts as a seasonal loss
options.rationale: Treats a manageable perception problem as fixed.

options.text: Add two staff and absorb the cost anyway
options.rationale: The case rules this out, so it is not an available move.

options.text: Shorten the menu to speed up the line
options.rationale: Plausible, but it cuts revenue and is not what the wait complaint names.

options.text: Order the queue and post a live estimate
options.rationale: With capacity fixed, the remaining lever is how the wait is experienced, and predictability is what stops walkouts.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: capacity is constrained, so the wait management concept has to carry the answer.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Matching Service Capacity to Demand, Managing Customer Wait Times. Without the capacity constraint hiring is obviously right. Without wait management there is no second lever once hiring is ruled out. Both are needed.

questions.question: A hotel writes an excellent recovery script, but front desk process still varies so much that failures happen daily. Recovery costs climb even though guests leave satisfied. What is the priority?

options.text: Move recovery approval to a manager
options.rationale: Slows the response that currently satisfies guests.

options.text: Rewrite the recovery script once more
options.rationale: Improves the half that is already succeeding.

options.text: Standardise check in so failures stop
options.rationale: Recovery is working as designed, so the rising cost points at the inconsistent process generating the failures.

options.text: Cap what staff may offer per incident
options.rationale: Cuts the cost by weakening the recovery.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: good recovery masks a bad process, and only holding both explains rising cost alongside happy guests.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Designing Service Recovery Procedures, Managing Service Operations. Without recovery the guests would be leaving angry and the case is simple. Without the operations view the cost has no source. The pairing is the diagnosis.

questions.question: A cafe staffs its peak correctly by the data, yet the line still backs up because each barista runs the order differently. What does the evidence point to?

options.text: Too few people during the peak
options.rationale: The staffing is stated as correct for the demand.

options.text: Demand arriving later than forecast
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the peak moved.

options.text: Equipment too slow for the volume
options.rationale: Machines would slow every barista equally.

options.text: Enough people, no shared method
options.rationale: When capacity matches demand and throughput still lags, the variation in how the work is done is what remains.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: capacity is ruled out by one concept so the other supplies the explanation.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Matching Service Capacity to Demand, Managing Service Operations. Without the capacity check understaffing is the obvious answer. Without the operations view there is no alternative explanation. Both are load bearing.

questions.question: A manager answers every stock question with order more to be safe. What is that ignoring?

options.text: The number of staff on shift
options.rationale: Staffing is unrelated to how much stock sits in the back.

options.text: The cash and space it ties up
options.rationale: Inventory has a carrying cost, so more stock is never free protection.

options.text: The price the supplier charges
options.rationale: Unit price is usually known and is not what extra stock hides.

options.text: The brand of the product sold
options.rationale: Which brand is stocked does not change the carrying cost logic.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the cost of over-ordering.

questions.question: A bakery drops its cheapest flour supplier after two missed delivery windows in one quarter. What does that decision weigh?

options.text: Reliability alongside unit price
options.rationale: Vendor choice balances cost, quality and dependability rather than taking the lowest bid on its own.

options.text: Only the price per bag of flour
options.rationale: Price alone would have kept the cheapest supplier.

options.text: The size of the bakery's storage
options.rationale: Storage is an inventory question, not a vendor one.

options.text: The distance to the supplier's mill
options.rationale: Location matters only through its effect on delivery.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the criteria behind a vendor switch.

questions.question: An online shoe store sends every returned pair to the same landfill bin regardless of condition. What is it losing?

options.text: Value in items it could resell
options.rationale: Returns should be routed by condition, since restocking and repair recover money that a single bin throws away.

options.text: The customer's original order data
options.rationale: Records are unaffected by how goods are disposed of.

options.text: The cost of the prepaid label
options.rationale: That cost is already spent either way.

options.text: The shelf space in the warehouse
options.rationale: Discarding frees space rather than losing it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: state what routing returns recovers.

questions.question: A bakery buys all its flour from one mill because the price is best. The mill shuts for a fortnight after a fire. What would have helped?

options.text: A second mill already set up
options.rationale: Spreading key inputs across more than one supplier is what keeps one failure from stopping the business.

options.text: A larger order placed each month
options.rationale: More volume from the same point of failure.

options.text: A lower price from the same mill
options.rationale: Price is not what failed.

options.text: A longer contract with the mill
options.rationale: A contract cannot bake through a fire.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the protection that was absent.

questions.question: A workshop reorders a part the day it runs out. The part takes three weeks to arrive. What is it not planning around?

options.text: The gap between order and arrival
options.rationale: Lead time is how long stock actually takes to become usable, and reordering at zero guarantees a gap of exactly that length.

options.text: Which supplier to buy the part from
options.rationale: A different supplier, same timing error.

options.text: How much storage space it has
options.rationale: Space is not the constraint.

options.text: The price the supplier charges
options.rationale: Cost is not the failure.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the interval being ignored.
