options.text: A SWOT that found the wrong opening
options.rationale: The opportunity is real and winnable.

options.text: A firm not placed to win the work
options.rationale: It is well placed.

options.text: A mission that should be dropped
options.rationale: Rewrites the commitment.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the analysis surfaces the option and the mission is the filter the recommendation never applied.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: SWOT analysis application, Vision and mission. Without the SWOT there is no opportunity on the table. Without the mission the recommendation is complete. Both are needed.

questions.question: A proposal describes a new kitchen display system in detail and says nothing about the cooks who have used paper tickets for a decade. What is missing?

options.text: A plan for getting people to adopt it
options.rationale: Change management is about adoption, and a system nobody uses delivers nothing.

options.text: A comparison with rival software vendors
options.rationale: Selection is a different decision.

options.text: A technical specification of the screens
options.rationale: The system is already described in detail.

options.text: A budget for the hardware purchase
options.rationale: Funding is a separate line.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the adoption gap.

questions.question: A new boutique gym signs a five year lease and equips the whole floor for one class format before testing demand. What does agility suggest instead?

options.text: Commit in steps that can be changed
options.rationale: Agility is a clear plan with room to adjust, which means avoiding irreversible commitments before the market answers.

options.text: Offer every class format at once
options.rationale: Spreads resources without learning anything.

options.text: Sign a longer lease for a better rate
options.rationale: Deepens the commitment being questioned.

options.text: Operate without any plan at first
options.rationale: Agility is not the absence of a plan.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the agile alternative.

questions.question: Warehouse pickers resist a new scanning system because they believe it will be used to discipline them. What does that tell a manager?

options.text: The resistance has a specific cause
options.rationale: Resistance is usually about a particular fear, and naming it is what makes it addressable.

options.text: The pickers dislike change in general
options.rationale: The generic reading the card warns against.

options.text: The system was chosen incorrectly
options.rationale: The objection is about use, not the tool.

options.text: The rollout should be cancelled now
options.rationale: Abandons a change over an addressable fear.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: read resistance as specific.

questions.question: Pickers fear the new scanner data will be used against them. Which response addresses that specific objection?

options.text: Explain again how the scanner works
options.rationale: Answers a question nobody asked.

options.text: Require adoption and monitor compliance
options.rationale: Escalates exactly the fear described.

options.text: Offer a bonus for hitting scan targets
options.rationale: Confirms the data will drive their treatment.

options.text: State in writing how the data may be used
options.rationale: The fear is about the use of the data, so a clear limit on that use is what answers it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: answer the actual objection.

questions.question: A restaurant is moving from paper tickets to digital displays. Which rollout gives the change its best chance?

options.text: A rule that paper tickets are now banned
options.rationale: Removes the fallback before the new way is proven.

options.text: A full switch on a Monday with training
options.rationale: Trains for a system nobody has stress tested.

options.text: A memo announcing the date of the change
options.rationale: Notification is not adoption work.

options.text: A two week pilot on one shift, then expand
options.rationale: A limited trial with the people affected surfaces problems and produces staff who can vouch for the system.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: design a rollout for adoption.

questions.question: A print shop sees local businesses moving ad budgets to social media. Which response counts as innovation tied to the shift?

options.text: Redesign the shop's own website this quarter
options.rationale: Internal work that does not change the offer.

options.text: Add a new paper stock to the print catalogue
options.rationale: A feature addition unrelated to the shift.

options.text: Discount printing to win the budgets back
options.rationale: Fights a structural move with price.

options.text: Launch a social content service for those clients
options.rationale: The new offer answers the specific change in where customer money is going.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: tie innovation to an observed shift.

questions.question: A well designed pilot of the scanning system runs smoothly, and pickers still refuse to use it at full rollout because nobody addressed their fear about performance monitoring. What does the case show?

options.text: The system should be replaced with another
options.rationale: The tool is not what is being objected to.

options.text: The pilot was too short to prove anything
options.rationale: The pilot ran smoothly on its own terms.

options.text: A good rollout cannot answer an unnamed fear
options.rationale: Adoption work covers how the change is introduced, and a specific objection still has to be identified and answered directly.

options.text: The pickers were always going to resist
options.rationale: The generic reading the case rules out.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the change process was sound and the specific resistance was unaddressed.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Change Management, Overcoming Organizational Resistance. Without the rollout there is no adoption effort to praise. Without the specific fear the refusal has no cause. Both are needed.

questions.question: A print shop wants to answer the shift to social media by building a full in-house agency, hiring six people on permanent contracts before any client signs. What does agility argue?

options.text: Abandon the service, since the shift may reverse
options.rationale: Refuses a real market change.

options.text: Hire all six, since half measures never work
options.rationale: Locks in cost before learning anything.

options.text: Wait a year and see what competitors build
options.rationale: Cedes the response to rivals.

options.text: Test the service before fixing the cost base
options.rationale: The response to the shift is right, and the commitment should stay reversible until demand from these clients is proven.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: innovation identifies the right response and agility governs how much to commit to it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Innovation as Strategic Response, Strategic Agility. Without innovation there is no new service to size. Without agility the full build looks decisive. Both shape the answer.

questions.question: A print shop launches its social content service. The press operators, who will keep running the presses, hear about it from a client and conclude the shop is abandoning printing. What was skipped?

options.text: A decision to close the printing side
options.rationale: Confirms the fear rather than addressing it.

options.text: A client agreement before hiring anyone
options.rationale: Commercial sequencing, not the internal gap.

options.text: Explaining the change to the people staying
options.rationale: A new offer changes how staff read their own future, so adoption work covers the people whose jobs are not changing as well.

options.text: A market study before launching the service
options.rationale: The shift is already evidenced.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the innovation is sound and the change was never managed with the existing staff.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Innovation as Strategic Response, Change Management. Without the innovation there is nothing for operators to misread. Without change management the misreading has no remedy. Both are needed.

questions.question: A coffee chain plans a 15 percent price cut to win back customers, treating the current market as fixed. What is the flaw in that planning?

options.text: It targets customers who already left
options.rationale: Winning back lapsed customers is a normal aim.

options.text: It assumes the rival will not respond
options.rationale: Competitive moves are answered, so a plan built on today's snapshot ignores the most predictable part of the outcome.

options.text: It cuts prices by too small a margin
options.rationale: A deeper cut deepens the same problem.

options.text: It should have raised prices instead
options.rationale: A different tactic, not the flaw in the reasoning.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the missing anticipation.

questions.question: Facing a national chain opening nearby, a regional coffee shop's only plan is to undercut its prices. Why is that a poor defence?

options.text: Customers are slow to notice price changes
options.rationale: They notice; the problem is who can sustain it.

options.text: It needs the landlord to agree to the change
options.rationale: Pricing is the shop's own decision.

options.text: A defensive move is weaker than attacking
options.rationale: Defending a position is legitimate; the chosen defence is not.

options.text: It starts a war the larger firm can win
options.rationale: A chain can absorb thinner margins for longer, so the one axis the shop picked is the one where size decides it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify why price cutting fails as defence.

questions.question: A rival launched a hydration tracker first and is still fixing its sensor problems publicly. What advantage does the follower hold?

options.text: Learning from mistakes it did not pay for
options.rationale: Following lets a company enter with the early costs already absorbed by someone else.

options.text: Protection from the rival's patents
options.rationale: Following does not confer legal cover.

options.text: A guaranteed larger share of the market
options.rationale: Nothing about following guarantees share.

options.text: Lower manufacturing costs by default
options.rationale: Costs do not fall simply by waiting.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the follower's advantage.

questions.question: A chain is considering a 15 percent cut. The rival across the street has lower rent and matched every previous move within a week. What should the plan include?

options.text: A deeper cut to discourage a response
options.rationale: Invites the war rather than planning through it.

options.text: The next step once the rival matches
options.rationale: Anticipation means planning past the first move, since the response is effectively certain here.

options.text: A decision to keep the cut permanent
options.rationale: Commits indefinitely to a contested position.

options.text: A public announcement of the new prices
options.rationale: Publicity does not change the rival's reply.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: plan beyond the first move.

questions.question: A company's smart bottle is six months from launch. A rival's early product is out with visible flaws, and customers are still learning what the category does. What does that suggest?

options.text: Abandon the category to the first mover
options.rationale: Treats being first as decisive, which the case disproves.

options.text: Enter second, with the flaws already solved
options.rationale: The rival is paying the education and debugging costs, which is what makes following the stronger position here.

options.text: Copy the rival's product exactly as it is
options.rationale: Copies the flaws along with the design.

options.text: Rush to launch before the rival improves
options.rationale: Trades the follower advantage for speed.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose entry timing.

questions.question: A local hardware store learns that a national chain will open two blocks away in six months. What counts as a defensive move?

options.text: Cut every price the week it opens
options.rationale: A price war against a bigger buyer is unwinnable.

options.text: Wait and see how many customers leave
options.rationale: Reacting after the loss is the opposite of defending.

options.text: Copy the chain's layout and hours
options.rationale: Imitation removes the reason to choose the local store.

options.text: Lock in trade accounts before it opens
options.rationale: Defence means making the position harder to attack while there is still time, and committed trade customers are the hardest business to take.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: pick the move that strengthens the position ahead of the attack.

questions.question: A chain can cut prices 15 percent, which the rival will match within a week, or spend the same money on a loyalty programme the rival cannot immediately copy. Which reasoning holds?

options.text: Neither, since the rival is better funded
options.rationale: Surrenders a defensible position.

options.text: Cut prices, since customers respond fastest
options.rationale: Speed of response is irrelevant once it is matched.

options.text: Do both, to cover every possible angle
options.rationale: The budget funds one, and the price war undoes the other.

options.text: Spend where the response is hardest to match
options.rationale: Anticipating the rival's reply is what reveals that one option is neutralised in days while the other builds a position.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: anticipation predicts the reply and defensive thinking chooses the move that survives it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Anticipating Competitor Moves, Defensive Strategy Tactics. Without anticipation both options look equivalent. Without the defensive view there is no criterion for choosing. Both are needed.

questions.question: A firm plans to follow the rival into smart bottles in six months, learning from its flaws. The rival has a history of cutting prices hard the moment a competitor appears. What should the plan account for?

options.text: An earlier launch to avoid the response
options.rationale: Gives up the learning the strategy depends on.

options.text: A price response timed to the second entry
options.rationale: The follower advantage is real and it arrives into a predictable reaction, so the entry has to be planned around that reply.

options.text: A plan to exit if the rival cuts prices
options.rationale: Plans the retreat rather than the entry.

options.text: Nothing, since following is the safer route
options.rationale: Safety in one dimension does not remove the reaction.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: timing choice and competitor reaction shape each other.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: First-Mover Versus Follower Strategy, Anticipating Competitor Moves. Without the timing decision there is no entry to defend. Without anticipation the follower walks into a predictable cut. Both are needed.

questions.question: A company was first into a category and now faces three followers with cheaper copies. Its early advantage is fading. What does a defensive posture call for now?

options.text: Exit the category and start a new one
options.rationale: Abandons a position that can still be defended.

options.text: Claim first-mover status in all advertising
options.rationale: Asserts an advantage that is already eroding.

options.text: Cut prices to the level of the copies
options.rationale: Fights on the followers' chosen ground.

options.text: Convert the head start into something sticky
options.rationale: Being first is temporary, so the defence is to turn early customers into a position rivals cannot simply undercut.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the first-mover position is expiring and defensive tactics decide what replaces it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: First-Mover Versus Follower Strategy, Defensive Strategy Tactics. Without the timing view there is no fading advantage. Without defence there is no answer to the erosion. Both are needed.

questions.question: A bakery's mission is handmade bread for neighborhood tables, baked before dawn. The owner turns down a supermarket contract that would require overnight industrial baking. What is the mission doing here?

options.text: Setting a measurable sales target
options.rationale: No number or deadline appears.

options.text: Acting as a filter on decisions
options.rationale: A mission earns its place when it rules options in and out, rather than sitting framed on a wall.

options.text: Serving as a marketing slogan
options.rationale: Nothing is being advertised in this choice.

options.text: Defining the company's legal form
options.rationale: Structure is unrelated to mission.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: recognise a mission being used.

questions.question: A meal kit startup writes: pre-portioned ingredients, recyclable packaging, twelve recipes weekly. Why is that not yet a value proposition?

options.text: It lists features, not the benefit
options.rationale: A value proposition names the problem solved for the customer, which a specification list never reaches.

options.text: It mentions too few recipes
options.rationale: Count is not what makes it a spec sheet.

options.text: It names no competitor by name
options.rationale: Naming a rival is optional; naming a benefit is not.

options.text: It omits the company's founding
options.rationale: History is not part of the form.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: distinguish features from a value proposition.

questions.question: A startup posts its values on the website but hires, promotes and rewards exactly as before. What has it actually changed?

options.text: Nothing about how people behave
options.rationale: Culture is carried by hiring, promotion and daily practice, so a statement alone changes nothing.

options.text: Its legal obligations to staff
options.rationale: Values statements are not employment terms.

options.text: The company's whole culture
options.rationale: That is the claim the case disproves.

options.text: The engineering team's output
options.rationale: Nothing about the work has been altered.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify culture as practice rather than statement.

questions.question: A meal kit startup competes against grocery stores, where shoppers can buy the same ingredients cheaper. Which value proposition holds up?

options.text: The freshest ingredients available anywhere
options.rationale: Competes on the dimension the grocery store already wins.

options.text: Dinner in 20 minutes with nothing to decide
options.rationale: It names what the grocery aisle cannot give: the planning and prep removed, which is the real problem being solved.

options.text: A lower price per meal than any store
options.rationale: Directly contradicted by the case.

options.text: Twelve new recipes published every week
options.rationale: A feature with no customer problem attached.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: build a proposition against a specific alternative.

questions.question: A bakery whose mission centres on neighborhood freshness is offered a profitable airport concession requiring frozen par-baked loaves. What does using the mission as a filter mean here?

options.text: Accept and keep the mission unchanged
options.rationale: Leaves a stated purpose the operation contradicts.

options.text: Decline, or change the mission openly
options.rationale: A mission that never blocks anything is decoration, so the choice is to honour it or revise it deliberately.

options.text: Decline and stop publishing the mission
options.rationale: Hides a filter that is working correctly.

options.text: Accept, since profit funds the mission
options.rationale: Any decision can be justified this way, which empties the filter.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: use a mission to decide a real trade.

questions.question: A software firm wants ship small, ship often to become real after hiring twenty engineers. Which change makes it stick?

options.text: Hold a workshop explaining the new value
options.rationale: Explanation without any consequence attached.

options.text: Promote and review people on shipping cadence
options.rationale: Culture follows what gets rewarded, so the value has to appear in hiring, review and promotion decisions.

options.text: Add the phrase to the careers page and site
options.rationale: A statement with nothing behind it.

options.text: Print the value on stickers and wall art
options.rationale: Decoration rather than practice.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: make a stated value operative.

questions.question: Research shows a meal kit's buyers most value low price, but the company's mission centres on reducing the mental load of cooking. A consultant proposes repositioning on price. What is the real decision?

options.text: Whether competitors would copy the new pitch
options.rationale: A secondary concern that does not resolve the conflict.

options.text: Whether the research sample was large enough
options.rationale: Sidesteps the strategic question with a methodology doubt.

options.text: Whether to run both propositions at once
options.rationale: Two contradictory promises confuse the market.

options.text: Whether to change the mission, not just the pitch
options.rationale: A value proposition has to be deliverable by the business the mission describes, so repositioning on price is a decision about what the company is.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the proposition must sit inside the mission, so changing one forces a decision about the other.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Crafting a Value Proposition, Vision and Mission. Without the proposition there is nothing to reposition. Without the mission the pivot is a marketing choice with no cost. The depth of the decision requires both.

questions.question: A bakery's mission promises handmade bread, while its promotions all reward speed and volume. New bakers learn quickly that output is what gets noticed. What is the consequence?

options.text: The rewarded behavior becomes the real mission
options.rationale: Culture is set by what an organisation actually recognises, so a contradicted mission is overruled in practice.

options.text: The mission will correct the promotions over time
options.rationale: A statement does not override incentives.

options.text: New bakers will ignore both of the signals
options.rationale: The case says they respond to the stronger one.

options.text: Both will coexist without any real tension
options.rationale: The bakers are already choosing between them.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the stated direction and the lived culture conflict, and the outcome depends on how each operates.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Vision and Mission, Setting Organizational Culture. Without the mission there is no contradiction to notice. Without culture the promotions are just administration. The displacement needs both.

questions.question: A company promises customers unhurried, expert advice, while its floor staff are measured purely on transactions per hour. Customers report feeling rushed. What explains the gap?

options.text: The measure teaches the opposite of the promise
options.rationale: What staff are held to becomes the culture, and that culture is what customers experience regardless of the promise.

options.text: Customers misunderstood the advertising claims
options.rationale: Blames the audience for an internal contradiction.

options.text: The promise was too ambitious to keep at all
options.rationale: It is deliverable if the incentives allow it.

options.text: Staff need additional product training time
options.rationale: Expertise is not what the metric squeezes out.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the external promise and the internal measure conflict, and the customer experiences the measure.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Crafting a Value Proposition, Setting Organizational Culture. Without the proposition there is no promise being broken. Without culture the metric is neutral. The gap only exists where both are in play.

questions.question: A store opening plan assigns hiring to the operations team and fit-out to the store team, with no names and no dates. What is wrong?

options.text: Hiring should come after the fit-out work
options.rationale: Sequence is a different question.

options.text: Tasks owned by groups are owned by nobody
options.rationale: Accountability needs one named person and a date, since a department cannot be asked whether it finished.

options.text: The opening has too many separate tasks
options.rationale: Task count is not what the structure gets wrong.

options.text: The teams need more people assigned to them
options.rationale: Headcount does not create ownership.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the accountability gap.

questions.question: Asked how the catering strategy will happen, a manager answers that the team will really focus on catering growth this year. What has been produced?

options.text: The strategy restated, not broken down
options.rationale: Turning strategy into action means specific steps with owners and dates, which a more emphatic restatement never supplies.

options.text: A complete implementation plan
options.rationale: No step, owner or date appears.

options.text: A change to the company's strategy
options.rationale: The strategy is unchanged.

options.text: A measurable goal for the year
options.rationale: There is no number attached.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: distinguish restatement from execution.

questions.question: A subscription box launch holds one kickoff meeting, then each department works separately until launch week. What does that miss?

options.text: Regular syncs while the work is live
options.rationale: Coordination is ongoing contact with shared goals and handoffs, not a single meeting at the start.

options.text: A project name everyone can remember
options.rationale: Naming does not coordinate work.

options.text: A bigger kickoff with more attendees
options.rationale: One larger meeting has the same flaw.

options.text: A budget approved before the kickoff
options.rationale: Funding is separate from coordination.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what coordination requires.

questions.question: A bakery's quick weekday breakfast push lists social ads, a new menu item and earlier opening hours, each described on its own. What makes it a coherent plan?

options.text: A larger budget behind all three pieces
options.rationale: Funds three disconnected actions.

options.text: Ads that name the item and the new hours
options.rationale: Coherence means the pieces reinforce each other, so the promotion points at the product available at the newly opened time.

options.text: A fourth idea added to widen the push
options.rationale: More unconnected pieces.

options.text: A decision to run them one at a time
options.rationale: Sequencing them separately keeps them separate.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: make separate actions reinforce each other.

questions.question: Grow catering revenue is the strategy. Which statement is an actual execution step?

options.text: Catering becomes everyone's shared responsibility
options.rationale: Shared responsibility removes ownership.

options.text: Marketing lead emails 40 offices by March 14
options.rationale: A named owner, a specific action and a date is what converts strategy into work that can be checked.

options.text: Catering will receive more attention this year
options.rationale: No action, owner or deadline.

options.text: The company will prioritise catering clients
options.rationale: A restatement with no step inside it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: recognise a real execution step.

questions.question: A store opening needs hiring, fit-out and stock in place within six weeks. What does an accountability structure look like?

options.text: A regional manager overseeing everything alone
options.rationale: One person owning all three is a bottleneck.

options.text: A weekly meeting where all three are discussed
options.rationale: Discussion without assigned ownership.

options.text: A shared document everyone can edit freely
options.rationale: Visibility is not accountability.

options.text: One named owner and date for each piece
options.rationale: Single ownership with a deadline and a check is what makes each strand answerable.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: design accountability for a project.

questions.question: A catering plan lists twelve specific steps with dates, all assigned to the sales department as a whole. Three months later half are untouched and nobody can say why. What failed?

options.text: Twelve steps is too many for one quarter
options.rationale: Half were completed, so the volume was workable.

options.text: Real steps with no individual owners
options.rationale: The strategy was broken down properly, and without a named person per step the plan had nobody to answer for it.

options.text: The catering strategy was poorly chosen
options.rationale: Nothing questions the strategy itself.

options.text: The steps themselves were far too vague
options.rationale: The case states they were specific and dated.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the breakdown was done and ownership was not, so only both together explain the stall.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Turning Strategy into Action, Setting Accountability Structures. Without the breakdown the plan is vague and the diagnosis is different. Without ownership the good steps have nobody behind them. Both are needed.

questions.question: A subscription launch has a coherent plan on paper: ads, fulfilment capacity and billing all support one launch date. Each department executes its own part perfectly, and boxes ship two weeks after the ads run. What broke?

options.text: The ads should have been delayed by a month
options.rationale: A remedy guessed without diagnosing the gap.

options.text: The plan was never coherent to begin with
options.rationale: The case states the pieces supported one date.

options.text: Fulfilment capacity was badly underestimated
options.rationale: Each part is described as executed correctly.

options.text: Nobody synced the timing between teams
options.rationale: A coherent plan still needs live coordination, because each department can hit its own dates while the handoffs between them drift.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: plan coherence and ongoing coordination are separate requirements and only one was met.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Coordinating a Coherent Plan, Cross-Functional Coordination. Without coherence the misalignment starts on paper. Without live coordination the plan cannot survive contact with three calendars. The failure needs both.

questions.question: Every task in a launch has a named owner with a date, but owners sit in three departments and each discovers late dependencies on the others. What should be added?

options.text: A single owner for the whole launch
options.rationale: Concentrates work that is properly distributed.

options.text: Named handoffs between the owners
options.rationale: Individual ownership covers the tasks, and what remains unowned is the transfer between them, which coordination defines.

options.text: Longer deadlines for every named task
options.rationale: Slack hides the dependency problem.

options.text: A rule that departments work in sequence
options.rationale: Serialises work that could run in parallel.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: ownership is in place and the gaps between owners are what coordination supplies.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Setting Accountability Structures, Cross-Functional Coordination. Without ownership the tasks themselves would drift. Without coordination the handoffs have no owner. Both are needed to close it.

questions.question: A chain entering a new country translates its menu and converts prices, changing nothing else. What does that leave undone?

options.text: The legal registration of the business
options.rationale: A compliance step, separate from adaptation.

options.text: The offer itself is still unchanged
options.rationale: Adapting reaches the product, portions and service model, not only the words and the currency.

options.text: The choice of a local advertising agency
options.rationale: A supplier decision rather than the strategy.

options.text: The exchange rate used for conversion
options.rationale: Currency conversion is already done.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify shallow adaptation.

questions.question: A furniture maker eyeing Mexico decides to license a local manufacturer rather than build its own plant. What is it doing?

options.text: Choosing a lower commitment entry mode
options.rationale: Licensing trades some control for far less capital and risk, which is an entry mode decision.

options.text: Benchmarking against local competitors
options.rationale: No comparison is being made.

options.text: Diversifying into an unrelated category
options.rationale: The product stays the same.

options.text: Integrating an earlier supply stage
options.rationale: Nothing in the supply chain is being acquired.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: classify the entry mode.

questions.question: A skincare brand entering Brazil flags high import tariffs on finished cosmetics and different labelling rules. What is it doing?

options.text: Mapping the differences that affect the plan
options.rationale: Cross-border work means identifying how law, tariffs and logistics vary and adjusting the plan to them.

options.text: Choosing a distribution partner to work with
options.rationale: Partner selection is a later step.

options.text: Setting the retail price for the market
options.rationale: Pricing follows from the analysis.

options.text: Deciding whether to enter Brazil at all
options.rationale: Entry is already assumed in the case.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the activity.

questions.question: A Texas fried chicken chain is opening in Seoul, where portions run smaller and side dishes matter more. Which adaptation is substantive?

options.text: Smaller portions and a local side menu
options.rationale: The offer itself changes to fit local eating norms, which is what real adaptation means.

options.text: Menus printed in Korean and won prices
options.rationale: Necessary and superficial, which the card names as the trap.

options.text: The same menu with a Seoul opening advert
options.rationale: Promotion around an unadapted offer.

options.text: A Texas theme emphasised in the store design
options.rationale: Leans harder into the unadapted original.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose substantive adaptation.

questions.question: A brand treats its international plan as one uniform strategy across six countries with different tariffs, labelling rules and payment norms. What follows?

options.text: Administration becomes simpler overall
options.rationale: Simplicity that does not survive contact with the rules.

options.text: Costs fall through shared processes
options.rationale: Rework in six markets raises them.

options.text: The brand gains consistency advantages
options.rationale: Consistency of identity is fine; uniform compliance is not.

options.text: The plan fails wherever the rules differ
options.rationale: Uniform strategies collide with country-specific requirements that do not bend to a corporate template.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: predict the result of a uniform plan.

questions.question: A bakery chain wants to test whether Canada works for it, with limited capital and nobody on the ground there. Which entry method fits those constraints?

options.text: Buy a Canadian bakery chain outright
options.rationale: An acquisition is a commitment, not a test.

options.text: Build and staff three owned stores
options.rationale: The most capital and the most local knowledge required.

options.text: Franchise to an operator already there
options.rationale: Franchising buys local knowledge and puts most of the capital risk on the partner, which is what a test with little money needs.

options.text: Ship product daily from the home city
options.rationale: Freight cost and freshness make this unworkable.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: match the entry method to the stated constraints.

questions.question: A skincare brand faces steep tariffs on finished cosmetics in Brazil but far lower duties on bulk ingredients. It is weighing exporting finished goods against licensing a local filler. What does the tariff picture argue?

options.text: Licence the brand for every product line
options.rationale: Extends a decision beyond what the analysis supports.

options.text: Export anyway and raise the retail price
options.rationale: Prices the brand out of the market it is entering.

options.text: Delay entry until the tariffs are reduced
options.rationale: Waits on policy rather than adapting.

options.text: The entry mode should follow the duty structure
options.rationale: Cross-border conditions determine which entry route is viable, so the tariff gap effectively selects local filling.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the entry decision is determined by the cross-border conditions rather than by preference.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Global Expansion Strategy, Managing Cross-Border Complexity. Without the entry question there is nothing to decide. Without the tariff detail both modes look equally open. Both are needed.

questions.question: A chain licenses its brand to an operator in Seoul, who adapts portions and sides well. Head office then insists on the Texas menu exactly as written. What does the conflict reveal?

options.text: Head office should open owned stores instead
options.rationale: Changes the mode after the fact rather than reading the conflict.

options.text: The operator exceeded its legal authority
options.rationale: Adapting the offer is normally within a licensee's remit.

options.text: Adaptation should never touch the menu
options.rationale: The menu is precisely what needed adapting.

options.text: The entry mode gave away that control
options.rationale: Licensing hands operating decisions to the partner, so demanding uniformity contradicts the mode chosen and the adaptation the market needs.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the entry mode determines who may adapt, and the market demands adaptation.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Global Expansion Strategy, Adapting Strategy Across Markets. Without the mode there is no question of who decides. Without adaptation there is no change to object to. Both are needed.

questions.question: A brand adapts its product beautifully for a new market but ships with labels that fail local ingredient disclosure rules. Stock is held at customs. What does the case show?

options.text: The brand should exit the market now
options.rationale: Abandons an entry over a fixable labelling issue.

options.text: The product adaptation was itself wrong
options.rationale: The case says the adaptation succeeded.

options.text: Market fit does not cover legal difference
options.rationale: Adapting to taste and adapting to regulation are separate obligations, and only one was met.

options.text: Customs delays are an unavoidable cost
options.rationale: This one was avoidable through compliance work.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: cultural adaptation and regulatory complexity are distinct requirements.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Adapting Strategy Across Markets, Managing Cross-Border Complexity. Without adaptation the failure would be commercial as well. Without the legal difference the shipment clears. The distinction needs both.

questions.question: A food truck sets the goal become popular downtown. What makes that unusable?

options.text: Food trucks cannot set goals
options.rationale: Nothing about the format prevents it.

options.text: Downtown is the wrong location
options.rationale: Location is not what the wording gets wrong.

options.text: Nobody could say when it is met
options.rationale: A strategic goal needs a measure and a date, or success stays a matter of opinion.

options.text: Popularity does not drive revenue
options.rationale: It often does; the flaw is the vagueness.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: test a goal for measurability.

questions.question: A bakery's quarterly goal is growing wholesale accounts by 20 percent, and the team spends most of its time polishing social posts. What is missing?

options.text: A second goal for social media
options.rationale: Adds a competing aim rather than ordering effort.

options.text: A larger marketing budget
options.rationale: Funds the misaligned work.

options.text: A longer quarter to finish both
options.rationale: Time does not create priority.

options.text: Work ranked against the stated goal
options.rationale: Alignment means the effort is ordered by what moves the main goal, not by what feels productive.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the alignment gap.

questions.question: A chain launches a value line to lift weak first-quarter sales while protecting its premium positioning long term. What is it managing?

options.text: A competitor's recent pricing decision
options.rationale: No rival action is described.

options.text: A short term need against a long one
options.rationale: The balance is exactly this: producing results now without spending the future position.

options.text: A staffing shortfall across the stores
options.rationale: Labour is not in the case.

options.text: A supply chain constraint this quarter
options.rationale: Nothing about sourcing appears.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the balance being struck.

questions.question: A food truck owner wants a goal the team can act on this quarter. Which one qualifies?

options.text: Build the strongest brand downtown
options.rationale: No definition of strongest.

options.text: Be busier than last year overall
options.rationale: Vague comparison with no threshold.

options.text: Serve 150 customers daily by March 31
options.rationale: A number and a date together make success checkable and give the team something to steer by.

options.text: Increase sales as much as possible
options.rationale: Measurable in principle, with no target or deadline.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: select a usable goal.

questions.question: A premium bakery needs cash this quarter. A deep discount would deliver it but train customers to wait for sales. What does balanced judgement suggest?

options.text: Run the discount indefinitely from now
options.rationale: Spends the long term position for a quarter.

options.text: Refuse any discount, to protect the brand
options.rationale: Treats the trade as all-or-nothing, which the card warns against.

options.text: Delay the decision to next quarter
options.rationale: The cash need is now.

options.text: A bounded promotion that ends clearly
options.rationale: Short term needs can be met without permanent damage when the concession has limits built into it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: bound a short term concession.

questions.question: With a goal of 20 percent wholesale growth, a team has four tasks and time for two. Which pair fits?

options.text: A store refresh and a loyalty card launch
options.rationale: Aimed at walk-in customers, not accounts.

options.text: A social content calendar and new packaging
options.rationale: Retail-facing work that leaves wholesale untouched.

options.text: Restaurant outreach and a wholesale price sheet
options.rationale: Both directly serve the stated goal, which is what ranking work against a main aim produces.

options.text: All four, done at a lower standard
options.rationale: Refuses to prioritise, which is the skill being tested.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: rank work against a goal.

questions.question: A company sets five measurable quarterly goals with dates, and every team picks whichever it prefers. Three months later two goals are met and three untouched. What went wrong?

options.text: The goals were not measurable enough
options.rationale: The case states they carried numbers and dates.

options.text: Measurable goals were never ranked
options.rationale: Good goals still need an order, since without one the limited effort scatters across all of them.

options.text: The teams lacked the necessary skills
options.rationale: Two goals were met, so capability existed.

options.text: Five goals is always too many
options.rationale: Count is workable when priority is clear.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: goals were well formed and unprioritised, so only the second concept explains the outcome.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Setting Strategic Goals, Goal Alignment and Prioritization. Without well-formed goals the failure is simply vagueness. Without prioritisation there is nothing else to blame. The diagnosis needs both.

questions.question: A quarter's priority is wholesale growth. A large retail promotion would hit the quarterly revenue number but consume the team's capacity for six weeks. What does sound reasoning say?

options.text: Take the promotion, since revenue is revenue
options.rationale: Ignores what the quarter was supposed to build.

options.text: The revenue gain costs the stated priority
options.rationale: Meeting a number by abandoning the ranked goal trades the longer aim for a short result, which is the trade to make explicit.

options.text: Run both by extending working hours
options.rationale: Pretends the capacity constraint is not real.

options.text: Refuse it, since promotions never help
options.rationale: Absolute rule rather than a weighed trade.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the priority defines what the quarter is for and the time horizon defines what the promotion costs.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Goal Alignment and Prioritization, Balancing Short and Long-Term Goals. Without the priority the promotion is free revenue. Without the horizon the capacity hit has no future cost. Both are needed.

questions.question: A chain's only goal is hit $2.4 million in revenue this year. Managers meet it by deferring equipment maintenance and cutting training. What does the goal set fail to include?

options.text: A penalty for managers who miss it
options.rationale: Sharpens the same incentive.

options.text: A target protecting the longer horizon
options.rationale: A single short-horizon measure invites borrowing from the future, so the goal set needs something that captures what is being spent.

options.text: A larger revenue figure to aim at
options.rationale: Raises the pressure that caused the behavior.

options.text: A monthly rather than annual measure
options.rationale: Shortens the horizon further.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the goal is well formed by one standard and unbalanced by the other.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Setting Strategic Goals, Balancing Short and Long-Term Goals. Without goal-setting there is no target driving behavior. Without the balance view a met target looks like success. The missing piece needs both.

questions.question: A taco chain's growth plan says it will launch new products, enter new states and win new customer segments all at once. What is the flaw?

options.text: New states are too expensive to enter
options.rationale: Cost is not what the plan gets wrong.

options.text: Products should always come before markets
options.rationale: There is no universal order.

options.text: No single path has been chosen
options.rationale: Growth strategy means picking one route and resourcing it, since each path demands different capability.

options.text: The chain is too small to grow at all
options.rationale: Eight locations can support growth.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the missing choice of path.

questions.question: A furniture maker losing margin to a lumber supplier considers buying a small mill. What kind of growth move is that?

options.text: Forming an alliance with a partner
options.rationale: Ownership, not partnership, is proposed.

options.text: Expanding into a new sales region
options.rationale: Geography is not what changes.

options.text: Taking over an earlier supply stage
options.rationale: Moving up or down your own supply chain is what vertical integration describes.

options.text: Entering an unrelated new category
options.rationale: Lumber is directly related to furniture.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: classify the move.

questions.question: A cold brew brand partners with a regional gym chain to stock its cans. What makes this a sound partner choice?

options.text: The gym chain is large and known
options.rationale: Fame without fit is the trap the card names.

options.text: The gym will pay the marketing cost
options.rationale: Nothing about who pays is stated.

options.text: The gym reaches its actual buyers
options.rationale: A partnership works when the partner's audience and the brand's customer genuinely overlap.

options.text: The gym has no other drink brands
options.rationale: Exclusivity is not what makes the fit.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: apply the partner fit test.

questions.question: A coffee roaster wants into canned cold brew. Building the capability would take three years; a small canned brand is for sale now. What is the core question about the deal?

options.text: Whether competitors are also making acquisitions
options.rationale: Industry activity is not a reason to buy.

options.text: Whether the target's brand name is well known
options.rationale: Recognition is one input among many.

options.text: Whether buying beats building for this capability
options.rationale: An acquisition is judged against the alternative of developing the same capability, including time and integration cost.

options.text: Whether the deal adds revenue and market share
options.rationale: Almost any purchase adds both, which is why it settles nothing.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: frame an acquisition against building.

questions.question: A coffee roaster has maxed out grocery shelf space. A board member proposes launching a line of pet products to reduce reliance on coffee. What is the objection?

options.text: Pet products run on thin margins
options.rationale: Margin is not the objection; relatedness is.

options.text: The roaster should leave coffee behind
options.rationale: Nobody proposed exiting the core business.

options.text: Shelf space could be expanded instead
options.rationale: The premise is that it is maxed out.

options.text: Nothing connects it to what the firm does
options.rationale: Diversifying into a category sharing no capability, buyer or channel means starting a second business rather than growing this one.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: test a diversification proposal for fit.

questions.question: A taco chain with eight locations has a proven format, loyal customers and no product development team. Which growth path fits?

options.text: Develop a packaged retail line for grocery
options.rationale: Needs product development capability it lacks.

options.text: Open in neighbouring towns with the same format
options.rationale: Market development leans on the capability the chain already has, which is a repeatable store format.

options.text: Acquire a competing chain in another state
options.rationale: Adds integration complexity to an untested expansion.

options.text: Launch a delivery-only brand in the same towns
options.rationale: A new concept competing with its own sites.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: match a growth path to existing capability.

questions.question: A roaster can buy a canned cold brew brand that fits its expertise, or a snack company in a category it knows nothing about. Both deals add similar revenue. Which reasoning holds?

options.text: Fit decides, since revenue is matched
options.rationale: With the financial gain equal, the deciding factor is whether the company can actually run what it buys, which is the diversification test.

options.text: Neither, since building is always cheaper
options.rationale: Building is slower here, and cost is not established.

options.text: Either one, since revenue is the point
options.rationale: Revenue parity is why other factors decide.

options.text: The snack deal, since it spreads the risk
options.rationale: Risk spreading without capability is the trap on the card.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the acquisition question and the diversification test combine to break a tie the numbers leave open.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Mergers and Acquisitions Strategy, Diversification Strategy. Without the acquisition frame there is nothing to buy. Without the diversification test the two deals look equivalent. Both are needed.

questions.question: A cold brew brand's chosen growth path is reaching new buyers in existing cities. A national supermarket chain offers a shelf deal requiring volumes it cannot yet produce. A gym chain offers a smaller placement. What does the path argue?

options.text: The gym fits the path and the capacity
options.rationale: A partner is judged against the chosen growth route and what the business can actually supply, and the supermarket fails the second test.

options.text: Neither, since partners dilute the brand
options.rationale: Rejects the route the company has chosen.

options.text: The supermarket, since the reach is larger
options.rationale: Reach it cannot serve produces failed deliveries.

options.text: Both, since partnerships rarely conflict
options.rationale: Capacity makes them mutually exclusive here.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the growth path sets the criterion and partner selection is where it gets applied.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Growth Strategy, Strategic Partnerships and Alliances. Without the path any large partner looks attractive. Without partner evaluation the path has no decision attached. Both are needed.

questions.question: A juice brand has settled on winning more supermarket shelf space as this year's growth path. It is then offered the chance to buy the orchard that supplies its fruit. What does the chosen path argue?

options.text: The orchard deal is too large to fund
options.rationale: Size is not given and is not the test.

options.text: Shelf space follows from supply control
options.rationale: Retailers do not allocate shelves on that basis.

options.text: Buying upstream does not win shelf space
options.rationale: Integration is a real strategy and it answers a supply question, while the path the brand chose is a distribution question.

options.text: Owning supply always lowers unit cost
options.rationale: Treats integration as automatically cheaper.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the integration move is judged against the specific growth path, not on its own merits.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Growth strategy, Vertical integration strategy. Without the chosen path the orchard looks attractive. Without the integration offer there is nothing to test the path against. Both are needed.

questions.question: A manager announces a decision confidently and never mentions what could go wrong with it. What is missing from the judgement?

options.text: The downside weighed against the gain
options.rationale: Judgement means showing the risks alongside the upside, not asserting a conclusion.

options.text: A longer explanation of the upside
options.rationale: More of the half already covered.

options.text: A more confident tone of delivery
options.rationale: Confidence is already present and is not the gap.

options.text: The approval of a second manager
options.rationale: Sign-off does not supply reasoning.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what judgement requires.

questions.question: Delivery costs are eating a bakery's profit and the owner immediately decides to raise prices. What step was skipped?

options.text: Comparing that against other options
options.rationale: Weighing alternatives means at least two candidates compared before one is chosen.

options.text: Informing staff before the change
options.rationale: Communication follows the decision.

options.text: Asking customers about a price rise
options.rationale: Research supports a decision already narrowed.

options.text: Calculating the exact delivery cost
options.rationale: Useful, but the gap is the single option.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the missing comparison.

questions.question: After comparing four suppliers, a student recommends the cheapest and says nothing about its much longer lead time. What does the recommendation lack?

options.text: A second quote for comparison
options.rationale: Four suppliers were already compared.

options.text: A lower price from the supplier
options.rationale: Price is the part already settled.

options.text: Approval from the finance team
options.rationale: Sign-off is not part of the reasoning.

options.text: An honest account of the downside
options.rationale: Judgement means naming the cost of the choice, not only the reason it wins.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: spot the missing half of the judgement.

questions.question: Delivery is unprofitable. The options are raising the delivery fee, setting a minimum order, or dropping delivery entirely. What does weighing them properly involve?

options.text: Naming what each costs and wins
options.rationale: Listing options is not comparing them; the trade-offs have to be set against each other.

options.text: Picking the one staff prefer most
options.rationale: Preference is not a comparison.

options.text: Choosing the fastest to implement
options.rationale: Speed is one factor presented as the whole test.

options.text: Listing all three in the final plan
options.rationale: Listing is exactly the trap the card names.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: compare rather than enumerate.

questions.question: A food truck weighs adding a $6 loaded fries item: it lifts the average ticket but slows service at peak. Which recommendation shows judgement?

options.text: Add it everywhere, since the ticket lift is real
options.rationale: Takes the upside and ignores the named downside.

options.text: Add it and raise prices to cover the slower line
options.rationale: Charges customers for an operational problem.

options.text: Reject it, since any slowdown is unacceptable
options.rationale: Treats one risk as disqualifying without weighing it.

options.text: Add it off-peak first and watch ticket times
options.rationale: It states the gain, acknowledges the specific risk, and structures the decision so the risk can be observed.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: produce a recommendation that carries its risk.

questions.question: Closing on Mondays would save a shop about $900 a month in wages and give up roughly $600 of Monday profit, along with some habit among weekday regulars. Which recommendation shows judgement?

options.text: Close every quiet day the same way
options.rationale: Generalises from one set of figures.

options.text: Close Mondays, since the saving is clear
options.rationale: Right call, with the risk left unmentioned.

options.text: Close Mondays, watching for regulars lost
options.rationale: It takes the favourable arithmetic and names the one effect the arithmetic does not capture.

options.text: Stay open, because closing looks weak
options.rationale: Appearance is not a weighed cost.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: weigh a stated upside against a stated risk and commit.

questions.question: A manager compares three delivery options carefully and picks the minimum order, but presents it as risk free. Small regular customers then leave. What was the fault?

options.text: Customers should have been consulted first
options.rationale: Helpful, but not the reasoning failure.

options.text: The wrong option was selected from the three
options.rationale: The choice may be right; the presentation hid its cost.

options.text: Only three options were placed on the table
options.rationale: Three is a real comparison.

options.text: A good comparison sold without its downside
options.rationale: The alternatives were weighed properly, and judgement failed at the point where the chosen option's cost went unstated.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: comparison was done and judgement was not, and only both together locate the fault.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Weighing Alternatives, Sound Business Judgment. Without the comparison the decision is arbitrary. Without judgement the comparison alone looks like a complete process. The fault sits between them.

questions.question: An option scores best on every financial measure and quietly contradicts the company's stated purpose. The analysis recommends it without mentioning that. What is incomplete?

options.text: Another financial option should be found
options.rationale: Avoids the conflict rather than naming it.

options.text: The financial measures need recalculating
options.rationale: The numbers are not in dispute.

options.text: The mission should simply be rewritten
options.rationale: A possible outcome, but it must be decided openly rather than assumed.

options.text: The cost to the stated purpose is unnamed
options.rationale: Judgement has to surface every material downside, and a decision that erodes the mission carries one the numbers do not show.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the mission supplies a cost that financial judgement alone cannot see.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Sound Business Judgment, Vision and Mission. Without judgement there is no obligation to name downsides. Without the mission there is no non-financial cost to name. Both are needed.

questions.question: A co-op compares three suppliers carefully on price and delivery time, and its stated purpose is to source locally. The winning bid ships from overseas. What went wrong?

options.text: Three suppliers was too small a field
options.rationale: Adding bidders does not add the missing criterion.

options.text: Price should not drive supplier choice
options.rationale: Price is a fair criterion, just not the only one.

options.text: The purpose statement needs rewriting
options.rationale: Rewrites the commitment instead of applying it.

options.text: The comparison left out its own purpose
options.rationale: The alternatives were weighed properly on the criteria chosen, and the criteria omitted the commitment that defines the business.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the comparison is competent and the criteria it runs on were never anchored to the mission.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Weighing alternatives, Vision and mission. Without the comparison there is no decision to fault. Without the stated purpose the overseas bid is simply the best one. Both are needed.

questions.question: A chief executive says site selection is delegated to the regional manager, then requires personal sign-off on every site. What has actually been delegated?

options.text: Both the work and the decision
options.rationale: The sign-off keeps the decision at the top.

options.text: Neither, since nothing was assigned
options.rationale: The work was assigned.

options.text: The budget for the new locations
options.rationale: Nothing about funding is described.

options.text: The work, but not the decision
options.rationale: Delegation of authority means the other person can decide, not merely prepare the recommendation.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: distinguish task assignment from authority.

questions.question: A manager announces a new scanning system in an all-hands meeting and considers buy-in achieved. What is the error?

options.text: Staff should have chosen the system
options.rationale: Selection and buy-in are different steps.

options.text: The system should be introduced sooner
options.rationale: Timing does not create support.

options.text: Announcing is not the same as convincing
options.rationale: Buy-in is built by addressing the concerns of those affected, which one announcement cannot do.

options.text: All-hands meetings are always too large
options.rationale: Format is not the fundamental issue.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what buy-in requires.

questions.question: Two senior engineers are launching a product line they have shipped before. Which leadership style fits the situation?

options.text: Hands-on, writing code alongside them
options.rationale: Adds a manager to work that is covered.

options.text: Directive, with daily task assignment
options.rationale: Close direction wastes proven capability.

options.text: Coaching, teaching them the basics
options.rationale: They already hold the skill.

options.text: Delegating, with checkpoints agreed
options.rationale: Style follows the situation, and experienced people on familiar work need room rather than direction.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: match style to situation.

questions.question: A warehouse is switching inventory systems. Which approach builds genuine support among shift leads?

options.text: Require attendance at a training session
options.rationale: Compliance rather than support.

options.text: Send a detailed memo explaining benefits
options.rationale: One-way communication with no response to concerns.

options.text: Meet them first, hear objections, adjust
options.rationale: Buy-in comes from addressing the specific concerns of the people affected before the change is fixed.

options.text: Offer a bonus for using the new system
options.rationale: Buys behavior without resolving objections.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: build buy-in in a specific case.

questions.question: A regional expansion needs faster site decisions. What does genuine delegation look like?

options.text: The manager recommends and waits for approval
options.rationale: The arrangement that created the delay.

options.text: The manager decides within agreed criteria
options.rationale: Real authority means deciding inside a defined boundary rather than forwarding each choice upward.

options.text: The manager shares decisions with the owner
options.rationale: Shared decisions are not delegated ones.

options.text: The manager decides only on small sites
options.rationale: Keeps the significant decisions centralised.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: define delegated authority.

questions.question: A new team of recent hires is launching an unfamiliar product under a tight deadline. The leader's habit is to delegate and step back. What should they do?

options.text: Delegate as usual, since it works for them
options.rationale: Comfort-driven style, the trap named on the card.

options.text: Lead more closely than habit suggests
options.rationale: Style is chosen for the situation, and inexperienced people on unfamiliar work under pressure need direction.

options.text: Replace the team with experienced staff
options.rationale: Avoids the leadership question entirely.

options.text: Extend the deadline to suit the team
options.rationale: Changes the situation rather than the leadership.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: adjust style against habit.

questions.question: A leader delegates site selection with clear criteria to a manager who has never opened a store. Two poor sites are signed before anyone notices. What was the error?

options.text: The leader should approve every site
options.rationale: Returns to the bottleneck delegation was meant to remove.

options.text: Authority given without matching the person
options.rationale: Delegation is sound in principle and the style has to fit the individual, so an inexperienced manager needed coaching before full authority.

options.text: Delegation is wrong for site decisions
options.rationale: It works with a manager ready for it.

options.text: The criteria were too detailed to follow
options.rationale: Clear criteria are described as given.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the delegation was structurally correct and the style was wrong for this person.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Delegation of Strategic Authority, Strategic Leadership Style. Without delegation nothing was handed over. Without style matching the handover looks correct. Both are needed.

questions.question: A manager is given real authority over a rollout but no chance to shape it, and is then asked to persuade her team to support it. Her advocacy falls flat. Why?

options.text: Her team was always going to resist it
options.rationale: Attributes the outcome to inevitability.

options.text: She was handed delivery without a voice
options.rationale: Buy-in has to be built with the person who will carry the change, and authority to execute is not the same as involvement in the decision.

options.text: Her authority was insufficient for the task
options.rationale: The case states the authority is real.

options.text: She lacked the presentation skills needed
options.rationale: Blames delivery for a structural gap.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: authority was delegated while buy-in was never built with the person holding it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Delegation of Strategic Authority, Building Stakeholder Buy-In. Without delegation she has no role to play. Without buy-in the flat advocacy has no cause. Both are needed.

questions.question: A directive leader pushes a system change through on schedule. Adoption stalls because nobody was asked what would break. What should change next time?

options.text: Abandon directive leadership altogether
options.rationale: Discards a style that fits some situations.

options.text: Assign adoption to a separate manager
options.rationale: Delegates the symptom rather than fixing the method.

options.text: Keep the pace, add the consultation step
options.rationale: A directive style can suit a deadline, and it still has to include the input that surfaces obstacles and builds support.

options.text: Slow every rollout to a consensus pace
options.rationale: Overcorrects into a different failure.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the style was defensible and buy-in was the missing component within it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Strategic Leadership Style, Building Stakeholder Buy-In. Without style there is no pace to defend. Without buy-in the stall has no explanation. Both are needed.

questions.question: A roaster lists being first in town with cold brew as its competitive advantage. Why is that weak?

options.text: The town is too small for advantage
options.rationale: Market size is not the test.

options.text: Advantages must always be financial
options.rationale: They can be operational or relational.

options.text: Any rival can copy it next month
options.rationale: A durable advantage is something competitors cannot easily replicate, and being early is not protected.

options.text: Cold brew is a declining product
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the category is fading.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: apply the durability test.

questions.question: A bakery can save $300 a month on flour by switching to a cheaper supplier whose protein content varies batch to batch. What does long term thinking add?

options.text: The bakery's current cash balance
options.rationale: That argues for the saving, not against it.

options.text: The supplier's delivery schedule
options.rationale: Logistics is not the long term issue.

options.text: The price of flour two years ago
options.rationale: History does not bear on the decision.

options.text: The cost of inconsistent bread later
options.rationale: The saving is immediate and the quality risk plays out over months, which is exactly what the longer view surfaces.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: extend a decision's horizon.

questions.question: A furniture manufacturer that depends on timber builds its responsibility strategy around sustainable forestry. Why does that fit?

options.text: Forestry causes are the most popular
options.rationale: Popularity is not the fit test.

options.text: It sits inside the firm's own operations
options.rationale: A responsibility commitment holds when it connects to what the business actually does and depends on.

options.text: Customers rarely ask about timber
options.rationale: Would be an argument against, not for.

options.text: It costs the company almost nothing
options.rationale: Cost is not what makes it fit.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: apply the CSR fit test.

questions.question: A regional roaster competes on price, location and direct relationships with five specific farms built over a decade. Which of these can be built into a durable advantage?

options.text: The farm relationships, hardest to replicate
options.rationale: Ten years of direct sourcing relationships cannot be bought quickly, while price and location can be matched.

options.text: All three equally, as a combined position
options.rationale: Combining copyable things does not make them durable.

options.text: The location, being on the main street
options.rationale: Another site nearby erases it.

options.text: The price point, if held below rivals
options.rationale: Any competitor can match a price.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: identify the defensible strength.

questions.question: A software company with no physical supply chain adopts ocean plastic cleanup as its flagship responsibility commitment. What is the risk?

options.text: It reads as unconnected to the business
options.rationale: A cause with no link to operations invites the charge that the commitment is presentation rather than substance.

options.text: Employees will object to the spending
options.rationale: Speculation rather than the fit problem.

options.text: Ocean cleanup is too expensive to fund
options.rationale: Cost is not the strategic objection.

options.text: Software firms cannot make commitments
options.rationale: They can, on issues they actually touch.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: test a CSR choice for connection.

questions.question: A chain can meet this year's profit target by cutting its apprenticeship programme, which supplies most of its future head bakers. What does the longer view require?

options.text: Deferring the decision to the next board
options.rationale: Avoids a choice that is due now.

options.text: Cutting it, since targets must be met
options.rationale: Takes the saving without pricing the loss.

options.text: Naming what the cut costs in three years
options.rationale: Long term thinking means stating the future consequence explicitly rather than using the phrase as decoration.

options.text: Keeping it, since training is always good
options.rationale: A slogan rather than a weighed judgement.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: make the long horizon explicit.

questions.question: A roaster's edge is ten years of direct farm relationships. A cheaper commodity broker would lift margin 4 points this year and end direct contact with the farms. What is the real cost?

options.text: Four points of margin in future years
options.rationale: Reverses the direction of the trade.

options.text: A small administrative burden each quarter
options.rationale: Trivialises the loss of the advantage.

options.text: Nothing, since the coffee quality is equal
options.rationale: Quality parity does not preserve the relationships.

options.text: Margin now, bought with the durable edge
options.rationale: The saving is immediate and the thing being spent is the one asset rivals cannot copy, which only the long view prices.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the advantage identifies what is at stake and the horizon prices it.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Building Sustainable Competitive Advantage, Long-Term and Sustainable Thinking. Without the advantage the switch is a routine saving. Without the horizon the cost lands invisibly later. Both are needed.

questions.question: A furniture maker's sustainable forestry programme has produced exclusive long-term agreements with certified mills that competitors cannot now access. How should that be understood?

options.text: A temporary edge until rivals certify too
options.rationale: The agreements are stated as exclusive and long term.

options.text: A marketing claim with no operational base
options.rationale: The opposite of what the case describes.

options.text: A commitment that became a real advantage
options.rationale: A responsibility strategy tied to operations can produce assets rivals cannot copy, which is what durable advantage requires.

options.text: A cost centre justified by reputation alone
options.rationale: The supply agreements are a commercial asset.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the CSR choice and the advantage test combine to explain why this commitment pays.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Corporate Social Responsibility Strategy, Building Sustainable Competitive Advantage. Without CSR there is no programme. Without the advantage test it is just a good deed. Both are needed to read it correctly.

questions.question: A timber-dependent manufacturer can meet its certification commitment at a 6 percent cost increase, or quietly buy uncertified stock for one year while prices spike. Nobody would notice this year. What does sound reasoning say?

options.text: Buy uncertified, since nobody will notice
options.rationale: Treats detection as the only consequence.

options.text: Pass the full 6 percent to customers now
options.rationale: A pricing tactic that skips the strategic question.

options.text: The quiet year would cost the commitment itself
options.rationale: A responsibility strategy holds only if it survives the year it is inconvenient, and the longer view is what makes that cost visible.

options.text: Drop certification and announce the change
