options.rationale: Honest, but it abandons an asset over one price spike.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the commitment's value is only defensible when the horizon beyond this year is counted.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Corporate Social Responsibility Strategy, Long-Term and Sustainable Thinking. Without the commitment there is nothing to break. Without the horizon a single quiet year looks costless. Both are needed.

questions.question: A loyalty app launch defines success as increasing customer engagement. What does that definition lack?

options.text: A marketing budget for the launch
options.rationale: Funding is separate from the measure.

options.text: A description of the app's features
options.rationale: Feature detail is not a success measure.

options.text: A list of competitors with loyalty apps
options.rationale: Comparison is a different exercise.

options.text: A number and a date to judge it by
options.rationale: Success has to be stated so that anyone could later say whether it happened.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: test a success definition.

questions.question: A meal kit company's strategy this year is retention over growth, and its headline metric is still new signups. What is wrong?

options.text: A single metric cannot carry a strategy
options.rationale: True in general, and the fault here is which one.

options.text: Retention is difficult to measure directly
options.rationale: Repeat rate and churn measure it well.

options.text: Signups are hard to measure accurately
options.rationale: They are easy to measure; that is their appeal.

options.text: The metric tracks the strategy it dropped
options.rationale: The company says it is chasing retention and keeps scoring itself on acquisition, so the measure will quietly pull the work back toward growth.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: match indicator to strategy.

questions.question: A plan promises to monitor and adjust as needed, with no metric, date or threshold named. What is that promise worth?

options.text: A great deal, since flexibility is valuable
options.rationale: Flexibility without a trigger is inertia.

options.text: Little, since nothing triggers a change
options.rationale: A review needs a named measure, a checkpoint and a level that prompts action.

options.text: Nothing, since strategies never change
options.rationale: Overstates and contradicts the concept.

options.text: Enough, provided the team meets weekly
options.rationale: Meetings do not supply the missing threshold.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: judge a review commitment.

questions.question: A coffee chain's strategy is faster service. Which scorecard tells it whether the strategy is working without hiding damage?

options.text: Website visits and social media followers
options.rationale: Easy to collect and unconnected to service speed.

options.text: Order time, staff turnover and repeat visits
options.rationale: A few measures across different areas show the gain and the cost of getting it, which one operational number cannot.

options.text: Total revenue compared with the prior year
options.rationale: Too broad to attribute to this strategy.

options.text: Average order time tracked hourly all week
options.rationale: One dimension, with no view of what speed is costing.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: build a balanced scorecard.

questions.question: A loyalty app is live. What makes the review commitment real rather than decorative?

options.text: A quarterly report circulated to managers
options.rationale: Reporting is not the same as deciding.

options.text: A 60 day check on signups and repeat visits
options.rationale: A named date with named measures is what forces an actual decision at a known moment.

options.text: An intention to watch the numbers closely
options.rationale: Watching without a checkpoint or threshold.

options.text: A promise to revisit it if problems appear
options.rationale: Leaves the trigger undefined.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: define a real review point.

questions.question: A meal kit firm has chosen retention over growth for the year. Which indicator set fits?

options.text: Website traffic and email open rates
options.rationale: Activity measures that flatter and decide nothing.

options.text: Repeat order rate and subscriber churn
options.rationale: Both measure whether existing customers stay, which is what the chosen strategy is about.

options.text: New signups and app store downloads
options.rationale: Growth metrics for a strategy that set growth aside.

options.text: Total revenue and marketing spend
options.rationale: Too coarse to show whether retention improved.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: select indicators for a stated strategy.

questions.question: A company holds disciplined quarterly strategy reviews, but the only numbers on the table are downloads and page views. Reviews always conclude that things look fine. What is happening?

options.text: The reviews are held too infrequently
options.rationale: Quarterly is a workable rhythm.

options.text: Reviews should be replaced by dashboards
options.rationale: Changes the format, not the inputs.

options.text: A real review is reading the wrong numbers
options.rationale: The cadence and discipline are in place, and vanity metrics guarantee the review never finds a reason to change course.

options.text: The strategy is genuinely performing well
options.rationale: The metrics cannot support that conclusion.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the review process works and the indicators feeding it do not.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Reviewing and Adjusting Strategy, Key Performance Indicator Selection. Without the review there is no process to mislead. Without the indicator fault the reviews would surface problems. Both are needed.

questions.question: A chain defines success for its faster service push as average order time under 90 seconds. It hits the number, while staff turnover doubles and repeat visits fall. What does that reveal?

options.text: Staff turnover is unrelated to service speed
options.rationale: The case links them in time.

options.text: Success should not be defined numerically
options.rationale: Overcorrects against measurable goals.

options.text: A single measure declared a costly win
options.rationale: Success was defined sharply on one dimension, and a scorecard across areas is what would have shown the price being paid.

options.text: The 90 second target was set too high
options.rationale: The target was met; the problem is what it omitted.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: a well defined success measure and a missing scorecard together produce a hollow win.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Measuring Success and Follow-Through, Strategic Scorecarding. Without the success definition nothing was claimed. Without the scorecard the damage stays invisible. Both are needed.

questions.question: A loyalty app misses its 500 signup target at the 60 day checkpoint, reaching 180. The team's instinct is to extend the deadline and keep going unchanged. What does the checkpoint exist for?

options.text: To confirm the original target was correct
options.rationale: Checkpoints test the plan, not the ambition.

options.text: To give the team a longer runway
options.rationale: Describes the instinct being questioned.

options.text: To force a decision about changing course
options.rationale: A review point is where evidence meets the plan, and moving the date rather than examining the miss empties the mechanism.

options.text: To report progress to senior managers
options.rationale: Reporting is a by-product, not the purpose.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the success measure produced the evidence and the review is where it has to be acted on.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Measuring Success and Follow-Through, Reviewing and Adjusting Strategy. Without the measure the miss is invisible. Without the review there is no moment that demands a response. Both are needed.

questions.question: A bakery announces that growing catering is its priority, then leaves the same one part-time employee on catering and funds nothing new. What is the problem?

options.text: The priority should have been announced earlier
options.rationale: Timing of the announcement changes nothing.

options.text: The spending does not follow the stated strategy
options.rationale: A strategy is visible in where money, people and time actually go, and nothing here moved.

options.text: The catering employee has not been trained well
options.rationale: Skill is not what the case identifies as missing.

options.text: Catering is the wrong market for this bakery
options.rationale: The choice of market is not being questioned.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: spot the misalignment.

questions.question: A bakery plans to add three wholesale cafes needing 200 extra loaves weekly and assumes its single oven will stretch to cover it. What step was skipped?

options.text: Checking what the oven can actually produce
options.rationale: Capacity planning means verifying the resource can deliver before the commitment is made.

options.text: Negotiating a better price with the cafes
options.rationale: Commercial terms are a separate question.

options.text: Deciding what to name the wholesale line
options.rationale: Branding is irrelevant to throughput.

options.text: Choosing which cafes to approach first
options.rationale: Sequencing does not address the ceiling.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the capacity check.

questions.question: A chain with $150,000 for the quarter lists a fourth location and a kitchen upgrade as both essential and plans to do both. What is missing?

options.text: A statement of what gets funded first
options.rationale: Allocation means naming the trade, since the budget cannot cover both in full.

options.text: A second quarter to spread the work
options.rationale: Assumes away the constraint being tested.

options.text: A longer list of options to consider
options.rationale: More options make the choice harder, not easier.

options.text: A bank willing to lend the difference
options.rationale: Changes the budget instead of allocating it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the missing trade-off.

questions.question: A chain has $150,000. A fourth location would add revenue in year two; upgrading the central kitchen would lift capacity for all three existing sites now. Wholesale demand is already being turned away. How should it choose?

options.text: Fund the location, since growth means more sites
options.rationale: Equates growth with footprint rather than with served demand.

options.text: Fund the kitchen, since demand already exists
options.rationale: Allocation weighs what each option returns against what is given up, and here one choice serves demand that is currently being refused.

options.text: Delay both until next year's budget arrives
options.rationale: Leaves the refused demand unserved for another year.

options.text: Split the budget evenly between both projects
options.rationale: Half-funds two projects that each need full funding.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: make an allocation call with a stated reason.

questions.question: Catering is the declared priority. Which change shows real alignment rather than a statement?

options.text: A note that everyone should think catering
options.rationale: Generic exhortation with nothing behind it.

options.text: A full-time catering lead and a delivery van
options.rationale: Naming the specific people and assets that move is what alignment looks like in practice.

options.text: A request for staff to add catering duties
options.rationale: Adds work without adding capacity.

options.text: A new slide about catering in the team deck
options.rationale: Communication without resourcing.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: identify genuine resource alignment.

questions.question: The oven runs 14 hours a day at full load and the wholesale plan needs four more hours of baking. What does capacity planning require before signing the cafes?

options.text: A clause allowing late deliveries when busy
options.rationale: Plans for failure instead of preventing it.

options.text: A promise from staff to work more quickly
options.rationale: Speed cannot create oven hours that do not exist.

options.text: A deposit from each cafe to cover the risk
options.rationale: Money does not bake the bread.

options.text: A second oven or a changed production schedule
options.rationale: The commitment has to be matched by real capacity, which means either more equipment or a genuine rescheduling.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: convert a capacity gap into a requirement.

questions.question: A bakery moves budget and staff onto its catering priority, but nobody checks whether the single oven can produce catering volume alongside retail. Orders are accepted and then missed. What failed?

options.text: The staff assigned lacked catering experience
options.rationale: Experience does not create oven hours.

options.text: Resources moved without a capacity check first
options.rationale: Alignment put money and people behind the strategy while the physical ceiling that governs delivery was never tested.

options.text: The budget allocated was far too small
options.rationale: Nothing suggests underfunding was the cause.

options.text: The catering strategy was the wrong choice
options.rationale: The strategy may be sound; the execution skipped a step.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: alignment happened and capacity planning did not, so only both together explain accepted orders being missed.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Aligning Resources to Strategy, Capacity Planning for Strategy. Without alignment nothing was committed. Without the capacity gap the committed resources would have delivered. The failure needs both.

questions.question: A fourth location promises the larger revenue gain, but the central kitchen is already at its ceiling and supplies every site. The budget funds one project. What does that change about the comparison?

options.text: Both projects should be deferred a full year
options.rationale: Avoids a decision the constraint has already clarified.

options.text: Nothing, since the revenue figure is larger
options.rationale: Compares projections while ignoring whether one can be produced.

options.text: The kitchen should be funded by borrowing
options.rationale: Changes the budget rather than making the choice.

options.text: The new site inherits a constraint it cannot fix
options.rationale: Capacity that is already binding means the expansion option cannot deliver its projected revenue, which reshapes the allocation decision.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the allocation comparison is invalid until the capacity ceiling is factored in.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Resource Allocation Trade-Offs, Capacity Planning for Strategy. Without the trade-off both get funded. Without the capacity ceiling the bigger projection simply wins. The reasoning requires both.

questions.question: A company names three equal strategic priorities and divides its budget evenly across them. A year later none has advanced far enough to matter. What does the case illustrate?

options.text: The three priorities were poorly chosen
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the priorities themselves were wrong.

options.text: Even funding is a refusal to prioritise
options.rationale: Resources signal strategy, and splitting them equally declares that nothing is actually the priority.

options.text: The budget was too small for any of them
options.rationale: Concentrated, it might have carried one.

options.text: A year is too short to judge a strategy
options.rationale: Excuses the outcome without explaining it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: alignment says resources reveal strategy and trade-offs say a limited budget forces a rank.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Aligning Resources to Strategy, Resource Allocation Trade-Offs. Without alignment the even split is neutral accounting. Without the trade-off there is no scarcity forcing a rank. Both are needed.

questions.question: A plan for a second bakery location lists six risks and proposes nothing for any of them. What is that document?

options.text: A crisis response plan for the chain
options.rationale: Nothing has gone wrong yet.

options.text: A complete strategic risk assessment
options.rationale: Assessment without response is half the work.

options.text: A list of worries, not a risk plan
options.rationale: Risk management attaches a reduction or an acceptance to each risk named.

options.text: A contingency plan for the opening
options.rationale: Contingency means the fallback, which is absent.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: distinguish a risk list from management.

questions.question: A truck's stadium launch depends on a commissary kitchen that might fall through. The plan says the team will handle it if it comes up. What does that lack?

options.text: A clearer description of the risk
options.rationale: The risk is already named precisely.

options.text: A later launch date for the truck
options.rationale: Delay is not a fallback.

options.text: A budget line for legal advice
options.rationale: Unrelated to kitchen access.

options.text: A named fallback decided in advance
options.rationale: Contingency planning is the specific alternative chosen before the risk lands, not a promise to improvise.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the missing fallback.

questions.question: A salad company's contamination plan covers recall logistics and legal steps but says nothing about who speaks to customers or when. What is the gap?

options.text: No legal review of the documents
options.rationale: Legal steps are included.

options.text: No estimate of the financial loss
options.rationale: Costing follows the response.

options.text: No plan for communicating outward
options.rationale: Crisis response includes who says what, how fast, since silence is itself a message during an incident.

options.text: No detail on the recall logistics
options.rationale: Logistics is the part already covered.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the missing element of crisis planning.

questions.question: A bakery opening a second site must hire half its staff new, and quality depends on trained bakers. What does managing that risk look like?

options.text: Open anyway and hire more staff if needed
options.rationale: Reacts after customers have seen the result.

options.text: Note the risk and monitor quality after opening
options.rationale: Watching a known risk arrive is not managing it.

options.text: Delay the opening until the market improves
options.rationale: Addresses a different risk entirely.

options.text: Train new hires at the first site beforehand
options.rationale: The risk is reduced by moving the learning ahead of the opening, which is a specific action attached to a named risk.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: attach an action to a strategic risk.

questions.question: A contamination report lands on a Friday evening. What does a sound crisis plan already specify?

options.text: Which law firm will defend any claims
options.rationale: Useful later, not what governs the first hours.

options.text: The exact wording of every statement
options.rationale: Wording depends on facts not yet known.

options.text: Who decides, who speaks, and how fast
options.rationale: Pre-assigned roles and timing are what let a business act in hours rather than days.

options.text: The financial reserve set aside for it
options.rationale: Funding does not organise a response.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: state what a crisis plan pre-decides.

questions.question: The commissary kitchen might fall through two weeks before a stadium launch. Which line is a real contingency?

options.text: A plan to search for kitchens if it happens
options.rationale: Starts the search at the worst moment.

options.text: A second kitchen quoted and held on standby
options.rationale: The alternative is identified and arranged in advance, so the launch survives the failure.

options.text: A decision to cancel if the kitchen is lost
options.rationale: Accepts the loss rather than planning around it.

options.text: A note that the risk is being monitored
options.rationale: Observation without a fallback.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: recognise a prepared fallback.

questions.question: A bakery reduces its staffing risk by training new hires early, and the second site opens well. Three weeks in, its only delivery van fails and wholesale orders stop. What was missing?

options.text: The staff training was clearly insufficient
options.rationale: The opening went well on that dimension.

options.text: A fallback for a risk nobody had reduced
options.rationale: Risk work covered one exposure and left another with neither mitigation nor a prepared alternative.

options.text: Wholesale accounts are too risky to hold
options.rationale: Abandons the business rather than planning for it.

options.text: The second site should not have opened
options.rationale: Rejects the strategy over a vehicle failure.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: one risk was managed and another had no fallback, which only a combined reading explains.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Strategic Risk Management, Contingency Planning. Without risk management the opening would have failed first. Without contingency the van has no backup. The pattern needs both.

questions.question: A food company can fund a supplier testing programme that reduces contamination odds, or a crisis response plan that shortens reaction time if one occurs. It can afford one this year. How should it decide?

options.text: Fund neither, since both costs are avoidable
options.rationale: Treats a known exposure as optional.

options.text: By likelihood against severity, then fund first
options.rationale: One lowers the chance and the other lowers the damage, so the choice depends on which dimension this business is most exposed on.

options.text: Fund the crisis plan, since incidents will happen
options.rationale: Assumes inevitability rather than weighing the odds.

options.text: Fund the testing, since prevention always wins
options.rationale: A maxim substituted for the comparison.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: reducing probability and reducing impact are different tools and the budget forces a comparison.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Strategic Risk Management, Crisis Response Planning. Without risk management there is no prevention option. Without crisis planning there is no impact option. The comparison requires both.

questions.question: A company has fallbacks for every operational failure it can name, but when a genuine safety incident occurs nobody knows who may speak publicly and the response stalls for a day. What does that show?

options.text: The incident was too rare to plan around
options.rationale: Safety incidents are exactly what crisis plans exist for.

options.text: Operational backups are not a crisis plan
options.rationale: Contingency keeps the work running while crisis response governs decisions and communication when people are at risk.

options.text: The fallbacks were never properly tested
options.rationale: They are not what failed here.

options.text: Public communication should be avoided
options.rationale: Silence is the failure being described.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: continuity planning is complete and crisis planning is absent, and the distinction is the answer.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Contingency Planning, Crisis Response Planning. Without contingency the company would be failing on ordinary disruptions too. Without crisis planning the stall has no explanation. The contrast needs both.

questions.question: A factory planning a four-day week lists everyone affected but does not sort them at all. What does that omission cause?

options.text: The plan taking longer to write up
options.rationale: Administrative, not strategic.

options.text: Legal problems with the union agreement
options.rationale: No legal breach is described.

options.text: A minor voice treated like a decisive one
options.rationale: Stakeholders are ranked by power and interest so that attention goes where it changes the outcome.

options.text: Some groups being left off the list
options.rationale: The case says everyone was listed.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the effect of not ranking.

questions.question: Shareholders want an underperforming store closed, staff want their jobs, and the town wants the service kept. A manager proposes fully satisfying shareholders alone. What is the flaw?

options.text: Shareholders have the weakest claim here
options.rationale: Ranking one claim lowest is the same mistake in reverse.

options.text: A town has no standing in the decision
options.rationale: The town is a stakeholder the manager named.

options.text: Other interests are simply written off
options.rationale: Closing satisfies one group completely and gives the other two nothing, which is a decision made rather than a balance struck.

options.text: The store was a poor decision to open
options.rationale: History does not help with the choice now.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the one-winner error.

questions.question: Investors want a 15 percent dividend increase while the factory needs safety upgrades. A board memo announces the dividend and says nothing about the upgrades. What is missing?

options.text: A legal review of the dividend decision
options.rationale: Compliance is a separate matter.

options.text: An apology to the factory workers
options.rationale: Sentiment rather than disclosure.

options.text: A statement of what was given up
options.rationale: A trade-off is only honest when the cost of the chosen path is named alongside the decision.

options.text: A larger dividend for the investors
options.rationale: Deepens the trade without naming it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name what an honest trade-off states.

questions.question: A factory is moving to a four-day week. The union has high power and high interest; a local newspaper has low power and high interest. What does the analysis imply?

options.text: Avoid both until the plan is finalised
options.rationale: Guarantees resistance from the powerful group.

options.text: Brief the newspaper before the union
options.rationale: Spends the first move on the lower power group.

options.text: Treat both groups identically throughout
options.rationale: Ignores the ranking the analysis produced.

options.text: Engage the union first and directly
options.rationale: Ranking by power and interest tells you where engagement changes the outcome and where information is enough.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: act on a power and interest map.

questions.question: An underperforming store is losing money, employs eleven people and is the only grocer in its town. Which path manages the competing claims best?

options.text: Close it immediately to stop the losses
options.rationale: Satisfies one group and writes off the rest.

options.text: Shrink the format and redeploy some staff
options.rationale: It addresses the financial claim while partly meeting the employment and access claims, which is what a workable path looks like.

options.text: Sell it to staff without any support
options.rationale: Transfers a losing operation and calls it a solution.

options.text: Keep it open unchanged indefinitely
options.rationale: Ignores the financial reality entirely.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: find a path across competing claims.

questions.question: The board chooses safety upgrades over the dividend increase this year. How should that be communicated to investors?

options.text: Name the deferral and why it was chosen
options.rationale: Trade-offs are negotiated honestly when the losing side hears what it lost and the reasoning behind it.

options.text: Frame it as a win for every stakeholder
options.rationale: The pretence the card warns against.

options.text: Promise a larger dividend next year
options.rationale: A commitment made to avoid the conversation.

options.text: Announce the upgrades without mentioning it
options.rationale: Hides the cost from the group paying it.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: communicate a trade-off honestly.

questions.question: A company maps its stakeholders carefully, then designs a store closure plan that fully satisfies the highest-power group and offers nothing to the others. Protests follow from a low-power group with high public sympathy. What did the analysis not settle?

options.text: How to address claims beyond the strongest
options.rationale: Ranking tells you where to focus, and managing competing interests still requires a path that does not write everyone else off.

options.text: Whether protests were legally permitted
options.rationale: Legality is not the strategic gap.

options.text: Which stakeholders held the most power
options.rationale: The mapping answered that correctly.

options.text: Whether the store was losing money
options.rationale: A financial question the analysis does not cover.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the mapping was correct and the management of the remaining claims was skipped.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Stakeholder Analysis, Managing Competing Stakeholder Interests. Without the analysis the focus would be random. Without the management step the ranking becomes a licence to ignore. Both are needed.

questions.question: Investors want a dividend rise, the factory needs safety work and the board can fund one. A director proposes announcing a partial dividend and quietly deferring the safety work indefinitely. What is wrong?

options.text: Investors are better off not hearing the costs
options.rationale: Concealment is the problem, not the remedy.

options.text: A partial dividend is a weak compromise
options.rationale: Splitting the difference can be fine when it is declared.

options.text: It hides the claim that was actually dropped
options.rationale: Announcing the dividend while saying nothing about the deferred safety work lets investors judge a trade-off they were never shown.

options.text: Safety work outranks returns in every case
options.rationale: A ranking, where the fault is the silence.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts interacting: the balancing looks reasonable while the trade-off is being hidden.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Managing Competing Stakeholder Interests, Negotiating Strategic Trade-Offs. Without the competing claims there is nothing to balance. Without the trade-off standard the quiet deferral passes as compromise. Both are needed.

questions.question: A four-day week will please staff, worry a major customer who needs Friday deliveries, and slightly raise costs. The customer holds high power and high interest. How should the decision be handled?

options.text: Offer staff the change without telling clients
options.rationale: Conceals a change that directly affects service.

options.text: Drop the four-day week to protect the account
options.rationale: Abandons the plan before testing a workable arrangement.

options.text: Announce the change and manage complaints
options.rationale: Leaves the decisive stakeholder to react publicly.

options.text: Negotiate Friday cover with the customer first
options.rationale: The map identifies whose objection can stop the plan, and the trade is then negotiated with that group rather than announced to it.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the analysis identifies who must be negotiated with and the trade-off is what gets negotiated.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Stakeholder Analysis, Negotiating Strategic Trade-Offs. Without the map the customer is one voice among many. Without the trade-off there is nothing to negotiate. Both are needed.

questions.question: An appliance company shifts from selling units to selling repair subscriptions, while every team still reports through regional sales managers paid on unit volume. What is wrong?

options.text: The company needs more sales staff
options.rationale: Adds capacity to the wrong structure.

options.text: Regional managers should be replaced
options.rationale: People are not the issue; the design is.

options.text: The structure still serves the old strategy
options.rationale: Reporting lines and incentives have to follow the strategy, or the organisation keeps producing the previous outcome.

options.text: Subscriptions are the wrong business model
options.rationale: The model is not what the case questions.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: spot structure lagging strategy.

questions.question: A coffee chain entering three countries lets regional teams set menus and prices while brand standards stay central. What is that?

options.text: Full decentralisation of the company
options.rationale: Brand standards remain centrally held.

options.text: A franchising arrangement by country
options.rationale: No third party ownership is described.

options.text: Deciding which choices sit where
options.rationale: The question is never all or nothing; it is which specific decisions are local and which stay central.

options.text: Full centralisation of the company
options.rationale: Menus and prices are local.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: name the mixed arrangement.

questions.question: A grocery chain's planning document lists what to analyse each year but never says who submits it, when, or who decides. What is missing?

options.text: Competitor data from other regions
options.rationale: More input, same missing structure.

options.text: More analytical categories to cover
options.rationale: Adds topics to a process with no mechanics.

options.text: The people, timing and decision points
options.rationale: A planning process needs steps, owners and a calendar, not only a list of topics to examine.

options.text: A longer planning horizon than a year
options.rationale: Horizon is not the gap.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept, one step: identify the missing process mechanics.

questions.question: A chain expanding into three countries must decide what regional managers control. Which split is sound?

options.text: Everything decided at head office centrally
options.rationale: Ignores the local knowledge the expansion needs.

options.text: Everything decided by the regional teams
options.rationale: Loses the consistency that makes it one brand.

options.text: Local menus and pricing, central brand rules
options.rationale: Decisions that depend on local knowledge go local, while those that protect a shared identity stay central.

options.text: Alternating control between them each year
options.rationale: Creates instability rather than a design.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: allocate decision rights sensibly.

questions.question: The appliance company wants subscriptions to succeed. Which structural change actually supports that?

options.text: A training course on subscription selling
options.rationale: Skill without structural support.

options.text: A service unit with its own targets and lead
options.rationale: Changing who reports where and what they are measured on is what makes a structure serve the new strategy.

options.text: A memo asking sales to promote subscriptions
options.rationale: Requests behaviour the incentives contradict.

options.text: A new subscription title for a sales manager
options.rationale: A title without changed reporting or measures.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: choose a real structural change.

questions.question: A 40-store grocery chain wants local knowledge to reach its annual plan. Which process design does that?

options.text: Head office analyses market data centrally
options.rationale: Leaves store level knowledge out of the plan.

options.text: An annual survey of customers in each store
options.rationale: Useful input, but not a planning process.

options.text: An open invitation to send ideas any time
options.rationale: No timing or structure, so little arrives.

options.text: Store managers submit data by a set date
options.rationale: A repeatable process names who contributes what and when, which is how local insight actually arrives.

notes.difficulty_justification: One concept applied: design a planning process.

questions.question: A chain's strategy depends on fast local response to competitors, yet every pricing change needs head office approval that takes three weeks. What does the structure reveal?

options.text: The approval process is merely inefficient
options.rationale: Reads a strategic misalignment as an administrative delay.

options.text: Local managers need more pricing training
options.rationale: They are not permitted to decide regardless of skill.

options.text: The strategy should be slowed to match
options.rationale: Bends the strategy to a structure that can be changed.

options.text: Decision rights contradict the stated strategy
options.rationale: A strategy built on speed requires the relevant decisions to sit where the speed is needed, which centralised pricing prevents.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: alignment says structure follows strategy and the centralisation choice is the specific misfit.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Aligning Structure to Strategy, Centralization Versus Decentralization. Without alignment the delay is just process. Without the centralisation question there is no specific fix. Both are needed.

questions.question: A chain wants store managers' local knowledge in the annual plan, but final capital allocation must stay with the board. How should the process be designed?

options.text: Keep planning entirely at head office
options.rationale: Discards the local knowledge being sought.

options.text: Rotate the decision between stores yearly
options.rationale: Neither a process nor a coherent allocation.

options.text: Let store managers allocate their own capital
options.rationale: Moves a decision the board has reserved.

options.text: Local input on a calendar, central decision
options.rationale: The process defines who contributes and when, while the decision rights question settles who ultimately decides.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the process supplies the mechanics and the centralisation question supplies who decides.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Strategic Planning Process Design, Centralization Versus Decentralization. Without the process the input never arrives. Without the decision rights the board's authority is unclear. Both are needed.

questions.question: A company runs a disciplined annual planning process, but the resulting strategy is always executed by the same unchanged divisions with the same targets. Strategy after strategy produces the old results. What explains it?

options.text: The planning process is poorly designed
options.rationale: The case describes it as disciplined.

options.text: Annual planning is too infrequent to work
options.rationale: Frequency is not what blocks execution.

options.text: Plans change while the structure does not
options.rationale: A sound process can produce a new strategy, and without matching changes to reporting and measures the organisation keeps doing what it did.

options.text: The strategies chosen are always wrong
options.rationale: Nothing indicates the content is at fault.

notes.difficulty_justification: Two concepts at once: the planning process works and the structure never follows, which only both together explain.
notes.synthesis_check: Concepts: Strategic Planning Process Design, Aligning Structure to Strategy. Without the process there would be no strategy to execute. Without the structural question the repeated results have no cause. Both are needed.
